quiz.question:
A product review from a user must appear inside

. Which line is safe?
options: review.innerHTML = userText
review.outerHTML = userText
review.textContent = userText
review.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', userText)
quiz.explanation: textContent inserts the string as plain text and never parses it, so tags in the review are shown as characters, not run. The other three all parse HTML.

quiz.question: The user types “Priya” into <input value="Guest">. What do input.getAttribute('value') and input.value return?
options: "Priya" and "Priya"
"Guest" and "Guest"
"Priya" and "Guest"
"Guest" and "Priya"
quiz.explanation: The value attribute is the default value and does not change as the user types. The value property holds the current value.

quiz.question: You write button.setAttribute('disabled', 'false'). What happens?
options: The button becomes disabled, because the attribute is present
The button becomes enabled
Nothing: setAttribute ignores the string "false"
It throws a TypeError
quiz.explanation: disabled is a boolean attribute: its presence means true, whatever the value. Use button.disabled = false or removeAttribute('disabled') (or toggleAttribute).

quiz.question: Why do you usually toggle a class instead of setting several el.style properties?
options: el.style is read-only
Classes keep the design in CSS, are easy to override and cover states like :hover, and one class change can update many properties
Inline styles do not work in modern browsers
classList is faster because it skips layout
quiz.explanation: Classes separate behaviour (JS decides the state) from design (CSS decides the looks). Inline styles have high specificity and scatter design values through your code. Both can trigger layout.

lessons.title: Creating, inserting and removing elements
lessons.summaryHtml:
Real pages build UI from data: notifications, product cards, table rows. You create elements with document.createElement, fill them with textContent and properties, and place them with the modern insertion methods: append, prepend, before, after, replaceWith, replaceChildren and remove.

For repeated markup, a <template> element holds an inert blueprint that you cloneNode(true) and fill. A DocumentFragment lets you assemble many nodes off-page and insert them in one operation. insertAdjacentHTML is handy for trusted, static strings only; never feed it user data.

You build a notification centre and a product grid rendered from an array, and you measure why batching matters.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Until now you changed elements that were already in the HTML. Real apps create UI from data: twenty products from an API, a new notification every minute, a row for each invoice. Creating DOM is like assembling furniture off to the side and then carrying it into the room: you make an element with createElement, fill it in while it is still detached (not on the page), then insert it where it belongs. Removing is one call: el.remove().

Why it matters

How you build DOM decides three things users and reviewers notice. Security: building with elements and textContent makes XSS impossible by construction. Correctness: inserting one item instead of re-rendering the whole list with innerHTML += keeps input focus, scroll position and event listeners intact. Speed: avoiding forced layouts while you insert keeps a 1,000-row table fast on a cheap phone. Every framework you will use later (React, Vue, Svelte) automates exactly the operations in this lesson.

How it works

Creating elements and a tiny helper

const card = document.createElement('article');   // detached
card.className = 'card';
card.dataset.id = '42';

const title = document.createElement('h2');
title.textContent = product.title;                // safe for any data

const price = document.createElement('span');
price.className = 'price';
price.textContent = inr.format(product.price);

card.append(title, price);                        // build the subtree
grid.append(card);                                // now it is on the page

Writing four lines per element gets tedious, so most vanilla projects write a small helper. el(tag, props, ...children) creates the element, copies properties with Object.assign (so className, textContent, disabled all work), and appends children, where strings become text nodes. It is the same shape as React.createElement, the function JSX compiles to. One catch: dataset is read-only (assigning to it throws) and style only accepts a whole CSS string, so passing objects for them does not work; set dataset.x and style.x after creating the element, as the product grid does.

Try it: Product grid built from data

HTML

<main class="store">
  <header class="top">
    <div><h1>Study desk essentials</h1><p class="muted" id="summary"></p></div>
    <div class="tools">
      <label class="check"><input type="checkbox" id="in-stock"> In stock only</label>
      <select id="sort" aria-label="Sort products">
        <option value="featured">Featured</option>
        <option value="low">Price: low to high</option>
        <option value="high">Price: high to low</option>
      </select>
      <span class="cart" id="cart">🛒 0</span>
    </div>
  </header>
  <section class="grid" id="grid" aria-live="polite"></section>
</main>

CSS

:root { --accent: #2563eb; --line: #e4e7ec; --muted: #667085; }
body { margin: 0; background: #f4f6fb; color: #1d2939; }
.store { padding: 16px; display: grid; gap: 14px; }
.top { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; align-items: flex-end; justify-content: space-between; gap: 12px; }
h1 { font-size: 18px; margin: 0; }
.muted { margin: 2px 0 0; font-size: 13px; color: var(--muted); }
.tools { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; align-items: center; gap: 8px; }
.check { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 6px; font-size: 13px; color: #344054; }
.check input { accent-color: var(--accent); width: 16px; height: 16px; }
select { font: inherit; font-size: 13px; padding: 7px 10px; border: 1px solid var(--line); border-radius: 10px; background: #fff; color: inherit; }
.cart { font-size: 13px; font-weight: 700; padding: 6px 10px; border-radius: 999px; background: #dbeafe; color: #1e40af; }
.grid { display: grid; gap: 12px; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(160px, 1fr)); }
.card { background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line); border-radius: 14px; padding: 10px; display: grid; gap: 6px;
  transition: box-shadow .2s, transform .2s; }
.card:hover { transform: translateY(-2px); box-shadow: 0 12px 24px -16px rgba(16,24,40,.35); }
.thumb { height: 88px; border-radius: 10px; display: grid; place-items: center; font-size: 40px; background: #f2f4f7; position: relative; }
.flag { position: absolute; top: 6px; left: 6px; font-size: 11px; font-weight: 700; padding: 2px 6px; border-radius: 6px; background: #fff; color: #b42318; }
.card h2 { font-size: 14px; margin: 0; }
.meta { font-size: 12px; color: var(--muted); }
.row { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; gap: 8px; }
.price { font-weight: 800; }
.add { font: inherit; font-size: 12px; font-weight: 600; padding: 6px 10px; border-radius: 8px; border: 0; background: var(--accent); color: #fff; cursor: pointer; }
.add:disabled { background: #e4e7ec; color: #98a2b3; cursor: not-allowed; }

JavaScript

const products = [
  { id: 1, title: 'Glow Desk Lamp', emoji: '💡', tint: '#fef9c3', price: 1299, rating: 4.6, stock: 31 },
  { id: 2, title: 'Tactile Keyboard', emoji: '⌨️', tint: '#e0e7ff', price: 3450, rating: 4.8, stock: 5 },
  { id: 3, title: 'Wave Pro Headphones', emoji: '🎧', tint: '#fce7f3', price: 4999, rating: 4.7, stock: 0 },
  { id: 4, title: 'Bamboo Pen Stand', emoji: '🖊️', tint: '#dcfce7', price: 349, rating: 4.3, stock: 58 },
  { id: 5, title: 'Focus Timer Cube', emoji: '⏱️', tint: '#ffedd5', price: 899, rating: 4.4, stock: 12 },
  { id: 6, title: 'Dot-grid Notebook', emoji: '📓', tint: '#e0f2fe', price: 249, rating: 4.9, stock: 0 },
];
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', {
  style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0,
});
const grid = document.querySelector('#grid');
let cartCount = 0;

// Tiny helper: el('p', { className: 'meta' }, 'text', otherNode)
function el(tag, props = {}, ...children) {
  const node = document.createElement(tag);
  Object.assign(node, props);
  node.append(...children);           // strings become text nodes
  return node;
}

function productCard(p) {
  const thumb = el('div', { className: 'thumb', role: 'img', ariaLabel: p.title }, p.emoji);
  thumb.style.background = p.tint;
  if (p.stock === 0) thumb.append(el('span', { className: 'flag' }, 'Sold out'));
  const add = el('button', { className: 'add', disabled: p.stock === 0 }, 'Add');
  add.addEventListener('click', () => {
    document.querySelector('#cart').textContent = `🛒 ${++cartCount}`;
  });
  const card = el('article', { className: 'card' },
    thumb,
    el('h2', {}, p.title),
    el('span', { className: 'meta' }, `★ ${p.rating} · ${p.stock ? p.stock + ' left' : 'restocking'}`),
    el('div', { className: 'row' }, el('span', { className: 'price' }, inr.format(p.price)), add),
  );
  card.dataset.id = p.id;
  return card;
}

function render() {
  const onlyInStock = document.querySelector('#in-stock').checked;
  const sort = document.querySelector('#sort').value;
  let list = onlyInStock ? products.filter((p) => p.stock > 0) : products;
  if (sort !== 'featured') list = list.toSorted((a, b) => sort === 'low' ? a.price - b.price : b.price - a.price);

  const t0 = performance.now();
  grid.replaceChildren(...list.map(productCard));   // one DOM update
  document.querySelector('#summary').textContent = `${list.length} of ${products.length} products`;
  console.log(`Rendered ${list.length} cards in ${(performance.now() - t0).toFixed(2)} ms`);
}

document.querySelector('#in-stock').addEventListener('change', render);
document.querySelector('#sort').addEventListener('change', render);
render();

Every card is built from the products array with a small el() helper. Sort or filter and the whole grid is rebuilt with one replaceChildren call.

Inserting, moving, replacing and removing

The modern methods (all current browsers) accept any number of nodes and strings; strings are inserted as text, never parsed as HTML.

MethodWhere the new content goesinsertAdjacentHTML position
target.before(...)Just before target, as a sibling'beforebegin'
target.prepend(...)Inside target, before its first child'afterbegin'
target.append(...)Inside target, after its last child'beforeend'
target.after(...)Just after target, as a sibling'afterend'
target.replaceWith(...)Target is removed and replacednone
target.replaceChildren(...)All children replaced (none given: emptied)none
target.remove()Target leaves the DOMnone

Older code uses appendChild, insertBefore and removeChild. They still work; the differences are that they take exactly one node and return it, while append returns undefined. Try each method and watch where the chip lands:

  border-radius: 8px; border: 1px solid #bfdbfe; background: #eff6ff; color: #1d4ed8; cursor: pointer; }

  border: 2px dashed #60a5fa; background: #f8fbff; }

JavaScript

const stage = document.querySelector('#parent');
const code = document.querySelector('#code');
const useAdjacent = document.querySelector('#adjacent');
const positions = {
  before: 'beforebegin', prepend: 'afterbegin', append: 'beforeend', after: 'afterend',
};
let target;
let count = 0;

function makeTarget() {
  const t = document.createElement('div');
  t.className = 'target';
  t.id = 'target';
  const caption = document.createElement('span');
  caption.className = 'caption';
  caption.textContent = 'target';
  t.append(caption);
  return t;
}

function reset() {
  target = makeTarget();
  stage.replaceChildren(stage.querySelector('.caption') ?? '', target);
  code.textContent = 'Pick a method.';
}

document.querySelector('#toolbar').addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const m = event.target.closest('button')?.dataset.m;
  if (!m) return;
  if (m === 'reset') return reset();
  if (!target.isConnected) reset();           // replaceWith removed it
  count += 1;
  if (useAdjacent.checked && positions[m]) {
    const pos = positions[m];
    // A constant string we wrote ourselves: safe for insertAdjacentHTML.
    target.insertAdjacentHTML(pos, `<span class="chip ${pos}">${pos} #${count}</span>`);
    code.textContent = `target.insertAdjacentHTML('${pos}', '<span…>')`;
  } else {
    const chip = document.createElement('span');
    chip.className = 'chip ' + m;
    chip.textContent = `${m} #${count}`;
    target[m](chip);                          // target.before(chip), target.append(chip)…
    code.textContent = `target.${m}(chip)`;
  }
  console.log(code.textContent, '→ parent now has', stage.children.length, 'children');
});

reset();
for (const m of ['before', 'append', 'after']) document.querySelector(`[data-m="${m}"]`).click();

Each button inserts a chip relative to the dashed target. Tick “insertAdjacentHTML” to do the same with the four position keywords and a trusted string.

Two rules explain most surprises. First, a node has only one parent: inserting a node that is already on the page moves it. That is handy for reordering (list.append(firstItem) sends it to the end) and a bug when you wanted a copy, which needs cloneNode(true). Second, insertAdjacentHTML parses HTML, so it follows the same rule as innerHTML: only for constant markup you wrote. Unlike innerHTML +=, though, it does not destroy the existing children.

Templates and cloneNode

For markup that repeats, such as a notification row, writing it with createElement hides the structure in JavaScript. The <template> element keeps it in HTML where designers can read it. Its content is parsed into a DocumentFragment but stays inert: nothing is rendered, images do not load and scripts do not run. You clone it for each item:

<template id="note-tpl">
  <li class="note">
    <span class="icon"></span>
    <p class="text"></p>
    <button class="dismiss" aria-label="Dismiss">✕</button>
  </li>
</template>
const tpl = document.querySelector('#note-tpl');

function createNote(note) {
  const li = tpl.content.firstElementChild.cloneNode(true);  // deep copy
  li.querySelector('.icon').textContent = note.icon;
  li.querySelector('.text').textContent = note.text;
  li.querySelector('.dismiss').addEventListener('click', () => li.remove());
  return li;
}

cloneNode(true) copies the element with all its descendants and attributes; cloneNode() without true copies only the element itself. Clones do not copy listeners added with addEventListener, and they copy id attributes, so never put ids inside a template you clone many times.

DocumentFragment and batching

A DocumentFragment is a parentless mini-document. You append many nodes to it, then append the fragment once; its children move into the target and the fragment is left empty. replaceChildren(...nodes) does the same job when you are rebuilding a whole list.

Is it faster? The honest answer surprises people. Browsers do not re-render after every append; they wait and lay out once before the next frame. So “append in a loop” and “append a fragment” usually cost about the same. What really hurts is layout thrashing: writing to the DOM and then reading geometry (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect, innerText) inside the same loop. Each read forces a full layout of everything changed so far. Measure it yourself; your numbers will differ from anyone else’s, so compare them rather than memorising them:

Try it: Batching and layout thrashing, measured

HTML

<main class="bench">
  <header><h1>Insert 1,000 order rows</h1><p class="muted">Press a strategy. Lower is better.</p></header>
  <div class="buttons" id="buttons">
    <button data-s="loop">append() in a loop</button>
    <button data-s="fragment">DocumentFragment</button>
    <button data-s="thrash" class="bad">loop + read offsetHeight</button>
  </div>
  <ul class="results" id="results"></ul>
  <ol class="rows" id="rows" aria-label="Rendered rows"></ol>
</main>

CSS

body { margin: 0; background: #f4f6fb; color: #1d2939; }
.bench { padding: 16px; display: grid; gap: 12px; }
h1 { font-size: 18px; margin: 0; }
.muted { margin: 2px 0 0; font-size: 13px; color: #667085; }
.buttons { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px; }
.buttons button { font: inherit; font-size: 13px; font-weight: 600; padding: 8px 12px; border-radius: 10px; cursor: pointer;
  border: 1px solid #2563eb; background: #2563eb; color: #fff; }
.buttons .bad { background: #fff; color: #b42318; border-color: #fecdca; }
.results { list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 12px; display: grid; gap: 8px; background: #fff; border: 1px solid #e4e7ec; border-radius: 12px; }
.results li { display: grid; grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 160px) minmax(60px, 1fr) auto; align-items: center; gap: 8px; font-size: 13px; }
.results li:empty::before { content: 'No runs yet'; color: #98a2b3; }
.track { height: 10px; border-radius: 999px; background: #f2f4f7; overflow: hidden; }
.fill { height: 100%; border-radius: inherit; background: #60a5fa; transition: width .4s; }
.fill.thrash { background: #f97066; }
.ms { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; font-weight: 700; }
.rows { margin: 0; padding: 8px 8px 8px 40px; height: 120px; overflow: auto; background: #fff; border: 1px solid #e4e7ec;
  border-radius: 12px; font-size: 12px; color: #475467; }

JavaScript

const rows = document.querySelector('#rows');
const results = document.querySelector('#results');
const N = 1000;
const timings = {};
const labels = { loop: 'append() in a loop', fragment: 'DocumentFragment', thrash: 'loop + offsetHeight' };

function makeRow(i) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = `Order #RZ-${2000 + i} · ₹${(i * 37) % 5000 + 99}`;
  return li;
}

const strategies = {
  loop() { for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) rows.append(makeRow(i)); },
  fragment() {
    const frag = document.createDocumentFragment();
    for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) frag.append(makeRow(i));
    rows.append(frag);
  },
  thrash() {
    for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
      rows.append(makeRow(i));
      void rows.offsetHeight;   // a read after a write forces layout now
    }
  },
};

function run(name) {
  rows.replaceChildren();
  void rows.offsetHeight;                   // start from a clean layout
  const t0 = performance.now();
  strategies[name]();
  void rows.offsetHeight;                   // include the final layout for all three
  timings[name] = performance.now() - t0;
  show();
  console.log(`${labels[name]}: ${timings[name].toFixed(1)} ms`);
}

function show() {
  const max = Math.max(...Object.values(timings));
  results.replaceChildren(...Object.entries(timings).map(([name, ms]) => {
    const fill = document.createElement('div');
    fill.className = 'fill ' + name;
    fill.style.width = (ms / max) * 100 + '%';
    const track = document.createElement('div');
    track.className = 'track';
    track.append(fill);
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    const label = document.createElement('span');
    label.textContent = labels[name];
    const value = document.createElement('span');
    value.className = 'ms';
    value.textContent = ms.toFixed(1) + ' ms';
    li.append(label, track, value);
    return li;
  }));
}

document.querySelector('#buttons').addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const name = event.target.closest('button')?.dataset.s;
  if (name) run(name);
});
['loop', 'fragment', 'thrash'].forEach(run);

Each strategy inserts 1,000 rows. Loop and fragment are close because browsers defer layout; reading offsetHeight inside the loop forces a layout every time. Numbers vary by machine: compare them, do not memorise them.

Fragments are still good practice: one insertion means one mutation record for observers, one moment where the list is incomplete, and a clear “build, then insert” structure. The rule to remember is batch your reads, then batch your writes. Lesson 5.1 goes deeper.

Removing elements and cleaning up

el.remove() detaches an element and everything inside it. The element object is not destroyed at that moment: JavaScript’s garbage collector frees it later, once no variable, array, closure or Map refers to it. Listeners attached to a removed element go away with it, so you do not need to remove them by hand in the normal case.

Problems start when something outside the element still points at it. A global selectedCards array, a timer created with setInterval that updates a removed clock, or a listener on window that closes over the element all keep it alive. DevTools calls these detached DOM nodes, and on a long-lived dashboard they pile up. The habit to build now: when you remove a component, also clear its timers, remove listeners you added to window or document (lesson 2.1 shows an AbortController trick that removes them all at once), and delete it from any collections.

Removing and re-inserting is also how you reorder. Because inserting an existing node moves it, sorting a list can be done without creating anything new:

const items = [...list.children];
items.sort((a, b) => Number(a.dataset.price) - Number(b.dataset.price));
list.append(...items);   // same nodes, new order; listeners and state kept

Compared with rebuilding every card from data, this keeps focus, input values and running animations intact. Frameworks call the same idea keyed updates, which you will build yourself in lesson 3.3.

Example: a notification centre

The Ralfiz Academy notification centre renders a list from an array of objects, adds new notifications at the top, lets users dismiss or mark them read, and keeps an unread badge in sync. The structure lives in a <template>; createNote clones and fills it; the first render builds all notes into a fragment; new ones go in with prepend and a small CSS entrance animation; dismiss calls li.remove(). After every change, updateCounts() re-derives the badge from the DOM with querySelectorAll('.note.unread').length instead of keeping a separate counter that could drift.

JavaScript

const list = document.querySelector('#list');
const template = document.querySelector('#note-tpl');
const badge = document.querySelector('#unread');
const empty = document.querySelector('#empty');

const notes = [
  { icon: '🛒', text: 'Order #RZ-1042 has shipped', time: '2 min ago', unread: true },
  { icon: '💬', text: 'Rahul replied to your question in Lesson 1.3', time: '1 h ago', unread: true },
  { icon: '⭐', text: 'You earned the DOM Explorer badge', time: 'Yesterday', unread: false },
];
const incoming = [
  { icon: '🔥', text: '7-day learning streak! Keep going', time: 'Just now', unread: true },
  { icon: '📦', text: 'Your Ralfiz Store refund was approved', time: 'Just now', unread: true },
  { icon: '🎓', text: 'Certificate ready: JavaScript Basics', time: 'Just now', unread: true },
];

function createNote({ icon, text, time, unread }) {
  const li = template.content.firstElementChild.cloneNode(true);
  li.querySelector('.icon').textContent = icon;
  li.querySelector('.text').textContent = text;
  li.querySelector('.time').textContent = time;
  li.classList.toggle('unread', unread);
  li.querySelector('.dismiss').addEventListener('click', () => { li.remove(); updateCounts(); });
  li.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
    if (event.target.closest('.dismiss')) return;
    li.classList.remove('unread');
    updateCounts();
  });
  return li;
}

function updateCounts() {
  const unread = list.querySelectorAll('.note.unread').length;
  badge.textContent = unread;
  badge.hidden = unread === 0;
  empty.hidden = list.children.length > 0;
  list.hidden = list.children.length === 0;
}

const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();
notes.forEach((n) => fragment.append(createNote(n)));
list.append(fragment);            // one insertion for all three
updateCounts();

let next = 0;
document.querySelector('#simulate').addEventListener('click', () => {
  const li = createNote(incoming[next++ % incoming.length]);
  li.classList.add('enter');
  list.prepend(li);
  updateCounts();
  console.log('Prepended:', li.querySelector('.text').textContent);
});
document.querySelector('#read-all').addEventListener('click', () => {
  list.querySelectorAll('.note.unread').forEach((li) => li.classList.remove('unread'));
  updateCounts();
});
console.log('Rendered', list.children.length, 'notes from', notes.length, 'objects');

Press Simulate new: each note is cloned from a <template>, filled with textContent and prepended. Click a note to mark it read, or ✕ to remove it.

In the lab you load the same notifications from a notifications.json file with fetch, handling a failed response by showing an error message instead of an empty list.

Common mistakes

1. Using innerHTML += to add one item.

// Wrong: re-parses the whole list; old listeners and focus are lost
list.innerHTML += `<li>${task.title}</li>`;

// Fix: create and append one node
const li = document.createElement('li');
li.textContent = task.title;
list.append(li);

2. Expecting append to copy. Appending the same element into two lists moves it. Use node.cloneNode(true) for the second list.

3. Cloning the template instead of its content.

// Wrong: clones the <template> element itself (still inert, renders nothing)
list.append(tpl.cloneNode(true));

// Fix: clone what is inside it
list.append(tpl.content.cloneNode(true));

4. Reading layout inside a build loop. list.offsetHeight or el.getBoundingClientRect() after each insert forces a layout per row. Insert everything, then measure once.

5. Emptying with a loop of removeChild. list.replaceChildren() empties an element in one clear call. (list.innerHTML = '' also works, but replaceChildren says what you mean.)

Interview and real-world notes

  • “How would you render 1,000 rows efficiently?” Build off-page (fragment or an array for replaceChildren), insert once, never read layout in the loop, and for really long lists render only the visible rows (virtualisation, lesson 5.1).
  • “append vs appendChild?” Multiple nodes and strings with no return value, versus one node that is returned.
  • The el() helper and <template> are two of the three ways frameworks describe UI; the third, JSX, compiles to calls just like el(). Seeing that connection makes React easier to learn.
  • When you remove an element, its listeners are freed once nothing else references the element. Keep references to removed nodes (for example in a global array) and they stay in memory: a classic leak that DevTools Memory calls “detached” DOM.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. One li, two lists. What is logged?

const a = document.createElement('ul');
const b = document.createElement('ul');
const li = document.createElement('li');
a.append(li);
b.append(li);
console.log(a.children.length, b.children.length);
  • A 1 1
  • B 1 0
  • C 0 0
  • D 0 1

Snippet 2. What happens to the fragment?

const ul = document.createElement('ul');
const frag = document.createDocumentFragment();
frag.append(document.createElement('li'), document.createElement('li'));
ul.append(frag);
console.log(frag.childNodes.length, ul.children.length);
  • A 2 2
  • B 0 2
  • C 2 0
  • D 0 1

Snippet 3. append() vs appendChild() return values:

const div = document.createElement('div');
const r1 = div.append('Hello ', 'there');
const r2 = div.appendChild(document.createElement('span'));
console.log(r1, r2.tagName, div.childNodes.length);
  • A undefined SPAN 3
  • B undefined SPAN 2
  • C div SPAN 3
  • D Hello there SPAN 2

Answers

  1. D. A node has only one parent. Appending li to b moves it out of a. To have it in both, append li.cloneNode(true) instead.
  2. B. Appending a fragment moves its children into the target. The fragment itself is never inserted and is left empty.
  3. A. append() returns undefined and turns each string into its own text node (2 nodes). appendChild() returns the appended node, the span, for a total of 3 child nodes.

terms.definition: Creates a new, detached element node. It appears on the page only after you insert it.
Insert one or more nodes or strings as the last / first children. Strings become text nodes, never HTML.
Insert nodes as siblings of an element, or swap the element for them.
Removes all children and inserts the given ones in one call. With no arguments it empties the element.
An element whose content is parsed but inert: nothing renders, no images load and no scripts run until you clone it into the page.
Copies a node. With true it copies all descendants. Listeners added with addEventListener are not copied.
A lightweight, parentless container. Appending it moves its children into the target and leaves the fragment empty.

quiz.question: You call list.append(card) where card is already inside another list. What happens?
options: The card is copied, so it appears in both lists
It throws a HierarchyRequestError
The card is moved: it leaves the old list and appears in the new one
Nothing, because the card already has a parent
quiz.explanation: A node can have only one parent. Inserting an existing node moves it. Use cloneNode(true) if you need a copy.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between append() and appendChild()?
options: append() accepts several nodes and strings and returns undefined; appendChild() takes one node and returns it
appendChild() is faster in all browsers
append() parses strings as HTML
They are identical
quiz.explanation: append() is the modern method: many arguments, strings become text nodes, no return value. appendChild() takes exactly one Node and returns it, which older code relies on.

quiz.question:
Why is list.innerHTML += '
  • New
    • ' a bad way to add one item?
options: += is not allowed on innerHTML
It re-parses and recreates every existing child, losing their listeners, focus and input state
It only works on ul elements
It escapes the HTML
quiz.explanation: innerHTML += reads the whole list as a string, adds to it and parses it all again. Every old node is destroyed and replaced, so listeners and state are lost, and it is slow on large lists.

quiz.question: When is insertAdjacentHTML acceptable?
options: For user comments, because it is faster than textContent
Never, it is deprecated
Only inside a <template>
For trusted, static markup you wrote yourself, never for data that came from users or APIs
quiz.explanation: insertAdjacentHTML parses HTML like innerHTML, so the same XSS rules apply. It is fine for your own constant strings; build user data with createElement and textContent (or sanitise it, covered in dm20).

domains.name: Events
domains.blurb: Listeners, propagation and delegation, keyboard, pointer and custom events.

lessons.title: Events and listeners
lessons.summaryHtml:
Everything a user does in the browser, and many things the browser does by itself, arrives in your code as an event: a click, a key press, a character typed into a box, a form being sent, the page finishing loading. You react to events by registering a listener with addEventListener(type, handler, options).

The browser calls your handler with an event object that says what happened (type), where it started (target), which element’s listener is running (currentTarget) and when (timeStamp). Options such as once, passive and signal control how long a listener lives and how it behaves, and one AbortController can remove many listeners at once.

In this lesson you build a Ralfiz Academy community post with a like button, a double-click-to-like gesture and a comment box with a live character counter, and you learn why inline onclick attributes belong in the past.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A web page on its own is a picture. It becomes an app when it reacts. Every time something happens, the browser creates an event: a small object that describes what happened. The user clicked. A key went down. The text in a box changed. A form was sent. The page finished loading. Your job is to say, "When this happens on that element, run this function."

Think of a shop counter bell. The bell (the element) does nothing clever by itself. You tell a staff member (the listener) to listen for the ring (the event type). When it rings, they walk over with a note that says who rang, where and when (the event object). One bell can have several staff listening, and a staff member can stop listening at the end of the shift.

const button = document.querySelector('.like');

button.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  console.log('Clicked!', event.type); // "click"
});

Why it matters

Almost every feature a front-end developer builds starts with an event. A cart total updates on input in a quantity box. A search box fetches suggestions as you type. A dashboard saves a draft when you press Ctrl+S. A checkout form checks the card number on submit. Getting events right is the difference between a page that feels solid and one that double-submits orders, leaks memory in long sessions, or ignores users who paste text instead of typing it.

Events are also where many bugs hide. A listener attached twice charges a customer twice. A listener that is never removed keeps a closed modal alive in memory. A handler that uses change instead of input makes a character counter lag behind. This lesson gives you the mental model to avoid all of these.

How it works

addEventListener: subscribe to what happens

element.addEventListener(type, listener, options) registers a listener. The type is a string such as 'click' (no "on" prefix). The listener is a function (or an object with a handleEvent method). The browser keeps a list of listeners per element and per type, and calls them in the order they were added when a matching event arrives.

The key detail: you pass the function itself, not the result of calling it. addEventListener('click', like) hands the browser your function to call later. addEventListener('click', like()) calls like right now, once, and registers whatever it returns (usually undefined).

Below is a Ralfiz Academy community post. One listener handles the heart button. Open the console and click in different places on the button: sometimes on the heart shape, sometimes on the number, sometimes on the padding.

JavaScript

const post = document.querySelector('.post');
const likeBtn = document.querySelector('.like');
const countEl = likeBtn.querySelector('.count');
const bigHeart = document.querySelector('.big-heart');

let liked = false;
let count = Number(countEl.textContent);

function setLiked(next) {
  if (next === liked) return;
  liked = next;
  count += liked ? 1 : -1;
  likeBtn.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(liked));
  countEl.textContent = count;
  likeBtn.classList.add('pop');
}

function handleLikeClick(event) {
  console.log(`${event.type} | target: <${event.target.localName}>` +
    ` | currentTarget: <${event.currentTarget.localName}>` +
    ` | at ${Math.round(event.timeStamp)} ms`);
  setLiked(!liked);
}

// Pass the function itself: no () after the name
likeBtn.addEventListener('click', handleLikeClick);

// animationend bubbles up from the svg, so we can replay the pop next time
likeBtn.addEventListener('animationend', () => likeBtn.classList.remove('pop'));

// Double-click the text to like (never un-like), like a photo app
post.querySelector('.post-body').addEventListener('dblclick', () => {
  setLiked(true);
  bigHeart.classList.add('show');
});
bigHeart.addEventListener('animationend', () => {
  bigHeart.classList.remove('show');
});

Click the heart, then click exactly on the number: target changes, currentTarget stays the button. Double-click the post text to like it.

Notice three more things in that code. First, the button uses aria-pressed, so a screen reader announces it as a toggle that is on or off. Second, CSS animations produce events too: animationend tells us when the pop has finished so we can remove the class and replay it next time. Third, dblclick on the text is a separate event type with its own listener; it only ever likes, never un-likes, which matches what users expect from photo apps.

The event object

Every listener receives one argument: the event object. Its exact class depends on the event (MouseEvent, KeyboardEvent, InputEvent, SubmitEvent), but they all share the properties of Event.

Property or methodWhat it tells youTypical use
typeThe event name, such as 'click'One handler serving several types
targetThe innermost element where the event startedFinding which item in a list was clicked
currentTargetThe element whose listener is running nowReading data from the element you registered on
timeStampMilliseconds since the page’s time originMeasuring gaps between events
isTrustedtrue if the user caused it, false if code dispatched itAnalytics, anti-automation checks
preventDefault()Cancels the browser’s default actionStop a form submit or a link navigation

target and currentTarget differ whenever the element you listen on has children. Click the heart shape and target is the <path> inside the <svg>; currentTarget is still the <button>. That happens because events travel up through ancestors (bubbling, the topic of the next lesson). So when you need "the element I attached to", use currentTarget. Note that currentTarget is only set while listeners run: if you log the event object and expand it later in DevTools, it shows null.

Common events you will use every day

EventFires whenTypical use
clickPointer press and release on the same element, or Enter/Space on a focused buttonButtons, toggles, menus
inputThe value of an input, textarea or select changes in any wayLive counters, search-as-you-type, previews
changeThe change is committed: blur for text, immediately for checkbox, radio and selectSaving a setting, filters
keydownA key goes down (repeats while held)Shortcuts, Escape to close
submitA form is submitted by a button or EnterSign-up, checkout, search
DOMContentLoadedHTML is fully parsed and deferred scripts have runStarting your app
load (on window)Everything, including images and styles, has loadedMeasuring images, hiding a splash screen

Notice that click is not only a mouse event. A real <button> fires click when a keyboard user presses Enter or Space. That is one big reason to use buttons, not clickable <div>s. The review box below shows the difference between input and change. It also counts characters the way people see them: with Intl.Segmenter, the emoji counts as one character, while text.length would count it as two UTF-16 units.

JavaScript

const LIMIT = 200;
const form = document.querySelector('#review');
const text = document.querySelector('#text');
const counter = document.querySelector('#counter');
const meter = document.querySelector('#meter');
const postBtn = document.querySelector('#post');
const status = document.querySelector('#status');
const badges = {
  input: document.querySelector('#n-input'),
  change: document.querySelector('#n-change'),
};
const seen = { input: 0, change: 0 };

// Count what a person sees as characters: an emoji is 1, not 2
const segmenter = new Intl.Segmenter('en', { granularity: 'grapheme' });
const countChars = (value) => [...segmenter.segment(value)].length;

function updateCounter() {
  const used = countChars(text.value);
  const left = LIMIT - used;
  const level = left < 0 ? 'over' : left <= 20 ? 'warn' : '';
  counter.textContent = left >= 0 ? `${left} left` : `${-left} over`;
  counter.className = `counter ${level}`;
  meter.className = `meter ${level}`;
  meter.style.setProperty('--p', Math.min(used / LIMIT, 1));
  postBtn.disabled = used === 0 || left < 0;
}

function trackEvent(event) {
  seen[event.type] += 1;
  badges[event.type].textContent = seen[event.type];
  document.querySelector('#last').textContent = event.type;
  status.textContent = '';
}

text.addEventListener('input', updateCounter);   // every edit
text.addEventListener('input', trackEvent);      // two listeners, same event
text.addEventListener('change', trackEvent);     // edit committed (blur)

form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault(); // stay on the page, we handle it in JS
  console.log('Posting:', text.value.trim());
  status.textContent = 'Thanks! Your review is waiting for moderation.';
  text.value = '';
  updateCounter();
});

updateCounter(); // draw the initial state

Type, paste or delete text: input fires every time. change fires only when you click outside the box. Add an emoji and watch it count as one character.

Two listeners are registered for input on the same textarea, and both run in order. That is the real advantage of addEventListener over the old textarea.oninput = fn property: a property holds one function, so a second assignment silently replaces the first. Also look at the submit listener: it goes on the form, not on the button, so it also catches Enter key submits.

Page lifecycle: DOMContentLoaded and load

When the browser parses HTML and meets a classic <script> with no attributes, it runs it right there, before the rest of the page exists. That is why beginners get null from querySelector. The modern fix is <script src="app.js" defer></script> (or type="module", which is deferred by default): the script runs after parsing, just before DOMContentLoaded. You rarely need the event itself, but it is useful for code that may load at an unknown time, like a widget or an analytics snippet.

Try it: Page lifecycle: readyState, DOMContentLoaded and load

JavaScript

console.log('1. script runs, readyState =', document.readyState);

document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', (event) => {
  // HTML fully parsed, DOM ready. Images may still be loading.
  console.log('2.', event.type, 'readyState =', document.readyState);
});

window.addEventListener('load', (event) => {
  // Everything loaded: images, styles, iframes.
  console.log('3.', event.type, 'readyState =', document.readyState);
});

// A safe "run when ready" helper for scripts that might load late
function onReady(fn) {
  if (document.readyState === 'loading') {
    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', fn, { once: true });
  } else {
    fn(); // already parsed: the DOM is ready, so run now (DOMContentLoaded may have fired already)
  }
}
onReady(() => console.log('onReady callback ran'));

The script runs while the page is still loading. Notice the order of the three lines and the value of readyState in each.

document.readyState moves from 'loading' to 'interactive' (parsed) to 'complete' (everything loaded). The onReady helper matters because events are not replayed: if you add a DOMContentLoaded listener after it fired, it never runs.

Removing listeners

removeEventListener(type, listener, options) removes a listener only if the type, the exact same function reference and the capture flag match. The browser compares functions by identity, not by their code. That also explains the opposite rule: adding the same function twice is ignored, so a named handler can never be doubled by accident, but an inline arrow can.

Try it: Listener identity: duplicates, removal and handleEvent

JavaScript

const cart = new EventTarget();

function onUpdate(event) {
  console.log('onUpdate ran for', event.type);
}

cart.addEventListener('update', onUpdate);
cart.addEventListener('update', onUpdate); // same function: ignored
cart.dispatchEvent(new Event('update'));   // runs once

// A NEW arrow function never matches the one that was added
cart.removeEventListener('update', (e) => onUpdate(e));
cart.dispatchEvent(new Event('update'));   // still runs

cart.removeEventListener('update', onUpdate); // same reference: removed
cart.dispatchEvent(new Event('update'));   // nothing
console.log('--- listener objects ---');

// A listener can be an object with a handleEvent method.
// Inside it, this is the object, so it can keep its own state.
const badge = {
  count: 0,
  handleEvent(event) {
    this.count += 1;
    console.log(`badge saw ${event.type} #${this.count}`);
  },
};
cart.addEventListener('add', badge);
cart.addEventListener('remove', badge);
cart.dispatchEvent(new Event('add'));
cart.dispatchEvent(new Event('add'));
cart.dispatchEvent(new Event('remove'));

EventTarget is the same machinery every element uses. Predict each line before you read the console.

The handleEvent object is a lesser-known pattern. The browser calls badge.handleEvent(event), so this is the object itself. It is handy for components that listen to many event types and keep state, and it avoids binding problems.

Listener options: once, passive, signal, capture

OptionEffectReal use
once: trueRemoved automatically after the first callClaim a coupon, a first-run tip, waiting for one transitionend
passive: truePromises no preventDefault(); calls to it are ignoredscroll, wheel, touchstart, touchmove handlers
signalRemoves the listener when its AbortController abortsTearing down a component, a modal or a page view
capture: trueRuns in the capture phase, on the way downCovered in the propagation lesson

Why does passive exist? For touch and wheel events, the browser cannot start scrolling until it knows whether your listener will cancel it. A slow listener makes scrolling stutter. A passive listener lets the browser scroll immediately on its compositor. Chrome and Firefox already treat wheel, touchstart and touchmove listeners on window, document and body as passive by default, so if you really need to block scrolling there, you must pass passive: false.

signal is the modern clean-up tool. One AbortController can be passed to ten listeners on different elements, and one controller.abort() removes them all. No need to keep references to every handler.

// once: the browser removes this listener after its first call
const claim = document.querySelector('#claim');
claim.addEventListener('click', () => {
  document.querySelector('#code').hidden = false;

const scroller = document.querySelector('#scroller');

const status = document.querySelector('#status');

let controller = null;

function updateProgress() {
  const max = scroller.scrollHeight - scroller.clientHeight;
  const ratio = max > 0 ? scroller.scrollTop / max : 1;
  bar.style.width = `${Math.round(ratio * 100)}%`;
  if (ratio > 0.98 && agree.disabled) {
    agree.disabled = false;
    status.textContent = 'Thanks for reading all the terms.';
  }
}

function startTracking() {
  controller = new AbortController();
  const { signal } = controller;
  // passive: we promise not to call preventDefault, so scrolling never waits
  scroller.addEventListener('scroll', updateProgress, { passive: true, signal });
  window.addEventListener('resize', updateProgress, { signal });
  signal.addEventListener('abort', () => {
    console.log('abort(): scroll and resize listeners removed together');
  });
  updateProgress();
}

toggle.addEventListener('change', () => {
  if (toggle.checked) {
    startTracking();
    console.log('tracking started with a new controller');
  } else {
    controller.abort();
  }
});

startTracking();
scroller.scrollTop = 90; // start part-way down so the bar shows

Claim the code twice: the second click does nothing because the listener is gone. Scroll the terms, then switch off Track reading and scroll again.

Remember: an AbortController is single-use. After abort(), its signal stays aborted forever, and adding a listener with an aborted signal does nothing. Create a new controller each time you start listening again, as startTracking() does.

Inline handlers and why to avoid them

<!-- Old style: avoid -->
<button onclick="like(this)">Like</button>

Inline on* attributes still work, but they cause problems in real projects. The code is a string, so it runs in the global scope and needs global functions, which clash across files and do not work with modules. You can only have one per event per element. HTML and behaviour are tangled, so a designer changing markup can break logic. Most importantly, a strict Content Security Policy (a security header you will meet in the security lesson) blocks inline handlers entirely, because they look exactly like injected script. Keep HTML for structure and attach behaviour from your JavaScript file.

Example: a Ralfiz Academy post card

The lab combines everything into one component: a post with a like button, double-click to like, a comment box with a live counter and a keyboard shortcut, a one-time tip, and a Close discussion button that removes every listener at once.

const controller = new AbortController();
const { signal } = controller;

likeBtn.addEventListener('click', toggleLike, { signal });
postText.addEventListener('dblclick', () => setLiked(true), { signal });
textarea.addEventListener('input', updateCounter, { signal });

textarea.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
  if (event.key === 'Enter' && (event.ctrlKey || event.metaKey)) {
    event.preventDefault();       // no new line
    form.requestSubmit();          // runs validation + submit listeners
  }
}, { signal });

form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = textarea.value.trim(); // user text: never innerHTML
  list.append(li);
  form.reset();
  updateCounter();
}, { signal });

tipButton.addEventListener('click', () => { tip.hidden = true; },
  { once: true });

closeBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
  controller.abort();             // every listener above is gone
  form.inert = true;
  closeBtn.textContent = 'Discussion closed';
}, { once: true });

Why form.requestSubmit() and not form.submit()? submit() sends the form directly: it skips validation and does not fire the submit event, so your handler never runs. requestSubmit() behaves exactly like clicking the submit button.

Common mistakes

  1. Calling the handler instead of passing it. Wrong: btn.addEventListener('click', save()); runs save immediately. Fix: btn.addEventListener('click', save); or () => save(id) when you need arguments.
  2. Removing with a new function. Wrong: el.removeEventListener('scroll', () => update());. Fix: keep a named reference, or register with { signal } and call controller.abort().
  3. Adding listeners inside a render function. Wrong: calling btn.addEventListener('click', () => …) every time a list re-renders adds another copy each time, so one click runs five times. Fix: attach once, outside the render, or use delegation (next lesson).
  4. Using change for live feedback. Wrong: textarea.addEventListener('change', updateCounter) updates only on blur. Fix: listen to input.
  5. Running before the element exists. Wrong: a plain <script> in <head> finds null. Fix: add defer or use type="module".
  6. Using this inside an arrow handler. Wrong: btn.addEventListener('click', () => this.classList.add('on')): arrows have no own this. Fix: use event.currentTarget, which works in every kind of function.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "What is the difference between target and currentTarget?" target is where the event started; currentTarget is where the running listener is attached. Give the icon-inside-a-button example.
  • "How do you remove an anonymous listener?" You cannot with removeEventListener, but you can with { signal } or { once: true }. Mentioning AbortController shows modern knowledge.
  • "Why are passive listeners faster?" The browser does not have to wait for your JavaScript before scrolling.
  • Accessibility: listen for click on real buttons and you get keyboard support for free. Listening for mousedown on a div leaves keyboard and switch users behind.
  • Memory: in single-page apps, listeners on window or document outlive the view that added them. Tie them to a controller and abort it when the view closes; frameworks do this for you in their clean-up hooks.
  • Deprecated APIs: event.keyCode, event.which and event.returnValue still appear in old tutorials. Use key, code and preventDefault().

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. The same named function is added twice, and one arrow function once. What is logged?

const bus = new EventTarget();
const onSave = () => console.log('saved');

bus.addEventListener('save', onSave);
bus.addEventListener('save', onSave);
bus.addEventListener('save', () => console.log('saved'));

bus.dispatchEvent(new Event('save'));
  • A saved
  • B 
    saved
saved
saved
  • C 
    saved
saved
  • D Nothing is logged

Snippet 2. What is the final value of clicks?

const button = new EventTarget();
const controller = new AbortController();
let clicks = 0;

button.addEventListener('click', () => clicks++, { once: true });
button.addEventListener('click', () => { clicks += 10; }, {
  signal: controller.signal,
});

button.dispatchEvent(new Event('click'));
controller.abort();
button.dispatchEvent(new Event('click'));
console.log(clicks);
  • A 22
  • B 1
  • C 12
  • D 11

Snippet 3. element.click() fires a click event from code. In what order do the lines appear?

const button = document.createElement('button');
button.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('handler'));

console.log('before');
button.click();
console.log('after');
  • A 
    before
after
handler
  • B 
    before
handler
after
  • C 
    handler
before
after
  • D 
    before
after

Answers

  1. C. Adding the same function with the same type and capture flag a second time is ignored, so onSave runs once. The arrow is a different function, so it runs too: two lines.
  2. D. The first dispatch runs both listeners (1 + 10). The once listener then removes itself and abort() removes the other, so the second dispatch runs nothing: 11.
  3. B. Dispatching an event is synchronous: click() runs every listener before it returns. Only the browser’s own events wait for their turn in the task queue.

input fires on every edit of a field’s value; change fires when the edit is committed, usually when the field loses focus.

quiz.question: A button contains an <svg> icon and you attach a click listener to the button. The user clicks the icon. What are event.target and event.currentTarget?
options: target is the svg (or its path); currentTarget is the button
Both are the button
target is the button; currentTarget is the svg
Both are the svg
quiz.explanation: target is where the event started (the innermost element clicked). currentTarget is always the element whose listener is running, which is the button you registered on.

quiz.question: You want a live character counter under a textarea. Which event should update it?
options: change, because it fires when the value changes
keydown, because every character is a key
input, because it fires on every edit, including paste and dictation
blur, because the user has finished typing
quiz.explanation: input fires after every change to the value, whatever caused it (typing, paste, autocorrect, drag and drop). change only fires when the edit is committed, and keydown misses paste and fires before the value updates.

quiz.question: Why does removeEventListener("click", () => save()) never remove anything?
options: removeEventListener only works for events added with once
Each arrow expression creates a new function, so it never matches the function that was added
removeEventListener needs the third argument to be true
Click listeners can only be removed by replacing the element
quiz.explanation: The browser removes a listener only when the type, the exact same function reference and the capture flag all match. Keep a named reference, or register with a signal and call abort().

quiz.question: What does { passive: true } promise the browser?
options: The listener will run after all other listeners
The listener will only run once
The listener runs in a background thread
The listener will never call preventDefault, so scrolling does not have to wait for it
quiz.explanation: For scroll-related events (wheel, touchstart, touchmove) the browser must wait to see if you cancel the default. A passive listener promises not to, so scrolling stays smooth. Chrome and Firefox already make these passive by default on window, document and body.

lessons.title: Propagation and event delegation
lessons.summaryHtml:
An event does not just happen on one element. It travels: down from window to the target in the capture phase, arrives at the target, then travels back up through every ancestor in the bubble phase. Any ancestor can listen along the way.

That journey makes event delegation possible: one listener on a list handles clicks on every row, including rows added later, by asking event.target.closest('li') which row was hit. You also learn the difference between stopPropagation() (stop the journey) and preventDefault() (cancel the browser’s default action), and which events do not bubble, such as focus, with focusin as the bubbling alternative.

The mini project is a Ralfiz Tasks to-do list driven by a handful of delegated listeners, with add, toggle, delete, inline edit, filters and clear completed.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

When you click a button, you are also clicking the card the button sits in, the section around the card, the page body, and the whole document. The browser models this honestly: the event is delivered along a path that includes every ancestor of the element you clicked.

Picture a parcel sent to flat 3B. It goes into the building through the gate, up to the third floor, into flat 3B (the target), and then the delivery receipt travels back down the same way. Anyone along the route (the guard at the gate, the floor manager) can look at it on the way in, on the way out, or both. That route is propagation, and it has three phases.

  1. Capture: from window down through each ancestor to the target’s parent.
  2. Target: at the element where the event happened.
  3. Bubble: back up from the target’s parent to window.

Why it matters

Propagation explains three things that confuse every beginner: why clicking an icon inside a button makes event.target the icon; why a click on a "Save" button inside a clickable card also opens the card; and why a dropdown that "closes when you click outside" suddenly stops closing after someone adds stopPropagation() somewhere else.

It also powers event delegation, one of the most useful patterns in front-end work. Instead of attaching a listener to each of 500 rows in an orders table, you attach one to the table. New rows work immediately, removed rows need no clean-up, and memory stays flat. React does something similar internally: it attaches its listeners at the root of your app rather than on each element.

How it works

The three phases in action

By default, addEventListener listens in the bubble phase. Pass { capture: true } (or just true as the third argument) to listen in the capture phase instead. The event object tells you where it is in its journey with eventPhase: 1 for capture, 2 at the target, 3 for bubble.

The page below registers two listeners on each of five nodes: window, document, the section, the article and the button. It logs each one as it runs. Click different places and compare the paths.

Try it: Watch an event travel: capture, target, bubble

HTML

<main class="app">
  <section class="stage">
    <section class="box shop" id="shop"><span class="tag">section#shop</span>
      <article class="box card" id="card"><span class="tag">article.card</span>
        <div class="lamp" aria-hidden="true">💡</div>
        <p class="title">Aurora Desk Lamp</p>
        <p class="price">₹1,499</p>
        <button class="buy" id="buy" type="button">Add to cart</button>
      </article>
    </section>
    <label class="check"><input type="checkbox" id="stop"> Call <code>stopPropagation()</code> in the article’s bubble listener</label>
  </section>
  <section class="log" aria-label="Event log">
    <h2>Event path <span id="count" class="pill">0 listeners</span></h2>
    <ol id="log"></ol>
  </section>
</main>

JavaScript

const log = document.querySelector('#log');
const count = document.querySelector('#count');
const stopBox = document.querySelector('#stop');
const shop = document.querySelector('#shop');
const PHASES = ['none', 'capture', 'target', 'bubble'];

let currentEvent = null;
let n = 0;

function write(event, label) {
  if (event !== currentEvent) {      // a new click: start a fresh log
    currentEvent = event;
    n = 0;
    log.replaceChildren();
  }
  const phase = PHASES[event.eventPhase];
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.className = phase;
  li.style.animationDelay = `${n * 60}ms`;
  const badge = document.createElement('span');
  badge.className = 'phase';
  badge.textContent = phase;
  const who = document.createElement('code');
  who.textContent = label;
  li.append(badge, who);
  log.append(li);
  n += 1;
  count.textContent = `${n} listeners`;
}

const nodes = [
  ['window', window],
  ['document', document],
  ['section#shop', shop],
  ['article.card', document.querySelector('#card')],
  ['button#buy', document.querySelector('#buy')],
];

for (const [label, node] of nodes) {
  node.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
    if (!shop.contains(event.target)) return; // ignore clicks elsewhere
    write(event, `${label}  (capture listener)`);
  }, { capture: true });

  node.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
    if (!shop.contains(event.target)) return;
    write(event, `${label}  (bubble listener)`);
    if (label === 'article.card' && stopBox.checked) {
      event.stopPropagation();
      const li = document.createElement('li');
      li.className = 'stopped';
      li.textContent = '✋ stopPropagation(): the event stops here';
      log.append(li);
    }
  });
}

document.querySelector('#buy').click(); // one click to start

Click the button, the card and the grey section. Then tick stopPropagation and click the button again: the journey ends at the article.

Click the button and you get ten lines: four capture listeners on the way down, two at the target, four bubble listeners on the way up. Click the grey section and the path is shorter, because the target is higher in the tree. At the target itself, both of its listeners report phase "target". Modern browsers run the target’s capture listeners before its normal ones, which is what you see.

You can inspect the full route in code with event.composedPath(), which returns the array of nodes from the target up to window. It is handy when debugging "who else is listening?"

buyButton.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const path = event.composedPath().map((n) => n.localName ?? n.constructor.name);
  console.log(path);
  // [ 'button', 'article', 'section', 'main', 'body', 'html',
  //   'HTMLDocument', 'Window' ]
});

stopPropagation, stopImmediatePropagation and preventDefault

These three methods are often mixed up. They do completely different jobs.

MethodWhat it stopsWhat still happens
preventDefault()The browser’s default action: following a link, submitting a form, ticking a checkbox, scrolling on wheelThe event keeps travelling; every listener still runs
stopPropagation()Delivery to further nodes on the pathOther listeners on the current node still run; the default action still happens
stopImmediatePropagation()Delivery to further nodes and to the remaining listeners on this nodeThe default action still happens

Tick the checkbox in the playground above and click the button: the log stops at the article’s bubble listener, and the section, document and window never hear about it. That is exactly the problem with stopPropagation() in real apps: code far away that relies on bubbling (analytics, "click outside to close" menus, keyboard shortcut managers) silently breaks. Use it rarely and deliberately.

Event delegation with closest()

Delegation means putting one listener on a stable ancestor and working out, inside it, which child was involved. The recipe has three steps:

  1. Listen on a container that exists for the lifetime of the feature, such as the <ul> of a list.
  2. Find the element you care about with event.target.closest(selector). closest checks the element itself and then walks up its ancestors, so it works even if the user clicked an icon or a <span> inside the button.
  3. Ignore the event if nothing matched, and read the item’s identity from a data-* attribute on the row.

This Ralfiz Tasks list has three listeners in total, whatever the number of rows: click on the list for delete buttons, change on the list for checkboxes, and click on the filter bar. Each render throws the old rows away and builds new ones, which would be a listener leak if every row had its own handlers.

const list = document.querySelector('#list');
const filters = document.querySelector('#filters');
const leftEl = document.querySelector('#left');
const form = document.querySelector('#new');
const input = document.querySelector('#title');

let tasks = [
  { id: 1, title: 'Review pull request #42', done: true },
  { id: 2, title: 'Fix cart total rounding', done: false },
  { id: 3, title: 'Write release notes for v2.3', done: false },
];
let filter = 'all';
let nextId = 4;

function renderItem(task) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.className = task.done ? 'item done' : 'item';
  li.dataset.id = task.id;               // the row remembers its task
  const row = document.createElement('label');
  row.className = 'row';
  const box = document.createElement('input');
  box.type = 'checkbox';
  box.className = 'toggle';
  box.checked = task.done;
  const text = document.createElement('span');
  text.className = 'text';
  text.textContent = task.title;
  row.append(box, text);
  const del = document.createElement('button');
  del.type = 'button';
  del.className = 'delete';
  del.textContent = '×';
  del.setAttribute('aria-label', `Delete ${task.title}`);
  li.append(row, del);
  return li;
}

function render() {
  const visible = tasks.filter((t) =>
    filter === 'all' ? true : filter === 'done' ? t.done : !t.done);
  list.replaceChildren(...visible.map(renderItem));
  if (!visible.length) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.className = 'empty';
    li.textContent = 'Nothing here. Enjoy your day!';
    list.append(li);
  }
  const left = tasks.filter((t) => !t.done).length;
  leftEl.textContent = `${left} ${left === 1 ? 'task' : 'tasks'} left`;
}

const idOf = (el) => Number(el.closest('li').dataset.id);

// ONE click listener for every delete button, now and in the future
list.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const del = event.target.closest('.delete');
  if (!del || !list.contains(del)) return;
  const id = idOf(del);
  tasks = tasks.filter((t) => t.id !== id);
  console.log(`delete #${id}: target <${event.target.localName}>,` +
    ` handled on <${event.currentTarget.localName}>`);
  render();
});

// ONE change listener for every checkbox ('change' bubbles)
list.addEventListener('change', (event) => {
  if (!event.target.matches('.toggle')) return;
  const task = tasks.find((t) => t.id === idOf(event.target));
  task.done = event.target.checked;
  console.log(`toggle #${task.id} -> ${task.done ? 'done' : 'active'}`);
  render();
});

filters.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const btn = event.target.closest('button[data-filter]');
  if (!btn) return;
  filter = btn.dataset.filter;
  for (const b of filters.querySelectorAll('button')) {
    b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(b === btn));
  }
  render();
});

form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const title = input.value.trim();
  if (!title) return;
  tasks.unshift({ id: nextId++, title, done: false });
  form.reset();
  render();
});

render();

Add tasks, tick them and delete them: every row, old or new, is handled by the listeners on the <ul>. Open the console to see who handled each click.

Two details deserve attention. First, the checkbox listener uses change, which bubbles, and matches('.toggle'), because the target is the checkbox itself. Second, the delete handler checks list.contains(del). In this demo it cannot fail, but in nested components closest() can walk past your container and match an element outside it, so the check is a good habit.

// The general shape of a delegated handler
container.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const button = event.target.closest('[data-action]');
  if (!button || !container.contains(button)) return;

  const id = button.closest('[data-id]').dataset.id;
  const actions = { edit: editItem, remove: removeItem, pin: pinItem };
  actions[button.dataset.action]?.(id);
});

The data-action map in that snippet scales nicely: adding a new button type means adding one entry, not another listener.

Clickable cards: handling nested interactive elements

Product cards often open a detail view when clicked anywhere, but they also contain a wishlist button and a link. A common beginner fix is stopPropagation() on the inner button. A cleaner approach is to handle everything in one delegated listener and decide in order: is it the heart? Handle it and return. Is it the link? Prevent navigation. Otherwise, open the card.

Events that do not bubble

Most user-input events bubble, but a few do not. They still go through the capture phase, so a capture listener on an ancestor can see them, or you can use a bubbling equivalent.

Does not bubbleUse instead for delegation
focus, blurfocusin, focusout
mouseenter, mouseleavemouseover, mouseout (or pointerover, pointerout)
load, error on images and scriptsA capture listener on a container
scroll on an elementListen on the scrolling element itself
invalid on form fieldsA capture listener on the form

click, input, change, keydown, submit and focusin all bubble. The checkout form below proves the difference with counters: the form’s normal focus listener never runs, while the capture listener and focusin fire on every field.

const form = document.querySelector('#address');
const hint = document.querySelector('#hint');
const counts = { focus: 0, capture: 0, focusin: 0 };
const show = (key) => {
  counts[key] += 1;
  document.querySelector(`#c-${key}`).textContent = counts[key];
};

// Never runs for the inputs: focus does not bubble up to the form
form.addEventListener('focus', () => show('focus'));

// Capture still works: every event goes DOWN through the form first
form.addEventListener('focus', () => show('capture'), { capture: true });

// focusin is the bubbling twin of focus: perfect for delegation
form.addEventListener('focusin', (event) => {
  show('focusin');
  const field = event.target.closest('.field');
  if (!field) return;
  field.classList.add('active');
  hint.textContent = field.dataset.hint;
});

form.addEventListener('focusout', (event) => {
  event.target.closest('.field')?.classList.remove('active');
  // relatedTarget is where focus is going next (null if leaving the form)
  if (!form.contains(event.relatedTarget)) {
    hint.textContent = 'Select a field to see a hint.';
  }
});

document.querySelector('#phone').focus();

Tab through the fields. The focus counter on the form stays at 0; the capture listener and focusin both see every change.

The focusout handler also uses event.relatedTarget: the element receiving focus next. If it is outside the form (or null), the user has left the form, so we reset the hint.

Example: Ralfiz Tasks with delegation

The lab extends the to-do list with inline editing and clear completed, still with listeners only on the list, the filter bar and the form. Editing is the interesting part, because it combines three delegated events.

// Double-click a title to edit it
list.addEventListener('dblclick', (event) => {
  const text = event.target.closest('.text');
  if (!text) return;
  const input = document.createElement('input');
  input.className = 'edit';
  input.value = text.textContent;
  text.replaceWith(input);
  input.focus();
  input.select();
});

// Enter saves, Escape cancels (keydown bubbles)
list.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
  if (!event.target.matches('.edit')) return;
  if (event.key === 'Enter') event.target.blur();       // triggers focusout
  if (event.key === 'Escape') { editing = false; render(); }
});

// Leaving the field saves (focusout bubbles, blur does not)
list.addEventListener('focusout', (event) => {
  if (!event.target.matches('.edit') || !editing) return;
  const task = findTask(event.target);
  task.title = event.target.value.trim() || task.title;
  render();
});

Notice that the edit input is created long after the listeners were attached, yet all three handlers work for it. That is the power of delegation.

Common mistakes

  1. Using event.target directly. Wrong: if (event.target.classList.contains('delete')) fails when the user clicks the icon inside the button. Fix: const del = event.target.closest('.delete');.
  2. Reaching for stopPropagation to fix a nested click. Wrong: favButton.addEventListener('click', (e) => e.stopPropagation()) also hides the click from analytics and "click outside" code. Fix: in the outer handler, check event.target.closest('.fav') and return early.
  3. Delegating a non-bubbling event. Wrong: form.addEventListener('focus', highlight) never fires for the inputs. Fix: use focusin, or pass { capture: true }.
  4. Mismatched capture when removing. Wrong: adding with { capture: true } and removing without it leaves the listener in place. Fix: pass the same capture flag to removeEventListener, or use a signal.
  5. Per-row listeners inside render. Wrong: rows.forEach((r) => r.querySelector('.delete').addEventListener('click', …)) after each render. Fix: one delegated listener, attached once.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "Explain event bubbling." Describe the three phases, the default bubble listeners and { capture: true }. Draw the path from window to target and back.
  • "What is event delegation and why use it?" One listener on a parent, closest() to find the child, and the benefits: dynamic content, fewer listeners, simpler clean-up.
  • "Click outside to close": document.addEventListener('click', (e) => { if (!menu.contains(e.target)) close(); }). It only works if nothing inside the page stops propagation, which is a good reason to avoid stopPropagation.
  • Shadow DOM: events crossing a shadow boundary are retargeted, so outside listeners see the host element as the target. You will see this in the Web Components lesson.
  • Performance: delegation is not about making each click faster; it saves memory and set-up time when lists are long, and it removes whole classes of bugs.

Answers

  1. C. The capture listener runs on the way down, before the target. The normal listener runs on the way back up, after the target. The order the listeners were added in does not matter across phases.
  2. B. stopPropagation stops the event from reaching other elements (so C never runs), but the remaining listeners on the current element still run. stopImmediatePropagation would stop B too.
  3. D. preventDefault cancels the default action but not the journey, so the event still bubbles to the form. defaultPrevented is true, and eventPhase is 3 because the form is an ancestor, reached in the bubble phase.

terms.definition: The path an event travels through the DOM: capture (down), target, then bubble (up).
The first phase: the event goes from window down to the target’s parent. Listeners run here only if added with capture: true.
The last phase: the event goes from the target’s parent back up to window. Normal listeners run here.
A number on the event: 1 capture, 2 at target, 3 bubble (0 when not being dispatched).
Handling events for many child elements with one listener on a common ancestor, using event.target to find the child.
Stops the event from reaching further elements on its path. Other listeners on the current element still run.
Bubbling versions of focus and blur, so a form can react to focus changes in any of its fields.

lessons.examTip: When an interviewer asks about delegation, mention three wins: fewer listeners, rows added later work automatically, and no clean-up when rows are removed. Then mention the catch: always use closest() and check the match is inside your container.
