quiz.question: A to-do list renders new <li> rows every time the user adds a task. What is the most robust way to handle the delete buttons?
options: Add a listener to each delete button inside the render function
Use inline onclick attributes on each button
Add one click listener to the <ul> and use event.target.closest(".delete")
Add a listener to document for every button on the page with the same function
quiz.explanation: Delegation handles rows that do not exist yet, needs no clean-up when rows are removed and cannot accidentally add duplicate listeners on re-render.

quiz.question: A link inside a clickable card calls event.preventDefault(). What happens to the event?
options: It stops travelling and the card’s listener never runs
The link does not navigate, but the event still bubbles to the card
The link navigates, but the card’s listener does not run
Both the navigation and the bubbling are cancelled
quiz.explanation: preventDefault cancels the browser’s default action (following the link). It does not affect propagation. stopPropagation is the one that stops the journey.

quiz.question: You want a form to highlight whichever field group has focus, with one listener on the form. Which event do you listen for?
options: focus, because it bubbles from inputs to the form
blur, because it fires first
change, because it fires when focus moves
focusin, because unlike focus it bubbles
quiz.explanation: focus and blur do not bubble, so a normal listener on the form never sees them. focusin and focusout fire at the same moments and do bubble. (A capture listener for focus would also work.)

lessons.title: Keyboard, mouse, pointer and custom events
lessons.summaryHtml:
Keyboard events tell you which character a key produced (event.key, such as 'k' or '!') and which physical key was pressed (event.code, such as 'KeyK' or 'Digit1'), plus the state of Ctrl, Shift, Alt and Meta. With them you build shortcuts like Ctrl+K for a command palette.

Pointer events unify mouse, touch and pen into one set of events (pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup), and pointer capture keeps a drag working even when the finger or mouse leaves the element. Finally, CustomEvent lets your own components announce things, such as budgetchange, with data in detail, so other code can listen without being tightly coupled.

You build a Ralfiz Admin command palette, a keyboard inspector, a draggable budget slider and a resizable sidebar.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

The last two lessons used mostly click and input. Real apps need more. Power users expect keyboard shortcuts. Touch users expect to drag things with a finger. And as your code grows, your own components need a way to say "something happened" without knowing who cares.

  • Keyboard events (keydown, keyup) tell you which key was pressed, what it produced and which modifiers were held.
  • Pointer events (pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup) describe a mouse, a finger or a pen with one API.
  • Custom events are events you create and dispatch yourself, carrying your own data.

Why it matters

Products like email clients, design tools and admin dashboards live or die on speed. A Ctrl+K command palette lets staff jump to any screen without the mouse. A slider that works with a mouse but not a finger fails half your users, because in India most traffic is on phones. And a price filter that directly calls the product grid’s functions becomes impossible to reuse. Custom events decouple the two: the slider announces budgetchange, and anything that cares listens.

How it works

Keyboard events: key vs code

Use keydown for almost everything. It fires when a key goes down and repeats while it is held (with event.repeat set to true). keyup fires on release. The old keypress event is deprecated, as are keyCode and which.

Key pressed (US layout)event.keyevent.code
A"a""KeyA"
Shift+A"A""KeyA"
Shift+1"!""Digit1"
Space bar" ""Space"
Down arrow"ArrowDown""ArrowDown"
A on a French AZERTY keyboard"a""KeyQ"

The last row is the important one. code names the physical position as if the keyboard were US QWERTY, so the A key on a French keyboard reports KeyQ. That makes code right for games (WASD movement should use positions) and key right for letter shortcuts like Ctrl+S (users think of the letter printed on their key).

Modifiers are booleans on every keyboard and mouse event: ctrlKey, shiftKey, altKey and metaKey (Cmd on a Mac). Press keys in the inspector below. It also shows isTrusted: the first event was dispatched by code, so it is false.

Try it: Keyboard inspector: key vs code

JavaScript

const cap = document.querySelector('#cap');
const history = document.querySelector('#history');
const toast = document.querySelector('#toast');
const trusted = document.querySelector('#trusted');

function show(event) {
  // Space is ' ' in event.key: give it a readable label
  cap.textContent = event.key === ' ' ? 'Space' : event.key;
  document.querySelector('#k').textContent = JSON.stringify(event.key);
  document.querySelector('#c').textContent = JSON.stringify(event.code);
  document.querySelector('#r').textContent = String(event.repeat);
  for (const chip of document.querySelectorAll('[data-mod]')) {
    chip.classList.toggle('on', event[chip.dataset.mod]);
  }
  trusted.textContent = event.isTrusted ? 'isTrusted: true (real key)'
    : 'isTrusted: false (dispatched by code)';
  trusted.classList.toggle('real', event.isTrusted);
  if (!event.repeat) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = `${event.key} · ${event.code}`;
    history.prepend(li);
    history.querySelectorAll('li:nth-child(n+7)').forEach((el) => el.remove());
  }
}

document.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
  show(event);
  cap.classList.add('down');

  // A shortcut: Ctrl+S on Windows/Linux, Cmd+S on a Mac
  const mod = event.ctrlKey || event.metaKey;
  if (mod && event.key.toLowerCase() === 's') {
    event.preventDefault(); // stop the browser's "Save page" dialog
    toast.textContent = '✓ Draft saved (Ctrl/Cmd+S intercepted)';
  }
});

document.addEventListener('keyup', () => cap.classList.remove('down'));

// Simulate Shift+1 so there is something to see before you type
document.dispatchEvent(new KeyboardEvent('keydown', {
  key: '!', code: 'Digit1', shiftKey: true, bubbles: true,
}));
cap.classList.remove('down');

Click inside the page, then press keys. Try Shift+1, Space, arrows and holding a key down. Press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on a Mac) to see a shortcut intercepted.

Three details in that code are worth copying into your own projects. event.key.toLowerCase() makes the shortcut work with Shift or Caps Lock on. Checking ctrlKey || metaKey gives Mac users Cmd+S. And preventDefault() stops the browser’s own "Save page" dialog. Some browser shortcuts (Ctrl+W, Ctrl+T, Ctrl+N) cannot be overridden by pages at all, so do not build features on them.

Building a command palette

A command palette combines global and local keyboard handling:

  • A global listener on document opens it with Ctrl/Cmd+K, or with / when the user is not already typing in a field. Without that check, typing a URL with a slash into a form would pop the palette open.
  • A local listener on the palette’s input handles ↑, ↓, Enter and Esc, and calls preventDefault() only for keys it uses, so normal typing still works.
  • Focus stays in the input the whole time. The highlighted option is announced with aria-activedescendant, the standard pattern for a combobox with a listbox.

Try it: Command palette with Ctrl+K

JavaScript

const COMMANDS = [
  { id: 'dashboard', group: 'Go to', label: 'Dashboard', icon: '🏠' },
  { id: 'orders', group: 'Go to', label: 'Orders', icon: '📦' },
  { id: 'products', group: 'Go to', label: 'Products', icon: '🏷️' },
  { id: 'customers', group: 'Go to', label: 'Customers', icon: '👥' },
  { id: 'invoice', group: 'Actions', label: 'Create invoice', icon: '🧾' },
  { id: 'theme', group: 'Actions', label: 'Toggle dark mode', icon: '🌙' },
];
const overlay = document.querySelector('#overlay');
const input = document.querySelector('#q');
const list = document.querySelector('#cmds');
const status = document.querySelector('#status');
let matches = [];
let active = 0;

function render() {
  const q = input.value.trim().toLowerCase();
  matches = COMMANDS.filter((c) => c.label.toLowerCase().includes(q));
  active = Math.min(active, Math.max(matches.length - 1, 0));
  list.replaceChildren();
  let group = '';
  matches.forEach((cmd, i) => {
    if (cmd.group !== group) {
      group = cmd.group;
      const h = document.createElement('li');
      h.className = 'group';
      h.setAttribute('role', 'presentation');
      h.textContent = group;
      list.append(h);
    }
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.className = 'opt';
    li.id = `cmd-${cmd.id}`;
    li.dataset.index = i;
    li.setAttribute('role', 'option');
    li.setAttribute('aria-selected', String(i === active));
    const ico = document.createElement('span');
    ico.className = 'ico';
    ico.textContent = cmd.icon;
    li.append(ico, cmd.label);
    list.append(li);
  });
  if (!matches.length) {
    list.innerHTML = '<li class="none">No commands found</li>'; // static text only
  }
  const current = matches[active];
  input.setAttribute('aria-activedescendant', current ? `cmd-${current.id}` : '');
  list.querySelector('[aria-selected="true"]')?.scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest' });
}

const isOpen = () => !overlay.hidden;
function open() {
  overlay.hidden = false;
  input.value = '';
  active = 0;
  render();
  input.focus();
}
function close() { overlay.hidden = true; }

function run(cmd, how) {
  if (!cmd) return;
  close();
  if (cmd.id === 'theme') document.querySelector('#shell').classList.toggle('dark');
  else document.querySelector('#page').textContent = cmd.label;
  status.textContent = `Ran "${cmd.label}" with ${how}`;
  status.classList.add('show');
  setTimeout(() => status.classList.remove('show'), 1600);
}

// Global shortcuts live on document
document.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
  const mod = event.ctrlKey || event.metaKey;          // Cmd on a Mac
  if (mod && event.key.toLowerCase() === 'k') {
    event.preventDefault();                             // browser uses Ctrl+K too
    isOpen() ? close() : open();
    return;
  }
  const typing = event.target.closest('input, textarea, [contenteditable]');
  if (event.key === '/' && !typing && !isOpen()) {
    event.preventDefault();
    open();
  }
});

// Keys inside the palette
input.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
  if (event.isComposing) return; // an IME is still building a character
  if (event.key === 'ArrowDown') active = (active + 1) % matches.length;
  else if (event.key === 'ArrowUp') active = (active - 1 + matches.length) % matches.length;
  else if (event.key === 'Enter') return run(matches[active], 'Enter');
  else if (event.key === 'Escape') return close();
  else return;                                          // let other keys type
  event.preventDefault();                               // no cursor jump
  render();
});

input.addEventListener('input', () => { active = 0; render(); });

list.addEventListener('pointermove', (event) => {
  const opt = event.target.closest('.opt');
  if (opt && Number(opt.dataset.index) !== active) {
    active = Number(opt.dataset.index);
    render();
  }
});
list.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const opt = event.target.closest('.opt');
  if (opt) run(matches[Number(opt.dataset.index)], 'a click');
});
overlay.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  if (event.target === overlay) close();               // click on the backdrop
});
document.querySelector('#trigger').addEventListener('click', open);

open();

The palette starts open. Type to filter, use ↑ ↓ and Enter, or click. Press Esc to close, then Ctrl+K (Cmd+K) or / to open it again.

Look at event.isComposing at the top of the input handler. Users typing Japanese, Chinese or Malayalam with an input method editor press Enter to confirm a character. Without this check, that Enter would also run a command. The palette also uses pointermove with delegation to follow the mouse, and a click on the backdrop (where event.target === overlay) closes it.

Mouse events vs pointer events

Mouse events came first, then touch events were added for phones, which meant writing everything twice. Pointer events replace both with one model. Every pointer has a pointerId, a pointerType ("mouse", "touch" or "pen") and extras such as pressure and isPrimary.

Mouse eventPointer eventNotes
mousedownpointerdownCheck event.button === 0 for the main button
mousemovepointermoveFires very often: keep the handler cheap
mouseuppointerupAlso listen for pointercancel
mouseover / mouseoutpointerover / pointeroutBubble; the enter/leave versions do not
(none)pointercancelThe browser took over, for example to scroll

For simple taps, click is still the right event: it works for mouse, touch and keyboard. Use pointer events when you need the movement itself: dragging, drawing, sliders, swipe gestures.

Dragging with pointer capture

The classic dragging bug: you listen for pointermove on the slider, the user moves quickly, the pointer leaves the slider, and the thumb freezes. Pointer capture fixes it. After element.setPointerCapture(event.pointerId) in pointerdown, every event from that pointer is sent to the element until the pointer is released, wherever it is on screen. Capture is released automatically after pointerup or pointercancel, and the element receives lostpointercapture, which is a single, reliable place for clean-up.

On touch screens there is one more piece: CSS touch-action: none on the slider. Without it, the browser treats a horizontal finger movement as a possible scroll or zoom, fires pointercancel and your drag stops.

Try it: A draggable budget slider with pointer capture and a custom event

JavaScript

const MIN = 500, MAX = 5000, STEP = 100;
const slider = document.querySelector('#slider');
const debug = document.querySelector('#debug');
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', {
  style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0,
});
let value = 2500;

// ---- The component: knows about pointers and keys, not about products ----
function draw() {
  const pct = ((value - MIN) / (MAX - MIN)) * 100;
  slider.style.setProperty('--pct', `${pct}%`);
  slider.setAttribute('aria-valuenow', value);
  slider.setAttribute('aria-valuetext', inr.format(value));
}

function setValue(raw, source) {
  const next = Math.min(MAX, Math.max(MIN, Math.round(raw / STEP) * STEP));
  if (next === value) return;
  value = next;
  draw();
  // Announce the change; anyone can listen, the slider does not care who
  slider.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('budgetchange', {
    detail: { value, source },
    bubbles: true,
  }));
}

function valueFromX(clientX) {
  const rect = slider.getBoundingClientRect();
  const ratio = (clientX - rect.left) / rect.width;
  return MIN + ratio * (MAX - MIN);
}

slider.addEventListener('pointerdown', (event) => {
  if (event.button !== 0) return;               // primary button / touch only
  slider.setPointerCapture(event.pointerId);    // all moves now come to us
  slider.classList.add('dragging');
  setValue(valueFromX(event.clientX), event.pointerType);
  debug.textContent = `pointerdown · pointerType: ${event.pointerType}` +
    ` · pointerId: ${event.pointerId} · captured: yes`;
});

slider.addEventListener('pointermove', (event) => {
  if (!slider.hasPointerCapture(event.pointerId)) return; // just hovering
  setValue(valueFromX(event.clientX), event.pointerType);
});

// Fires after pointerup AND after pointercancel: one clean-up place
slider.addEventListener('lostpointercapture', () => {
  slider.classList.remove('dragging');
  debug.textContent += ' → released';
});

slider.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
  const steps = { ArrowRight: 1, ArrowUp: 1, ArrowLeft: -1, ArrowDown: -1,
    PageUp: 10, PageDown: -10 };
  if (event.key === 'Home') setValue(MIN, 'keyboard');
  else if (event.key === 'End') setValue(MAX, 'keyboard');
  else if (event.key in steps) setValue(value + steps[event.key] * STEP, 'keyboard');
  else return;
  event.preventDefault(); // arrows would scroll the page
});

// ---- The page: only listens for the custom event ----
const PRODUCTS = [
  ['Brew Mug', 399], ['Desk Mat', 899], ['Aurora Lamp', 1499],
  ['Trail Backpack', 1899], ['Pulse Headphones', 2999],
  ['Smart Speaker', 3499], ['Mech Keyboard', 4299], ['Studio Monitor', 4999],
];

function showProducts(max) {
  document.querySelector('#value').textContent = inr.format(max);
  const list = document.querySelector('#products');
  list.replaceChildren(...PRODUCTS.map(([name, price]) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.className = price <= max ? 'in' : 'out';
    li.textContent = `${name} · ${inr.format(price)}`;
    return li;
  }));
  const n = PRODUCTS.filter(([, price]) => price <= max).length;
  document.querySelector('#result').textContent = `${n} of ${PRODUCTS.length} products in budget`;
}

document.addEventListener('budgetchange', (event) => {
  showProducts(event.detail.value);
});

draw();
showProducts(value);

Drag the thumb, then drag past the edge of the page area: capture keeps it following. Click the slider and use the arrow keys, Home and End too.

This slider is also keyboard accessible: it has role="slider", tabindex="0", the aria-value* attributes and arrow, Page Up/Page Down, Home and End support. If a native <input type="range"> fits your design, prefer it; you get all of this for free. Build a custom one only when the design truly needs it.

Custom events

Look at the bottom half of the slider code. The product list never touches the slider, and the slider never touches the product list. The slider announces a budgetchange event with the new value in detail, and the page listens on document. That works because the event was created with bubbles: true.

OptionDefaultMeaning
detailnullAny data you want to send with the event
bubblesfalseTravel up through ancestors (needed for delegation)
cancelablefalseListeners may call preventDefault(); dispatchEvent then returns false
composedfalseCross a shadow DOM boundary (Web Components)

Custom events are not only for elements. Any class can extend EventTarget and get addEventListener and dispatchEvent for free, which gives you a tiny, standard publish/subscribe system. A cancelable "before" event is a neat way to let outside code veto an action.

Try it: Custom events on your own objects

JavaScript

class Cart extends EventTarget {
  #items = new Map();

  add(name, price) {
    // Ask first: listeners may cancel by calling preventDefault()
    const allowed = this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('beforeadd', {
      detail: { name, price },
      cancelable: true,
    }));
    if (!allowed) {
      console.warn(`blocked: ${name}`);
      return false;
    }
    this.#items.set(name, price);
    // Then announce what happened
    this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('change', {
      detail: { count: this.#items.size, total: this.total },
    }));
    return true;
  }

  get total() {
    return [...this.#items.values()].reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0);
  }
}

const cart = new Cart();

// A spending rule, written without touching the Cart class
cart.addEventListener('beforeadd', (event) => {
  if (event.detail.price > 50000) event.preventDefault();
});

// Two independent parts of the UI react to the same event
cart.addEventListener('change', (event) => {
  console.log('badge shows', event.detail.count, 'items');
});
cart.addEventListener('change', (event) => {
  console.log('total is', event.detail.total.toLocaleString('en-IN'));
});

cart.add('Pulse Headphones', 2999);
cart.add('Aurora Desk Lamp', 1499);
cart.add('Ralfiz Laptop Pro', 84999);
console.log('final:', cart.total);

A Cart extends EventTarget and announces changes. One listener vetoes expensive items with preventDefault. Try changing the limit.

Remember: dispatchEvent is synchronous. All listeners run before it returns, which is why add() can check the return value straight away. Name custom events in lowercase with no "on" prefix (budgetchange, cart:updated). A namespace with a colon, as in cart:updated, also guarantees the name can never clash with a future built-in event.

Example: Ralfiz Admin command palette

The lab builds an admin shell with a sidebar you can resize by dragging, and a command palette. The palette does not change the page itself. It dispatches a command event, and the app decides what each command does. You could later trigger the same commands from a menu or a keyboard shortcut without touching the palette.

// palette.js side: announce, do not act
function runCommand(cmd) {
  closePalette();
  palette.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('command', {
    detail: { id: cmd.id, label: cmd.label },
    bubbles: true,
  }));
}

// app side: one place that decides what commands mean
document.addEventListener('command', (event) => {
  const { id, label } = event.detail;
  if (id === 'theme') document.body.classList.toggle('dark');
  else if (id.startsWith('go:')) showPage(label);
  statusEl.textContent = `Last command: ${label}`;
});

// Resizable sidebar with pointer capture
handle.addEventListener('pointerdown', (event) => {
  handle.setPointerCapture(event.pointerId);
});
handle.addEventListener('pointermove', (event) => {
  if (!handle.hasPointerCapture(event.pointerId)) return;
  const width = Math.min(360, Math.max(160, event.clientX));
  document.body.style.setProperty('--sidebar', `${width}px`);
});

Common mistakes

  1. Using keyCode. Wrong: if (event.keyCode === 13). It is deprecated and unreadable. Fix: if (event.key === 'Enter').
  2. Forgetting Shift and Caps Lock. Wrong: event.key === 'k' fails when Caps Lock is on. Fix: event.key.toLowerCase() === 'k'.
  3. Shortcuts that fire while typing. Wrong: a global / handler that opens search even inside a textarea. Fix: ignore events whose target.closest('input, textarea, [contenteditable]') matches.
  4. Dragging without capture. Wrong: thumb.addEventListener('mousemove', drag) stops when the pointer leaves the thumb and never works with touch. Fix: pointer events plus setPointerCapture, and touch-action: none in CSS.
  5. Custom events that never arrive. Wrong: new CustomEvent('rate', { detail: 4 }) with a listener on the parent. Fix: add bubbles: true.
  6. Cleaning up only on pointerup. Wrong: removing the dragging style in pointerup only; a phone call or scroll gesture sends pointercancel instead. Fix: clean up in lostpointercapture.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "key vs code?" key is the produced value and follows the layout; code is the physical key. Give the Shift+1 and AZERTY examples.
  • "Why pointer events?" One code path for mouse, touch and pen, plus capture and pointercancel.
  • "How do components communicate without a framework?" Custom events with detail, bubbling to a shared ancestor, or an EventTarget subclass as a small event bus.
  • Accessibility: every drag interaction needs a keyboard alternative (WCAG 2.2 also asks for a single-pointer alternative to dragging). Arrow keys on a slider and move-up/move-down buttons on a sortable list are typical solutions.
  • Discoverability: show shortcuts in tooltips and menus (Ctrl K on the search button), and on a Mac, display ⌘ instead of Ctrl.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. The listener calls preventDefault() on both events. What is logged?

const target = new EventTarget();
target.addEventListener('save', (event) => event.preventDefault());

const a = target.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('save'));
const b = target.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('save', { cancelable: true }));

console.log(a, b);
  • A false false
  • B true true
  • C true false
  • D false true

Snippet 2. Which of these key presses count as the Save shortcut?

const isSave = (e) =>
  (e.ctrlKey || e.metaKey) && e.key.toLowerCase() === 's';

const presses = [
  new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 's', ctrlKey: true }),
  new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 'S', ctrlKey: true, shiftKey: true }),
  new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 's' }),
  new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 's', metaKey: true }),
];
console.log(presses.map(isSave));
  • A [ true, false, false, true ]
  • B [ true, true, false, false ]
  • C [ true, false, false, false ]
  • D [ true, true, false, true ]

Snippet 3. The list listens for rate. Two events are dispatched on the item. What is logged?

const list = document.createElement('ul');
const item = document.createElement('li');
list.append(item);

list.addEventListener('rate', (event) => {
  console.log('list heard', event.detail);
});

item.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('rate', { detail: 4 }));
item.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('rate', { detail: 5, bubbles: true }));
  • A list heard 5
  • B 
    list heard 4
list heard 5
  • C Nothing is logged
  • D list heard 4

Answers

  1. C. dispatchEvent returns false only if the event is cancelable and a listener called preventDefault. Events you create are not cancelable by default, so preventDefault is ignored on the first one.
  2. D. Shift turns key into "S", but toLowerCase() handles that, so Ctrl+Shift+S matches too. The plain "s" has no modifier. metaKey is Cmd on a Mac, which the check accepts.
  3. A. Events you create do not bubble unless you pass bubbles: true. The first event stays on the item; only the second travels up to the list.

terms.definition: The value the key produces with the current layout and modifiers, such as "a", "A", "!", "Enter" or "ArrowDown".
The physical key position, independent of layout, such as "KeyA", "Digit1" or "Space".
Ctrl, Shift, Alt and Meta (Cmd on a Mac, the Windows key on Windows), exposed as ctrlKey, shiftKey, altKey and metaKey.
One event family for mouse, touch and pen: pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup, pointercancel, with pointerType telling them apart.
element.setPointerCapture(pointerId) sends all further events of that pointer to the element until release, even if the pointer leaves it.
An event you create with new CustomEvent(type, { detail, bubbles, cancelable }) and send with dispatchEvent.
A CSS property that tells the browser which touch gestures it may handle itself; none lets your pointer code own the gesture.

lessons.examTip: For shortcuts, match letters with event.key (it follows the user’s keyboard layout) and games or physical positions with event.code. Accept both ctrlKey and metaKey so Mac users can press Cmd.

quiz.question: A user on a US keyboard presses Shift+1. What are event.key and event.code?
options: key "1", code "Digit1"
key "!", code "Digit1"
key "!", code "Exclamation"

quiz.explanation: key is the character produced (with Shift, "!"); code is the physical key, which is still Digit1. A separate keydown with key "Shift" fires for the Shift key itself.

quiz.question: Your draggable slider stops following the finger as soon as it slides off the thumb. What is the best fix?
options: Listen to mousemove on document instead
Make the thumb larger
Use setTimeout to poll the pointer position
Call setPointerCapture(event.pointerId) in pointerdown so every move comes to the slider
quiz.explanation: Pointer capture retargets all events for that pointer to the element until pointerup or pointercancel, whichever element the pointer is over. It works the same for mouse, touch and pen.

quiz.question: A rating component dispatches new CustomEvent("rate", { detail: 4 }) on a star. A listener on the parent list never runs. Why?
options: CustomEvent does not bubble unless you pass bubbles: true
detail must be an object
Custom event names must contain a hyphen
Custom events can only be heard on window
quiz.explanation: Events you create yourself default to bubbles: false. Pass bubbles: true when ancestors (or delegated listeners) should hear them.

quiz.question: Your Ctrl+K handler shows the palette, but in Chrome the address bar also gets focus. What is missing?
options: stopPropagation()
Listening on keyup instead of keydown
event.preventDefault() on the keydown
A passive: true option
quiz.explanation: Ctrl+K has a default browser action. preventDefault() on the keydown cancels it (when the page has focus). Some shortcuts, like Ctrl+W or Ctrl+T, cannot be overridden at all, so choose shortcuts carefully.

lessons.title: Forms and validation
lessons.summaryHtml:
Forms are how users give your app data: sign-ups, checkouts, bookings, enrolments. The browser already does a lot for you. Every control with a name becomes a key/value pair in FormData, and attributes such as required, type="email", pattern and min give you built-in constraint validation with no code at all.

You learn to handle submit (not button clicks), turn a form into an object with Object.fromEntries and getAll, read the validity state of each field, add your own rules with setCustomValidity, style errors with :user-invalid, and write error messages that screen readers announce, using aria-invalid and aria-describedby.

The mini project is a Ralfiz Academy enrolment form with live validation, a password checklist, an error summary, a real POST request and a success state.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A form is a group of controls (inputs, selects, textareas, checkboxes, radio buttons) that together describe one thing the user wants to send: a delivery address, a new account, a booking. Working with forms in JavaScript comes down to three jobs:

  • Collect the values, preferably with FormData instead of reading every input by hand.
  • Validate them: use the browser’s built-in rules first, then add your own.
  • Communicate clearly: show errors next to the right field, in a way that sighted users, keyboard users and screen-reader users all understand, and show a clear success state at the end.

Why it matters

Forms are where businesses make money. A checkout that rejects a valid PIN code, a sign-up that only complains after you press submit, or an error that says "Invalid input" without saying which input: each one loses customers. Front-end interviews often include "build a sign-up form with validation" for this reason. It tests events, DOM updates, accessibility and async code in one small task.

One rule before we start: client-side validation is for the user, not for security. Anyone can remove required in DevTools or call your API with curl. The server must validate every request again.

How it works

Handle submit, then read the form with FormData

Listen for submit on the <form>, not click on the button. Submit fires for a button click and for Enter in a text field, and it only fires after built-in validation passes. Call event.preventDefault() to stop the browser from navigating away, then build a FormData.

form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const fd = new FormData(form);          // every named, enabled control
  const data = Object.fromEntries(fd);    // { fullName: 'Asha', city: 'Kochi', ... }
  data.extras = fd.getAll('extras');      // repeated names need getAll
  console.log(data, event.submitter);     // submitter = the button that was pressed
});

What ends up in FormData follows the same rules as a classic form post:

ControlWhat FormData contains
Text, email, tel, number, textareaThe value as a string (numbers too, so convert with Number())
SelectThe selected option’s value (or its text if it has no value)
Radio groupThe checked radio’s value, or nothing if none is checked
CheckboxIts value ('on' by default) only if checked; one entry per ticked box
File inputA File object, so FormData can upload files as multipart/form-data
Disabled or unnamed controlsNothing at all

The live page below is a checkout step. One input listener on the form keeps a preview up to date, because input bubbles and fires for every kind of control.

Try it: Delivery details: from a form to an object

HTML

<main class="page">
  <form id="checkout" class="card">

    <h2>Delivery details</h2>
    <div class="row">
      <label>Full name<input name="fullName" value="Asha Menon" autocomplete="name"></label>
      <label>Phone<input name="phone" type="tel" value="9876543210" inputmode="numeric"></label>
    </div>
    <label>City
      <select name="city">
        <option>Kochi</option><option selected>Bengaluru</option>
        <option>Chennai</option><option>Mumbai</option>
      </select>
    </label>
    <fieldset>

        <label><input type="radio" name="slot" value="morning" checked><span>🌅 9am–12pm</span></label>

CSS

JavaScript

const form = document.querySelector('#checkout');
const out = document.querySelector('#out');
const count = document.querySelector('#count');

function readForm() {
  const fd = new FormData(form);
  const data = Object.fromEntries(fd); // one value per name
  data.extras = fd.getAll('extras');   // checkboxes can repeat a name
  return data;
}

function preview() {
  const data = readForm();
  out.textContent = JSON.stringify(data, null, 2);
  count.textContent = `${Object.keys(data).length} fields`;
}

// input bubbles and fires for every control (text, select, radio, checkbox),
// so one listener on the form keeps the preview in sync
form.addEventListener('input', preview);

// Listen for submit, not for button clicks: Enter in a field submits too
form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault(); // stay on this page, we handle the data
  console.log('Submitting', readForm());
  document.querySelector('#done').hidden = false;
  event.submitter.textContent = 'Saved ✓';
});

preview();

Change any field and watch the object update. Tick both extras: FormData keeps both, and getAll returns them. Then press Continue to payment.

FormData is also a standalone tool. You can create an empty one, append values and send it straight to fetch as the body (the browser sets the multipart Content-Type for you). If an API wants JSON, convert it first. For a search URL, new URLSearchParams(formData) gives you a query string.

Try it: FormData up close

JavaScript

// FormData does not need a <form>: handy for building requests
const fd = new FormData();
fd.append('name', 'Asha Menon');
fd.append('course', 'dom');
fd.append('topics', 'events');
fd.append('topics', 'forms'); // same name twice, like two ticked checkboxes

console.log('entries:', [...fd]);
console.log('get:', fd.get('topics'), '| getAll:', fd.getAll('topics'));

// Object.fromEntries keeps only the LAST value for a repeated name
console.log('fromEntries:', Object.fromEntries(fd));

// A safe conversion that keeps repeated names as arrays
function formToObject(formData) {
  const out = {};
  for (const key of new Set(formData.keys())) {
    const all = formData.getAll(key);
    out[key] = all.length > 1 ? all : all[0];
  }
  return out;
}
console.log('as JSON:', JSON.stringify(formToObject(fd)));

// For a GET search URL, URLSearchParams accepts FormData directly
console.log('query:', new URLSearchParams(fd).toString());

// set() replaces every value for a name, delete() removes them, has() checks
fd.set('course', 'js');
fd.delete('topics');
console.log('after set/delete:', Object.fromEntries(fd), fd.has('topics'));

FormData works without any form element. Notice what Object.fromEntries does to the repeated topics key, and how URLSearchParams turns it into a query string.

Careful: Object.fromEntries silently keeps only the last value of a repeated name. For checkbox groups and multi-selects, always use getAll.

Built-in constraint validation

Before you write any validation code, describe the rules in HTML. The browser checks them, blocks the submit, shows a localised message and exposes the result to JavaScript.

AttributeRulevalidity flag
requiredMust not be empty (for radios, one in the group must be checked)valueMissing
type="email", type="url"Must look like an email or URLtypeMismatch
patternMust match the regex, anchored to the whole valuepatternMismatch
minlength, maxlengthLength limits, checked only after the user edits the valuetooShort, tooLong
min, max, stepNumber and date rangesrangeUnderflow, rangeOverflow, stepMismatch
setCustomValidity(msg)Your own rulecustomError

Every field has a validity object (a ValidityState) with those booleans plus valid, and a validationMessage string. The form and each field have two methods: checkValidity() returns true or false and fires an invalid event on each bad field, and reportValidity() does the same and also shows the browser’s bubble.

const form = document.querySelector('#addr');
const FLAGS = [
  'valueMissing', 'typeMismatch', 'patternMismatch', 'tooShort',
  'rangeUnderflow', 'rangeOverflow', 'stepMismatch', 'badInput',
  'customError', 'valid',
];

function inspect(field) {
  document.querySelector('#which').textContent = field.name;
  const items = FLAGS.map((flag) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = flag;
    li.classList.toggle('on', field.validity[flag]);
    li.classList.toggle('total', flag === 'valid');
    return li;
  });
  document.querySelector('#flags').replaceChildren(...items);
  document.querySelector('#msg').textContent =
    field.validationMessage || 'validationMessage is empty: the field is valid.';
}

form.addEventListener('focusin', (e) => e.target.matches('input') && inspect(e.target));
form.addEventListener('input', (e) => inspect(e.target));

// invalid does not bubble, so listen in the capture phase to hear every field
form.addEventListener('invalid', (e) => {
  console.warn(`invalid: ${e.target.name}: ${e.target.validationMessage}`);
}, true);

// submit only fires once every field is valid (no novalidate on this form)
form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  console.log('All valid, sending', Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form)));
});

inspect(form.elements.email);

Click into each field and type: the panel shows its validity flags. Try "asha@", PIN 012345 and quantity 12, then press Place order to see the browser’s own bubbles.

Three details from that demo matter in real work. First, the invalid event does not bubble, so the demo listens in the capture phase. Second, the email check is loose on purpose: asha@ralfiz passes because intranet addresses exist. Third, pattern="[1-9][0-9]{5}" behaves as if wrapped in ^(?:…)$, so you never write the anchors. Current browsers compile it with the v regex flag, which is stricter, so escape a literal - inside a character class as \-.

Your own rules with setCustomValidity

Some rules can’t be written as attributes: "confirm password must match", "at least one number", "delivery date is not a Sunday". Put them into the same system with setCustomValidity. A non-empty message makes the field invalid (so :invalid, checkValidity and the submit block all respect it). An empty string makes it valid again.

function checkPasswords() {
  const { password, confirm } = form.elements;
  confirm.setCustomValidity(
    confirm.value && confirm.value !== password.value
      ? 'Passwords do not match.'
      : ''                       // must clear it, or it stays invalid forever
  );
}
form.addEventListener('input', checkPasswords);

Styling errors: :invalid vs :user-invalid

:invalid matches an empty required field the moment the page loads, so a form styled with it starts out covered in red. :user-invalid (and :user-valid) only match after the user has changed the field and moved on, or tried to submit. It is supported in all current major browsers since late 2023; check the MDN compatibility table if you support older ones. When you take over error display yourself, style [aria-invalid="true"] instead, because then your code decides when a field counts as touched.

Accessible error messages

The browser’s bubbles disappear after a few seconds, can’t be styled and show one error at a time. Most product teams add novalidate to the form, which keeps the whole validity API but turns off the bubbles and the submit block, and then render their own messages. When you do, follow these rules:

  • Each input has a real <label for>. Placeholders are not labels.
  • The error text lives in an element next to the field, and the input points to it with aria-describedby, so a screen reader reads "Email, invalid entry, Enter an email like asha@example.com".
  • Set aria-invalid="true" on invalid fields and remove it (or set "false") when they are fixed.
  • On submit, move focus to the first invalid field and show a short summary in a role="alert" region.
  • Don’t rely on colour alone: the message text and an icon carry the meaning too.

The sign-up below puts it all together: built-in attributes for the simple rules, setCustomValidity for the password rules, validation when a field loses focus (focusout, which bubbles), live re-validation for touched fields, a loading state, a real POST and a success state that receives focus.

JavaScript

const form = document.querySelector('#signup');
const inputs = form.querySelectorAll('input');
const summary = document.querySelector('#summary');
const submitBtn = document.querySelector('#submit');
const success = document.querySelector('#success');

// Our own rules, on top of the HTML attributes
function customChecks() {
  const { password, confirm } = form.elements;
  const pw = password.value;
  const rules = { len: pw.length >= 8, letter: /[a-z]/i.test(pw), digit: /\d/.test(pw) };
  for (const li of form.querySelectorAll('[data-rule]')) {
    li.classList.toggle('ok', rules[li.dataset.rule]);
  }
  password.setCustomValidity(
    pw && !(rules.letter && rules.digit) ? 'Add at least one letter and one number.' : '');
  confirm.setCustomValidity(
    confirm.value && confirm.value !== pw ? 'Passwords do not match.' : '');
}

function messageFor(field) {
  const v = field.validity;
  if (v.valid) return '';
  if (v.valueMissing) {
    return field.type === 'checkbox' ? 'Please accept the terms to continue.'
      : `${field.labels[0].textContent} is required.`;
  }
  if (v.typeMismatch) return 'Enter an email like asha@example.com.';
  if (v.tooShort) return `Use at least ${field.minLength} characters.`;
  return field.validationMessage; // our custom messages
}

function show(field) {
  const msg = messageFor(field);
  field.setAttribute('aria-invalid', String(msg !== ''));
  document.getElementById(`${field.id}-err`).textContent = msg;
  return msg === '';
}

// Validate when the user leaves a field (focusout bubbles, blur does not)
form.addEventListener('focusout', (e) => {
  if (!e.target.matches('input')) return;
  e.target.dataset.touched = '';
  customChecks();
  show(e.target);
});
// ...then live on every keystroke, but only for fields already touched
form.addEventListener('input', () => {
  customChecks();
  for (const f of inputs) if ('touched' in f.dataset) show(f);
});

form.addEventListener('submit', async (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  customChecks();
  const bad = [...inputs].filter((f) => !show(f));
  inputs.forEach((f) => { f.dataset.touched = ''; });
  if (bad.length) {
    summary.hidden = false;
    summary.textContent = `Please fix ${bad.length} field${bad.length > 1 ? 's' : ''} below.`;
    bad[0].focus();
    return;
  }
  summary.hidden = true;
  const { name, email } = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));
  submitBtn.disabled = true;
  submitBtn.textContent = 'Creating account…';
  try {
    // Demo API: send only name and email, never a real password to a test server
    const res = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ name, email }),
    });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    const user = await res.json();
    console.log('Created', user);
    document.querySelector('#welcome').textContent = `Welcome, ${name.split(' ')[0]}!`;
    document.querySelector('#detail').textContent =
      `Account #${user.id} is ready. We sent a confirmation link to ${email}.`;
    form.hidden = true;
    success.hidden = false;
    success.focus(); // move focus so screen readers announce the new state
  } catch (err) {
    summary.hidden = false;
    summary.textContent = `Could not create your account (${err.message}). Try again.`;
  } finally {
    submitBtn.disabled = false;
    submitBtn.textContent = 'Create account';
  }
});

document.querySelector('#again').addEventListener('click', () => {
  form.reset();
  for (const f of inputs) {
    delete f.dataset.touched;
    f.removeAttribute('aria-invalid');
    document.getElementById(`${f.id}-err`).textContent = '';
  }
  customChecks();
  success.hidden = true;
  form.hidden = false;
  form.elements.name.focus();
});

Press Create account on the empty form first. Then fill it in: errors clear as you fix them, and the password checklist ticks live. A valid form is POSTed and swaps to a success card.

Example: Ralfiz Academy enrolment form

The lab form enrols a student: name, email, Indian mobile number, course, batch, password, confirm password and terms. The core is two small functions. messageFor turns a ValidityState into friendly words, and showError writes them next to the field.

function messageFor(field) {
  const v = field.validity;
  if (v.valid) return '';
  if (v.valueMissing) return REQUIRED[field.name];
  if (v.typeMismatch) return 'Enter an email address like asha@example.com.';
  if (v.patternMismatch) return 'Enter a 10-digit mobile number starting with 6-9.';
  if (v.tooShort) return `Use at least ${field.minLength} characters.`;
  return field.validationMessage;   // our setCustomValidity messages
}

function showError(field) {
  const message = messageFor(field);
  field.setAttribute('aria-invalid', String(message !== ''));
  document.getElementById(`${field.name}-error`).textContent = message;
  return message === '';
}

On submit, the handler validates every control, counts invalid names (two radios in one group are one problem), focuses the first bad field, and only then sends the data. It deletes the password fields from the object before logging it, disables the button while the request runs, and handles !res.ok and network errors with a message instead of silence.

Common mistakes

  1. Listening for the button click. Wrong: button.addEventListener('click', save) misses Enter and skips validation. Fix: form.addEventListener('submit', save) with preventDefault().
  2. Forgetting name attributes. Wrong: <input id="email"> never appears in FormData. Fix: <input id="email" name="email">.
  3. Losing checkbox values. Wrong: Object.fromEntries(fd).topics for a group. Fix: fd.getAll('topics').
  4. A custom error that never clears. Wrong: calling setCustomValidity('Passwords do not match') once on submit. Fix: re-check on every input and pass '' when the rule passes.
  5. Shouting at the user while they type. Wrong: validating on the very first keystroke of an email address. Fix: validate on focusout, then live only for touched fields.
  6. Using disabled for "read only". Wrong: a disabled price field that you expect to be sent. Fix: readonly, which is submitted but not editable.
  7. Trusting the client. Wrong: skipping server checks because the form has required. Fix: validate again on the server, always.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "How would you validate a form?" HTML attributes first, setCustomValidity for custom rules, novalidate plus your own accessible messages for a polished UI, and server validation as the real gate.
  • Double submits: disable the submit button (or ignore submits) while a request is in flight, and re-enable it in finally.
  • Autofill: correct autocomplete values (name, email, tel, new-password) and inputmode="numeric" make forms much faster on phones and let password managers help.
  • Libraries: React projects often use React Hook Form with a schema library such as Zod. Underneath, the same ideas apply: touched state, error messages and one schema shared with the server.
  • Security: never put user input back into innerHTML in a success message; use textContent, as every example here does.

Answers

  1. B. An empty required field is valueMissing, and "asha" has no @. The browser’s email check does not require a dot in the domain, so asha@ralfiz passes. Add a pattern (or check on the server) if you need a dot.
  2. D. Changing the value does not clear a custom error: it stays until you call setCustomValidity with an empty string. That is why custom checks must run again on every input.
  3. A. Unchecked checkboxes and disabled controls are not submitted, so news and city are missing. FormData holds both topic entries, but Object.fromEntries keeps the last one. Use getAll('topic') for the list, and readonly instead of disabled if a value must be sent.

terms.definition: An object holding the name/value pairs of a form, built with new FormData(form). It supports get, getAll, set, append, delete and has, and can be sent directly as a fetch body.
The browser’s built-in checking driven by attributes such as required, type, pattern, min, max, step, minlength and maxlength.
The object in field.validity. It has one boolean per kind of problem (valueMissing, typeMismatch, patternMismatch, tooShort, rangeUnderflow, customError…) plus valid.
Gives a field your own error message and makes it invalid. It stays invalid until you call setCustomValidity('').
Both return true or false and fire invalid events. reportValidity also shows the browser’s error bubble on the first invalid field.
A CSS pseudo-class that matches an invalid field only after the user has interacted with it or tried to submit, so empty forms do not start out red.
A form attribute that turns off the browser’s error bubbles and submit blocking, so your own JavaScript and messages take over. The validity API still works.

lessons.examTip: Validate a field when the user leaves it, re-validate it on every keystroke once it has been touched, and validate everything on submit. Users are not shouted at while typing, and errors disappear the moment they are fixed.

quiz.question: What is the practical difference between :invalid and :user-invalid?
options: :user-invalid only works on inputs inside a form with novalidate
There is none; :user-invalid is just the newer name
An empty required field matches :invalid as soon as the page loads, but :user-invalid only after the user interacts with it or tries to submit
Only :user-invalid can be changed with setCustomValidity
quiz.explanation: :invalid matches from the start, so a styled sign-up form begins covered in red. :user-invalid waits for user interaction, which is almost always what you want for error styles.

quiz.question: Your sign-up form checks every field in JavaScript before sending. Why must the server validate the same data again?
options: Anyone can bypass client-side checks by editing the page in DevTools or calling the API directly
Browsers skip validation on slow connections
FormData changes values while sending
Client-side validation only runs in Chrome
quiz.explanation: Client-side validation is for the user’s convenience and speed. It is not security: the server must treat every request as untrusted and validate it again.

quiz.question: A form has two checkboxes named topics, and both are ticked. What does Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form)).topics give you?
options: An array of both values
The first ticked value
undefined, because checkboxes are skipped
Only the last ticked value, so use formData.getAll('topics') for the full list
quiz.explanation: Object.fromEntries keeps one value per key, and later entries overwrite earlier ones. FormData itself keeps both entries, and getAll returns them as an array.

quiz.question: You call confirm.setCustomValidity('Passwords do not match'). The user then types the matching password, but the form still refuses to submit. Why?
options: The confirm field needs a pattern attribute
A custom error stays until you clear it with setCustomValidity(''), so you must re-check on every input
setCustomValidity only works with novalidate
The password field must be re-rendered
quiz.explanation: The browser cannot know when your rule is satisfied again. Run your custom checks on input and pass an empty string when the value is valid.

lessons.title: Building UI components
lessons.summaryHtml:
Real products are built from a small set of UI components: modal dialogs, tabs, accordions, dropdown menus and toast notifications. Each one has a visual design, but also a behaviour contract: which keys it answers to, where focus goes, what it announces to screen readers and how it closes.

Modern HTML does much of this for you. <dialog> with showModal() gives you a real modal with a backdrop, focus handling and Esc to close. <details>/<summary> is a working accordion with no JavaScript. For tabs, menus and toasts you add ARIA roles and a few keyboard handlers.

In this lesson you build all five as live pages and learn a reusable pattern: find the root element, keep the state in attributes such as aria-selected and aria-expanded, and use one delegated listener per component.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A UI component is a piece of interface that behaves the same way every time you use it: a pop-up that asks “Are you sure?”, a row of tabs on a product page, a list of FAQ questions that open and close, an account menu under your avatar, a little message in the corner that says “Saved”. Users have seen thousands of these. They already know that Esc closes a pop-up and that arrow keys move between tabs. Your job is to meet those expectations.

So a component is two things. The look comes from HTML and CSS. The behaviour contract covers what happens on click, which keys work, where keyboard focus goes, what a screen reader announces and how the thing closes. Beginners build the look and forget the contract. Professionals start from the contract.

Why it matters

Every client project uses these five components. An admin dashboard has a “Delete customer?” dialog. A shop has product tabs and a cart toast. A course site has an FAQ accordion. If the dialog does not close with Esc, or a keyboard user gets stuck behind it, that is a bug report, and in many countries it is also an accessibility compliance problem.

The good news: the browser now ships most of the hard parts. <dialog> and <details> replace hundreds of lines of old jQuery plugins. Knowing what the platform gives you for free, and what you must add yourself, is exactly what interviewers probe when they ask you to “build a modal”.

How it works

All five components follow one recipe:

  1. Semantic HTML first: a real <button>, a real <dialog>, a real <details>.
  2. State lives in attributes: aria-selected, aria-expanded, hidden, open. CSS styles those attributes, so the look can never disagree with the state.
  3. One delegated listener per component, using closest() as you learned in lesson 2.2.
  4. Focus management: decide where focus goes when the component opens and where it returns when it closes.

Modal dialogs with <dialog>

A modal blocks the rest of the page until the user answers. Before <dialog>, you had to build a backdrop, trap focus with key listeners, hide the page from screen readers and restore focus by hand. Now dialog.showModal() does it in one call:

  • the dialog goes into the top layer, above every z-index, so no stacking bugs;
  • the ::backdrop pseudo-element appears and you can style it;
  • the rest of the page becomes inert: it cannot be clicked or focused, and screen readers ignore it;
  • focus moves into the dialog, and Esc fires a cancel event and then closes it;
  • when it closes, browsers return focus to the element that was focused before it opened.

A <form method="dialog"> inside the dialog closes it on submit instead of sending a request. The value of the button that submitted becomes dialog.returnValue, so you know which choice the user made. Built-in validation still runs first: a required field that is empty keeps the dialog open.

openBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
  dialog.returnValue = '';   // forget the last answer
  dialog.showModal();
});

dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
  if (dialog.returnValue === 'delete') deleteProject();
  openBtn.focus();           // explicit, in case the opener changed
});

// Clicking the backdrop: the target is the dialog element itself
dialog.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  if (e.target === dialog) dialog.close('cancel');
});

The backdrop trick works only when the dialog has no padding of its own and a child (the form) fills it. Then any click inside the box lands on a child, and only clicks on the backdrop report the dialog as the target. The live page below is a “type the project name to delete” confirmation, the pattern cloud dashboards use for destructive actions.

Try it: Confirm delete with <dialog>

HTML

<main class="page">
  <section class="card">
    <header class="head">
      <div class="logo" aria-hidden="true">R</div>
      <div>
        <h1>Project settings</h1>
        <p class="muted">ralfiz-store-prod · Mumbai region · 3 deployments</p>
      </div>
    </header>
    <div class="row">
      <div>
        <h2>Delete this project</h2>
        <p class="muted">Removes the database, uploaded files and every deployment. This cannot be undone.</p>
      </div>
      <button class="btn danger" id="open-delete" type="button">Delete project</button>
    </div>
    <p class="status" id="status" role="status"></p>
  </section>
</main>

<dialog id="confirm" aria-labelledby="confirm-title" aria-describedby="confirm-desc">
  <form method="dialog">
    <div class="badge" aria-hidden="true">!</div>
    <h2 id="confirm-title">Delete ralfiz-store-prod?</h2>
    <p class="muted" id="confirm-desc">Type <strong>ralfiz-store-prod</strong> to confirm.</p>
    <input id="confirm-name" autocomplete="off" aria-label="Project name" placeholder="ralfiz-store-prod">
    <div class="actions">
      <button class="btn ghost" value="cancel">Cancel</button>
      <button class="btn danger" value="delete" id="confirm-btn" disabled>Delete forever</button>
    </div>
  </form>
</dialog>

CSS

:root { --ink: #0f172a; --muted: #64748b; --line: #e2e8f0; --ac: #4f46e5; --red: #dc2626; }
body { margin: 0; background: #f1f5f9; color: var(--ink); }
body:has(dialog[open]) { overflow: hidden; }
.page { padding: 24px 16px; }
.card { max-width: 560px; margin: 0 auto; background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line);
  border-radius: 16px; box-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgb(15 23 42 / .06); }
.head { display: flex; gap: 12px; align-items: center; padding: 16px;
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--line); }
.logo { width: 40px; height: 40px; border-radius: 12px; display: grid; place-items: center;
  background: linear-gradient(135deg, #6366f1, #8b5cf6); color: #fff; font-weight: 700; }
h1 { font-size: 17px; margin: 0; }
h2 { font-size: 15px; margin: 0 0 4px; }
.muted { color: var(--muted); margin: 0; font-size: 13px; }
.row { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 16px; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between;
  padding: 16px; margin: 16px; border: 1px solid #fecaca; background: #fef2f2; border-radius: 12px; }
.row > div { flex: 1 1 240px; }
.status { margin: 0 16px 16px; min-height: 1.5em; font-size: 13px; color: var(--muted); }
.btn { font: inherit; font-weight: 600; font-size: 14px; border-radius: 10px; padding: 8px 14px;
  border: 1px solid transparent; cursor: pointer; }
.btn.danger { background: var(--red); color: #fff; }
.btn.danger:hover { background: #b91c1c; }
.btn.danger:disabled { opacity: .45; cursor: not-allowed; }
.btn.ghost { background: #fff; border-color: var(--line); color: var(--ink); }
.btn:focus-visible, input:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid rgb(79 70 229 / .35); outline-offset: 2px; }
dialog { border: 0; padding: 0; border-radius: 16px; width: min(400px, calc(100% - 32px));
  box-shadow: 0 24px 48px -12px rgb(15 23 42 / .35); color: var(--ink); }
dialog[open] { animation: pop .18s ease-out; }
dialog::backdrop { background: rgb(15 23 42 / .45); backdrop-filter: blur(2px); }
dialog form { padding: 24px; }
.badge { width: 40px; height: 40px; border-radius: 50%; display: grid; place-items: center;
  background: #fee2e2; color: var(--red); font-weight: 800; margin-bottom: 12px; }
dialog input { width: 100%; box-sizing: border-box; margin: 12px 0 16px; padding: 10px 12px;
  font: inherit; border: 1px solid #cbd5e1; border-radius: 10px; }
.actions { display: flex; justify-content: flex-end; gap: 8px; }
@keyframes pop { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(8px) scale(.98); } }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { dialog[open] { animation: none; } }

JavaScript

const dialog = document.querySelector('#confirm');
const openBtn = document.querySelector('#open-delete');
const input = document.querySelector('#confirm-name');
const confirmBtn = document.querySelector('#confirm-btn');
const status = document.querySelector('#status');
const PROJECT = 'ralfiz-store-prod';

openBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
  input.value = '';
  confirmBtn.disabled = true;
  dialog.returnValue = '';
  dialog.showModal(); // top layer + backdrop + inert page + focus moves in
});

input.addEventListener('input', () => {
  confirmBtn.disabled = input.value.trim() !== PROJECT;
});

// A click on the backdrop has the <dialog> itself as its target,
// because the form fills the dialog and has no gaps around it.
dialog.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  if (event.target === dialog) dialog.close('cancel');
});

// Esc fires "cancel" first: you may preventDefault() it for unsaved work.
dialog.addEventListener('cancel', () => console.log('Esc pressed'));

dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
  const choice = dialog.returnValue || 'dismissed';
  console.log('dialog closed, returnValue =', choice);
  status.textContent = choice === 'delete'
    ? 'Project scheduled for deletion. You have 7 days to restore it.'
    : 'Nothing was deleted.';
  openBtn.focus(); // make the focus return explicit
});

console.log('Click "Delete project", then try Esc, the backdrop and Tab.');

Click Delete project, then close it three ways: Cancel, Esc and a click on the backdrop. Watch returnValue in the console and where focus lands.

APIBackdrop and inert pageEsc closesUse for
dialog.showModal()YesYesConfirmations, forms that must be answered
dialog.show()NoNoNon-blocking panels, such as a chat window
popover attributeNo (light dismiss)YesMenus, tooltips, pickers that close on outside click

Two finishing touches: body:has(dialog[open]) { overflow: hidden; } stops the page scrolling behind the modal, and a short CSS animation on dialog[open] makes it feel polished. Newer HTML adds a closedby attribute for backdrop-click closing and command/commandfor buttons that open dialogs with no JavaScript; check MDN’s compatibility table before relying on them.

Tabs with ARIA roles and arrow keys

Tabs have no native HTML element, so you describe them with ARIA. The container gets role="tablist", each button role="tab" with aria-selected and aria-controls, and each panel role="tabpanel" with aria-labelledby. A screen reader then says “Specs, tab, 2 of 3, selected”.

The keyboard pattern is called a roving tabindex. Only the selected tab has tabindex="0"; the others have -1. So Tab enters the tab list once and the next Tab goes into the panel, instead of walking through every tab. Inside the list, ← and → move (wrapping at the ends) and Home/End jump. This is “automatic activation”: moving focus also shows the panel. If panels are slow to load, use manual activation, where arrows only move focus and Enter selects.

<div role="tablist" aria-label="Product details">
  <button role="tab" id="tab-specs" aria-controls="panel-specs"
          aria-selected="false" tabindex="-1">Specs</button>
</div>
<section role="tabpanel" id="panel-specs"
         aria-labelledby="tab-specs" tabindex="0" hidden>…</section>

The whole behaviour is one function, selectTab(tab), that loops over all tabs and sets three things per tab. Click and keyboard handlers both call it, so they can never get out of step. Try the keys on the product page below.

Try it: Accessible product tabs

HTML

<main class="product">

  text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--ac); }

[role="tab"]:hover { color: var(--ink); background: #f1f5f9; }
[role="tab"][aria-selected="true"] { color: var(--ac); box-shadow: inset 0 -2px 0 var(--ac); }
[role="tab"]:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid rgb(79 70 229 / .35); outline-offset: -3px; }

[role="tabpanel"] { background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line); border-top: 0;
  border-radius: 0 0 12px 12px; padding: 16px; font-size: 14px; }
[role="tabpanel"]:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid rgb(79 70 229 / .25); }
[role="tabpanel"] p { margin: 0 0 12px; }

.chips li { font-size: 12px; padding: 4px 10px; border-radius: 99px; border: 1px solid var(--line); }

JavaScript

const tablist = document.querySelector('[role="tablist"]');
const tabs = [...tablist.querySelectorAll('[role="tab"]')];

function selectTab(tab, { focus = false } = {}) {
  for (const t of tabs) {
    const selected = t === tab;
    t.setAttribute('aria-selected', String(selected));
    t.tabIndex = selected ? 0 : -1; // roving tabindex: one tab stop
    document.getElementById(t.getAttribute('aria-controls')).hidden = !selected;
  }
  if (focus) tab.focus();
  console.log('selected:', tab.id);
}

tablist.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const tab = event.target.closest('[role="tab"]');
  if (tab) selectTab(tab);
});

tablist.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
  const i = tabs.indexOf(document.activeElement);
  const last = tabs.length - 1;
  const moves = {
    ArrowRight: i === last ? 0 : i + 1,
    ArrowLeft: i === 0 ? last : i - 1,
    Home: 0,
    End: last,
  };
  if (!(event.key in moves)) return;
  event.preventDefault(); // stop Home/End scrolling the page
  selectTab(tabs[moves[event.key]], { focus: true });
});

console.log('Click a tab, then use ← → Home End. Tab moves into the panel.');

Click a tab, then use the arrow keys, Home and End. Only one tab is a Tab stop, and the underline is styled from aria-selected.

Remember: style the state, not a class. [aria-selected="true"] { … } means the underline can only appear when assistive technology also hears “selected”.

Accordions: details/summary vs custom

<details> and <summary> are a complete disclosure widget: clickable, keyboard accessible, announced as expanded or collapsed, and searchable with the browser’s find-in-page (Chromium browsers, and recent versions of others, even open the matching section; check MDN compatibility). Give several <details> the same name attribute and they become an exclusive accordion: opening one closes the others. That attribute is supported in all current major browsers, but check caniuse.com if you support older ones. The toggle event tells you when one opens.

A custom accordion is a <button aria-expanded> inside a heading, controlling a region. You choose it when you need a smooth height animation, analytics, or a design <summary> cannot express. The live page shows both. The custom one animates with a modern trick: the panel is a grid whose row goes from 0fr to 1fr, and visibility: hidden on the closed panel removes its links from the tab order.

Try it: Native vs custom accordion

    </details>

    <h2><button class="acc-btn" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="p3" id="b3">Do you offer company billing?</button></h2>

CSS

:root { --ink: #0f172a; --muted: #64748b; --line: #e2e8f0; --ac: #4f46e5; }
body { margin: 0; background: #f8fafc; color: var(--ink); }
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(260px, 1fr)); gap: 16px;
  padding: 16px; align-items: start; }
.card { background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line); border-radius: 16px; padding: 16px;
  box-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgb(15 23 42 / .05); }
.tag { margin: 0; font-size: 11px; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: .06em; text-transform: uppercase;
  color: var(--ac); }

summary, .acc-btn { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; gap: 12px;
  width: 100%; padding: 12px 0; font: inherit; font-weight: 600; font-size: 14px; color: inherit;
  background: none; border: 0; cursor: pointer; text-align: left; list-style: none; }
summary::-webkit-details-marker { display: none; }
summary::after, .acc-btn::after { content: '+'; flex: none; width: 24px; height: 24px;
  border-radius: 50%; display: grid; place-items: center; background: #f1f5f9; color: var(--muted);
  transition: transform .2s; }
details[open] > summary::after, .acc-btn[aria-expanded="true"]::after { transform: rotate(45deg);
  background: #eef2ff; color: var(--ac); }

  outline-offset: 2px; border-radius: 6px; }

JavaScript

// Native: the browser handles open/close, keyboard and semantics.
// name="faq" makes the group exclusive: opening one closes the others.
for (const d of document.querySelectorAll('details')) {
  d.addEventListener('toggle', () => {
    const q = d.querySelector('summary').textContent;
    if (d.open) console.log('native opened:', q);
  });
}

// Custom: you own the state (aria-expanded) and the behaviour.
const custom = document.querySelector('#custom');
custom.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const btn = event.target.closest('.acc-btn');
  if (!btn) return;
  const willOpen = btn.getAttribute('aria-expanded') !== 'true';
  // Exclusive mode: close every other section first
  for (const other of custom.querySelectorAll('.acc-btn')) {
    other.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
  }
  btn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(willOpen));
  console.log('custom', willOpen ? 'opened:' : 'closed:', btn.textContent);
});

The left card needs no JavaScript for opening; name="faq" makes it exclusive. The right card owns its state in aria-expanded and animates with grid rows.

JavaScript neededNoneA click handler
AccessibilityBuilt inYou add aria-expanded, aria-controls
Find-in-page opens itYes in Chromium; check MDN for other browsersNo (hidden="until-found" can help; newer, check support)
AnimationHarderFull control

Dropdown menus and the Popover API

An account menu is a button with aria-haspopup="menu" and aria-expanded, controlling a list with role="menu" and items with role="menuitem". The contract: Enter or ↓ opens it and focuses the first item, ↑ opens on the last, arrows move, Esc closes and returns focus to the button, Tab closes and moves on, and a click outside closes it. For a plain list of navigation links, skip the menu roles and use a simple disclosure (a button plus a list of links) instead: menu roles promise arrow-key behaviour, and a broken promise is worse than none.

The Popover API handles the “show on top, close on outside click or Esc” part with attributes alone, and has been Baseline since 2024:

<button popovertarget="share">Share</button>
<div id="share" popover>…</div>   <!-- light dismiss, top layer -->

It does not add menu roles or arrow keys, so for a true menu you still write the key handling. The live page combines a full keyboard menu with toasts: each menu item triggers a notification.

JavaScript

// ---------- toast(): one small, reusable function ----------
const region = document.querySelector('#toasts');
const reduced = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;

function toast(message, { type = 'success', duration = 4000 } = {}) {
  const el = document.createElement('div');
  el.className = `toast ${type}`;
  const dot = document.createElement('span');
  dot.className = 'dot';
  const text = document.createElement('p');
  text.textContent = message; // never innerHTML for messages
  const close = document.createElement('button');
  close.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Dismiss');
  close.textContent = '✕';
  el.append(dot, text, close);
  region.append(el);
  el.animate([{ opacity: 0, transform: 'translateY(8px)' }, { opacity: 1 }],
    { duration: reduced ? 0 : 180, easing: 'ease-out' });

  let timer, started, remaining = duration;
  const start = () => { started = Date.now(); timer = setTimeout(dismiss, remaining); };
  const pause = () => { clearTimeout(timer); remaining -= Date.now() - started; };
  function dismiss() {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    el.animate([{ opacity: 1 }, { opacity: 0 }], { duration: reduced ? 0 : 150 })
      .finished.then(() => el.remove());
  }
  el.addEventListener('mouseenter', pause); // hover pauses the timer
  el.addEventListener('mouseleave', start);
  close.addEventListener('click', dismiss);
  start();
  return { dismiss };
}

// ---------- dropdown menu ----------
const btn = document.querySelector('#menu-btn');
const menu = document.querySelector('#menu');
const items = [...menu.querySelectorAll('[role="menuitem"]')];

function openMenu(focusIndex = 0) {
  menu.hidden = false;
  btn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');
  items.at(focusIndex).focus();
}
function closeMenu({ returnFocus = true } = {}) {
  menu.hidden = true;
  btn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
  if (returnFocus) btn.focus();
}

btn.addEventListener('click', () => (menu.hidden ? openMenu() : closeMenu()));
btn.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  if (e.key === 'ArrowDown') { e.preventDefault(); openMenu(0); }
  if (e.key === 'ArrowUp') { e.preventDefault(); openMenu(-1); }
});

menu.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  const i = items.indexOf(document.activeElement);
  if (e.key === 'ArrowDown') items[(i + 1) % items.length].focus();
  else if (e.key === 'ArrowUp') items.at(i - 1).focus();
  else if (e.key === 'Escape') closeMenu();
  else if (e.key === 'Tab') closeMenu({ returnFocus: false });
  else return;
  if (e.key !== 'Tab') e.preventDefault();
});

const messages = {
  profile: ['Opening your profile…'],
  invite: ['Invite link copied: academy.ralfiz.dev/join/AK42'],
  invoice: ['Invoice INV-2026-0918 is ready'],

};

  const item = e.target.closest('[role="menuitem"]');
  if (!item) return;
  closeMenu();
  const [msg, type] = messages[item.dataset.action];
  toast(msg, { type });
  console.log('action:', item.dataset.action);
});

// Click outside closes the menu (without stealing focus)
document.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => {
  if (!menu.hidden && !e.target.closest('.menu-wrap')) closeMenu({ returnFocus: false });
});

toast('Welcome back, Asha. 2 new lessons are waiting.');

Open the menu with Enter or ArrowDown, move with the arrows, press Esc to close. Each item fires a toast; hover one to pause its timer.

Toast notifications

A toast is a short, non-blocking status message. Three rules make it accessible. First, put toasts inside one container that exists from page load, marked role="status" (which implies aria-live="polite"), so screen readers announce new text without interrupting. Second, give people time: pause the timer on hover and focus, and keep important errors until they are dismissed. Third, never put the only copy of important information, or the only way to undo, in a toast that vanishes.

The toast() function in the live page returns a handle with dismiss(), so callers can close it early, for example when a request finishes. The message is set with textContent: toasts often echo user input (“Saved ‘<b>hi’”), and innerHTML would turn that into an XSS hole.

Example: Ralfiz Academy course page

The lab puts all of this on one page: a hero with a “Reserve a seat” button, course tabs, an FAQ accordion, an enrol dialog and a toast. Each component gets an initX(root) function. That is the seed of a component system: the same function can run on every matching element on the page.

function initAccordion(root) {
  root.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
    const btn = event.target.closest('.acc-btn');
    if (!btn) return;
    const open = btn.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true';
    btn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(!open));
    const panel = document.getElementById(btn.getAttribute('aria-controls'));
    panel.hidden = open;
  });
}

document.querySelectorAll('.faq').forEach(initAccordion);

The enrol dialog reads its form with FormData only when returnValue is 'enroll'. The Cancel button is type="button", not a submit button, so pressing Enter in a field submits “Reserve” rather than the first button in the form.

dialog.addEventListener('close', () => {
  openBtn.focus();
  if (dialog.returnValue !== 'enroll') return;
  const { name, batch } = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));
  toast(`Seat reserved for ${name} (${batch}).`);
});

Common mistakes

1. A div pretending to be a modal. A fixed div with a high z-index leaves the page behind it focusable, so keyboard users tab “under” the modal.

// Wrong
modal.style.display = 'block';
// Right
dialog.showModal();

2. Clickable divs as tabs or menu items. A div with a click handler cannot be focused or pressed with Enter. Use <button> and add roles on top.

<!-- Wrong -->  <div class="tab" onclick="show(2)">Specs</div>
<!-- Right -->  <button role="tab" aria-selected="false">Specs</button>

3. State in a class, not in ARIA. Toggling .active updates the look but a screen reader still hears “collapsed”.

// Wrong
btn.classList.toggle('open');
// Right: one source of truth, CSS styles [aria-expanded="true"]
btn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(!isOpen));

4. Forgetting where focus goes. After closing a menu with Esc, focus must return to the button. If you remove the focused element, focus drops to <body> and keyboard users lose their place.

5. Toasts built with innerHTML.

// Wrong: product names come from users or an API
el.innerHTML = `Added ${product.title}`;
// Right
el.textContent = `Added ${product.title}`;

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Build a modal” is a classic interview task. Mention showModal(), the top layer, inert background, Esc and cancel, focus return and returnValue. That list alone shows seniority.
  • Know the difference between a disclosure (button that shows content), a menu (list of actions with arrow keys) and a listbox (a choice, like a select). Using the wrong role is a common accessibility audit finding.
  • The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) documents the keyboard contract for every component in this lesson. Teams link to it in code reviews.
  • Component libraries (Radix, Headless UI, shadcn/ui, Angular CDK) exist mainly to get these contracts right. Knowing the contract helps you pick, debug and extend them.
  • Avoid alert() and confirm() in real products: they block the whole tab, cannot be styled and look like the browser is warning the user.

terms.definition: A native dialog element. showModal() puts it in the top layer with a ::backdrop, makes the rest of the page inert, moves focus inside and closes on Esc.
The string a dialog closes with: the value of the submit button in a form method="dialog", or the argument passed to dialog.close(value).
A keyboard pattern where only the active item in a group has tabindex="0" and the rest have -1, so Tab enters the group once and arrow keys move inside it.
ARIA state attributes that tell assistive technology which tab is selected and whether a button’s content is open. Style them in CSS so the look matches the state.
A button that shows and hides a section of content, such as details/summary or a custom accordion item.
The popover attribute and popovertarget buttons: content shown in the top layer that closes on outside click (light dismiss) or Esc.
An element with role="status" or aria-live whose text changes are announced by screen readers without moving focus; used for toasts.

lessons.examTip: When asked to “build a modal” in an interview, list the contract before coding: showModal, top layer, inert background, Esc and the cancel event, focus return, returnValue.
