lessons.title: State-driven rendering
lessons.summaryHtml:
As pages grow, changing the DOM directly from every event handler turns into a mess: the counter says 3 but the list shows 4. State-driven rendering fixes this with one rule: keep all changing data in a single state object, and draw the UI from it with a render(state) function.

Every interaction follows the same loop: event → update state → render. Values you can calculate, such as “2 items left” or the filtered list, are derived state: computed in render, never stored. Saving the state to localStorage after each update makes the app survive a reload.

You also learn the cost of re-rendering everything (lost focus, lost typing, wasted work) and the fix that frameworks use: keyed updates, which reuse existing elements by id. You finish with a complete Task Board with filters, counters and “Clear completed”.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Think of a scoreboard at a cricket ground. The operator does not repaint the board by hand after every ball. There is one scorebook (the state). After each ball the scorer writes in the book, and the board is redrawn from the book. The board can never disagree with the book, because the book is the only thing the board looks at.

State-driven rendering works the same way. All the data that can change lives in one JavaScript object. A function called render reads that object and makes the page match it. Event handlers never edit the page themselves; they change the state and call render. This idea, often written as UI = f(state), is the heart of React, Vue, Svelte and every other modern framework. Here you learn it with plain JavaScript, so frameworks will feel familiar later.

Why it matters

In lessons 1.3 and 2.2 you changed the DOM directly: add an li here, update a counter there. That is fine for one feature. Now imagine a to-do list with a counter, filters, a “Clear completed” button and a saved copy in storage. Adding a task must update the list, the counter and storage. Deleting must do the same. Toggling must update the row, the counter, maybe hide the row if a filter is on, and enable the Clear button. With direct edits, every handler has to remember every side effect. Forget one and the counter says 3 while the list shows 4.

With state-driven rendering, handlers only answer “what changed in the data?”. render answers “what should the screen look like for this data?” once, in one place. Bugs become easier to find because there is one source of truth, and features become easier to add because you add them to render and they work for every event.

How it works

A single state object and a pure render

Start by listing everything that can change and would change the screen: the tasks, the current filter, which task is being edited. Put exactly those things in one object. Then write render(state) so it depends only on its argument. The console example below separates the pieces completely. render returns text here instead of DOM, which makes the idea easy to see: same state in, same output out.

Try it: UI = f(state) in the console

JavaScript

// 1. ONE object holds everything that can change
const state = {
  todos: [
    { id: 1, text: 'Send the March invoice', done: true },
    { id: 2, text: 'Fix cart total rounding', done: false },
  ],
  filter: 'all',
};

// 2. Derived data is computed, never stored
const left = (s) => s.todos.filter((t) => !t.done).length;

// 3. render is a pure function: same state in, same UI out
function render(s) {
  const lines = s.todos.map((t) => `${t.done ? '[x]' : '[ ]'} ${t.text}`);
  return [...lines, `${left(s)} item(s) left · filter: ${s.filter}`].join('\n');
}

// 4. Events never touch the UI: they produce a NEW state
function update(s, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'add':
      return { ...s, todos: [...s.todos, { id: Date.now(), text: action.text, done: false }] };
    case 'toggle':
      return { ...s, todos: s.todos.map((t) => (t.id === action.id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)) };
    case 'filter':
      return { ...s, filter: action.value };
    default:
      return s;
  }
}

console.log(render(state));

let next = update(state, { type: 'toggle', id: 2 });
next = update(next, { type: 'add', text: 'Call the design team' });
console.log('\n' + render(next));

console.log('\nold state untouched?', state.todos[1].done === false);
console.log('same object?', state === next);

render is pure and update returns a new state. Change the actions at the bottom and run again: the old state never changes.

Notice update(state, action). It never changes the old object; it returns a new one with the spread operator. This is called an immutable update. It has two benefits. You can compare oldState === newState to know if anything changed, which is how React and Redux skip work. And you can keep old states for undo. The pattern of “actions” with a type and a function that turns (state, action) into the next state is called a reducer.

// Mutating: the old state is gone, nobody can tell what changed
state.tasks.push(task);

// Immutable: a new object and a new array, the old ones untouched
state = { ...state, tasks: [...state.tasks, task] };
Watch out: spread copies only one level. { ...state } still shares the same tasks array, so copy.tasks.push() changes the original too. Copy every level you change, or use structuredClone when you need a deep copy.

Event → update state → render

In the browser, the loop looks like this. Every handler ends with the same call, usually hidden inside a small setState helper that also saves:

let state = { tasks: [], filter: 'all' };

function setState(patch) {
  state = { ...state, ...patch };
  localStorage.setItem('taskboard:v1', JSON.stringify(state));
  render();
}

list.addEventListener('change', (e) => {
  const id = Number(e.target.closest('li').dataset.id);
  setState({
    tasks: state.tasks.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)),
  });
});

The handler contains no DOM code at all: no classList, no counter update. That is the goal. It also uses one delegated listener on the list, so rows created by render later work automatically.

Full re-render vs keyed updates

The simplest render throws the old list away and builds a new one, with innerHTML or replaceChildren(). It is easy and, for a few dozen rows, fast enough. But it has real costs:

  • Focus is lost. The checkbox you just pressed with Space no longer exists, so focus falls back to <body>.
  • Uncontrolled input is lost. Anything typed into a field that is not in the state disappears, and so do scroll positions and text selections inside the list.
  • Work is wasted. Creating elements, parsing HTML and running layout for rows that did not change.
  • CSS transitions do not run, because a new element has no “before” state.

A keyed update keeps a Map from each item’s id to its element. On render it reuses the element for ids it has seen, creates elements only for new ids, removes elements for ids that disappeared and changes only the text that differs. This is what the key prop does in React and :key in Vue. The live page updates flash-sale stock every two seconds. Type a quantity in both lists and watch what happens at the next tick.

const state = {
  items: [
    { id: 'p1', name: '🎧 Ralfiz Buds Pro', stock: 42 },
    { id: 'p2', name: '⌚ Ralfiz Watch S', stock: 18 },
    { id: 'p3', name: '🔋 Power Bank 20K', stock: 67 },
  ],
};

// A) Full re-render: throw the old DOM away, build it again from a string
//    (innerHTML is OK here only because the data is hard-coded and trusted)
const full = document.querySelector('#full');
let fullCreated = 0;
function renderFull(s) {
  full.innerHTML = s.items.map((item) => `
    <li><span class="name">${item.name}</span>
      <span class="stock">${item.stock} left</span>
      <input type="number" min="1" aria-label="Quantity"></li>`).join('');
  fullCreated += full.querySelectorAll('*').length;
  document.querySelector('#full-meter').textContent = `${fullCreated} elements created so far`;
}

// B) Keyed update: find each row by its id and change only what differs
const keyed = document.querySelector('#keyed');
const rows = new Map(); // id -> { li, stock }
let keyedCreated = 0;
let keyedUpdated = 0;
function renderKeyed(s) {
  for (const item of s.items) {
    let row = rows.get(item.id);
    if (!row) {
      const li = document.createElement('li');
      const name = document.createElement('span');
      name.className = 'name';
      name.textContent = item.name;
      const stock = document.createElement('span');
      stock.className = 'stock';
      const qty = document.createElement('input');
      Object.assign(qty, { type: 'number', min: 1 });
      qty.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Quantity');
      li.append(name, stock, qty);
      keyed.append(li);
      row = { li, stock };
      rows.set(item.id, row);
      keyedCreated += 4;
    }
    const text = `${item.stock} left`;
    if (row.stock.textContent !== text) { row.stock.textContent = text; keyedUpdated++; }
  }
  document.querySelector('#keyed-meter').textContent =
    `${keyedCreated} elements created · ${keyedUpdated} text updates`;
}

function render(s) { renderFull(s); renderKeyed(s); }

// Every 2 s: new state arrives (like a server push), UI re-renders
let ticks = 0;
setInterval(() => {
  state.items = state.items.map((i) => ({ ...i, stock: Math.max(0, i.stock - Math.floor(Math.random() * 3)) }));
  render(state);
  if (++ticks <= 2) console.log(`tick ${ticks}: full=${fullCreated} created, keyed=${keyedCreated} created`);
}, 2000);

render(state);
console.log('Type a quantity in each list and wait for the next tick.');

A middle path, used in the Task Board: keep the full re-render, but remember document.activeElement.id before rendering and focus the element with the same id afterwards. It works because each row’s controls have stable ids derived from the task id.

Derived state

Derived state is any value you can compute from the state: the number of items left, the filtered list, a cart subtotal, whether the Clear button is enabled. The rule is simple: store the minimum, compute the rest. If you store itemsLeft as well as the tasks, every handler must remember to update both, and one day one of them will not. If you compute it inside render, it is always right.

The cart below stores only the lines (price and quantity) and the applied coupon. Subtotal, discount, GST, total and the item count all come from one pure totals(state) function. Change a quantity or apply RALFIZ10, and every number updates, because there is only one place that calculates them.

// Source of truth: only what the user changed. Prices in whole rupees.
const state = {
  lines: [
    { id: 'buds', icon: '🎧', name: 'Ralfiz Buds Pro', price: 6499, qty: 1 },
    { id: 'cable', icon: '🔌', name: 'USB-C cable (2 m)', price: 499, qty: 2 },
    { id: 'case', icon: '🧳', name: 'Travel case', price: 899, qty: 1 },
  ],
  coupon: null, // e.g. { code: 'RALFIZ10', percent: 10 }
};
const COUPONS = { RALFIZ10: 10, WELCOME5: 5 };

// Derived values: pure functions of state. Never stored, so never stale.
function totals(s) {
  const subtotal = s.lines.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l.price * l.qty, 0);
  const discount = Math.round(subtotal * (s.coupon?.percent ?? 0) / 100);
  const gst = Math.round((subtotal - discount) * 0.18);
  const count = s.lines.reduce((n, l) => n + l.qty, 0);
  return { subtotal, discount, gst, total: subtotal - discount + gst, count };
}

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', {
  style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0,
});
const $ = (s) => document.querySelector(s);

function render() {
  const t = totals(state);
  $('#lines').replaceChildren(...state.lines.map((l) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.dataset.id = l.id;
    li.innerHTML = `<span class="thumb" aria-hidden="true"></span>
      <div class="info"><b></b><small></small></div>
      <div class="qty"><button data-d="-1" aria-label="Fewer">−</button>
      <output></output><button data-d="1" aria-label="More">+</button></div>`;
    li.querySelector('.thumb').textContent = l.icon;   // static markup above,
    li.querySelector('b').textContent = l.name;        // data only via textContent
    li.querySelector('small').textContent = `${inr.format(l.price)} each`;
    li.querySelector('output').textContent = l.qty;
    return li;
  }));
  $('#count').textContent = `${t.count} items`;
  $('#subtotal').textContent = inr.format(t.subtotal);
  $('#discount').textContent = t.discount ? `− ${inr.format(t.discount)}` : '—';
  $('#gst').textContent = inr.format(t.gst);
  $('#total').textContent = inr.format(t.total);
}

$('#lines').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const btn = e.target.closest('[data-d]');
  if (!btn) return;
  const id = btn.closest('li').dataset.id;
  state.lines = state.lines
    .map((l) => (l.id === id ? { ...l, qty: l.qty + Number(btn.dataset.d) } : l))
    .filter((l) => l.qty > 0); // qty 0 removes the line
  render();
  // the old button was replaced: put focus on its twin in the new row
  $(`li[data-id="${id}"] [data-d="${btn.dataset.d}"]`)?.focus();
  console.log('total is now', inr.format(totals(state).total));
});

$('#coupon').addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  const code = e.target.code.value.trim().toUpperCase();
  const percent = COUPONS[code];
  const msg = $('#coupon-msg');
  msg.classList.toggle('bad', !percent);
  msg.textContent = percent ? `${code} applied: ${percent}% off` : 'That code is not valid.';
  if (percent) { state.coupon = { code, percent }; render(); }
});

render();
console.table(totals(state));

Only quantities and the coupon are state. Subtotal, GST and total come from one totals() function. Try + and − and the code RALFIZ10.

Computing on every render is cheap for normal data sizes. If a calculation becomes expensive, for example sorting ten thousand rows, cache it by remembering the last input and output (memoisation) rather than storing it in the state.

Persisting state

Because all the data lives in one object, saving it is one line: JSON.stringify in setState, and JSON.parse when the page loads. Three habits make this robust. Put a version in the key (taskboard:v1) so you can change the shape later without reading old data as new. Wrap JSON.parse in try/catch so a corrupted value starts the app fresh instead of crashing it. And decide what not to save: the id of the task being edited, or a loading flag, belongs to this visit only. Lesson 4.2 goes deeper into storage.

const KEY = 'taskboard:v1';
const seed = {
  filter: 'all',
  tasks: [
    { id: 1, text: 'Design the pricing page', done: true },
    { id: 2, text: 'Write the invoice PDF export', done: false },
    { id: 3, text: 'Review the Flutter PR', done: false },
  ],
};

function load() {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY)) ?? seed;
  } catch {
    return seed; // corrupted JSON: start fresh instead of crashing
  }
}

let state = load();

// ---- one way to change state: setState → save → render ----
function setState(patch) {
  state = { ...state, ...patch };
  localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(state));
  render();
}

// ---- derived state: computed on every render, never saved ----
const visible = () => state.tasks.filter({
  all: () => true, active: (t) => !t.done, done: (t) => t.done,
}[state.filter]);

const $ = (s) => document.querySelector(s);

function render() {
  // Full list re-render destroys the focused checkbox: remember and restore it
  const focusedId = document.activeElement?.id;
  const items = visible().map((task) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.dataset.id = task.id;
    li.classList.toggle('done', task.done);
    const box = document.createElement('input');
    box.type = 'checkbox';
    box.id = `t${task.id}`;
    box.checked = task.done;
    const label = document.createElement('label');
    label.htmlFor = box.id;
    label.textContent = task.text; // user text: always textContent
    const del = document.createElement('button');
    del.className = 'del';
    del.setAttribute('aria-label', `Delete ${task.text}`);
    del.textContent = '✕';
    li.append(box, label, del);
    return li;
  });
  $('#list').replaceChildren(...items);
  if (focusedId) document.getElementById(focusedId)?.focus();

  const left = state.tasks.filter((t) => !t.done).length;
  const doneCount = state.tasks.length - left;
  $('#left').textContent = `${left} item${left === 1 ? '' : 's'} left`;
  $('#summary').textContent = `${doneCount}/${state.tasks.length} done`;
  $('#empty').hidden = items.length > 0;
  $('#clear').disabled = doneCount === 0;
  for (const b of document.querySelectorAll('[data-filter]')) {
    b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(b.dataset.filter === state.filter));
  }
}

// ---- events: translate user intent into new state ----
$('#add').addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  const text = e.target.text.value.trim();
  if (!text) return;
  setState({ tasks: [{ id: Date.now(), text, done: false }, ...state.tasks] });
  e.target.reset();
});

  const id = Number(e.target.closest('li').dataset.id);
  setState({ tasks: state.tasks.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)) });
});

  const id = Number(e.target.closest('li').dataset.id);

The core of render builds rows with createElement and textContent (task text is user input, so never innerHTML) and swaps them in with one replaceChildren call:

const FILTERS = {
  all: () => true,
  active: (t) => !t.done,
  done: (t) => t.done,
};

function render() {
  const focusedId = document.activeElement?.id;
  const visible = state.tasks.filter(FILTERS[state.filter]);
  list.replaceChildren(...visible.map(taskItem));
  if (focusedId) document.getElementById(focusedId)?.focus();

  const left = state.tasks.filter(FILTERS.active).length;
  leftEl.textContent = `${left} item${left === 1 ? '' : 's'} left`;
  clearBtn.disabled = left === state.tasks.length;
}

The lab extends it: the filter moves into the URL hash (#/active) so the Back button works and links can be shared, and double-clicking a task switches that row into edit mode by setting editingId in the state. Edit mode is just another piece of state that render reads.

Common mistakes

1. Changing the DOM in a handler and the state somewhere else. The two drift apart.

// Wrong: the DOM is updated, the state is not
checkbox.closest('li').classList.add('done');
// Right: change the data, let render draw it
setState({ tasks: state.tasks.map(toggle(id)) });

2. Storing derived values.

// Wrong: two sources of truth
state.itemsLeft = state.itemsLeft - 1;
// Right: compute it where it is shown
const itemsLeft = state.tasks.filter((t) => !t.done).length;

3. Mutating the state you were given. state.tasks.sort() sorts in place and changes the stored order. Use toSorted() for a sorted copy.

4. innerHTML with user data during re-render.

// Wrong: a task named <img src=x onerror=...> runs code
list.innerHTML = tasks.map((t) => `<li>${t.text}</li>`).join('');
// Right
li.textContent = t.text;

5. Unguarded JSON.parse on load. JSON.parse('undefined') throws and the whole app stays blank. Always try/catch and fall back to a default state.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to explain UI = f(state) and why frameworks re-render: it removes a whole class of “UI out of sync” bugs.
  • “Why does React need a key on list items?” Because without stable keys it cannot tell which element belongs to which item, so it reuses the wrong elements and inputs keep the wrong values. Never use the array index as the key for lists that can be reordered or filtered.
  • Know the words single source of truth, immutable update, reducer and derived state. Redux, Zustand, NgRx and Pinia are all variations of this lesson.
  • Batch renders: if one click changes state three times, render once. Frameworks do this automatically; in vanilla code, make handlers call setState once with the full change, or schedule render with queueMicrotask or requestAnimationFrame.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const state = { todos: [{ id: 1, done: false }] };
const next = {
  ...state,
  todos: state.todos.map((t) => ({ ...t, done: true })),
};
console.log(state === next, state.todos[0].done, next.todos[0].done);
  • A true true true
  • B false true true
  • C false false true
  • D true false true

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const state = { items: ['pen'] };
const copy = { ...state };
copy.items.push('book');
console.log(state.items.length);
  • A 1
  • B undefined
  • C TypeError
  • D 2

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const todos = [
  { t: 'a', done: true },
  { t: 'b', done: false },
  { t: 'c', done: false },
];
const filters = { all: () => true, active: (x) => !x.done };
const view = todos.filter(filters.active).map((x) => x.t);
console.log(view, todos.length);
  • A [ 'b', 'c' ] 3
  • B [ 'b', 'c' ] 2
  • C [ 'a' ] 3
  • D 3 [ 'b', 'c' ]

Answers

  1. C. The spread creates a new outer object and map creates new todo objects, so the old state keeps done: false and the objects are not the same.
  2. D. Spread is a shallow copy: copy.items is the same array as state.items, so pushing to it changes the original state too.
  3. A. The visible list is derived with filter and map; the original array is not changed, so it still has 3 items.

terms.definition: The data that can change and affects what the user sees, kept in one object: the single source of truth.
A function that makes the page match the state. Given the same state it always produces the same UI.
Values computed from the state (counts, filtered lists, totals) instead of stored, so they can never be out of date.
Creating a new object or array with the change ({ ...state, tasks: [...] }) instead of modifying the old one.
A function (state, action) → newState that describes every possible change in one place.
Re-rendering by matching items to existing elements by a stable id, so unchanged elements (and their focus and input) are reused.

lessons.examTip: If a value can be calculated from the state, calculate it in render. Storing it too creates a second source of truth, and one day they will disagree.

quiz.question: In the event → update state → render loop, what should a click handler for “toggle task” do?
options: Add the done class to the list item and update the counter
Create a new state with the task toggled, then call render

Which task is being edited

quiz.question: Why does a full re-render with innerHTML make a checkbox lose keyboard focus?
options: The old checkbox element is destroyed and replaced by a new one, so the focused element no longer exists
innerHTML always blurs the document
Checkboxes cannot be focused after a click
localStorage resets focus
quiz.explanation: Focus belongs to a specific element. When that element is removed, focus falls back to the body. Keyed updates reuse the element, or you restore focus by id.

quiz.question: What does a keyed update use to decide whether to reuse an element?

The element’s class name
A stable id for each item, mapped to its element
The text content of the element

lessons.title: Fetching data into the page
lessons.summaryHtml:
Most real pages show data from a server, and a request can be loading, fail, return nothing or succeed. A professional UI designs all four states, usually with one status field instead of scattered booleans, and uses skeleton loaders so the layout does not jump.

You render DummyJSON products into cards with <template> and textContent, page through them with limit/skip and a Load more button, and build a search box that is debounced (one request after typing stops), cancels stale requests with AbortController so an old response never overwrites a newer one, and caches results in a Map.

The mockup is the Ralfiz Store product browser, the same shape as search pages in real shops and dashboards.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

When you order food in an app, the screen is never just “the result”. First you see a spinner or grey placeholder shapes. Then either your restaurants appear, or a message says “No restaurants deliver here”, or “Something went wrong, try again”. Each of those screens was designed on purpose.

Fetching data into a page means two jobs. The first is the request itself, which you learned in the JavaScript track with fetch, response.ok and try/catch. The second, the subject of this lesson, is the user interface around the request: what the user sees while waiting, when it fails, when there is nothing to show and when data arrives; how more data is loaded; and how a search box avoids flooding the server and showing wrong results.

Why it matters

Networks are slow and unreliable, especially on mobile data. A page that shows a blank area for two seconds feels broken. A page that silently fails leaves users tapping a button that does nothing. A search box that sends a request for every letter wastes the server’s capacity and, worse, can show results for “pho” after the user finished typing “phone”, because responses do not always arrive in the order the requests were sent.

These are the bugs testers and clients find first. Handling them well is a visible sign of a junior developer who is ready for real projects, and the patterns (status field, skeletons, pagination, debounce, abort, cache) are exactly what libraries such as TanStack Query and SWR automate. Knowing them by hand means you understand what those libraries do for you.

How it works

Four UI states and one status field

Every request-driven area of a page has four states:

StateWhat the user seesTypical UI
loadingSomething is happeningSkeleton cards, a spinner in the button, aria-busy="true"
errorWhat went wrong and what to doA short message and a Try again button
emptyThe request worked but found nothingA friendly message and a way out (“clear filters”)
successThe dataCards, a list, a table

Beginners often track these with booleans: isLoading, hasError, isEmpty. With three booleans there are eight combinations, and some are impossible (“loading and error at the same time”) but still reachable through a bug. A single status field that is exactly one of 'idle' | 'loading' | 'error' | 'success' makes impossible states impossible. Empty is simply success with zero items.

let state = { status: 'idle', products: [], error: null };

async function load() {
  state = { ...state, status: 'loading' };
  render();
  try {
    const res = await fetch(url);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Server answered ${res.status}`);
    const data = await res.json();
    state = { ...state, status: 'success', products: data.products };
  } catch (err) {
    state = { ...state, status: 'error', error: err.message };
  }
  render();
}

Remember that fetch only rejects for network failures. A 404 or 500 is a successful HTTP exchange, so you must check response.ok yourself. Use the segmented control in the live page to force each state: Slow adds an artificial delay, Error requests a product that does not exist, and Empty searches for nonsense.

Try it: Loading, error, empty and success

HTML

<main class="shop">
  <header class="head">
    <div>
      <p class="eyebrow">Ralfiz Store</p>
      <h1>Top picks</h1>
    </div>
    <div class="seg" role="group" aria-label="Simulate a response">
      <button data-mode="ok" aria-pressed="true">Normal</button>
      <button data-mode="slow">Slow</button>
      <button data-mode="error">Error</button>
      <button data-mode="empty">Empty</button>
    </div>
  </header>
  <section id="view" aria-live="polite" aria-busy="false"></section>
</main>

CSS

:root { --ink: #0f172a; --muted: #64748b; --line: #e2e8f0; --ac: #4f46e5; }
body { margin: 0; background: #f8fafc; color: var(--ink); }
.shop { padding: 16px; }
.head { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; justify-content: space-between; align-items: end; gap: 12px; margin-bottom: 16px; }
.eyebrow { margin: 0; font-size: 12px; font-weight: 600; color: var(--ac); }
h1 { margin: 0; font-size: 20px; }
.seg { display: flex; padding: 3px; background: #eef2f7; border-radius: 10px; }
.seg button { font: inherit; font-size: 13px; font-weight: 600; color: var(--muted); background: none;
  border: 0; border-radius: 8px; padding: 6px 12px; cursor: pointer; }
.seg button[aria-pressed="true"] { background: #fff; color: var(--ink); box-shadow: 0 1px 3px rgb(15 23 42 / .12); }
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(170px, 1fr)); gap: 12px; }
.card { background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line); border-radius: 14px; padding: 12px; }
.thumb { height: 72px; border-radius: 10px; display: grid; place-items: center; font-size: 32px;
  background: linear-gradient(135deg, #eef2ff, #f5f3ff); margin-bottom: 10px; }
.card h3 { margin: 0; font-size: 14px; line-height: 1.3; height: 2.6em; overflow: hidden; }
.meta { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; margin-top: 6px; font-size: 13px; }
.price { font-weight: 700; }
.rating { color: #b45309; }
.sk { background: linear-gradient(90deg, #eef2f7 25%, #f8fafc 50%, #eef2f7 75%);
  background-size: 200% 100%; animation: shimmer 1.2s infinite; border-radius: 8px; }
.sk.line { height: 12px; margin-top: 8px; }
.sk.short { width: 50%; }
.state { text-align: center; padding: 32px 16px; background: #fff; border: 1px dashed #cbd5e1; border-radius: 14px; }
.state .big { font-size: 36px; }
.state h2 { margin: 8px 0 4px; font-size: 16px; }
.state p { margin: 0 0 12px; color: var(--muted); font-size: 14px; }
.state.error { border-color: #fecaca; background: #fef2f2; }
.btn { font: inherit; font-weight: 600; font-size: 14px; color: #fff; background: var(--ac); border: 0;
  border-radius: 10px; padding: 8px 16px; cursor: pointer; }
@keyframes shimmer { to { background-position: -200% 0; } }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .sk { animation: none; } }

JavaScript

const API = 'https://dummyjson.com';
const URLS = {
  ok: `${API}/products?limit=8&select=title,price,rating,category`,
  slow: `${API}/products?limit=8&skip=8&select=title,price,rating,category`,
  error: `${API}/products/99999`,                 // 404 from the server
  empty: `${API}/products/search?q=zzzzzz&limit=8`, // 200 but no results
};
const ICONS = { beauty: '💄', fragrances: '🌸', furniture: '🛋️', groceries: '🛒',
  laptops: '💻', smartphones: '📱', 'home-decoration': '🏺', 'kitchen-accessories': '🍳' };

const view = document.querySelector('#view');
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
let state = { status: 'idle', products: [], error: null, mode: 'ok' };

function el(tag, className, text) {
  const node = document.createElement(tag);
  if (className) node.className = className;
  if (text !== undefined) node.textContent = text;
  return node;
}

// ONE status field instead of isLoading + isError + isEmpty booleans
function render() {
  view.setAttribute('aria-busy', String(state.status === 'loading'));
  if (state.status === 'loading') {
    const grid = el('div', 'grid');
    for (let i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
      const card = el('div', 'card');
      card.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
      card.append(el('div', 'thumb sk'), el('div', 'sk line'), el('div', 'sk line short'));
      grid.append(card);
    }
    view.replaceChildren(grid);
  } else if (state.status === 'error') {
    const box = el('div', 'state error');
    const retry = el('button', 'btn', 'Try again');
    retry.addEventListener('click', () => load(state.mode));
    box.append(el('div', 'big', '⚠️'), el('h2', '', 'Could not load products'),
      el('p', '', state.error), retry);
    view.replaceChildren(box);
  } else if (state.status === 'success' && state.products.length === 0) {
    const box = el('div', 'state');
    box.append(el('div', 'big', '🔍'), el('h2', '', 'No products found'),
      el('p', '', 'Try another search or clear the filters.'));
    view.replaceChildren(box);
  } else if (state.status === 'success') {
    const grid = el('div', 'grid');
    for (const p of state.products) {
      const card = el('article', 'card');
      const meta = el('div', 'meta');
      meta.append(el('span', 'price', `$${p.price}`), el('span', 'rating', `★ ${p.rating}`));
      card.append(el('div', 'thumb', ICONS[p.category] ?? '📦'), el('h3', '', p.title), meta);
      grid.append(card);
    }
    view.replaceChildren(grid);
  }
}

async function load(mode) {
  state = { ...state, status: 'loading', mode, error: null };
  render();
  try {
    if (mode === 'slow') await sleep(1500);
    const res = await fetch(URLS[mode]);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Server answered ${res.status} ${res.statusText}`.trim());
    const data = await res.json();
    state = { ...state, status: 'success', products: data.products };
    console.log(`${mode}: ${data.products.length} products`);
  } catch (err) {
    state = { ...state, status: 'error', error: err.message };
    console.warn(`${mode}: ${err.message}`);
  }
  render();
}

document.querySelector('.seg').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const mode = e.target.dataset.mode;
  if (!mode) return;
  for (const b of e.currentTarget.children) b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(b === e.target));
  load(mode);
});

load('ok');

Switch between Normal, Slow, Error and Empty. One status field decides what renders; skeletons keep the layout steady while loading.

Skeleton loaders

A skeleton is a grey placeholder with the same shape as the content that will replace it. It does two things a spinner cannot. It tells users what is coming (eight product cards, not a table), which makes the wait feel shorter. And it reserves the space, so the page does not jump when data arrives. That jump is measured by Core Web Vitals as Cumulative Layout Shift, which you meet again in lesson 5.1.

Build skeletons from the same CSS grid as the real cards, give them aria-hidden="true" so screen readers skip them, and mark the container aria-busy="true" while loading. The shimmer is a moving gradient; switch it off under prefers-reduced-motion.

Rendering cards safely with a template

Product titles and descriptions come from a server you do not control. Rendering them with innerHTML and a template literal means one malicious product name can run script in your page. The clean pattern is an HTML <template> for the structure and textContent for the data:

const card = cardTemplate.content.firstElementChild.cloneNode(true);
const img = card.querySelector('img');
img.src = product.thumbnail;
img.alt = product.title;          // meaningful alt text
card.querySelector('.title').textContent = product.title;
card.querySelector('.price').textContent = `$${product.price.toFixed(2)}`;

The template’s <img> has width, height and loading="lazy". Width and height let the browser reserve the right space before the image downloads (no layout shift), and lazy loading skips images far below the fold. The live pages here use emoji instead of photos, because the playground allows no external images; the lab uses the real thumbnail URLs.

Pagination with limit and skip

APIs rarely return everything at once. DummyJSON uses offset pagination: limit is the page size and skip is how many items to jump over. The response includes total, so you know when to stop. URLSearchParams builds the query string and encodes values correctly.

const params = new URLSearchParams({ limit: 5, skip, select: 'title,price' });
const res = await fetch(`https://dummyjson.com/products?${params}`);
// → /products?limit=5&skip=10&select=title%2Cprice

There are three common UIs. Numbered pages suit tables and admin screens where users jump around. Load more suits shops and feeds: the user stays in control and the footer stays reachable. Infinite scroll loads automatically near the bottom, which you build with IntersectionObserver in lesson 4.4. The live page uses Load more with skeleton rows appended at the end and the button disabled while a page is loading, so a double click cannot load the same page twice.

Try it: Load more with limit and skip

HTML

<main class="shop">
  <header class="head">
    <h1>All products</h1>
    <p class="count" id="count" aria-live="polite">Loading…</p>
  </header>
  <ul class="list" id="list"></ul>
  <div class="more">
    <button class="btn" id="more" disabled>Load more</button>
  </div>
</main>

CSS

:root { --ink: #0f172a; --muted: #64748b; --line: #e2e8f0; --ac: #4f46e5; }
body { margin: 0; background: #f8fafc; color: var(--ink); }
.shop { max-width: 640px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 16px; }
.head { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: baseline; gap: 12px; margin-bottom: 12px; }
h1 { margin: 0; font-size: 18px; }
.count { margin: 0; font-size: 13px; color: var(--muted); font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
.list { list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 0; background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line); border-radius: 14px; overflow: hidden; }
.list li { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px; padding: 10px 14px; border-top: 1px solid var(--line); }
.list li:first-child { border-top: 0; }
.list li.new { animation: fade .3s ease-out; }
.num { width: 28px; font-size: 12px; color: var(--muted); font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
.title { flex: 1; min-width: 0; font-size: 14px; white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }
.cat { font-size: 11px; color: var(--ac); background: #eef2ff; padding: 2px 8px; border-radius: 99px; }
.price { font-weight: 700; font-size: 14px; min-width: 64px; text-align: right; }
.sk { height: 14px; flex: 1; border-radius: 6px; background: linear-gradient(90deg, #eef2f7 25%, #f8fafc 50%, #eef2f7 75%);
  background-size: 200% 100%; animation: shimmer 1.2s infinite; }
.more { display: flex; justify-content: center; padding: 16px 0 0; }
.btn { font: inherit; font-weight: 600; font-size: 14px; color: var(--ac); background: #fff;
  border: 1px solid #c7d2fe; border-radius: 10px; padding: 8px 20px; cursor: pointer; }
.btn:hover:not(:disabled) { background: #eef2ff; }
.btn:disabled { color: var(--muted); border-color: var(--line); cursor: default; }
@keyframes shimmer { to { background-position: -200% 0; } }

JavaScript

const PAGE_SIZE = 5;
const list = document.querySelector('#list');
const moreBtn = document.querySelector('#more');
const count = document.querySelector('#count');
let skip = 0;
let total = Infinity;

function skeletonRows(n) {
  return Array.from({ length: n }, () => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.className = 'sk-row';
    li.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
    const bar = document.createElement('div');
    bar.className = 'sk';
    li.append(bar);
    return li;
  });
}

function row(p, index) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.className = 'new';
  const parts = [
    ['num', `#${index + 1}`], ['title', p.title], ['cat', p.category], ['price', `$${p.price}`],
  ];
  for (const [cls, text] of parts) {
    const span = document.createElement('span');
    span.className = cls;
    span.textContent = text;
    li.append(span);
  }
  return li;
}

async function loadPage() {
  moreBtn.disabled = true;
  moreBtn.textContent = 'Loading…';
  list.append(...skeletonRows(PAGE_SIZE));
  const params = new URLSearchParams({
    limit: PAGE_SIZE, skip, select: 'title,price,category',
  });
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`https://dummyjson.com/products?${params}`);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    const data = await res.json();
    list.querySelectorAll('.sk-row').forEach((r) => r.remove());
    list.append(...data.products.map((p, i) => row(p, skip + i)));
    skip += data.products.length;
    total = data.total;
    console.log(`GET ?${params} → ${data.products.length} items (skip=${data.skip})`);
  } catch (err) {
    list.querySelectorAll('.sk-row').forEach((r) => r.remove());
    console.warn('Page failed:', err.message);
  } finally {
    const done = skip >= total;
    count.textContent = `Showing ${skip} of ${total === Infinity ? '…' : total}`;
    moreBtn.disabled = done;
    moreBtn.textContent = done ? 'You have seen everything' : 'Load more';
  }
}

moreBtn.addEventListener('click', loadPage);
loadPage();

Each click fetches the next 5 products with URLSearchParams. The console shows the query; the button stops when skip reaches total.

Remember: select asks DummyJSON for only the fields you display. Smaller responses load faster on mobile. Many real APIs offer the same idea (sparse fieldsets, GraphQL fields).

Search: debounce, abort and cache

A search-as-you-type box needs three techniques that work together.

Debounce waits until the user pauses typing (300 ms is typical) before sending a request. Typing “phone” produces one request instead of five. You wrote debounce in the JavaScript track: every call clears the previous timer and starts a new one.

Abort stale requests. Debounce reduces requests but does not remove the race. The user types “pho”, pauses, the request starts, then types “ne”. Now two requests are in flight, and if the “pho” response is slower, it arrives last and overwrites the “phone” results. The fix is to keep the AbortController of the request in flight and call abort() before starting a new one. The aborted fetch rejects with an error whose name is 'AbortError', which you ignore because it is expected, not a failure.

let controller = null;

async function search(q) {
  controller?.abort();                       // the old request is stale
  const ctrl = (controller = new AbortController());
  try {
    const res = await fetch(urlFor(q), { signal: ctrl.signal });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    render(await res.json());
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') return;   // expected: ignore
    showError(err.message);
  }
}

Cache responses in a Map keyed by the full URL. When the user deletes a letter and retypes it, or clicks back to a category, the result appears instantly with no request. Cache only successful responses, and remember that a cache in memory lasts until reload, which is fine for search. Real apps also expire entries after some time.

The live page combines all three with category chips loaded from /products/categories. Type quickly, then slowly, and watch the console: “aborted stale request” and “cache hit” show each technique working. Note the finally block only clears the spinner if its request is still the latest one.

HTML

<main class="store">
  <header class="top">
    <strong class="brand"><span aria-hidden="true">◆</span> Ralfiz Store</strong>

      <span aria-hidden="true">🔍</span>

:root { --ink: #0f172a; --muted: #64748b; --line: #e2e8f0; --ac: #4f46e5; }

JavaScript

const API = 'https://dummyjson.com/products';
const FIELDS = 'title,price,discountPercentage,category';
const ICONS = { beauty: '💄', fragrances: '🌸', furniture: '🛋️', groceries: '🛒',
  laptops: '💻', smartphones: '📱', 'home-decoration': '🏺', 'kitchen-accessories': '🍳' };
const $ = (s) => document.querySelector(s);

const cache = new Map();   // url → data: repeat searches are instant
let controller = null;     // the request currently in flight
let category = '';

function buildUrl(q) {
  const params = new URLSearchParams({ limit: 12, select: FIELDS });
  if (q) { params.set('q', q); return `${API}/search?${params}`; }
  if (category) return `${API}/category/${encodeURIComponent(category)}?${params}`;
  return `${API}?${params}`;
}

function setBusy(busy) {
  $('#spin').hidden = !busy;
  $('#grid').classList.toggle('dim', busy);
}

async function search(q) {
  const url = buildUrl(q);
  controller?.abort();                 // whatever is in flight is now stale
  if (cache.has(url)) {
    console.log('cache hit:', q || category || 'all');
    setBusy(false);
    return render(cache.get(url), q);
  }
  const ctrl = (controller = new AbortController());
  setBusy(true);
  try {
    const res = await fetch(url, { signal: ctrl.signal });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    const data = await res.json();
    cache.set(url, data);              // only successful responses
    render(data, q);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') return console.log('aborted stale request');
    $('#status').textContent = `Something went wrong (${err.message}). Try again.`;
  } finally {
    if (controller === ctrl) setBusy(false); // only the latest request
  }
}

function render(data, q) {
  const cards = data.products.map((p) => {
    const card = document.createElement('article');
    card.className = 'card';
    card.innerHTML = `<div class="thumb" aria-hidden="true"></div><h3></h3>
      <div class="row"><span class="price"></span><span class="off"></span></div>`;
    card.querySelector('.thumb').textContent = ICONS[p.category] ?? '📦';
    card.querySelector('h3').textContent = p.title;
    card.querySelector('.price').textContent = `$${p.price}`;
    card.querySelector('.off').textContent = `−${Math.round(p.discountPercentage)}%`;
    return card;
  });
  if (!cards.length) {
    const empty = document.createElement('p');
    empty.className = 'empty';
    empty.textContent = `No products match “${q}”.`;
    cards.push(empty);
  }
  $('#grid').replaceChildren(...cards);
  $('#status').textContent = `${data.total} result${data.total === 1 ? '' : 's'}` +
    (q ? ` for “${q}”` : category ? ` in ${category}` : '');
}

// Debounce: wait until the user stops typing for 300 ms
function debounce(fn, ms) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => { clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms); };
}
$('#q').addEventListener('input', debounce((e) => {
  const q = e.target.value.trim();
  console.log('search:', JSON.stringify(q));
  search(q);
}, 300));

// Category chips come from the API too
async function loadCategories() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`${API}/categories`);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    const cats = await res.json();
    $('#chips').append(...cats.slice(0, 6).map(({ slug, name }) => {
      const b = document.createElement('button');
      b.dataset.cat = slug;
      b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', 'false');
      b.textContent = name;
      return b;
    }));
  } catch (err) {
    console.warn('No categories:', err.message);
  }
}
$('#chips').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const chip = e.target.closest('button');
  if (!chip) return;
  category = chip.dataset.cat;
  for (const b of $('#chips').children) b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(b === chip));
  $('#q').value = '';
  search('');
});

loadCategories();
search('');

Type fast, then slowly. Debounce waits 300 ms, stale requests are aborted and repeated searches come from the Map cache. Chips filter by category.

A reusable request helper

In a real project you do not repeat the response.ok check in twenty places. Wrap fetch once so every failure becomes an Error with a message you can show: network failures, timeouts, HTTP errors with the server’s own message, and cancellation passed through untouched. AbortSignal.timeout(ms) gives a signal that aborts itself; AbortSignal.any([...]) combines it with the caller’s signal. AbortSignal.any is newer, so the helper checks for it (see the MDN compatibility table).

Try it: A getJSON helper with clear errors

JavaScript

// One helper that turns every failure into a clear, catchable Error
async function getJSON(url, { signal, timeout = 8000 } = {}) {
  // Combine the caller's signal with a timeout (AbortSignal.any is newer:
  // check MDN compatibility; fall back to the timeout alone)
  const timer = AbortSignal.timeout(timeout);
  const combined = signal && AbortSignal.any ? AbortSignal.any([signal, timer]) : timer;

  let res;
  try {
    res = await fetch(url, { signal: combined });
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') throw err;       // caller cancelled
    if (err.name === 'TimeoutError') throw new Error('The server took too long');
    throw new Error('Network error: check your connection', { cause: err });
  }
  if (!res.ok) {
    const body = await res.json().catch(() => ({}));
    throw new Error(body.message ?? `HTTP ${res.status}`);
  }
  return res.json();
}

async function demo(label, url, options) {
  try {
    const data = await getJSON(url, options);
    console.log(`✔ ${label}:`, data.title ?? data);
  } catch (err) {
    console.log(`✘ ${label}: ${err.name}: ${err.message}`);
  }
}

await demo('found', 'https://dummyjson.com/products/1?select=title');
await demo('404', 'https://dummyjson.com/products/0');
await demo('offline', 'https://api.ralfiz.invalid/products');

const controller = new AbortController();
const pending = demo('cancelled', 'https://dummyjson.com/products/2', { signal: controller.signal });
controller.abort(); // e.g. the user typed another letter
await pending;

Runs as a module (top-level await). Every failure becomes an Error with a useful message, and cancellation stays an AbortError.

Example: Ralfiz Store product browser

The lab puts every piece into one page. The state is small: { query, skip, total, status, error }. One load({ reset }) function does all fetching: a new search resets skip and clears the grid, Load more keeps both. One renderStatus() derives the status line (“Showing 24 of 194”), the error box and the Load more button from the state.

async function load({ reset = false } = {}) {
  controller?.abort();
  const ctrl = (controller = new AbortController());
  if (reset) { state.skip = 0; grid.replaceChildren(); }
  state.status = 'loading';
  renderStatus();
  showSkeletons(reset ? PAGE_SIZE : 4);
  try {
    const data = await fetchPage(pageUrl(state.query, state.skip), ctrl.signal);
    removeSkeletons();
    grid.append(...data.products.map(productCard));
    state.skip += data.products.length;
    state.total = data.total;
    state.status = 'success';
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') return;
    removeSkeletons();
    Object.assign(state, { status: 'error', error: err.message });
  }
  renderStatus();
}

Test the unhappy paths on purpose: DevTools → Network → throttling “Slow 4G” shows your skeletons, and “Offline” shows your error box. If you never looked at those states, your users will be the first to see them.

Common mistakes

1. Treating a 404 as success.

// Wrong: data is { message: 'Product not found' } and the page breaks later
const data = await (await fetch(url)).json();
// Right
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);

2. No loading or error state. An empty area during loading and a silent console error on failure. Every fetch in the UI needs all four states.

3. Race conditions in search. Without abort(), an older, slower response can replace newer results. Debounce alone does not fix it.

4. Showing AbortError to the user.

// Wrong: "The operation was aborted" flashes on every keystroke
catch (err) { showError(err.message); }
// Right
catch (err) { if (err.name !== 'AbortError') showError(err.message); }

5. innerHTML with API data. card.innerHTML = `<h3>${p.title}</h3>` trusts the server completely. Use a template and textContent.

6. Images without dimensions. Cards jump as each image loads. Always set width, height and alt.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “How would you build a search box?” is a favourite. Mention debounce, AbortController for stale requests, a cache, the loading/empty/error states and a minimum query length.
  • Know debounce vs throttle: debounce fires after activity stops (search), throttle fires at most once per interval during activity (scroll, resize).
  • Offset pagination (limit/skip) is simple but can skip or repeat items when data changes between pages. Large feeds use cursor pagination (“give me 20 after id X”).
  • In React and Next.js projects, TanStack Query or SWR handle caching, deduplication, retries and stale data. They are this lesson, packaged.
  • For accessibility, announce result counts in a role="status" region, and do not move focus when results update while the user is typing.

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const cache = new Map();
function getPage(n) {
  if (cache.has(n)) return 'hit ' + n;
  cache.set(n, ['item']);
  return 'miss ' + n;
}

  • A miss 1 miss 2 hit 1 2
  • B miss 1 miss 2 miss 1 3
  • C hit 1 hit 2 hit 1 2
  • D miss 1 miss 2 hit 1 3

Answers

  1. B. abort() fires the abort event synchronously, before the next line runs. The default reason is a DOMException named AbortError.
  2. D. Each call clears the previous timer, so only the last one survives, and it runs after the synchronous log.
  3. A. The first request for each key is a miss and stores it; the repeat of page 1 is a hit. Two keys are stored.

terms.definition: The four things a data-driven area can show: loading, error, empty and success. Designing all four is part of the feature.
Grey placeholder shapes that match the coming content, so the wait feels shorter and the layout does not jump.
Fetching a page with limit (page size) and skip (items to jump over); the response’s total tells you when to stop.
Delaying a function until calls stop for a set time, so typing “phone” sends one request instead of five.
An object whose signal is passed to fetch; calling abort() cancels the request and fetch rejects with an AbortError.
A bug where results depend on timing, such as an older, slower response arriving last and overwriting newer results.
A Map from request URL to parsed data, so repeated requests are answered instantly without the network.

quiz.question: Why use one status field ('loading' | 'error' | 'success') instead of isLoading and hasError booleans?
options: Booleans are slower to read
Booleans cannot be stored in objects
JSON cannot serialise booleans
A single field makes impossible combinations, like loading and error at once, impossible
quiz.explanation: Two or three booleans allow combinations that should never happen. One status value can only be in one state at a time.

quiz.question: A user types “pho”, pauses, then finishes “phone”. The “pho” response arrives last. What prevents it from replacing the “phone” results?
options: Debouncing the input by 300 ms
Aborting the previous request with its AbortController before starting the new one
Caching responses in a Map
Using response.ok
quiz.explanation: Debounce reduces requests but two can still be in flight. Aborting the stale one guarantees its response is never rendered.

quiz.question: fetch() resolves for https://dummyjson.com/products/0 with status 404. What should your code do?
options: Check response.ok and throw (or show the error state) because it is false
Nothing: fetch would have rejected if something was wrong
Retry forever until it succeeds
Call response.json() and render it as a product
quiz.explanation: fetch only rejects on network failure. HTTP errors resolve normally, so check response.ok yourself.

quiz.question: Why give product images width and height attributes and use skeleton cards?
options: They make images download faster
They are required for alt text to work
They reserve space so the layout does not jump when content arrives
They stop the browser caching images
quiz.explanation: Reserved space prevents layout shift (CLS). Skeletons also show what kind of content is coming.

lessons.title: Browser storage
lessons.summaryHtml:
Browsers give every site several places to keep data on the user’s device. localStorage keeps small strings until they are deleted; sessionStorage keeps them for one tab; cookies are tiny and are sent to the server with every request; IndexedDB is an asynchronous database for larger, structured data.

Web Storage only stores strings, so you save data with JSON.stringify and read it back with JSON.parse inside try/catch, remembering that Dates, Maps and Sets do not survive the trip. You also handle quota errors, keep tabs in sync with the storage event and version your keys.

Just as important is what never goes into storage: any script on the page can read localStorage, so a single XSS bug leaks every token kept there. Session cookies set by the server with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite are the safer home for authentication.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A web page forgets everything when it reloads. Every variable, every array, every piece of state from lesson 3.3 is gone. Browser storage gives your site small drawers on the user’s device where it can put things it wants to find again: the dark-mode choice, the last products someone looked at, a half-written message, a list of offline notes.

There are four drawers, and they differ in size, lifetime, who can see them and whether the server receives them. Picking the right drawer, and knowing what must never go in any of them, is the whole skill.

Why it matters

Users expect a site to remember them. If Ralfiz Academy resets the video speed on every visit, or the shop loses the cart when someone refreshes on a slow connection, the product feels broken. Storage also makes apps faster: preferences apply before the first paint, and data kept locally does not need a request.

Storage is also where many security incidents start. Access tokens kept in localStorage are one XSS bug away from being stolen, and a badly configured cookie can be sent with requests from other sites. Interviewers ask about storage choices precisely because the answer shows whether you think about security.

How it works

The four options

localStorage, sessionStorage and IndexedDB are scoped to the origin: scheme, host and port. https://shop.ralfiz.dev cannot read the storage of https://academy.ralfiz.dev. Cookies follow older, looser rules: they are scoped by domain and path (the port is ignored), and a cookie set with Domain=ralfiz.dev is shared by every subdomain.

localStoragesessionStorageCookiesIndexedDB
LifetimeUntil deletedUntil the tab closesUntil Max-Age/Expires, or the session endsUntil deleted
Shared between tabsYesNo (one per tab)YesYes
SizeAbout 5 MB per originAbout 5 MB per originAbout 4 KB per cookieLarge: a share of free disk
Sent to the serverNoNoWith every matching requestNo
APISynchronous, stringsSynchronous, stringsOne string, document.cookieAsynchronous, structured objects
Use forPreferences, small caches, recently viewedDrafts, wizard steps, one-tab stateServer sessions, language for server renderingOffline data, large lists, files

A simple decision path: if the server needs it on every request, it is a cookie (usually set by the server). If it is big, structured or needed offline, use IndexedDB. If it belongs to one tab, use sessionStorage. Otherwise, a small preference, use localStorage. Exact limits vary by browser, and Safari may clear script-written storage for sites the user has not visited for a while, so treat all of it as a cache that can disappear.

Web Storage stores strings: JSON in, JSON out

localStorage.setItem(key, value) converts value with String(). Save an object directly and you store the text "[object Object]". So you serialise with JSON.stringify and read with JSON.parse. Three details catch people:

  • getItem returns null for a missing key, and JSON.parse(null) is null, so always provide a default.
  • JSON.parse throws on corrupted text, for example after a user edits storage in DevTools or an older version of your app wrote a different shape. Wrap it in try/catch.
  • JSON only knows strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and plain objects. A Date becomes an ISO string, Map and Set become {}, undefined properties disappear and NaN becomes null. Convert them yourself on the way in and out.

The console example shows each loss and a small storage wrapper that never throws at the caller. Most real projects have exactly such a wrapper.

Try it: JSON round trip and a safe wrapper

JavaScript

// Storage keeps STRINGS. JSON turns data into strings, but not everything survives.
const order = {
  id: 'ORD-1042',
  placedAt: new Date('2026-09-28T10:30:00Z'),
  items: new Map([['buds', 1]]),
  tags: new Set(['gift']),
  total: 7499,
  note: undefined,
};
const json = JSON.stringify(order);
console.log(json);
const back = JSON.parse(json);
console.log(typeof back.placedAt, back.items, back.tags, 'note' in back);

// A small wrapper: JSON in and out, safe defaults, never throws at callers
const storage = {
  get(key, fallback) {
    try {
      const raw = localStorage.getItem(key);
      return raw === null ? fallback : JSON.parse(raw);
    } catch {
      return fallback; // corrupted or unavailable
    }
  },
  set(key, value) {
    try {
      localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(value));
      return true;
    } catch (err) {
      console.warn('storage.set failed:', err.name); // QuotaExceededError, SecurityError
      return false;
    }
  },
};

// Convert types that JSON cannot represent yourself
storage.set('order', { ...order, placedAt: order.placedAt.toISOString(), items: [...order.items] });
const saved = storage.get('order', null);
const restored = { ...saved, placedAt: new Date(saved.placedAt), items: new Map(saved.items) };
console.log(restored.placedAt.getUTCHours(), restored.items.get('buds'));

localStorage.setItem('broken', '{not json');
console.log(storage.get('broken', 'fallback used'));
console.log(storage.get('missing', { theme: 'light' }));

See what JSON loses (Date, Map, Set, undefined) and how a small wrapper converts types and never throws at callers.

Writes can fail too. When the quota is full, setItem throws a DOMException named QuotaExceededError; some privacy modes and blocked-storage settings throw a SecurityError just for reading localStorage. Catch it, keep the app working with in-memory state, and optionally tell the user. For large data, navigator.storage.estimate() reports usage and quota.

Example: a remember-me preferences panel

The preferences panel below saves on every change. The “Remember me on this device” switch decides where: on, the settings go to localStorage and survive restarts; off, they go to sessionStorage and vanish when the tab closes, which is what a user on a shared college computer wants. Reading merges the saved object over DEFAULTS, so a setting added in a later release still gets a value for old users. The key includes a version, academy:prefs:v1; if the shape changes incompatibly, you move to v2 and migrate or ignore the old one.

Try it: Remember-me preferences panel

  <section class="panel">
    <header class="head">
      <div>
        <h1>Learning preferences</h1>

      </div>

        <legend>Theme</legend>
        <div class="seg">
          <label><input type="radio" name="theme" value="light"> ☀️ Light</label>
          <label><input type="radio" name="theme" value="dark"> 🌙 Dark</label>
        </div>
      </fieldset>
      <label class="field">

Example: a recently viewed list

“Recently viewed” is a classic localStorage feature. The list keeps the most recent first, removes duplicates, and is capped so it cannot grow forever. It stores only product ids and timestamps, not whole product objects: that keeps it small, and prices or titles shown later always come from fresh data, never from a stale copy. Ids for products that no longer exist are simply skipped when rendering. Intl.RelativeTimeFormat turns the timestamps into “5 minutes ago”.

The storage event: keeping tabs in sync

When one tab changes localStorage, every other tab of the same origin receives a storage event with key, oldValue and newValue. The tab that made the change does not. This is how a “log out everywhere” or a theme switch reaches all open tabs. sessionStorage is per tab, so its changes do not reach other tabs. The playground runs one page, so this is shown here and practised in the lab with two real tabs:

addEventListener('storage', (event) => {
  if (event.key !== 'notes:prefs:v1') return;
  applyPrefs(JSON.parse(event.newValue ?? '{}'));
});

Cookies and their attributes

A cookie is a small name/value pair that the browser attaches to requests to the server. That is its purpose, and also why it should stay small. From JavaScript, document.cookie is odd: reading returns all visible cookies as one string ("lang=en-IN; theme=dark"), and writing sets or replaces one cookie. The attributes you write cannot be read back.

AttributeMeaning
Max-Age / ExpiresLifetime. Without them the cookie ends with the browser session. Max-Age=0 deletes it.
Path, DomainWhich URLs receive it.
SecureSent only over HTTPS.
SameSiteStrict: never on cross-site requests. Lax (the default in Chromium): cross-site only on top-level navigations such as following a link. None: always, requires Secure. Protects against CSRF.
HttpOnlyInvisible to JavaScript. Only the server can set it, with the Set-Cookie header.

The storage inspector below is a small version of DevTools → Application. It lists all three string stores, parses document.cookie into an object, and writes cookies with encodeURIComponent so values with spaces or semicolons stay intact.

// document.cookie is ONE string: "a=1; b=2". Parse it into an object.
function readCookies() {
  return Object.fromEntries(
    document.cookie.split('; ').filter(Boolean).map((pair) => {
      const i = pair.indexOf('=');
      return [decodeURIComponent(pair.slice(0, i)), decodeURIComponent(pair.slice(i + 1))];
    }),
  );
}

// Writing adds or replaces ONE cookie; the attributes are not readable later.
function writeCookie(name, value, days = 7) {
  document.cookie = `${encodeURIComponent(name)}=${encodeURIComponent(value)}; ` +
    `Max-Age=${days * 86400}; Path=/; SameSite=Lax; Secure`;
}
const deleteCookie = (name) => {
  document.cookie = `${encodeURIComponent(name)}=; Max-Age=0; Path=/`;
};

const STORES = {
  local: { label: 'localStorage', note: 'Per origin · survives restarts · ~5 MB',
    entries: () => Object.entries({ ...localStorage }),
    set: (k, v) => localStorage.setItem(k, v), remove: (k) => localStorage.removeItem(k) },
  session: { label: 'sessionStorage', note: 'Per tab · gone when the tab closes',
    entries: () => Object.entries({ ...sessionStorage }),
    set: (k, v) => sessionStorage.setItem(k, v), remove: (k) => sessionStorage.removeItem(k) },
  cookie: { label: 'Cookies', note: 'Sent to the server with every request · ~4 KB each',
    entries: () => Object.entries(readCookies()), set: writeCookie, remove: deleteCookie },
};

// UTF-16 strings: roughly 2 bytes per character count toward the quota
const bytes = (entries) => entries.reduce((n, [k, v]) => n + (k.length + v.length) * 2, 0);

function render() {
  const cols = Object.entries(STORES).map(([id, store]) => {
    const entries = store.entries();
    const col = document.createElement('section');
    col.className = 'col';
    col.innerHTML = '<h2><span></span><small></small></h2><p class="note"></p>';
    col.querySelector('span').textContent = store.label;
    col.querySelector('small').textContent = `${entries.length} · ${bytes(entries)} B`;
    col.querySelector('.note').textContent = store.note;
    if (!entries.length) {
      const none = document.createElement('div');
      none.className = 'none';
      none.textContent = 'Empty';
      col.append(none);
    } else {
      const table = document.createElement('table');
      for (const [k, v] of entries) {
        const row = table.insertRow();
        Object.assign(row.insertCell(), { className: 'k', textContent: k });
        row.insertCell().textContent = v;
        const x = Object.assign(row.insertCell(), { className: 'x' });
        const del = Object.assign(document.createElement('button'), { textContent: '✕' });
        del.setAttribute('aria-label', `Remove ${k} from ${store.label}`);
        del.addEventListener('click', () => { store.remove(k); render(); });
        x.append(del);
      }
      col.append(table);
    }
    col.dataset.store = id;
    return col;
  });
  document.querySelector('#cols').replaceChildren(...cols);
}

  try {
    STORES[target].set(key.trim(), value);
    console.log(`${STORES[target].label}: ${key} = ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);

What never to store

Any JavaScript running on your origin can read localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB and non-HttpOnly cookies. That includes every third-party script you load and any script an attacker injects through an XSS bug. So:

  • Never store passwords, card numbers or personal documents in browser storage.
  • Access tokens in localStorage are readable by any XSS. Many tutorials do it; the safer default for web apps is a session cookie set by the server with HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax, which scripts cannot read. If you must hold a token in the browser, keep it short-lived and in memory, and treat XSS prevention (lesson 5.3) as critical.
  • Do not trust stored data: a user can edit it in DevTools. Prices, roles and permissions are always checked on the server.

IndexedDB with a small wrapper

IndexedDB is a real database in the browser: object stores (like tables) of structured objects, keys, indexes and transactions. It is asynchronous, so it never blocks the page, and it stores Dates, Maps, Blobs and files directly. Its original API uses request objects with onsuccess callbacks, so projects wrap it in promises (or use the small idb library). The playground does not support IndexedDB, so here is the wrapper from the lab:

export function openDB() {
  dbPromise ??= new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const request = indexedDB.open('ralfiz-notes', 1);
    request.onupgradeneeded = () => {     // first open or new version
      const store = request.result.createObjectStore('notes',
        { keyPath: 'id', autoIncrement: true });
      store.createIndex('byDate', 'createdAt');
    };
    request.onsuccess = () => resolve(request.result);
    request.onerror = () => reject(request.error);
  });
  return dbPromise;
}

const done = (req) => new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  req.onsuccess = () => resolve(req.result);
  req.onerror = () => reject(req.error);
});

export async function addNote(note) {
  const db = await openDB();
  return done(db.transaction('notes', 'readwrite').objectStore('notes').add(note));
}

Schema changes happen only in onupgradeneeded, which runs when you raise the version number. That is how IndexedDB migrates existing users’ data.

Common mistakes

1. Storing an object without JSON.

// Wrong: stores "[object Object]"
localStorage.setItem('prefs', prefs);
// Right
localStorage.setItem('prefs', JSON.stringify(prefs));

2. Unguarded parsing.

// Wrong: one corrupted value and the app never starts
const cart = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('cart'));
cart.items.push(item);   // TypeError when nothing was saved
// Right
const cart = storage.get('cart', { items: [] });

3. Tokens in localStorage.

// Risky: any injected script can send this token anywhere
localStorage.setItem('accessToken', data.accessToken);
// Safer: the server sets the session cookie
// Set-Cookie: sid=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/

4. Trying to set HttpOnly from JavaScript. document.cookie = 'sid=1; HttpOnly' is ignored by browsers; only a server response can create an HttpOnly cookie.

5. Storing whole API responses forever. Stale prices and a full quota. Store ids or small, versioned caches with a timestamp, and refresh from the server.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies?” Answer with lifetime, scope, size, whether the server receives it, and a security note about XSS and HttpOnly.
  • Know that the storage event fires in other tabs only.
  • Web Storage is synchronous and runs on the main thread: large reads and writes can cause jank. IndexedDB is asynchronous.
  • Under GDPR and similar laws, non-essential cookies and similar storage for tracking need consent. Preferences the user explicitly set are usually treated differently, but check with the client’s legal team.
  • For offline-first apps, IndexedDB plus a service worker (Cache Storage) is the standard stack.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const s = JSON.stringify({
  at: new Date(0),
  tags: new Set(['a']),
  n: NaN,
  u: undefined,
});
console.log(s);
  • A {"at":{},"tags":["a"],"n":null}
  • B {"at":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z","tags":{},"n":null}
  • C {"at":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z","tags":["a"],"n":NaN,"u":null}
  • D TypeError: cannot serialise a Set

Snippet 2. localStorage.setItem converts values with String(). This snippet copies that behaviour. What is logged?

const store = {};
function setItem(key, value) {
  store[key] = String(value); // what Web Storage does
}
setItem('prefs', { theme: 'dark' });
setItem('count', 5);
console.log(store.prefs, typeof store.count);
  • A { theme: 'dark' } number
  • B {"theme":"dark"} string
  • C [object Object] number
  • D [object Object] string

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const raw = null; // what getItem returns for a missing key
const prefs = { theme: 'light', ...JSON.parse(raw) };
console.log(prefs.theme, JSON.parse(raw));
  • A light null
  • B TypeError
  • C light {}
  • D undefined null

Answers

  1. B. Dates become ISO strings through toJSON, a Set has no own enumerable properties so it becomes {}, NaN becomes null and undefined properties are dropped.
  2. D. String() of a plain object is "[object Object]" and every value becomes a string. That is why you JSON.stringify before saving.
  3. A. JSON.parse(null) turns null into the text "null" and parses it back to null. Spreading null adds nothing, so the default stays.

terms.definition: Per-origin key/value storage of strings that lasts until deleted and is shared by all tabs of the origin.
Like localStorage, but separate for each tab and cleared when the tab closes.
A small name/value pair the browser sends to the server with matching requests; configured with Max-Age, Path, Secure, SameSite and HttpOnly.
A cookie attribute, set only by the server, that hides the cookie from JavaScript so XSS cannot read it.
A cookie attribute (Strict, Lax, None) that controls whether the cookie is sent on cross-site requests; a key defence against CSRF.
Fired in the other tabs of the same origin when localStorage changes, with key, oldValue and newValue.
An asynchronous, transactional database in the browser for large, structured data such as offline records and files.

lessons.examTip: Treat browser storage as a cache the user (or an attacker’s script) can read and edit: parse it defensively, never store secrets, and check anything important on the server.
