lessons.title: URLs, history and a tiny router
lessons.summaryHtml:
The address bar is part of your app’s interface. A good web app keeps its important state in the URL, so a page can be bookmarked, shared, refreshed and navigated with the Back button. The URL and URLSearchParams classes parse and build addresses safely, and location is the page’s own URL.

history.pushState and replaceState change the URL without reloading, and the popstate event tells you when the user moves through history. With those pieces you can write a small client-side router: match the path to a view, render it, and keep links, titles and focus correct.

In the playground you use hash routing (#/courses). In the lab you build a real history router served by a dev server, and learn why the server must send index.html for every route.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Every page you open has an address: https://shop.ralfiz.dev/products?cat=audio&sort=price-asc#reviews. That address is not just “where the page lives”. It also says what the user is looking at: the audio category, sorted by price, scrolled to the reviews. When the user copies the link to a friend, bookmarks it or presses refresh, the URL is the only thing that survives.

This lesson has three parts. First you learn to read and build URLs safely with the URL and URLSearchParams classes. Then you learn the History API, which lets a page change the address bar without loading a new page. Finally you combine them into a router: a small piece of code that looks at the URL, picks a view and renders it, so one HTML page behaves like a whole website.

Why it matters

Think about the Ralfiz Store. A customer filters to “Audio, under ₹5,000, top rated” and sends the link to a colleague. If the filters live only in JavaScript variables, the colleague sees the default page. If they live in the query string, the colleague sees exactly the same list. The same is true for the open tab on a settings page, the page number of an invoice list, or the step in a checkout.

Users also expect the Back button to work. In a single-page app nothing is loaded from the server when the view changes, so the browser does not know that “a page change” happened unless you tell it with history.pushState. Get this wrong and Back throws the user out of your app. Get it right and your app feels like a normal website, which is also what search engines and screen-reader users expect.

Every front-end framework has a router (React Router, the Next.js App Router, Vue Router). They are all built on the same browser APIs you learn here, so understanding them makes framework routing much less magical.

How it works

Reading a URL with the URL object

Never take a URL apart with split('?') and string slicing if you can avoid it. The URL constructor parses an address exactly as the browser does and gives you named parts. It throws a TypeError for anything that is not a full URL, so wrap user input in try/catch, or check first with URL.canParse(). Pass a second argument, the base, to resolve relative addresses the way links in a page are resolved.

const url = new URL('https://shop.ralfiz.dev/products?cat=audio#reviews');
url.origin;    // 'https://shop.ralfiz.dev'  (protocol + host + port)
url.pathname;  // '/products'
url.search;    // '?cat=audio'
url.hash;      // '#reviews'

new URL('../cart', 'https://shop.ralfiz.dev/store/products/42').href;
// 'https://shop.ralfiz.dev/store/cart'

Run the example below and change the address. Notice that searchParams is live: when you call set or delete, url.href changes too, with every special character encoded for you.

Try it: Take a URL apart and build a new one

JavaScript

const url = new URL(
  'https://shop.ralfiz.dev/products?cat=audio&sort=price-asc&tag=new&tag=sale#reviews'
);

console.log('origin:  ', url.origin);
console.log('pathname:', url.pathname);
console.log('search:  ', url.search);
console.log('hash:    ', url.hash);

const params = url.searchParams;        // a live view of url.search
console.log(params.get('cat'), params.get('page'));   // missing key → null
console.log(params.getAll('tag'));
console.log(Object.fromEntries(params)); // repeated keys: the last one wins

params.set('page', '2');
params.delete('tag');
params.append('q', 'noise cancelling & wireless');
console.log(url.href);                   // spaces become + and & becomes %26

// Relative URLs are resolved against a base, like links in a page
const base = 'https://shop.ralfiz.dev/store/products/42';
console.log(new URL('reviews', base).href);
console.log(new URL('../cart', base).href);
console.log(new URL('/help', base).href);

console.log(URL.canParse('/cart'), URL.canParse('/cart', base));
try {
  new URL('/cart');                      // no base → not a full URL
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name + ':', err.message);
}

Change the address in the first line, run again and watch every part update. Notice how set, append and delete rewrite the query string with the right encoding.

Query strings with URLSearchParams

The query string is a list of key and value pairs. URLSearchParams is the right tool to read and write it. You can build one from a string, from location.search, from an object or from a form with new URLSearchParams(new FormData(form)).

MethodWhat it doesWatch out
get(key)First value for the keyReturns null when missing, '' when empty
getAll(key)Every value, as an arrayUse for filters like ?tag=new&tag=sale
set(key, v)Replace all values with oneValues become strings
append(key, v)Add another valueCreates repeated keys
delete(key) / has(key)Remove or test a key
toString()Encode back to a=1&b=2No leading ?; spaces become +

Every value that comes out of a URL is a string typed by a stranger. Anyone can edit the address bar, so treat query values like form input: convert them, check them against an allow-list, and fall back to a default. Never put them into innerHTML.

const params = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const SORTS = ['featured', 'price-asc', 'price-desc'];
const sort = SORTS.includes(params.get('sort')) ? params.get('sort') : 'featured';
const page = Math.max(1, Number.parseInt(params.get('page'), 10) || 1);

location: the page’s own address

location is the URL of the current document, with the same parts as a URL object (location.pathname, location.search, location.hash). Some of its operations navigate:

  • location.href = '/login' or location.assign('/login') loads a new page and adds a history entry.
  • location.replace('/login') loads a new page and replaces the current entry, so Back skips it. Use it for redirects.
  • location.reload() reloads the page.
  • location.hash = '#/about' does not load anything. It adds a history entry and fires popstate and then hashchange. Hash routing is built on this.

Filters in the URL

Here is the pattern used by most real product lists: the URL is the single source of truth. A click does not change a variable; it writes the URL, and render() reads the state back from the URL. Because of that, refresh, Back, Forward and a shared link all show the same view with no extra code. Two details make it pleasant: default values are left out, so URLs stay short, and the search box uses replaceState, so typing “buds” does not create four history entries.

Try it: Filters that live in the URL

HTML

<div class="shop">
  <header class="top">
    <span class="logo">R</span><strong>Ralfiz Store</strong>
    <span class="crumb">/ Products</span>
  </header>
  <div class="bar">
    <div class="chips" id="cats" role="group" aria-label="Category">
      <button data-cat="all">All</button>
      <button data-cat="laptops">Laptops</button>

        <option value="featured">Featured</option>
        <option value="price-asc">Price: low to high</option>

        <option value="rating">Top rated</option>

JavaScript

const PRODUCTS = [
  { title: 'Ralfiz Book 14', cat: 'laptops', price: 64990, rating: 4.6, icon: '💻' },
  { title: 'Ralfiz Book Air', cat: 'laptops', price: 82990, rating: 4.8, icon: '💻' },
  { title: 'Pulse Buds', cat: 'audio', price: 2499, rating: 4.2, icon: '🎧' },
  { title: 'Studio Cans', cat: 'audio', price: 7999, rating: 4.7, icon: '🎧' },
  { title: 'Mini Speaker', cat: 'audio', price: 1899, rating: 3.9, icon: '🔊' },
  { title: 'Ralfiz One', cat: 'phones', price: 29999, rating: 4.4, icon: '📱' },
  { title: 'Ralfiz One Pro', cat: 'phones', price: 45999, rating: 4.5, icon: '📱' },
];
const DEFAULTS = { cat: 'all', sort: 'featured', q: '' };
const CATS = ['all', 'laptops', 'audio', 'phones'];
const SORTS = ['featured', 'price-asc', 'price-desc', 'rating'];
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN',
  { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0 });
// The playground page lives at about:srcdoc, so build full URLs.
// On a real site you can pass '#/products?...' (or '/products?...') directly.
const hashUrl = (hash) => location.href.split('#')[0] + hash;

// The URL is the single source of truth: #/products?cat=audio&sort=rating
function readState() {
  const params = new URLSearchParams(location.hash.split('?')[1] ?? '');
  const cat = params.get('cat');
  const sort = params.get('sort');
  return {                                   // never trust URL input blindly
    cat: CATS.includes(cat) ? cat : DEFAULTS.cat,
    sort: SORTS.includes(sort) ? sort : DEFAULTS.sort,
    q: (params.get('q') ?? '').slice(0, 40),
  };
}

function writeState(patch, { replace = false } = {}) {
  const next = { ...readState(), ...patch };
  const params = new URLSearchParams();
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(next)) {
    if (value !== DEFAULTS[key]) params.set(key, value); // short, clean URLs
  }
  const qs = params.toString();
  const url = hashUrl('#/products' + (qs ? '?' + qs : ''));
  history[replace ? 'replaceState' : 'pushState'](null, '', url);
  render();
}

function render() {
  const { cat, sort, q } = readState();
  document.querySelectorAll('#cats button').forEach((b) =>
    b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(b.dataset.cat === cat)));
  document.querySelector('#sort').value = sort;
  const search = document.querySelector('#q');
  if (document.activeElement !== search) search.value = q;

  let items = PRODUCTS.filter((p) =>
    (cat === 'all' || p.cat === cat) &&
    p.title.toLowerCase().includes(q.toLowerCase()));
  if (sort === 'price-asc') items = items.toSorted((a, b) => a.price - b.price);
  if (sort === 'price-desc') items = items.toSorted((a, b) => b.price - a.price);
  if (sort === 'rating') items = items.toSorted((a, b) => b.rating - a.rating);

  const grid = document.querySelector('#grid');
  grid.replaceChildren(...items.map(card));
  if (!items.length) grid.innerHTML = '<li class="empty">No products match.</li>';
  document.querySelector('#count').textContent = items.length + ' products';
  document.querySelector('#link').textContent =
    'https://shop.ralfiz.dev/' + location.hash;
}

function card(p) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.className = 'card';
  li.innerHTML = '<div class="art"></div><h3></h3><p><strong></strong><span></span></p>';
  li.querySelector('.art').textContent = p.icon;
  li.querySelector('h3').textContent = p.title;       // data → textContent
  li.querySelector('strong').textContent = inr.format(p.price);
  li.querySelector('span').textContent = '★ ' + p.rating;
  return li;
}

document.querySelector('#cats').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const btn = e.target.closest('button[data-cat]');
  if (btn) writeState({ cat: btn.dataset.cat });            // a new entry
});
document.querySelector('#sort').addEventListener('change', (e) =>
  writeState({ sort: e.target.value }));
document.querySelector('#q').addEventListener('input', (e) =>
  writeState({ q: e.target.value.trim() }, { replace: true })); // no entry per key
addEventListener('popstate', render);                        // Back / Forward

// Pretend the user opened a link a colleague shared:
if (!location.hash) {
  history.replaceState(null, '', hashUrl('#/products?cat=audio&sort=price-asc'));
}
render();
console.log('State from URL:', readState());

Click a chip, change the sort or type in search. The address bar and the share link update; use the page’s Back arrow in the toolbar or reload, and the same view comes back from the URL.

pushState, replaceState and popstate

The History API keeps a stack of entries for the tab. Each entry has a URL and an optional state object (anything structuredClone can copy, such as { step: 2 }).

history.pushState({ step: 2 }, '', '/checkout/payment'); // new entry
history.replaceState({ step: 2, speed: 'express' }, '', location.href); // same entry
history.state;   // the state of the current entry
history.back();  // like the Back button; history.go(-2) jumps two
addEventListener('popstate', (event) => render(event.state));

Three rules explain almost every History API bug:

  1. pushState and replaceState never load a page and never fire popstate. You change the URL, and then you render yourself.
  2. popstate fires when the user (or your code) moves through history with Back, Forward, history.back() or history.go(), and also when the hash changes through a #link click or location.hash. Its event.state is the state you stored for the entry being shown (null for a new hash entry).
  3. The new URL must be the same origin, or the call throws a SecurityError. The second argument (title) is ignored by browsers; pass ''.

The checkout below stores the step in each history entry. Continue pushes; Back calls history.back(), and the render happens in the popstate listener. The delivery speed uses replaceState, because changing an option should not create a new Back step.

Try it: Checkout steps with pushState and popstate

    <li>Cart</li><li>Address</li><li>Payment</li><li>Done</li>

</div>

JavaScript

const STEPS = [
  { slug: 'cart', title: 'Your cart', text: '2 items · Pulse Buds and Mini Speaker' },
  { slug: 'address', title: 'Delivery address', text: 'Ralfiz Towers, Perinthalmanna, Kerala' },
  { slug: 'payment', title: 'Payment', text: 'UPI ending •• 4821' },
  { slug: 'done', title: 'Order placed 🎉', text: 'Order #RZ-2481 is on its way.' },
];
const $ = (s) => document.querySelector(s);
// Playground pages live at about:srcdoc, so build full URLs from it.
const hashUrl = (hash) => location.href.split('#')[0] + hash;

function log(kind, detail) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.innerHTML = '<b></b> ';
  li.firstChild.textContent = kind;
  li.append(detail + '  · history.length = ' + history.length);
  $('#log').prepend(li);
}

function render(state, moveFocus = true) {
  const step = state?.step ?? 0;
  const speed = state?.speed ?? 'standard';
  const s = STEPS[step];
  $('#heading').textContent = s.title;
  $('#body').textContent = s.text;
  document.querySelectorAll('#steps li').forEach((li, i) => {
    li.classList.toggle('done', i < step);
    if (i === step) li.setAttribute('aria-current', 'step');
    else li.removeAttribute('aria-current');
  });
  document.querySelectorAll('[data-speed]').forEach((b) =>
    b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(b.dataset.speed === speed)));
  $('.speed').hidden = step !== 1;
  $('#back').disabled = step === 0;
  $('#next').hidden = step === STEPS.length - 1;
  document.title = s.title + ' · Ralfiz Store';
  if (moveFocus) $('#heading').focus();  // announce the new step
}

$('#next').addEventListener('click', () => {
  const step = (history.state?.step ?? 0) + 1;
  const state = { ...history.state, step };
  history.pushState(state, '', hashUrl('#/checkout/' + STEPS[step].slug));
  log('pushState', JSON.stringify(state));
  render(state);                         // pushState never fires popstate
});

$('#back').addEventListener('click', () => {
  if ((history.state?.step ?? 0) > 0) history.back();   // popstate does the render
});

$('.speed').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const btn = e.target.closest('[data-speed]');
  if (!btn) return;
  const state = { ...history.state, speed: btn.dataset.speed };
  history.replaceState(state, '', location.href);         // same entry, new state
  log('replaceState', JSON.stringify(state));
  render(state);
});

addEventListener('popstate', (event) => {
  log('popstate', JSON.stringify(event.state));
  render(event.state);
});

history.replaceState({ step: 0, speed: 'standard' }, '', hashUrl('#/checkout/cart'));
render(history.state, false);            // no focus jump on first load
log('start', JSON.stringify(history.state));

Press Continue twice, then Back. Each step is a real history entry, so the address bar and the event log follow along. Switching the delivery speed uses replaceState and adds no entry.

Remember: playground pages run in a sandboxed frame whose address is about:srcdoc, so the plays push #hash URLs built from location.href (a small hashUrl() helper). On your own site you simply write history.pushState(state, '', '/checkout/payment'); the lab does that.

Hash routing vs history routing

Change the viewlocation.hash = '#/courses/2' or a plain <a href="#/courses/2">history.pushState plus a click handler on links
Listenhashchangepopstate
Server setupNone: the server only ever sees /Needs an SPA fallback that returns index.html for every route
URLsLook technical; the part after # is never sent to the serverClean, and pages can be rendered on the server for SEO

A 30-line router

A router needs only four jobs: match the path against a table of routes, extract params such as the :id in /courses/:id, render the view, and re-run whenever the URL changes. The trick for params is to compile each pattern into a regular expression once: /courses/:id becomes ^/courses/([^/]+)$ and remembers that group 1 is called id.

A good router also does the small things a normal page load gives you for free: it updates document.title, marks the current nav link with aria-current="page", and moves focus to the new content so keyboard and screen-reader users know the page changed. Views build elements with a tiny h() helper, so data always goes in as text, never as HTML.

JavaScript

const COURSES = [
  { id: 'js', icon: '🟨', name: 'JavaScript: Zero to Job-Ready', lessons: 31, level: 'Beginner' },
  { id: 'dom', icon: '🧩', name: 'DOM & Browser', lessons: 24, level: 'Beginner' },
  { id: 'flutter', icon: '🦋', name: 'Flutter Apps', lessons: 40, level: 'Intermediate' },
  { id: 'pbi', icon: '📊', name: 'Power BI in Practice', lessons: 18, level: 'Beginner' },
];

// Tiny helper: build elements safely (text goes in with textContent)
function h(tag, props = {}, ...kids) {
  const el = Object.assign(document.createElement(tag), props);
  el.append(...kids);
  return el;
}

const home = () => h('section', {},
  h('h1', {}, 'Learn by building'),
  h('p', { className: 'lead' }, 'Short lessons, live code and real projects.'),
  h('a', { className: 'btn', href: '#/courses' }, 'Browse courses'));

const courses = () => h('section', {},
  h('h1', {}, 'Courses'),
  h('div', { className: 'grid' }, ...COURSES.map((c) =>
    h('a', { className: 'course', href: '#/courses/' + c.id },
      h('span', { className: 'ico' }, c.icon), h('h2', {}, c.name),
      h('p', {}, c.lessons + ' lessons · ' + c.level)))));

function course({ id }) {
  const c = COURSES.find((x) => x.id === id);
  if (!c) return notFound();
  return h('section', {}, h('h1', {}, c.icon + ' ' + c.name),
    h('p', {}, h('span', { className: 'pill' }, c.level),
      h('span', { className: 'pill' }, c.lessons + ' lessons')),
    h('p', { className: 'lead' }, 'Route param id = "' + id + '"'),
    h('a', { href: '#/courses' }, '← All courses'));
}
const about = () => h('section', {}, h('h1', {}, 'About'),
  h('p', { className: 'lead' }, 'Ralfiz Academy is the training arm of Ralfiz Technologies.'));
const notFound = () => h('section', {}, h('h1', {}, 'Page not found'),
  h('p', { className: 'lead' }, 'Nothing lives at ' + location.hash), h('a', { href: '#/' }, 'Go home'));

// ---- the router: about 30 lines ----
const routes = [
  { path: '/', view: home, title: 'Home' },
  { path: '/courses', view: courses, title: 'Courses' },
  { path: '/courses/:id', view: course, title: 'Course' },
  { path: '/about', view: about, title: 'About' },
];
function compile(path) {                     // '/courses/:id' → /^\/courses\/([^/]+)$/
  const keys = [];
  const source = path.replace(/:(\w+)/g, (_, key) => { keys.push(key); return '([^/]+)'; });
  return { re: new RegExp('^' + source + '$'), keys };
}
routes.forEach((r) => Object.assign(r, compile(r.path)));

function match(pathname) {
  for (const route of routes) {
    const m = pathname.match(route.re);
    if (m) {
      const params = Object.fromEntries(
        route.keys.map((k, i) => [k, decodeURIComponent(m[i + 1])]));
      return { route, params };
    }
  }
  return null;
}

function router(event) {
  const [pathname] = (location.hash.slice(1) || '/').split('?');
  const found = match(pathname);
  const view = document.querySelector('#view');
  view.replaceChildren(found ? found.route.view(found.params) : notFound());
  document.title = (found?.route.title ?? 'Not found') + ' · Ralfiz Academy';
  document.querySelectorAll('[data-nav]').forEach((a) => {
    const here = a.getAttribute('href').slice(1) === pathname;
    if (here) a.setAttribute('aria-current', 'page');
    else a.removeAttribute('aria-current');
  });
  if (event) view.focus();          // after navigation: announce the new page
  console.log('route', pathname, found?.params ?? '(404)');
}

addEventListener('hashchange', router);
// Start on #/courses (the playground page URL is about:srcdoc)
if (!location.hash) history.replaceState(null, '', location.href + '#/courses');
router();

Click the nav links and a course card, then use the toolbar Back arrow. Try typing #/courses/99 or #/nope after the address in the code and run again to see the 404 view.

Example: Ralfiz Academy with a history router

The lab turns the hash router into a history router with clean paths. The route table, compile and match stay the same. Only three things change: links, the listener and the server.

// 1. Links: one delegated listener turns clicks into pushState
document.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const link = event.target.closest('a[data-to]');
  if (!link) return;
  // Let Ctrl/Cmd-click, Shift-click and middle-click open a new tab
  if (event.button !== 0 || event.metaKey || event.ctrlKey || event.shiftKey) return;
  event.preventDefault();
  navigate(link.dataset.to);
});

function navigate(path, { replace = false } = {}) {
  const url = toUrl(path);                  // adds the app's base folder
  if (url === location.pathname + location.search) return; // no duplicate entry
  history[replace ? 'replaceState' : 'pushState']({}, '', url);
  render();
}

// 2. Back and Forward
addEventListener('popstate', render);

3. The server. In-app clicks never reach the server, but a refresh on /courses/js does: the browser asks the server for that path. A plain static server has no such file and answers 404. The fix is an SPA fallback: npx serve -s, Vite’s dev server, Netlify and Vercel rewrites, or an Nginx try_files $uri /index.html; rule all return index.html for unknown paths. The lab README walks through it, including the second trap: relative asset paths such as app.js resolve to /courses/app.js on a nested route, so production apps use root-absolute paths (/app.js).

Common mistakes

  • Building query strings by hand. '?q=' + term breaks when the term contains &, # or a space. 
    // Wrong: 'a&b' becomes two parameters
fetch('/api/search?q=' + term);
// Right
fetch('/api/search?' + new URLSearchParams({ q: term }));
  • Expecting pushState to fire popstate. Nothing re-renders, so the URL changes but the page does not. 
    // Wrong
history.pushState({}, '', '/about');   // and wait for popstate…
// Right
history.pushState({}, '', '/about');
render();
  • Pushing on every keystroke. Ten letters means ten Back presses. Use replaceState for typing and sliders, and pushState for real navigation. 
    // Wrong: one history entry per letter
search.addEventListener('input', () => {
  history.pushState({}, '', '#/search?' + new URLSearchParams({ q: search.value }));
});
// Right: replace the current entry while typing
search.addEventListener('input', () => {
  history.replaceState({}, '', '#/search?' + new URLSearchParams({ q: search.value }));
});
  • Trusting query values. Number(params.get('page')) is 0 for a missing key and NaN for ?page=abc. Validate and fall back to a default. 
    // Wrong: 0 or NaN slips into your fetch
const page = Number(params.get('page'));
// Right: validate, then fall back
const n = Number.parseInt(params.get('page') ?? '', 10);
const page = Number.isInteger(n) && n > 0 ? n : 1;
  • Hijacking every click. A router that calls preventDefault on Ctrl-click, on external links or on download links breaks normal browser behaviour. Mark your internal links (data-to) and leave the rest alone. 
    // Wrong: every link, every kind of click
document.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const a = e.target.closest('a');
  if (a) { e.preventDefault(); navigate(a.href); }
});
// Right: plain left clicks on your own links only
document.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const a = e.target.closest('a[data-to]');
  if (!a || e.button !== 0 || e.ctrlKey || e.metaKey || e.shiftKey) return;
  e.preventDefault();
  navigate(a.getAttribute('href'));
});

Interview and real-world notes

  • “How does client-side routing work?” Intercept internal link clicks, call history.pushState, render the matching view, and listen for popstate for Back and Forward. The server needs a fallback to index.html.
  • Hash vs history: the hash is never sent to the server, so hash routing needs no server setup; history routing gives clean URLs and allows server rendering.
  • What belongs in the URL: anything a user may want to share or return to (filters, sort, page, tab, selected item). Temporary UI state (a hover, an open tooltip) does not.
  • Scroll restoration: browsers restore scroll on Back by default (history.scrollRestoration = 'auto'). Routers often set it to 'manual' and restore scroll themselves after rendering.
  • Newer API: the Navigation API (navigation.addEventListener('navigate', …)) is designed to replace the pushState/popstate pattern with one event. Check the MDN compatibility table and caniuse.com before relying on it; the History API works everywhere.

Answers

  1. C. get() returns the first value for a repeated key and getAll() returns all of them. toString() uses form encoding, where a space becomes +.
  2. A. Relative URLs resolve like links: ../ goes up from the folder /store/products/ to /store/, a leading slash starts at the origin, and a bare ?query keeps the path.
  3. D. An empty value gives '' and a missing key gives null, and Number() turns both into 0. Only ?? notices the null, so validate query values instead of converting them blindly.

An object that reads and writes the query string (?a=1&b=2), handling encoding and repeated keys for you.
The current page’s URL as an object. Setting location.href or calling location.assign() loads a new page; changing location.hash does not.
Adds a new history entry with a state object and a same-origin URL, without loading a page or firing popstate.
The event fired on window when the active history entry changes because of Back, Forward, history.back()/go() or a same-page hash change. pushState and replaceState never fire it.
Code that maps the current URL to a view and renders it in the page, instead of asking the server for a new HTML page.
A server rule that returns index.html for any unknown path, so deep links to client-side routes work on refresh.

lessons.title: Observers: Intersection, Resize and Mutation
lessons.summaryHtml:
Observers let the browser tell you when something changes, instead of you checking again and again. IntersectionObserver reports when an element enters or leaves the viewport (or another scroll box), which powers lazy loading, infinite scroll and reveal-on-scroll effects without scroll listeners.

ResizeObserver reports when an element’s own size changes, so a component can adapt to the space it is given rather than to the window. MutationObserver reports changes to the DOM tree itself: added or removed nodes, attributes and text.

All three share one shape: create the observer with a callback, observe() targets, receive batched entries asynchronously, and unobserve() or disconnect() when you are done. For images, the native loading="lazy" attribute is usually all you need.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

An observer is a helper you hire to watch something and tap you on the shoulder when it changes. You do not stand there asking “has it changed yet?” every few milliseconds. The browser has three of these helpers for the DOM:

  • IntersectionObserver watches whether an element is on screen (or inside a scroll box), and how much of it is showing.
  • ResizeObserver watches an element’s size.
  • MutationObserver watches the DOM tree: nodes added or removed, attributes and text changed.

With them you build lazy loading, infinite feeds, scroll animations, components that adapt to their container, and code that reacts to DOM changes made by someone else’s script.

Why it matters

Before observers, developers listened to scroll and resize events and called getBoundingClientRect() on every card, on every event. A scroll can fire many events per second, and each geometry read may force the browser to recalculate layout. On a product feed with a hundred cards, that is how you get a janky page and a bad INP score on a mid-range phone.

Observers flip the model. The browser already computes layout and visibility while rendering, so it can tell you about changes at the right moment, in one batch, without extra layout work in your code. The result is smoother pages and simpler code: “when the last card is near the screen, load more” is five lines.

How it works

One pattern, three observers

All three follow the same life cycle, so learn it once:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver(callback, options); // 1. create
observer.observe(element);         // 2. start watching one or more targets
function callback(entries, obs) {  // 3. called later with a batch of entries
  for (const entry of entries) { /* entry.target is the element */ }
}
observer.unobserve(element);       // 4a. stop watching one target
observer.disconnect();             // 4b. stop watching everything
IntersectionObserverResizeObserverMutationObserver
WatchesVisibility inside a rootAn element’s box sizeDOM changes under a node
Callback getsIntersectionObserverEntry[]ResizeObserverEntry[]MutationRecord[]
When it runsDuring rendering, after a threshold is crossedDuring rendering, after layout, before paintIn a microtask after the change
Fires on observe?Yes, once, with the current stateYes, once, if the size is not 0×0No
Typical useLazy load, infinite scroll, reveal, analytics “seen”Charts, responsive components, text fittingReacting to third-party DOM, editors, auto-scrolling logs

IntersectionObserver: root, rootMargin and threshold

Three options shape an IntersectionObserver. root is the box you measure against; leave it out (or null) for the viewport, or pass a scrolling container. rootMargin grows or shrinks that box using CSS margin syntax: '0px 0px 300px 0px' means “pretend the viewport is 300px taller at the bottom”, so loading starts before the user arrives. threshold is how much of the target must be visible: 0 means any pixel, 1 means all of it, and an array like [0, 0.5, 1] calls you at each point.

Each entry has isIntersecting (the useful yes or no), intersectionRatio (0 to 1), boundingClientRect, rootBounds and time. You get geometry for free, already measured.

Infinite scroll with a sentinel

Put an empty element, the sentinel, after the list and observe it. When it intersects, fetch the next page with limit and skip. Three guards make it production-ready: a loading flag so a fast scroll cannot fire two requests, a check that stops when skip >= total, and disconnect() at the end. There is one subtle bug to avoid: the callback runs only when the intersection changes. If the new page is short and the sentinel never leaves the screen, you are never called again. Re-observing the sentinel after each load (unobserve then observe) gives you a fresh initial callback.

const feed = document.querySelector('#feed');
const sentinel = document.querySelector('#sentinel');
const status = document.querySelector('#status');
const PAGE = 12;
let skip = 0;
let total = Infinity;
let loading = false;
const usd = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' });

// The playground cannot load outside images, so each product gets a tiny
// SVG "photo". On a real page use img.src = p.thumbnail instead.
const ICONS = { beauty: '💄', fragrances: '🌸', furniture: '🛋️', groceries: '🥑',
  laptops: '💻', smartphones: '📱', 'home-decoration': '🪴', 'kitchen-accessories': '🍳' };
const TINTS = ['#fde68a', '#bfdbfe', '#fbcfe8', '#bbf7d0', '#ddd6fe', '#fed7aa'];
function art(p) {
  const svg = `<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="160" height="120">
    <rect width="160" height="120" fill="${TINTS[p.id % TINTS.length]}"/>
    <text x="80" y="76" font-size="44" text-anchor="middle">${ICONS[p.category] ?? '🛍️'}</text></svg>`;
  return 'data:image/svg+xml,' + encodeURIComponent(svg);
}

function card(p) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.className = 'card';
  const img = Object.assign(document.createElement('img'), {
    alt: p.title, width: 160, height: 120,    // reserves space: no layout shift
    loading: 'lazy', decoding: 'async',        // native lazy loading
  });
  img.src = art(p);
  const body = document.createElement('div');
  body.innerHTML = '<h3></h3><p><b></b><span></span></p>';
  body.querySelector('h3').textContent = p.title;
  body.querySelector('b').textContent = usd.format(p.price);
  body.querySelector('span').textContent = '★ ' + p.rating.toFixed(1);
  li.append(img, body);
  return li;
}

async function loadMore() {
  if (loading || skip >= total) return;       // one request at a time
  loading = true;
  const skeletons = Array.from({ length: 4 }, () =>
    Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { className: 'card skeleton' }));
  feed.append(...skeletons);
  try {
    const res = await fetch(
      `https://dummyjson.com/products?limit=${PAGE}&skip=${skip}&select=title,price,rating,category`);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status);
    const data = await res.json();
    total = data.total;
    skip += data.products.length;
    skeletons.forEach((s) => s.remove());
    feed.append(...data.products.map(card));
    status.textContent = `${skip} of ${total}`;
    console.log(`Loaded ${data.products.length} more (skip was ${skip - data.products.length})`);
    if (skip >= total) {
      observer.disconnect();                  // nothing left to watch
      sentinel.textContent = `You have seen all ${total} products ✨`;
    }
  } catch (err) {
    skeletons.forEach((s) => s.remove());
    sentinel.textContent = 'Could not load products. ';
    const retry = Object.assign(document.createElement('button'), { textContent: 'Retry' });
    retry.onclick = () => { sentinel.textContent = ''; loadMore(); };
    sentinel.append(retry);
    console.warn('Feed failed:', err.message);
  } finally {
    loading = false;
  }
  // Still visible after the new cards? Re-observing gives a fresh callback.
  if (skip < total) { observer.unobserve(sentinel); observer.observe(sentinel); }
}

const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  if (entries[0].isIntersecting) loadMore();
}, { rootMargin: '0px 0px 300px 0px' });     // start 300px before the end
observer.observe(sentinel);

Scroll inside the page. The next 12 products load before you reach the bottom; skeleton cards show while the request runs, and the observer disconnects at the end.

For accessibility, infinite scroll hides the footer and makes “go back to item 40” hard. Many shops add a visible Load more button as well, and keep the page number in the URL (dm13), so Back returns to the same place.

Lazy-loading images

For images and iframes you rarely need an observer: loading="lazy" is built into every modern browser. The browser loads the file when the element comes near the viewport, with its own distance rules tuned for the connection. Always set width and height (or a CSS aspect-ratio) so the space is reserved and nothing jumps when the image arrives; that jump is counted in CLS.

<img src="/img/buds-640.webp" alt="Pulse Buds in charging case"
     width="640" height="480" loading="lazy" decoding="async">

<!-- The hero image is the LCP element: load it eagerly and early -->
<img src="/img/hero.webp" alt="Ralfiz POS on a shop counter"
     width="1200" height="600" fetchpriority="high">

Do not lazy-load images that are visible on first paint. It delays your Largest Contentful Paint. Use an IntersectionObserver version (swap data-src into src) only when you need custom behaviour, such as lazy-loading CSS backgrounds or starting a video.

Reveal on scroll

Scroll animations follow the same pattern: observe each block with threshold: 0.15, add a class when it intersects, and unobserve it so the work is done once. Two details separate a professional version from a tutorial one. First, hide elements only when JavaScript runs (.js .reveal), so the content is never lost if a script fails. Second, respect prefers-reduced-motion: people who turn motion off still see the content, just without the slide.

ResizeObserver: components that know their own size

Media queries answer “how wide is the window?”. A dashboard widget needs a different question: “how wide is my box?”. The same card can sit in a narrow sidebar and in a wide main column on the same screen. ResizeObserver reports the element’s box whenever it changes, for any reason: a window resize, a sidebar collapsing, a font loading or a user dragging a handle.

const ro = new ResizeObserver((entries) => {
  for (const entry of entries) {
    const { inlineSize, blockSize } = entry.contentBoxSize[0]; // width, height
    entry.target.dataset.size = inlineSize < 280 ? 'sm' : 'lg';
  }
});
ro.observe(document.querySelector('.widget'));

Use contentBoxSize (or the older contentRect) for the inside size and borderBoxSize when borders and padding matter. Canvas charts (dm16) use ResizeObserver to redraw at the new size. For pure styling, CSS container queries (container-type: inline-size and @container (width < 280px)) now do this without JavaScript; reach for ResizeObserver when you need to run code, such as redrawing a chart or choosing how many items fit.

MutationObserver: watching the DOM itself

MutationObserver tells you when the DOM changes, whoever changed it. That is its real value: reacting to markup you do not control, such as a chat widget, a CMS embed or a rich-text editor. You choose what to watch with options:

OptionReports
childList: trueChildren added or removed (addedNodes, removedNodes)
attributes: true, attributeFilter: ['data-read']Attribute changes, optionally only the listed ones
characterData: trueText node content changes
subtree: trueThe same, for every descendant, not only direct children
attributeOldValue, characterDataOldValueInclude the previous value in the record

Records are delivered in one batch, as a microtask after the current script. Ten appends in a loop give one callback with ten records, so do one piece of work per batch (update the badge once), not per record. takeRecords() hands you the pending records immediately, which is useful right before disconnect().

document.querySelector('#readall').onclick = () =>
  inbox.querySelectorAll('li').forEach((li) => { li.dataset.read = 'true'; });
document.querySelector('#pause').onclick = (e) => {
  const paused = e.currentTarget.getAttribute('aria-pressed') !== 'true';
  e.currentTarget.setAttribute('aria-pressed', paused);
  if (paused) {
    observer.disconnect();
    log('observer paused: changes are not tracked');
  } else {
    observer.observe(inbox, options);
    updateBadge();                            // catch up on what we missed
    log('observer resumed');
  }
};

// Three tickets arrive in one go, then more over time
chatWidget.push(); chatWidget.push(); chatWidget.push();
setTimeout(() => chatWidget.push(), 700);
setTimeout(() => chatWidget.push(), 1400);
console.log('Watching', inbox.id, 'with', options);

New tickets are added by a “third-party” widget we do not control. The observer notices each insertion and each read flag, and updates the badge and the log. Click a ticket to mark it read, or pause the observer.

MutationObserver has a cost. Observing document.body with subtree: true and characterData: true means the browser creates a record for every text change on the page. Observe the smallest node you can, filter attributes, and never use a MutationObserver to react to changes your own code just made: call your update function directly instead.

Disconnecting and memory

An observer keeps doing work, and keeps its callback and everything that callback closes over, for as long as it is observing. In a single-page app, a view that is removed but never cleaned up can leave observers running and, depending on the observer type and the browser, keep its nodes and closures alive. Call unobserve when you are done with an element (after revealing it), disconnect() when the component is destroyed (for example in a Web Component’s disconnectedCallback, dm23), and pass an AbortSignal to event listeners you add next to it.

Example: the Ralfiz Store infinite feed

The lab combines all three ideas in one page. The feed loads 12 real DummyJSON products at a time with a sentinel; images use loading="lazy" with width and height; each new card fades in through a second IntersectionObserver; and a ResizeObserver on the grid switches to compact cards in a narrow space.

const feedObserver = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
  if (entry.isIntersecting) loadMore();
}, { rootMargin: '0px 0px 400px 0px' });
feedObserver.observe(sentinel);

const revealObserver = new IntersectionObserver((entries, obs) => {
  for (const e of entries) {
    if (e.isIntersecting) { e.target.classList.add('in'); obs.unobserve(e.target); }
  }
}, { threshold: 0.15 });

function addCards(products) {
  const cards = products.map(card);
  grid.append(...cards);
  cards.forEach((c) => revealObserver.observe(c));
}

new ResizeObserver(([entry]) => {
  const width = entry.contentBoxSize[0].inlineSize;
  grid.dataset.size = width < 520 ? 'compact' : 'regular';
}).observe(grid);

Common mistakes

  • Using a scroll listener for visibility. 
    // Wrong: layout work on every scroll event
addEventListener('scroll', () => {
  if (sentinel.getBoundingClientRect().top < innerHeight) loadMore();
});
// Right
new IntersectionObserver(([e]) => e.isIntersecting && loadMore()).observe(sentinel);
  • Forgetting that the first callback is immediate. IntersectionObserver calls you once on observe(), even when the target is off screen. Always check entry.isIntersecting instead of assuming “called means visible”. 
    // Wrong: loads a page as soon as observe() runs
new IntersectionObserver(() => loadMore()).observe(sentinel);
// Right
new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  if (entries.some((e) => e.isIntersecting)) loadMore();
}).observe(sentinel);
  • Double requests. Without a loading flag, a quick scroll can call loadMore() twice with the same skip, and you render duplicate products. 
    // Wrong: nothing stops a second call while the first is in flight
async function loadMore() { render(await getPage(skip)); skip += PAGE; }
// Right: a guard flag, reset in finally
async function loadMore() {
  if (loading || skip >= total) return;
  loading = true;
  try { render(await getPage(skip)); skip += PAGE; }
  finally { loading = false; }
}
  • Lazy-loading the hero image. loading="lazy" on the first visible image makes the page feel slower. Lazy-load only what starts below the fold. 
    <!-- Wrong: the first thing users see waits for layout -->
<img src="hero.webp" loading="lazy" alt="Ralfiz POS on a counter">
<!-- Right: hero loads eagerly with high priority; cards lower down are lazy -->
<img src="hero.webp" fetchpriority="high" width="1200" height="600" alt="Ralfiz POS on a counter">
<img src="card.webp" loading="lazy" width="300" height="300" alt="Barcode scanner">
  • Observing too much. 
    // Wrong: every text change on the page creates a record
mo.observe(document.body, { subtree: true, childList: true, characterData: true });
// Right: the smallest node, only what you need
mo.observe(inbox, { childList: true });

Interview and real-world notes

  • “How would you lazy-load images?” Native loading="lazy" with width and height; IntersectionObserver for custom cases; never for the LCP image.
  • “How would you track that an ad or product was seen?” IntersectionObserver with threshold: 0.5, plus a timer that checks it stayed visible for a second, then unobserve.
  • ResizeObserver vs container queries: CSS for styles, ResizeObserver for code such as redrawing a canvas.
  • MutationObserver timing: microtask, batched. It replaced the old synchronous “mutation events” (DOMNodeInserted), which were slow, are deprecated and have already been removed from Chromium-based browsers. Never use them in new code.
  • All three observers are supported in every evergreen browser. Check the MDN compatibility tables for newer options such as IntersectionObserver v2 (trackVisibility), which is not available everywhere.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged, in order?

const list = document.createElement('ul');
const observer = new MutationObserver((records) => {
  console.log('records: ' + records.length);
});
observer.observe(list, { childList: true });

list.append(document.createElement('li'));
list.append(document.createElement('li'));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise'));
console.log('sync done');
  • A 
    records: 1
records: 1
sync done
promise
  • B 
    sync done
records: 2
promise
  • C 
    sync done
promise
records: 2
  • D 
    records: 2
sync done
promise

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const box = document.createElement('div');
const observer = new MutationObserver(() => console.log('callback'));
observer.observe(box, { attributes: true });

box.dataset.state = 'open';
box.className = 'panel';
const pending = observer.takeRecords();
observer.disconnect();

console.log(pending.length, pending[0].attributeName);
setTimeout(() => console.log('done'), 0);
  • A 
    callback
2 data-state
done
  • B 
    0 undefined
callback
done
  • C 
    1 class
done
  • D 
    2 data-state
done

Answers

  1. B. Mutation records are batched and delivered in a microtask. That microtask was queued at the first append, before the promise callback, so both records arrive together after the synchronous code and before promise.
  2. D. takeRecords() empties the queue and returns the two records, so the callback has nothing left to deliver, and disconnect() stops future ones. dataset.state is the data-state attribute.

quiz.question: Why is IntersectionObserver better than a scroll listener that calls getBoundingClientRect() on every card?
options: It works in older browsers only
The browser computes intersections off your scroll handler and calls you only when a threshold is crossed, so there is no layout work on every scroll event
It makes images download faster
It can see elements inside cross-origin iframes
quiz.explanation: Reading geometry on every scroll forces layout work on the main thread. The observer batches that work and calls you only when something meaningful changes.

quiz.question: An infinite list stops loading after the first page even though the sentinel is still on screen. What is the likely cause?
options: The threshold is 0
rootMargin must be negative
The callback runs only when intersection changes; the sentinel never left the viewport, so it was never reported again
fetch() is cached
quiz.explanation: Re-observe the sentinel (unobserve then observe) or check its position after each load, so a sentinel that stays visible triggers the next page.

quiz.question: A card component should switch to a compact layout when its own column is narrower than 320px, whatever the window size. Which tool fits best?

A resize listener on window
MutationObserver
quiz.explanation: Media queries and window resize events describe the viewport. ResizeObserver and container queries describe the element’s own box.

quiz.question: When does a MutationObserver callback run?
options: Synchronously, inside each DOM change
On the next animation frame
After a setTimeout of 0
In a microtask after the current script, with all the records collected so far
quiz.explanation: Mutation records are queued and delivered in one batch as a microtask, so ten appends in a row produce one callback with ten records.

lessons.title: Timers and animation
lessons.summaryHtml:
setTimeout and setInterval schedule work for later, but the delay is a minimum, not a promise: timers are clamped, drift, and slow down in background tabs. For anything the user watches, such as a countdown, calculate from a fixed end time instead of counting ticks.

For motion, use requestAnimationFrame, which runs your code right before the browser paints, and base movement on elapsed time so it looks the same at 60 Hz and 120 Hz. Most UI animation is best done in CSS, triggered by toggling a class, or with the Web Animations API (element.animate) when you need JavaScript control and a finished promise.

The FLIP technique (First, Last, Invert, Play) makes list reordering glide smoothly, and prefers-reduced-motion lets you respect users who turn motion off.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Web pages often need to do something later or smoothly: close a toast after three seconds, count down to the end of a flash sale, grow a number on a dashboard, or slide a list into its new order. This lesson covers the tools for time-based work in the browser and when to use each one.

  • Timers (setTimeout, setInterval) for “run this later”.
  • requestAnimationFrame for “run this before every paint” when JavaScript drives the motion.
  • CSS transitions and animations, triggered by adding a class, for most UI motion.
  • The Web Animations API (element.animate) when you need CSS-quality animation with JavaScript control.

Why it matters

Motion tells users what happened: an item flew into the cart, the list re-sorted, the order was saved. Timers drive real business features: session timeouts, OTP resend countdowns, auto-save, polling for new orders. Done badly, they cause real problems. A countdown that drifts shows the wrong time at the end of a sale. A setInterval animation stutters on a busy phone. An animation that changes top and width on every frame drops frames and hurts INP. And for people with vestibular disorders, large motion can cause dizziness, which is why prefers-reduced-motion exists.

How it works

setTimeout and setInterval: “at least”, not “exactly”

A timer asks the browser to queue a task after a delay. When that time comes, the callback still has to wait until the call stack is empty and all microtasks have run (js19). So the delay is a minimum. Several rules make it later still:

  • Clamping: after timers are nested five levels deep, the HTML standard forces a minimum of 4ms, so setTimeout(fn, 0) in a chain does not run every 0ms.
  • Background tabs: browsers throttle timers in hidden tabs, typically to at most once per second and sometimes much less often, to save battery.
  • Long tasks: if your code, or a big render, blocks the main thread for 150ms, every timer due in that window fires late.
  • Drift: setInterval promises a gap of at least the delay between runs, and each run can be late. Browsers do not make up for lost time, so counting ticks slowly adds up the error.

Both functions return an id. Keep it, and always clear timers you no longer need with clearTimeout(id) or clearInterval(id), especially when a component is removed, or you leak work and memory. Extra arguments after the delay are passed to the callback. Very large delays (above 2 ** 31 - 1 ms, about 24.8 days) overflow and fire immediately.

Try it: Timers: order, clearing and drift

JavaScript

console.log('1. script starts');
setTimeout(() => console.log('4. timeout 0 runs as a task, after microtasks'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3. microtask'));

const id = setTimeout(() => console.log('never logged'), 50);
clearTimeout(id);                               // cancelled before it fired

// Extra arguments are passed to the callback
setTimeout((name, qty) => console.log(`5. ${qty} × ${name} added`), 20, 'Pulse Buds', 2);
console.log('2. script ends');

// setInterval promises "about every 100ms", never exactly
const start = performance.now();
let tick = 0;
const timer = setInterval(() => {
  tick++;
  const expected = tick * 100;
  const actual = Math.round(performance.now() - start);
  console.log(`tick ${tick}: expected ${expected}ms, actual ${actual}ms (+${actual - expected})`);
  if (tick === 2) {
    const t = performance.now();
    while (performance.now() - t < 150) {}      // a long task: nothing else can run
    console.warn('tick 2 blocked the main thread for 150ms');
  }
  if (tick === 5) clearInterval(timer);
}, 100);

Read the numbered logs, then look at the ticks: each one is a little late, and tick 3 is very late because tick 2 blocked the main thread for 150ms.

A countdown that never drifts

The fix for drift is simple: never count ticks, always compute from a fixed end time. Store endAt = performance.now() + duration when the timer starts. On each tick compute remaining = endAt - performance.now() and display that. A late tick then shows the correct time; it just updates a little later. performance.now() is better than Date.now() here because it is monotonic: it never jumps when the computer clock is corrected. Use Date only when the end is a real calendar moment, such as “the sale ends at 23:59 IST”.

function tick() {
  const remaining = Math.max(0, endAt - performance.now());
  render(remaining);
  if (remaining === 0) return finish();
  // Schedule just after the next whole second, not a fixed 1000ms
  timer = setTimeout(tick, (remaining % 1000) + 5);
}

A recursive setTimeout like this is often better than setInterval: each wait is computed fresh, and a slow tick can never cause two ticks to pile up.

Try it: Focus timer that never drifts

HTML

  <div class="presets" role="group" aria-label="Session length">
    <button data-min="25" aria-pressed="true">Focus 25:00</button>
    <button data-min="5">Break 5:00</button>
    <button data-min="0.1667">Demo 0:10</button>
  </div>
  <div class="ring" id="ring">
    <div class="face">
      <output id="time" aria-live="off">25:00</output>
      <span id="label">Ready to focus</span>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="controls">
    <button id="toggle" class="primary">Start</button>
    <button id="reset" class="ghost">Reset</button>
  </div>
</main>

JavaScript

const $ = (s) => document.querySelector(s);
let duration = 25 * 60_000;      // ms for the chosen preset
let remaining = duration;        // ms left while paused
let endAt = null;                // performance.now() when time runs out (while running)
let timer = 0;

const fmt = (ms) => {
  const total = Math.ceil(ms / 1000);
  return String(Math.floor(total / 60)).padStart(2, '0') + ':' + String(total % 60).padStart(2, '0');
};

function draw(label) {
  $('#time').textContent = fmt(remaining);
  $('#ring').style.setProperty('--p', remaining / duration);
  if (label) $('#label').textContent = label;
  document.title = (endAt ? fmt(remaining) + ' · ' : '') + 'Focus timer';
}

function tick() {
  remaining = Math.max(0, endAt - performance.now());   // truth comes from the clock
  draw();
  if (remaining === 0) return finish();
  // Wake up just after the next whole second, however late this tick was
  timer = setTimeout(tick, (remaining % 1000) + 5);
}

function start() {
  endAt = performance.now() + remaining;
  $('#toggle').textContent = 'Pause';
  draw('Stay on task');
  tick();
}
function pause() {
  clearTimeout(timer);
  remaining = Math.max(0, endAt - performance.now());
  endAt = null;
  $('#toggle').textContent = 'Resume';
  draw('Paused');
}
function reset(min) {
  clearTimeout(timer);
  endAt = null;
  if (min) duration = min * 60_000;
  remaining = duration;
  document.body.classList.remove('done');
  $('#toggle').textContent = 'Start';
  draw('Ready to focus');
}
function finish() {
  endAt = null;
  document.body.classList.add('done');
  $('#toggle').textContent = 'Start';
  draw('Session complete ✓');
  document.title = 'Time’s up! · Focus timer';
  console.log('Finished at', new Date().toLocaleTimeString('en-IN'));
  remaining = duration;                                  // ready for the next run
}

$('#toggle').addEventListener('click', () => (endAt ? pause() : start()));
$('#reset').addEventListener('click', () => reset());
$('.presets').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const btn = e.target.closest('[data-min]');
  if (!btn) return;
  document.querySelectorAll('.presets button').forEach((b) =>
    b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(b === btn)));
  reset(Number(btn.dataset.min));
});
reset();

Choose Demo 0:10 and press Start. The timer computes the time left from a fixed end time, so pausing, a busy page or a background tab cannot make it wrong. The tab title shows the time too.

requestAnimationFrame and delta time

requestAnimationFrame(callback) runs your callback once, just before the browser’s next paint. Screens refresh 60, 90, 120 or more times per second, so a loop that calls rAF again inside its callback runs once per frame, in step with the display. The browser passes a timestamp (the same clock as performance.now()), pauses rAF in hidden tabs and hidden frames, and gives you the right moment to write styles for the frame.

Never move things by a fixed amount per frame. On a 120 Hz screen that runs twice as fast, and a dropped frame makes it stutter. Move by speed × elapsed time instead:

let last = performance.now();
let x = 0;
const SPEED = 120;                       // pixels per second

function frame(now) {
  const dt = Math.min(0.1, (now - last) / 1000); // seconds, capped after a pause
  last = now;
  x = (x + SPEED * dt) % 300;
  scooter.style.transform = `translateX(${x}px)`;
  frameId = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}
frameId = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
// later: cancelAnimationFrame(frameId);

For a tween with a fixed duration, like a number counting up, compute progress from the start time: t = (now - start) / duration, clamp it to 1, and pass it through an easing function such as 1 - (1 - t) ** 3. That is exactly what the dashboard below does, with one loop for all three cards.

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0 });
const int = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN');
const KPIS = [
  { value: 948250, target: 1200000, format: (v) => inr.format(v) },
  { value: 1624, target: 2000, format: (v) => int.format(Math.round(v)) },
  { value: 38.6, target: 45, format: (v) => v.toFixed(1) + '%' },
];
const cards = [...document.querySelectorAll('.kpi')];
const reduce = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');
const DURATION = 1200;
const easeOutCubic = (t) => 1 - (1 - t) ** 3;
let frameId = 0;

function draw(progress) {                     // progress 0 → 1
  KPIS.forEach((kpi, i) => {
    const v = kpi.value * progress;
    cards[i].querySelector('.num').textContent = kpi.format(v);
    // transform only: no layout work on each frame
    cards[i].querySelector('.track i').style.transform = `scaleX(${v / kpi.target})`;
  });
}

function play() {
  cancelAnimationFrame(frameId);              // restart cleanly on Replay
  if (reduce.matches) { draw(1); return; }
  let start = null;
  let last = null;
  const deltas = [];
  const frame = (now) => {                    // now = the frame's timestamp
    start ??= now;
    if (last !== null) deltas.push(now - last);
    last = now;
    const t = Math.min(1, (now - start) / DURATION);
    draw(easeOutCubic(t));
    if (t < 1) {
      frameId = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
    } else {
      const avg = deltas.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / deltas.length;
      document.querySelector('#fps').textContent =
        `${deltas.length + 1} frames · avg ${avg.toFixed(1)}ms per frame (≈${Math.round(1000 / avg)} Hz)`;
      console.log('animation done in', Math.round(now - start), 'ms');
    }
  };
  frameId = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}

document.querySelector('#replay').addEventListener('click', play);
play();

Press Replay. One rAF loop drives every number and bar from the frame timestamp, eased over 1.2 seconds. The footer shows the measured frame time on your screen.

CSS transitions and animations, triggered from JavaScript

For most UI motion, the best JavaScript is one line: el.classList.add('open'). CSS does the rest with a transition (from the current value to the new one) or a @keyframes animation. The browser can run these off the main thread when they change only transform and opacity, so they stay smooth even while your script is busy.

NeedBest tool
Hover, open/close, show/hide, state changesCSS transition + class toggle
Looping or multi-step decoration (spinner, shimmer)CSS @keyframes
Motion with values known only at runtime (fly to the cart), or you need to await the endWeb Animations API
Physics, games, canvas, numbers that tween, scroll-linked effects in JSrequestAnimationFrame
Run code later (toast timeout, polling, auto-save)setTimeout / setInterval

Listen for transitionend or animationend when something must happen after the motion, such as moving focus into a drawer. transitionend fires once per property, so check event.propertyName. It does not fire if the transition is interrupted or if reduced motion removed it, so never make essential logic depend on it alone.

The Web Animations API

element.animate(keyframes, options) is the engine behind CSS animations, exposed to JavaScript. You pass keyframes as an array of style objects (optionally with an offset) and options such as duration, easing, delay, iterations and fill. It returns an Animation object that you can pause(), reverse(), cancel() or speed up with playbackRate, and its finished property is a promise, so await animation.finished replaces fragile setTimeout guesses. el.getAnimations() lists what is running on an element.

const reduce = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');
const cartBtn = document.querySelector('#cart');
const badge = document.querySelector('#count');

let count = 0;

async function fly(fromEl, toEl, emoji) {
  const a = fromEl.getBoundingClientRect();
  const b = toEl.getBoundingClientRect();
  const flyer = Object.assign(document.createElement('span'), { className: 'flyer', textContent: emoji });
  flyer.style.left = a.left + a.width / 2 - 16 + 'px';
  flyer.style.top = a.top + a.height / 2 - 16 + 'px';

  const dy = b.top + b.height / 2 - (a.top + a.height / 2);

    { transform: 'translate(0, 0) scale(1)' },
    { transform: `translate(${dx * 0.4}px, ${dy - 60}px) scale(1.2)`, offset: 0.4 },
    { transform: `translate(${dx}px, ${dy}px) scale(0.3)`, opacity: 0.4 },
  ], { duration: 650, easing: 'cubic-bezier(.45,0,.55,1)' });
  await animation.finished;                  // a promise: no timeout guessing
  flyer.remove();
}

Remember: after an animation ends, the element goes back to its own styles. Instead of fill: 'forwards', which keeps an animation alive forever, set the final style yourself (or call animation.commitStyles()) and let the animation only handle the journey.

FLIP: smooth reordering

When a list is sorted, the DOM order changes instantly and cards jump. You cannot transition “position in the grid”. FLIP solves it with four steps, all within one frame:

  1. First: record each element’s getBoundingClientRect().
  2. Last: make the DOM change (re-append in the new order), then measure again.
  3. Invert: the difference between First and Last is how far each element moved. Apply a transform that puts it back where it was.
  4. Play: animate that transform to none.

The user sees cards glide from old to new positions, and because only transform animates, it is cheap. Two details matter. Elements must be keyed: the same product keeps the same element, which is moved with append rather than recreated (dm10). And cancel running animations after measuring First, so a second click starts from where cards currently are. Libraries such as Motion and the View Transitions API (document.startViewTransition, now in evergreen browsers; check caniuse.com) build on the same idea.

  { name: 'Smart Bulb', icon: '💡', price: 699, rating: 4.1 },
  { name: 'Ralfiz Cam', icon: '📷', price: 3499, rating: 4.3 },
  { name: 'Desk Lamp', icon: '🪔', price: 1299, rating: 4.8 },
];
const grid = document.querySelector('#grid');
const reduce = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');

// Keyed elements: each product keeps the same <li> for its whole life
const items = new Map(PRODUCTS.map((p) => {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.className = 'item';
  li.innerHTML = '<span class="rank"></span><div class="art"></div><h2></h2><p><b></b><span></span></p>';
  li.querySelector('.art').textContent = p.icon;

  li.querySelector('b').textContent = '₹' + p.price.toLocaleString('en-IN');
  li.querySelector('p span').textContent = '★ ' + p.rating;
  return [p, li];
}));

function flip(change) {
  const els = [...grid.children];
  const first = new Map(els.map((el) => [el, el.getBoundingClientRect()])); // F
  els.forEach((el) => el.getAnimations().forEach((a) => a.cancel()));
  change();                                                          // DOM moves
  if (reduce.matches) return;
  for (const el of els) {
    const f = first.get(el);
    const l = el.getBoundingClientRect();                            // L
    const dx = f.left - l.left;
    const dy = f.top - l.top;
    if (!dx && !dy) continue;
    el.animate(                                                      // I + P
      [{ transform: `translate(${dx}px, ${dy}px)` }, { transform: 'none' }],
      { duration: 450, easing: 'cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1)' });
  }
}

function show(list) {
  list.forEach((p, i) => {
    const li = items.get(p);
    li.querySelector('.rank').textContent = i + 1;
    grid.append(li);                         // append moves an existing node
  });
}

const orders = {
  price: () => PRODUCTS.toSorted((a, b) => a.price - b.price),
  rating: () => PRODUCTS.toSorted((a, b) => b.rating - a.rating),
  shuffle: () => PRODUCTS.map((p) => [Math.random(), p]).sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]).map(([, p]) => p),
};

  console.log(btn.dataset.sort, '· measured and started in', (performance.now() - t0).toFixed(1), 'ms');
});

Respecting prefers-reduced-motion

Operating systems let users ask for less motion. Honour it in CSS with @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce), and in JavaScript with matchMedia. Reduced motion does not mean no feedback: replace movement with an instant change or a quick fade.

const reduce = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');
if (reduce.matches) {
  showFinalState();
} else {
  animateToFinalState();
}
reduce.addEventListener('change', () => { /* the user changed the setting */ });

The lab is a Ralfiz Academy quiz leaderboard. A 90-second clock counts down from a fixed end time. Every two seconds some players score, each score counts up with a rAF tween, and rows glide to their new rank with FLIP. When the clock hits zero, all timers are cleared and the winner pulses. function round() {

Common mistakes

  • Counting ticks for a countdown. 
    // Wrong: drifts, and freezes in background tabs
setInterval(() => { seconds--; show(seconds); }, 1000);
// Right: compute from the end time every tick
const left = Math.max(0, endAt - performance.now());
  • Animating with setInterval. A 16ms interval is not synced to the display and keeps running in hidden tabs. Use requestAnimationFrame. 
    // Wrong: fixed step, not synced to the display
setInterval(() => { x += 2; box.style.transform = `translateX(${x}px)`; }, 16);
// Right: once per frame, moved by elapsed time
function frame(now) {
  x += SPEED * (now - last) / 1000;
  last = now;
  box.style.transform = `translateX(${x}px)`;
  frameId = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}
  • Animating layout properties. 
    /* Wrong: layout on every frame */
.drawer { transition: right .3s; }
/* Right: compositor-friendly */
.drawer { transition: transform .3s; transform: translateX(100%); }
.drawer.open { transform: none; }
  • Forgetting to cancel. A Replay button that starts a new rAF loop without cancelAnimationFrame runs two loops that fight each other. Keep the id and cancel first. 
    // Wrong: each click adds another loop
replay.addEventListener('click', () => requestAnimationFrame(frame));
// Right
replay.addEventListener('click', () => {
  cancelAnimationFrame(frameId);
  frameId = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
});
  • Restarting a CSS animation by removing and adding a class in the same frame. The browser sees no change. Use element.animate() instead, or read el.offsetWidth between the two to force a style update (and know that it forces layout). 
    // Wrong: removed and re-added in one frame, nothing replays
badge.classList.remove('bump');
badge.classList.add('bump');
// Right: a fresh animation every time
badge.animate([{ transform: 'scale(1.4)' }, { transform: 'none' }], { duration: 300 });

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Is setTimeout(fn, 0) immediate?” No. It queues a task that runs after the current script and all microtasks, with a minimum delay after deep nesting.
  • “setInterval vs recursive setTimeout?” Recursive setTimeout recalculates each delay after the callback finishes, so there is always a gap; setInterval ignores how long the callback took, so slow callbacks can run back to back, and it drifts.
  • “Why requestAnimationFrame?” It runs in step with the display, before paint, and pauses in background tabs; use delta time for frame-rate independence.
  • Smooth animation checklist: transform and opacity only, no layout reads and writes mixed in the same frame (dm18), reduced motion respected.
  • FLIP is a classic senior front-end question: be ready to explain First, Last, Invert, Play in one sentence each.

quiz.question: A 60-second sale countdown decrements a counter in setInterval(…, 1000). After a few minutes in a background tab it is clearly wrong. What is the best fix?
options: Use a 100ms interval instead
Store the end time and compute the remaining time from the clock on each tick
Use requestAnimationFrame so it runs in background tabs
Use setTimeout with a delay of 0
quiz.explanation: Intervals drift and are throttled, so counting ticks accumulates error. Computing from a fixed end time is always correct, however late a tick runs.

quiz.question: Why does a requestAnimationFrame loop multiply speed by the time since the last frame?
options: Because rAF always runs at exactly 60 frames per second
To make the loop run faster
So the motion covers the same distance per second on 60 Hz and 120 Hz screens and after dropped frames
Because rAF has no timestamp argument
quiz.explanation: Frame rates vary by display and load. Moving by speed × deltaTime ties the animation to real time, not to the number of frames.

quiz.question: Which properties are cheapest to animate for smooth motion?
options: width and height
top and left
margin and padding
transform and opacity
quiz.explanation: transform and opacity changes can usually be handled by the compositor without re-running layout or paint for the page.

quiz.question: In FLIP, what happens in the Invert step?
options: Each element gets a transform that moves it back to where it was before the change
The list order is reversed
The animation is played backwards
The DOM change is undone
quiz.explanation: After the DOM change (Last), a transform makes each element look like it is still in its First position; then you animate that transform to none (Play).

lessons.title: Canvas and SVG graphics
lessons.summaryHtml:
The browser has two built-in ways to draw graphics. A <canvas> is a bitmap: you get a 2D context and paint shapes, paths and text into pixels with JavaScript, and the browser forgets what you drew, so you redraw whenever anything changes. SVG is a tree of vector elements (circle, path, text) that live in the DOM, stay sharp at any zoom, and can be styled with CSS and given events and accessible names.

For sharp canvas drawing you size the backing bitmap by devicePixelRatio and scale the context. SVG elements must be created with document.createElementNS and the SVG namespace. In this lesson you draw a data-driven sales bar chart on canvas, animate it with requestAnimationFrame, and build a donut chart and icons in SVG, then learn when each tool, or plain HTML and CSS, is the right choice.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Sooner or later every dashboard needs a chart, every delivery app a map, and every product a few sharp icons. The browser gives you two drawing surfaces, and they work in opposite ways.

  • Canvas is a painting. You get a rectangle of pixels and a 2D context with commands such as “fill a rectangle here” or “draw this text there”. Once painted, the browser forgets the shapes: only coloured pixels remain. To change anything, you clear and paint again.
  • SVG is a set of drawing objects. Each circle, path or text is an element in the DOM. You can change its attributes later, style it with CSS, listen for its events, and a screen reader can read its title. It is vector-based, so it is sharp at any size.

Canvas is called immediate mode (you draw now, it is gone as an object), and SVG, like the rest of the DOM, is retained mode (the browser keeps a tree you can change).

Why it matters

A sales dashboard for a shop owner, an expense tracker, a live delivery map, a signature pad, an image cropper, a seat picker for a cinema: these are everyday front-end tasks. Chart libraries exist, but they are built on exactly these two APIs, and when a chart is blurry on a phone, slow with 10,000 points, or invisible to a screen reader, you need to know what is underneath. Interviewers ask “canvas or SVG?” because the answer shows whether you understand rendering cost, accessibility and interactivity.

How it works

The canvas element and its 2D context

A <canvas> has two sizes. Its width and height attributes set the real bitmap, called the backing store (300 × 150 by default). Its CSS size only sets how big that bitmap is displayed. If they differ, the browser stretches the pixels. You draw through a context:

const canvas = document.querySelector('#chart');
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');

ctx.fillStyle = '#2563eb';        // state: applies to later fills
ctx.fillRect(20, 20, 120, 60);    // x, y, width, height
ctx.strokeStyle = '#0f172a';
ctx.lineWidth = 2;
ctx.strokeRect(20, 20, 120, 60);
ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);  // erase an area

The origin (0, 0) is the top-left corner, and y grows downwards. The context holds state: colours, line width, font, text alignment, alpha and the current transform. ctx.save() pushes that state on a stack and ctx.restore() pops it, which keeps helper functions from leaking a colour into the next drawing. Setting canvas.width, even to the same value, clears the bitmap and resets all state.

Paths, arcs and text

Anything beyond rectangles is a path: call beginPath(), add segments with moveTo, lineTo, arc(x, y, r, start, end) (angles in radians), bezierCurveTo or roundRect, then paint with fill() or stroke(). closePath() joins the last point to the first. Text uses ctx.font (CSS font syntax), textAlign, textBaseline and fillText, and measureText(text).width tells you how wide it will be, so you can draw a label box that fits.

// A map pin: the round top is an arc, the point is a line
ctx.beginPath();
ctx.arc(x, y - 16, 10, Math.PI * 0.8, Math.PI * 2.2);
ctx.lineTo(x, y);
ctx.closePath();
ctx.fillStyle = '#ef4444';
ctx.fill();

ctx.font = '600 12px system-ui, sans-serif';
const w = ctx.measureText('Home').width + 16;   // label box width

The delivery tracker below draws a street grid, a dashed Bézier route, the travelled part, three arcs and two measured labels. Every button press repaints everything from the current progress value: that is the canvas way.
