domains.blurb: Rendering performance, accessible interactive UI and front-end security.

lessons.title: Rendering performance
lessons.summaryHtml:
Every time your JavaScript changes the page, the browser may have to recalculate styles, redo layout (sizes and positions), paint pixels and composite layers. Which of these steps runs depends on what you changed, and the cost grows with the size of the page.

The biggest mistakes are layout thrashing (alternating reads like offsetWidth with writes like style.width in a loop), animating layout properties such as left instead of transform, and rendering thousands of rows the user cannot see.

You will measure with performance.now(), marks and the DevTools Performance panel, fix each problem, and connect the fixes to Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP and CLS.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A browser draws your page in a pipeline, a bit like a print shop. First it works out which CSS rules apply to each element (style). Then it measures where every box goes (layout, also called reflow). Then it fills in the pixels: text, colours, shadows (paint). Finally the GPU stacks the painted layers into the image you see (composite).

When your JavaScript changes something, the browser only redoes the steps it has to. Change a colour and it can skip layout. Change transform and it can often skip layout and paint. Change a width and it has to redo everything from layout onwards, possibly for many elements. Rendering performance is the skill of making changes that cost as little of this pipeline as possible, as rarely as possible.

Why it matters

A display refreshes about 60 times a second, which gives the browser roughly 16 ms per frame for your JavaScript and all of its own work. Go over and the page stutters. Block the main thread for 200 ms and a tap on “Pay now” feels ignored. On the mid-range Android phones many of your users have, the CPU is several times slower than your laptop, so a 30 ms task on your machine can be well over 100 ms for them.

This is not only about feel. Google’s Core Web Vitals measure real users, feed into search ranking, and are what managers look at. The three metrics, with Google’s “good” thresholds at the 75th percentile of visits:

MetricMeasuresGoodWhat your JavaScript does to it
LCP, Largest Contentful PaintWhen the main content appears≤ 2.5 sRender-blocking scripts and rendering the hero image from JS delay it
INP, Interaction to Next PaintHow quickly the page responds to clicks, taps and keys≤ 200 msLong tasks, heavy event handlers and big re-renders make it worse
CLS, Cumulative Layout ShiftHow much content jumps around≤ 0.1Inserting banners, images or ads without reserved space

INP replaced the older FID metric in 2024. It is the one JavaScript developers affect most.

How it works

What each change costs

Different CSS properties trigger different parts of the pipeline. You do not need to memorise every property: learn the three groups.

You change…ExamplesBrowser redoes
Geometry or DOM structurewidth, height, top, left, margin, padding, font-size, adding or removing nodes, changing textStyle → layout → paint → composite
Appearance onlycolor, background, box-shadow, border-color, visibilityStyle → paint → composite
Layer transformstransform, opacity (on an element with its own layer)Often composite only

Layout is the expensive step because boxes depend on each other: making one card taller pushes everything below it. So the two big rules are: animate transform and opacity, and never make the browser do layout more often than once per frame.

Layout thrashing and forced synchronous layout

Normally the browser is lazy in a good way. When you write el.style.width = '200px', it just marks the layout as “dirty” and carries on; the real layout happens once, before the next paint. But if you then read a layout value such as offsetWidth, getBoundingClientRect(), clientHeight, scrollTop or getComputedStyle(el).width, the browser must give you a correct answer now, so it runs layout immediately. That is a forced synchronous layout. Do read-write-read-write in a loop and you force layout on every iteration: layout thrashing.

// Thrashing: N layouts
cards.forEach((card) => {
  const w = card.parentElement.offsetWidth; // read (forces layout)
  card.style.height = w * 0.75 + 'px';      // write (dirties layout)
});

// Batched: 1 layout
const widths = cards.map((c) => c.parentElement.offsetWidth); // all reads
cards.forEach((c, i) => { c.style.height = widths[i] * 0.75 + 'px'; }); // all writes

The live page does exactly this with 600 stock bars. Both versions produce the same result; only the order of reads and writes differs.

Try it: Bad vs good: layout thrashing

HTML

<main class="wrap">
  <header class="head">
    <div>
      <h1>Warehouse stock</h1>
      <p class="muted">600 products · each bar is sized from its track width</p>
    </div>
    <div class="btns">
      <button id="bad" class="btn warn" type="button">Update (thrashing)</button>
      <button id="good" class="btn primary" type="button">Update (batched)</button>
    </div>
  </header>
  <section class="stats">
    <div class="stat"><p class="k">Read → write in a loop</p><p class="v" id="badMs">–</p>
      <div class="meter"><span id="badBar" class="m-bad"></span></div></div>
    <div class="stat"><p class="k">All reads, then all writes</p><p class="v" id="goodMs">–</p>
      <div class="meter"><span id="goodBar" class="m-good"></span></div></div>
  </section>
  <ul id="list" class="list"></ul>
</main>

CSS

:root { --accent: #4f46e5; --line: #e5e7eb; --muted: #6b7280; }
body { margin: 0; background: #f6f7fb; }
.wrap { max-width: 760px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 16px; }
.head { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 12px; justify-content: space-between;
  align-items: flex-end; margin-bottom: 12px; }
h1 { font-size: 20px; margin: 0; }
.muted { margin: 2px 0 0; color: var(--muted); font-size: 13px; }
.btns { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px; }
.btn { font: inherit; font-size: 14px; font-weight: 600; border-radius: 10px;
  padding: 8px 12px; cursor: pointer; border: 1px solid transparent; }
.btn:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px; }
.primary { background: var(--accent); color: #fff; }
.warn { background: #fff; color: #b91c1c; border-color: #fecaca; }
.stats { display: grid; gap: 12px; margin-bottom: 12px;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)); }
.stat { background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line); border-radius: 14px; padding: 12px 16px; }
.k { margin: 0; font-size: 13px; color: var(--muted); }
.v { margin: 2px 0 8px; font-size: 24px; font-weight: 700; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
.meter { height: 8px; background: #f1f5f9; border-radius: 99px; overflow: hidden; }
.meter span { display: block; height: 100%; width: 0; transition: width .4s; }
.m-bad { background: #ef4444; } .m-good { background: #10b981; }
.list { list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 4px 12px; max-height: 150px; overflow: auto;
  background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line); border-radius: 14px; }
.list li { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 72px 1fr 40px; gap: 12px; align-items: center;
  padding: 6px 0; font-size: 13px; border-bottom: 1px solid #f3f4f6; }
.track { height: 8px; background: #eef2ff; border-radius: 99px; }
.bar { display: block; height: 100%; background: var(--accent); border-radius: 99px; }
.qty { text-align: right; color: var(--muted); font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }

JavaScript

const list = document.querySelector('#list');
const N = 600;
const frag = document.createDocumentFragment();
for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.innerHTML = '<span>SKU-' + (1001 + i) + '</span>' +
    '<span class="track"><span class="bar"></span></span><span class="qty"></span>';
  frag.append(li); // static, trusted markup: fine for innerHTML
}
list.append(frag);
const bars = [...list.querySelectorAll('.bar')];
const qtys = [...list.querySelectorAll('.qty')];
const levels = () => bars.map(() => Math.random());

function updateThrashing(lv) {
  bars.forEach((bar, i) => {
    const trackWidth = bar.parentElement.offsetWidth; // READ: forces layout
    bar.style.width = trackWidth * lv[i] + 'px';       // WRITE: invalidates it
    qtys[i].textContent = Math.round(lv[i] * 500);
  });
}

function updateBatched(lv) {
  const widths = bars.map((bar) => bar.parentElement.offsetWidth); // all reads
  bars.forEach((bar, i) => {                                        // all writes
    bar.style.width = widths[i] * lv[i] + 'px';
    qtys[i].textContent = Math.round(lv[i] * 500);
  });
}

function measure(fn) {
  const lv = levels();
  const t0 = performance.now();
  fn(lv);
  void list.offsetHeight; // include the final layout in both timings
  return performance.now() - t0;
}

const last = { bad: 0, good: 0 };
function show() {
  const max = Math.max(last.bad, last.good, 1);
  for (const k of ['bad', 'good']) {
    document.querySelector('#' + k + 'Ms').textContent = last[k] ? last[k].toFixed(1) + ' ms' : '–';
    document.querySelector('#' + k + 'Bar').style.width = (last[k] / max) * 100 + '%';
  }
}
document.querySelector('#bad').onclick = () => { last.bad = measure(updateThrashing); show(); };
document.querySelector('#good').onclick = () => { last.good = measure(updateBatched); show(); };

last.bad = measure(updateThrashing);
last.good = measure(updateBatched);
show();
console.log('Thrashing ms > batched ms?', last.bad > last.good);
console.log('Speed-up this run: ' + (last.bad / last.good).toFixed(0) + 'x');

Both buttons set 600 bar widths from their track widths. The thrashing version reads, writes, reads, writes… Click each a few times and compare. Numbers include the final layout, so the comparison is fair.

In real apps the reads and writes are often in different functions, so thrashing is hidden. The DevTools Performance panel shows it plainly: purple Layout blocks repeated many times inside one task, with a warning about a forced reflow that links to the line of code. A common structure is to do all reads first, then schedule writes inside requestAnimationFrame. Even simpler: often you do not need to read at all, because CSS (aspect-ratio, percentages, grid) can size things for you.

Animate transform and opacity

Animating left or top runs layout on every frame, on the main thread. Animating transform: translateX() can be handed to the compositor thread, which moves an already-painted layer on the GPU. That has a second, bigger benefit: a CSS transform animation keeps running smoothly even while the main thread is busy with your JavaScript. Try it below: block the main thread and watch which lanes freeze.

Try it: transform vs left under a busy main thread

HTML

<main class="wrap">
  <header class="head">
    <h1>Animation lab</h1>
    <button id="block" class="btn" type="button">⏳ Block main thread 1 s</button>
  </header>
  <div class="lane"><span class="label">JS rAF · left</span><span id="js" class="ball b1"></span></div>
  <div class="lane"><span class="label">CSS · left</span><span class="ball b2 anim-left"></span></div>
  <div class="lane"><span class="label">CSS · transform</span>
    <span class="runner anim-transform"><span class="ball b3"></span></span></div>
  <p class="note">Longest frame gap: <b id="gap">–</b></p>
</main>

CSS

:root { --accent: #0d9488; --line: #e5e7eb; }
body { margin: 0; background: #f8fafc; }
.wrap { max-width: 640px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 16px; }
.head { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px; justify-content: space-between;
  align-items: center; margin-bottom: 12px; }
h1 { font-size: 20px; margin: 0; }
.btn { font: inherit; font-weight: 600; font-size: 14px; border: 0; border-radius: 10px;
  padding: 8px 14px; background: #111827; color: #fff; cursor: pointer; }
.btn:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px; }
.lane { position: relative; height: 48px; margin-bottom: 10px; border-radius: 12px;
  background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line); overflow: hidden; }
.label { position: absolute; right: 10px; top: 14px; font-size: 12px; color: #94a3b8; }
.ball { position: absolute; top: 7px; left: 7px; width: 32px; height: 32px;
  border-radius: 10px; box-shadow: 0 4px 10px rgba(0, 0, 0, .15); }
.b1 { background: #f59e0b; } .b2 { background: #ef4444; } .b3 { background: var(--accent); }
.runner { position: absolute; inset: 0; }
.anim-left { animation: slide-left 1.6s ease-in-out infinite alternate; }
@keyframes slide-left { to { left: calc(100% - 39px); } }
.anim-transform { animation: slide-x 1.6s ease-in-out infinite alternate; }
@keyframes slide-x { to { transform: translateX(calc(100% - 46px)); } }
.note { font-size: 13px; color: #475569; margin: 4px 0 0; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .anim-left, .anim-transform { animation-duration: 6s; }
}

JavaScript

const ball = document.querySelector('#js');
const lane = ball.parentElement;
let travel = 0;
// Read the lane width only when it changes, never inside the animation loop
new ResizeObserver(() => { travel = lane.clientWidth - 46; }).observe(lane);

let lastTime = performance.now();
let longest = 0;
function frame(now) {
  const gap = now - lastTime;
  lastTime = now;
  if (gap > longest) {
    longest = gap;
    document.querySelector('#gap').textContent = gap.toFixed(0) + ' ms';
  }
  const t = (now % 3200) / 1600;          // 0 → 2
  const p = t < 1 ? t : 2 - t;            // ping-pong 0 → 1 → 0
  const eased = (1 - Math.cos(Math.PI * p)) / 2;
  ball.style.left = 7 + eased * travel + 'px'; // layout property on purpose
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}
requestAnimationFrame(frame);

document.querySelector('#block').addEventListener('click', () => {
  longest = 0;
  const end = performance.now() + 1000;
  while (performance.now() < end) { /* a long task: nothing else can run */ }
  console.log('Blocked the main thread for 1000 ms');
});
console.log('Animations running. Watch the lanes, then block.');

Press Block main thread. The two left animations freeze for a second; the transform lane keeps gliding because the compositor moves it on the GPU.

will-change: transform tells the browser to prepare a layer in advance. Use it on the few elements that are about to animate, not on everything: each layer costs GPU memory. And respect users who asked for less motion: wrap big movement in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) or check matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') in JavaScript.

Keep the DOM small: virtualisation and content-visibility

Every element costs memory, style calculation and layout. A table of 10,000 orders with five cells each is 60,000 elements, and the page is slow before the user does anything. Virtualisation renders only what is visible. The idea is simple:

  1. A scrolling viewport with a fixed height.
  2. Inside it, a spacer as tall as all rows would be (count × rowHeight), so the scrollbar looks right.
  3. On scroll, compute the first visible index from scrollTop / rowHeight, render that slice plus a few extra rows (overscan), and move the slice down with transform: translateY().

Try it: Virtualised list: 10,000 orders, a handful of rows

HTML

<main class="wrap">
  <header class="head">
    <h1>Orders</h1>
    <span class="chip">DOM rows: <b id="count">0</b> of <b id="total">0</b></span>
  </header>
  <div class="thead"><span>#</span><span>Customer</span><span>City</span><span>Status</span><span>Total</span></div>
  <div id="viewport" class="viewport" tabindex="0" aria-label="Orders list">
    <div id="spacer" class="spacer"><div id="rows" class="rows"></div></div>
  </div>
  <p class="foot">Last render: <b id="ms">–</b></p>
</main>

CSS

:root { --accent: #4f46e5; --line: #e5e7eb; --row: 44px; }
body { margin: 0; background: #f6f7fb; }
.wrap { max-width: 760px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 16px; }
.head { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px; align-items: center;
  justify-content: space-between; margin-bottom: 12px; }
h1 { font-size: 20px; margin: 0; }
.chip { font-size: 13px; background: #eef2ff; color: #3730a3; padding: 4px 10px; border-radius: 99px; }
.thead, .row { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 64px 1.3fr 1fr 90px 80px;
  gap: 8px; align-items: center; padding: 0 12px; }
.thead { font-size: 12px; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: .04em;
  color: #6b7280; padding-bottom: 6px; }
.viewport { height: 220px; overflow: auto; background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line);
  border-radius: 14px; position: relative; }
.viewport:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px; }
.spacer { position: relative; }
.rows { position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; right: 0; will-change: transform; }
.row { height: var(--row); border-bottom: 1px solid #f3f4f6; font-size: 14px; }
.row span { white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }
.num { color: #9ca3af; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
.amt { text-align: right; font-weight: 600; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
.st { font-size: 12px; font-weight: 600; padding: 2px 8px; border-radius: 99px; justify-self: start; }
.Paid { background: #e0f2fe; color: #075985; } .Packed { background: #fef3c7; color: #92400e; }
.Shipped { background: #ede9fe; color: #5b21b6; } .Delivered { background: #dcfce7; color: #166534; }
.foot { font-size: 13px; color: #6b7280; margin: 8px 0 0; }
@media (max-width: 480px) { .thead span:nth-child(3), .row span:nth-child(3) { display: none; }
  .thead, .row { grid-template-columns: 60px 1fr 84px 72px; } }

JavaScript

const ROW_H = 44;
const OVERSCAN = 5;
const cities = ['Kochi', 'Kozhikode', 'Thrissur', 'Bengaluru', 'Dubai', 'Toronto'];
const names = ['Anu', 'Rahul', 'Fatima', 'Arjun', 'Meera', 'Omar', 'Neha', 'Joel'];
const statuses = ['Paid', 'Packed', 'Shipped', 'Delivered'];
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0 });
const orders = Array.from({ length: 10000 }, (_, i) => ({
  id: 10001 + i,
  customer: names[i % 8] + ' ' + String.fromCharCode(65 + (i % 26)) + '.',
  city: cities[(i * 7) % 6],
  status: statuses[(i * 3) % 4],
  total: 199 + ((i * 7919) % 9800),
}));

const viewport = document.querySelector('#viewport');
const rowsEl = document.querySelector('#rows');
document.querySelector('#spacer').style.height = orders.length * ROW_H + 'px';
document.querySelector('#total').textContent = orders.length.toLocaleString('en-IN');

function rowFor(o) {
  const row = document.createElement('div');
  row.className = 'row';
  const cells = [['num', '#' + o.id], ['', o.customer], ['', o.city],
    ['st ' + o.status, o.status], ['amt', inr.format(o.total)]];
  for (const [cls, text] of cells) {
    const span = document.createElement('span');
    span.className = cls;
    span.textContent = text;
    row.append(span);
  }
  return row;
}

let lastFirst = -1;
function render() {
  const t0 = performance.now();
  const first = Math.max(0, Math.floor(viewport.scrollTop / ROW_H) - OVERSCAN);
  const visible = Math.ceil(viewport.clientHeight / ROW_H) + OVERSCAN * 2;
  if (first === lastFirst) return; // nothing new to show
  lastFirst = first;
  const slice = orders.slice(first, first + visible);
  rowsEl.replaceChildren(...slice.map(rowFor));
  rowsEl.style.transform = 'translateY(' + first * ROW_H + 'px)';
  document.querySelector('#count').textContent = rowsEl.children.length;
  document.querySelector('#ms').textContent = (performance.now() - t0).toFixed(2) + ' ms';
}

// At most one render per frame, however fast scroll events arrive
let queued = false;
viewport.addEventListener('scroll', () => {
  if (queued) return;
  queued = true;
  requestAnimationFrame(() => { queued = false; render(); });
}, { passive: true });

render();
console.log('Orders:', orders.length, '| row elements in the DOM:', rowsEl.children.length);

Scroll fast. The counter shows how many row elements exist: it stays small no matter how many orders there are.

Libraries such as TanStack Virtual handle variable row heights and keyboard focus, but the core is these 30 lines. Note that scroll handling is throttled to one render per animation frame, and the listener is passive so the browser never waits for it before scrolling.

For long pages that are not lists (a report with many sections), CSS can skip the work for you:

.report-section {
  content-visibility: auto;          /* skip layout/paint while off-screen */
  contain-intrinsic-size: auto 600px; /* placeholder height to keep the scrollbar stable */
}

content-visibility is supported in all major browsers since 2024 (check caniuse.com for your audience). The content is still in the DOM, so find-in-page and screen readers keep working.

Measure, do not guess

performance.now() gives a high-resolution timestamp. performance.mark() and performance.measure() name the spans, and they appear in the Timings track of the DevTools Performance panel so you can line your code up with the browser’s own work.

Try it: Measure with marks and measures

JavaScript

const list = document.createElement('ul');
document.body.append(list);

performance.mark('build-start');
const frag = document.createDocumentFragment();
for (let i = 0; i < 3000; i++) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = 'Invoice INV-' + (5000 + i);
  frag.append(li);
}
list.append(frag);
performance.mark('build-end');

void list.offsetHeight; // forces style + layout right now
performance.mark('layout-end');

performance.measure('build nodes', 'build-start', 'build-end');
performance.measure('first layout', 'build-end', 'layout-end');

for (const m of performance.getEntriesByType('measure')) {
  console.log(m.name.padEnd(14), m.duration.toFixed(2), 'ms');
}
console.log('Rows in list:', list.children.length);

// Measures also show up in the DevTools Performance panel, under Timings
performance.clearMarks();
performance.clearMeasures();
list.remove();

Building DOM nodes is cheap until something forces layout. The measures split the cost so you can see where the time goes.

In the Performance panel: press record, do the slow action, stop. Look for long tasks (red corner marks, over 50 ms), then zoom in: yellow is scripting, purple is style and layout, green is paint. Turn on CPU throttling (4x or 6x slowdown) to feel what a budget phone feels. Lighthouse gives lab scores; real-user numbers come from the field, for example the web-vitals library sending LCP, INP and CLS to your analytics.

Debounced resize and breaking up long tasks

resize fires many times per second while the user drags a window. If your handler measures and redraws a chart, debounce it so it runs once after the dragging stops (or use a ResizeObserver on the one element that matters):

function debounce(fn, ms = 150) {
  let id;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(id);
    id = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms);
  };
}
addEventListener('resize', debounce(redrawChart));

// Long work: give the browser a chance to handle input between chunks
const yieldToMain = () => globalThis.scheduler?.yield
  ? scheduler.yield()
  : new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));

async function importRows(rows) {
  for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i++) {
    saveRow(rows[i]);
    if (i % 250 === 0) await yieldToMain(); // keeps INP low
  }
}

scheduler.yield() is newer: Chromium-based browsers and Firefox have it, Safari does not yet (check caniuse.com), so feature-detect it as above. For truly heavy computation (parsing a big CSV, image processing) move it off the main thread entirely with a Web Worker.

Example: fixing the Order Dashboard

The lab gives you a dashboard that works but feels heavy. Here is the order a professional would fix it in, measuring after each step:

  1. Measure. Marks around the first render show roughly how long building 5,000 rows takes. The Performance panel shows a long task on load.
  2. Virtualise the orders table. The biggest win: the DOM goes from tens of thousands of elements to a few hundred, and load time drops accordingly.
  3. Batch the revenue bars. updateBars() read clientWidth and wrote style.width in one loop. Two loops fix it.
  4. Throttle scroll and debounce resize. Scroll renders at most once per frame; resize work runs once after dragging stops.
  5. Fix the toast. It moved by changing bottom in a setInterval. Now a class toggles a transform/opacity transition, with a reduced-motion fallback.
  6. Skip off-screen work. The monthly report section below the fold gets content-visibility: auto.

Common mistakes

1. Reading layout inside an animation loop.

function tick() {
  box.style.left = box.offsetLeft + 2 + 'px'; // read + write every frame
  requestAnimationFrame(tick);
}

Fix: keep the position in a variable and animate transform: x += 2; box.style.transform = `translateX(${x}px)`;

2. Appending rows one by one to the live DOM while measuring.

for (const o of orders) {
  table.append(rowFor(o));
  total += table.offsetHeight; // forced layout per row
}

Fix: build into a DocumentFragment, append once, and measure once afterwards (or not at all).

3. Adding will-change everywhere. * { will-change: transform; } creates a layer for every element and can use more memory than it saves. Fix: apply it only to elements that are about to animate, and remove it afterwards.

4. Images without dimensions. <img src="banner.jpg"> has zero height until it loads, then shoves the page down (CLS). Fix: <img src="banner.jpg" width="1200" height="400" alt="…"> or CSS aspect-ratio.

5. Optimising without a profile. Rewriting a loop that takes 0.2 ms while a 400 ms image decode is the real problem. Fix: record first, then fix the biggest bar.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be able to draw the pipeline: JavaScript → style → layout → paint → composite, and say which properties skip which steps.
  • Define layout thrashing in one sentence and give the fix: batch reads before writes, or read in one frame and write in the next.
  • Know the three Core Web Vitals, their “good” thresholds, and one JavaScript cause and fix for each.
  • For huge lists, say “virtualise” and explain the spacer plus visible slice idea. Mention that frameworks use the same technique through libraries.
  • The 16 ms frame budget, the 50 ms long-task threshold and throttled CPU testing show you think about real devices.
  • Performance work is a loop: measure, change one thing, measure again, and keep the measurements in the pull request.

terms.definition: The browser working out the size and position of elements. Triggered by changes to geometry such as width, height, top, font-size or the DOM structure.
Redrawing pixels for elements whose look changed without moving, such as color, background or box-shadow.
Combining already-painted layers on the GPU. Changing transform or opacity can often be handled here without layout or paint.
Forcing the browser to run layout many times in one task by reading layout values right after writing styles, usually in a loop.
Rendering only the rows that are visible (plus a small buffer) in a long list, and reusing them as the user scrolls.
Any main-thread task over 50 ms. While it runs, the page cannot respond to clicks or typing.
Google’s user-experience metrics: LCP (loading), INP (responsiveness) and CLS (visual stability), measured at the 75th percentile of real visits.

lessons.examTip: When asked “how would you make this page faster?”, start with “I would measure first in the Performance panel”, then name the specific cause you found. Guessing is the junior answer.

quiz.question: Which change can usually be handled by the compositor alone, without layout or paint?
options: Changing width from 200px to 240px
Changing transform: translateX(40px)
Changing font-size
Changing padding-left
quiz.explanation: transform and opacity changes can be applied to an existing layer on the GPU. Geometry properties like width, padding and font-size trigger layout, then paint and composite.

quiz.question: This loop runs 500 times: el.style.height = h + 'px'; total += el.offsetHeight. Why is it slow?
options: offsetHeight is a slow property to spell
style.height only works in CSS files
Each read after a write forces the browser to recompute layout synchronously, 500 times
The loop needs to be async
quiz.explanation: That is layout thrashing. Batch the reads before the writes (or use requestAnimationFrame) so the browser lays out once.

quiz.question: A page shows 20,000 transactions and is slow to open and scroll. What helps the most?
options: Virtualise the list so only about 30 rows exist in the DOM at a time
Add will-change: transform to every row
Use innerHTML instead of createElement
Increase the font size so fewer rows fit
quiz.explanation: The cost is proportional to the number of nodes. Virtualising keeps the DOM small whatever the data size. will-change on every row wastes memory.

quiz.question: Users report the Buy button “jumps” just as they tap it, because a banner loads above it. Which Core Web Vital suffers and how do you fix it?
options: LCP; lazy-load the banner
INP; debounce the click
FCP; inline the CSS
CLS; reserve the banner’s space with fixed dimensions or aspect-ratio before it loads
quiz.explanation: Unexpected movement is layout shift (CLS). Reserve space with width/height attributes, aspect-ratio or min-height so late content does not push the page.

lessons.title: Accessible interactive UI
lessons.summaryHtml:
An accessible interface works for everyone: keyboard users, screen reader users, people zoomed to 200%, people with tremors or low vision, and anyone on a phone in bright sun. Most of it comes free when you use semantic HTML: a real <button> is focusable, works with Enter and Space and announces itself as a button.

JavaScript is where accessibility usually breaks. When you build menus, carts and deletes, you must keep keyboard access and a visible focus, move focus sensibly after actions, and expose state with a few ARIA attributes such as aria-expanded and aria-live.

You will build an accessible disclosure menu, a cart that announces updates through a live region and a list that manages focus after a delete, then learn to test with the keyboard, a screen reader, Lighthouse and axe.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Accessibility means people can use your interface whatever their body, device or situation. Some users never touch a mouse and move with Tab. Some cannot see the screen and listen to a screen reader, which reads out each element’s role (“button”), name (“Add Desk Lamp to cart”) and state (“expanded”). Some zoom to 200%, use a switch device or just have a cracked phone screen in the sun.

The browser builds an accessibility tree from your DOM: a simplified tree of roles, names and states that assistive technology reads. Semantic HTML fills this tree in correctly for free. Your JavaScript’s job is to keep it true as the page changes: when a menu opens, when the cart updates, when an item disappears.

Why it matters

Around one in six people worldwide live with a significant disability, according to the WHO, and everyone has temporary or situational limits. Accessibility is also a legal requirement in many markets: public sector sites in India, the EU (the European Accessibility Act applies to many products and services from June 2025), the UK, Canada and the US are expected to meet WCAG, usually version 2.1 or 2.2 at level AA. Client contracts increasingly say so too.

It is also just better engineering. Keyboard support makes power users faster, good labels make forms easier for everyone, and the semantic markup that screen readers need is the same structure that search engines and automated tests rely on. Fixing accessibility late is expensive; building it in while you write the component costs almost nothing.

How it works

Semantic HTML first, and the first rule of ARIA

ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of attributes that change what the accessibility tree says. It does not add behaviour. That is why the first rule of ARIA is: if a native element does the job, use it. Compare what you get:

Feature<button><div role="button" tabindex="0">
Announced as a buttonYesYes (because of role)
Reachable with TabYesYes (because of tabindex)
Enter and Space activate itYesNo: you must write a keydown handler
Can be disabledYesNo: you fake it with aria-disabled and code
Submits forms, works with form attributeYesNo

The same goes for <a href> for navigation, <label> for inputs, <dialog> for modals, <details> for simple disclosures, headings for structure and landmarks such as <nav>, <main> and <header>. Reach for ARIA to express things HTML has no word for: whether a toggle is expanded, which panel it controls, or that a region should announce updates.

Keyboard access, focus order and visible focus

The Tab order follows the DOM order. So the first fix for a confusing tab order is to put the HTML in a sensible order, not to add tabindex. The three values you need:

  • No tabindex on native controls: they are already in the order.
  • tabindex="0": puts a custom widget into the natural order (rarely needed if you use native elements).
  • tabindex="-1": focusable from JavaScript with .focus() but skipped by Tab. Perfect for headings and containers you move focus to.

Never use positive values like tabindex="3": they jump ahead of everything else and make the order unpredictable. And never remove focus rings with outline: none without a replacement. Use :focus-visible, which shows a ring for keyboard users but not for mouse clicks, with enough contrast (at least 3:1 against the background). WCAG 2.2 also asks that focused elements are not hidden behind sticky headers, and that small targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels or well spaced.

A skip link (“Skip to content”) as the first focusable element lets keyboard users jump past the header on every page. It can stay off-screen until focused, as in the live page below.

ARIA states: the disclosure pattern

A “Courses ▾” button that shows and hides a list of links is a disclosure. It needs very little: a native button, aria-expanded kept in sync, aria-controls pointing to the panel’s id, and the panel shown with the hidden attribute. Then add keyboard polish: Escape closes and returns focus to the button, and moving focus out of the menu closes it. Note it is not role="menu": that role is for application menus like a desktop app’s File menu and promises arrow-key behaviour users will then expect. Site navigation is just a list of links.

Try it: Accessible disclosure menu

HTML

<a class="skip" href="#main">Skip to content</a>
<header class="nav">
  <strong class="brand"><span class="logo" aria-hidden="true">R</span> Ralfiz Academy</strong>
  <nav aria-label="Main">
    <ul class="menu">
      <li class="item">
        <button type="button" class="toggle" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="courses-panel">
          Courses <span class="chev" aria-hidden="true">▾</span>
        </button>
        <ul id="courses-panel" class="panel" hidden>
          <li><a href="#js">JavaScript: Zero to Job-Ready</a></li>
          <li><a href="#dom">DOM & Browser</a></li>
          <li><a href="#flutter">Flutter and Dart</a></li>
        </ul>
      </li>
      <li><a class="link" href="#pricing">Pricing</a></li>
      <li><a class="link" href="#blog">Blog</a></li>
    </ul>
  </nav>
</header>
<main id="main" tabindex="-1">
  <h1>Learn by building</h1>
  <p>Open the Courses menu with your keyboard.</p>
</main>
<p class="inspect">aria-expanded: <b id="state">false</b> · focus: <b id="focus">body</b></p>

CSS

:root { --accent: #4f46e5; --line: #e5e7eb; --text: #111827; }
body { margin: 0; background: #f8fafc; color: var(--text); }
.skip { position: absolute; left: 8px; top: -48px; background: var(--accent); color: #fff;
  padding: 8px 12px; border-radius: 8px; z-index: 10; }
.skip:focus { top: 8px; }
.nav { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px 16px; align-items: center; padding: 12px 16px;
  background: #fff; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--line); }
.brand { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px; margin-right: auto; }
.logo { width: 28px; height: 28px; border-radius: 8px; background: var(--accent); color: #fff;
  display: grid; place-items: center; }
.menu { display: flex; gap: 4px; list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 0; }
.item { position: relative; }
.toggle, .link { font: inherit; font-weight: 500; color: var(--text); background: none;
  border: 0; padding: 8px 12px; border-radius: 8px; cursor: pointer; text-decoration: none;
  display: inline-block; }
.toggle:hover, .link:hover { background: #f3f4f6; }
.toggle[aria-expanded="true"] { background: #eef2ff; color: var(--accent); }
.toggle[aria-expanded="true"] .chev { display: inline-block; transform: rotate(180deg); }
.panel { position: absolute; top: calc(100% + 6px); left: 0; min-width: 240px; z-index: 5;
  list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 6px; background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line);
  border-radius: 12px; box-shadow: 0 12px 32px rgba(17, 24, 39, .12); }
.panel a { display: block; padding: 10px 12px; border-radius: 8px; color: var(--text);
  text-decoration: none; }
.panel a:hover { background: #f3f4f6; }
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px; }
main { padding: 24px 16px; }
main:focus { outline: none; }
h1 { margin: 0 0 4px; font-size: 24px; }
.inspect { margin: 0 16px; font: 12px ui-monospace, monospace; color: #475569;
  background: #fff; border: 1px dashed #cbd5e1; border-radius: 8px; padding: 6px 10px; }

JavaScript

const toggle = document.querySelector('.toggle');
const panel = document.getElementById(toggle.getAttribute('aria-controls'));
const item = toggle.closest('.item');

function setOpen(open) {
  toggle.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(open)); // attributes are strings
  panel.hidden = !open;
  document.querySelector('#state').textContent = open;
}

toggle.addEventListener('click', () => {
  setOpen(toggle.getAttribute('aria-expanded') !== 'true');
});

// Escape closes and puts focus back on the button that opened it
item.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
  if (event.key === 'Escape' && !panel.hidden) {
    setOpen(false);
    toggle.focus();
  }
});

// Close when focus moves somewhere outside the menu (Tab past the last link)
item.addEventListener('focusout', (event) => {
  if (!item.contains(event.relatedTarget)) setOpen(false);
});

// Close on a click outside
document.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  if (!item.contains(event.target)) setOpen(false);
});

// Teaching aid: show where focus is
document.addEventListener('focusin', (event) => {
  const el = event.target;
  const name = el.textContent.trim().split('\n')[0] || el.tagName.toLowerCase();
  document.querySelector('#focus').textContent = el.tagName.toLowerCase() + ' "' + name + '"';
});
console.log('Menu ready. aria-expanded =', toggle.getAttribute('aria-expanded'));

Use only the keyboard: Tab to Courses, press Enter, Tab through the links, press Escape. The strip at the bottom shows the ARIA state and where focus is.

One trap: attributes are strings. setAttribute('aria-expanded', false) stores the text "false", which is truthy. Always compare with === 'true'. The Predict the output widget below this lesson tests exactly this. aria-controls is part of the recommended pattern, though screen reader support for it varies; the expanded state is what users actually hear.

Names and labels

Every interactive element needs an accessible name. The browser computes it in roughly this order: aria-labelledby (text of other elements), aria-label, a <label> (for inputs), the element’s own text content, and finally title. Rules of thumb:

  • Visible text is best: it is what sighted users see and what voice-control users say (“click Add”).
  • Icon-only buttons need aria-label, such as aria-label="Close dialog" on a ✕.
  • Repeated buttons need context. Ten “Add” buttons all sound the same in a screen reader’s list of controls; add the product name in a visually hidden span so the name is “Add Wireless Mouse to cart” while the button still shows “Add”.
  • Placeholders are not labels: they vanish when you type and are often low contrast.
/* Hidden visually, still in the accessibility tree */
.sr-only {
  position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; padding: 0; margin: -1px;
  overflow: hidden; clip-path: inset(50%); white-space: nowrap; border: 0;
}

Compare with display: none, hidden and aria-hidden="true": all three remove content from the accessibility tree. Use aria-hidden for decorative emoji and icons so they are not read out.

Live regions: announcing updates

When content changes somewhere the user is not focused, such as a cart badge, a “Saved” message or search results count, a screen reader user will not know. A live region fixes this. role="status" (polite: waits until the user pauses) suits most updates; role="alert" (assertive: interrupts) is for errors that need attention now. Two rules make them reliable: the region must already be in the DOM before you change its text, and you should put a short, complete sentence in it.

Try it: Live region cart updates

HTML

<header class="bar">
  <strong>Ralfiz Store</strong>
  <span class="cart" aria-hidden="true">🛒 <b id="badge">0</b></span>
</header>
<main class="wrap">
  <h1 class="sr-only">Products</h1>
  <ul class="grid" id="products"></ul>
  <section class="said" aria-hidden="true">
    <p class="said-h">🔊 Screen reader hears</p>
    <ol id="said"><li class="none">Nothing yet: press Add or −.</li></ol>
  </section>
</main>
<div id="live" class="sr-only" role="status"></div>

CSS

:root { --accent: #059669; --line: #e5e7eb; }
body { margin: 0; background: #f6f7fb; }
.sr-only { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; padding: 0; margin: -1px;
  overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); clip-path: inset(50%); white-space: nowrap; border: 0; }
.bar { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center;
  padding: 12px 16px; background: #fff; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--line); }
.cart { font-size: 14px; background: #ecfdf5; color: #065f46; padding: 4px 10px; border-radius: 99px; }
.wrap { padding: 16px; max-width: 760px; margin: 0 auto; }
.grid { list-style: none; padding: 0; margin: 0 0 12px; display: grid; gap: 12px;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(160px, 1fr)); }
.card { background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line); border-radius: 14px; padding: 12px; }
.emoji { font-size: 32px; height: 56px; display: grid; place-items: center;
  background: #f3f4f6; border-radius: 10px; margin-bottom: 8px; }
.card h2 { font-size: 14px; margin: 0; }
.price { margin: 2px 0 8px; color: #374151; font-size: 14px; }
.row { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 6px; }
.btn { font: inherit; font-size: 14px; font-weight: 600; border-radius: 8px; cursor: pointer;
  min-height: 32px; min-width: 32px; border: 1px solid var(--line); background: #fff; }
.add { flex: 1; background: var(--accent); color: #fff; border-color: transparent; }
.qty { min-width: 20px; text-align: center; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
.btn:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #1d4ed8; outline-offset: 2px; }
.said { background: #0f172a; color: #e2e8f0; border-radius: 12px; padding: 10px 14px; }
.said-h { margin: 0 0 4px; font-size: 12px; color: #94a3b8; }
.said ol { margin: 0; padding-left: 20px; font-size: 13px; min-height: 20px; }
.said .none { list-style: none; margin-left: -20px; color: #64748b; }

JavaScript

const products = [
  { id: 1, name: 'Wireless Mouse', price: 799, emoji: '🖱️' },
  { id: 2, name: 'Desk Lamp', price: 1499, emoji: '💡' },
  { id: 3, name: 'Notebook Set', price: 349, emoji: '📓' },
];
const cart = new Map(); // id -> qty
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0 });
const live = document.querySelector('#live');

function card(p) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.className = 'card';
  li.innerHTML = '<div class="emoji" aria-hidden="true"></div><h2></h2><p class="price"></p>' +
    '<div class="row"><button class="btn minus" type="button">−</button>' +
    '<span class="qty">0</span>' +
    '<button class="btn add" type="button">Add <span class="sr-only"></span></button></div>';
  li.querySelector('.emoji').textContent = p.emoji;
  li.querySelector('h2').textContent = p.name;
  li.querySelector('.price').textContent = inr.format(p.price);
  li.querySelector('.add .sr-only').textContent = p.name + ' to cart';
  li.querySelector('.minus').setAttribute('aria-label', 'Remove one ' + p.name);
  li.dataset.id = p.id;
  return li;
}
document.querySelector('#products').append(...products.map(card));

function announce(message) {
  live.textContent = message; // the region already exists, so this is read out
  document.querySelector('#said .none')?.remove();
  const said = document.createElement('li');
  said.textContent = message;
  document.querySelector('#said').prepend(said);
}

document.querySelector('#products').addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const btn = event.target.closest('button');
  if (!btn) return;
  const li = btn.closest('.card');
  const p = products.find((x) => x.id === Number(li.dataset.id));
  const qty = (cart.get(p.id) ?? 0) + (btn.classList.contains('add') ? 1 : -1);
  if (qty < 0) return announce(p.name + ' is not in your cart.');
  qty ? cart.set(p.id, qty) : cart.delete(p.id);
  li.querySelector('.qty').textContent = qty;

  const count = [...cart.values()].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const total = [...cart].reduce((s, [id, q]) => s + products.find((x) => x.id === id).price * q, 0);
  document.querySelector('#badge').textContent = count;
  const verb = btn.classList.contains('add') ? 'added' : 'removed';
  announce(p.name + ' ' + verb + '. ' + count + ' item' + (count === 1 ? '' : 's') + ', ' + inr.format(total) + '.');
});

console.log('Button names:', [...document.querySelectorAll('.add')].map((b) => b.textContent.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()));

Add and remove items. The dark panel shows what a screen reader would hear from the role="status" region; the real region is visually hidden.

Managing focus after actions

When the focused element disappears, for example the Remove button you just pressed, focus falls back to <body>. A keyboard user is thrown to the top of the page and a screen reader goes silent. Always decide where focus goes next:

ActionMove focus to
Delete an item in a listThe next item’s control, else the previous one, else the list heading
Open a modalThe first control in it, or the dialog itself (showModal() does this)
Close a modal or menuThe button that opened it
Route change in a single-page appThe new page’s h1 (with tabindex="-1")
Form submit with errorsThe first invalid field, or an error summary

Try it: Managing focus after a delete

HTML

<main class="wrap">
  <h1 id="heading" tabindex="-1">Saved addresses</h1>
  <p class="hint">Remove an address with the keyboard and watch where focus lands.</p>
  <ul id="list" class="list" aria-labelledby="heading"></ul>
  <p id="empty" class="empty" hidden>No saved addresses. Add one at checkout.</p>
  <div id="status" class="toast" role="status"></div>
</main>

JavaScript

const addresses = [
  { id: 'a1', label: 'Home', line: '12 MG Road, Kochi 682016' },
  { id: 'a2', label: 'Office', line: 'Infopark Phase 2, Kakkanad' },
  { id: 'a3', label: 'Parents', line: 'Near KIMS, Perinthalmanna' },
];
const list = document.querySelector('#list');

function render() {
  list.replaceChildren(...addresses.map((a) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.className = 'addr';
    li.dataset.id = a.id;
    li.innerHTML = '<span class="pin" aria-hidden="true">📍</span><div><strong></strong><span></span></div>' +
      '<button class="remove" type="button">Remove</button>';
    li.querySelector('strong').textContent = a.label;
    li.querySelector('div span').textContent = a.line;
    li.querySelector('.remove').setAttribute('aria-label', 'Remove ' + a.label + ' address');
    return li;
  }));
  document.querySelector('#empty').hidden = addresses.length > 0;
}

list.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const btn = event.target.closest('.remove');
  if (!btn) return;
  const index = addresses.findIndex((a) => a.id === btn.closest('li').dataset.id);
  const [removed] = addresses.splice(index, 1);
  render(); // the focused button no longer exists after this

  // Next item, else previous item, else the heading
  const buttons = list.querySelectorAll('.remove');
  const target = buttons[index] ?? buttons[index - 1] ?? document.querySelector('#heading');
  target.focus();
  document.querySelector('#status').textContent = removed.label + ' address removed.';
  console.log('Removed', removed.label, '→ focus on', document.activeElement.getAttribute('aria-label') ?? document.activeElement.textContent);
});

render();
console.log('Addresses:', addresses.length);

Tab to a Remove button and press Enter. Focus moves to the next address (or the heading when the list is empty) and the change is announced.

Reduced motion

Some users get dizzy or nauseous from large movement. Respect prefers-reduced-motion: in CSS, shorten or remove transitions inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce); in JavaScript, check matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches before running scroll animations or auto-playing carousels, and use behavior: 'auto' instead of 'smooth' in scrollIntoView.

Testing: keyboard, screen reader and tools

  1. Keyboard only. Unplug the mouse. Can you reach and operate everything with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, arrows and Escape? Can you always see where focus is?
  2. Screen reader basics. NVDA (free, Windows), VoiceOver (built into macOS and iOS: Cmd+F5 on Mac) and TalkBack (Android). Tab through your component and listen: role, name and state should all make sense.
  3. Automated tools. Lighthouse’s Accessibility audit in Chrome DevTools and the axe DevTools extension find missing names, labels, alt text and contrast problems. The Elements panel has an Accessibility pane that shows each element’s computed name and role.

Try it: A tiny accessibility audit

JavaScript

document.body.innerHTML = `
  <img src="data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'/%3E" width="40" height="40">
  <img src="data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'/%3E" width="40" height="40" alt="Ralfiz logo">
  <button></button>
  <button aria-label="Close dialog">✕</button>
  <input id="email" type="email">
  <label for="phone">Phone</label><input id="phone" type="tel">
  <div class="btn" onclick="void 0">Buy now</div>
  <a href="#top" tabindex="3">Back to top</a>`; // fixed, trusted demo markup

const issues = [];
const describe = (el) => el.outerHTML.replace(/src="[^"]*"/, 'src="…"').slice(0, 40);

document.querySelectorAll('img:not([alt])').forEach((el) =>
  issues.push({ rule: 'img needs alt', element: describe(el) }));

document.querySelectorAll('button, a[href]').forEach((el) => {
  const name = el.getAttribute('aria-label') || el.textContent.trim();
  if (!name) issues.push({ rule: 'control has no name', element: describe(el) });
});

document.querySelectorAll('input').forEach((el) => {
  const labelled = el.labels.length > 0 || el.hasAttribute('aria-label');
  if (!labelled) issues.push({ rule: 'input has no label', element: describe(el) });
});

document.querySelectorAll('[onclick]:not(button):not(a)').forEach((el) =>
  issues.push({ rule: 'click on non-interactive element', element: describe(el) }));

document.querySelectorAll('[tabindex]').forEach((el) => {
  if (el.tabIndex > 0) issues.push({ rule: 'positive tabindex', element: describe(el) });
});

console.table(issues);
console.log(issues.length + ' issues found');

Automated checks catch missing names, labels and alt text. They cannot tell you whether the page makes sense: that still needs a keyboard and a screen reader.

Automated tools find only part of the problems. A page can score 100 and still be unusable if the focus order is illogical or a menu cannot be closed. Always do the keyboard pass.

Example: an accessible Ralfiz Store header and cart

The lab starts from a header that looks fine but fails every keyboard test. You fix it in this order:

  1. Semantics. Div “buttons” become <button type="button">; the logo gets alt text; the search input gets a real <label> (visually hidden).
  2. Focus styles. Remove outline: none, add a strong :focus-visible ring and a skip link.
  3. Categories disclosure. aria-expanded, aria-controls, the hidden attribute, Escape to close with focus returned, close on focus out.
  4. Names. Each Add button gets a visually hidden product name; the ✕ Remove buttons get aria-label.
  5. Announcements. A role="status" region says “Desk Lamp added. 2 items, ₹2,998.”
  6. Focus after remove. Focus moves to the next line or the cart heading.

Then run Lighthouse and axe on both versions and compare.

Common mistakes

1. Clickable divs.

<div class="btn" onclick="addToCart(3)">Add</div>

Fix: <button type="button" class="btn" data-id="3">Add</button> with a listener in JavaScript.

2. Removing focus rings.

*:focus { outline: none; } /* keyboard users are now lost */

Fix: :focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #4f46e5; outline-offset: 2px; }

3. Adding ARIA that lies. <button role="menu"> or aria-expanded that never updates is worse than nothing, because it tells users something false. Fix: fewer attributes, always kept in sync by the same function that changes the UI.

4. Creating the live region at the moment of the update.

const div = document.createElement('div');
div.setAttribute('role', 'status');
div.textContent = 'Item added'; // often not announced
document.body.append(div);

Fix: put the empty region in the HTML at load and only change its textContent later.

5. Using aria-label that hides visible text. A button showing “Buy” with aria-label="Purchase" confuses voice-control users who say “click Buy”. Fix: make the accessible name start with the visible text, or add context with a hidden span.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Say “semantic HTML first” and quote the first rule of ARIA. Then name the few ARIA attributes you use most: aria-expanded, aria-controls, aria-label, aria-describedby, aria-live/role="status", aria-hidden.
  • Explain focus management with a concrete example: “after deleting a row I move focus to the next row’s button and announce the change”.
  • Know how you test: keyboard pass, one screen reader, Lighthouse and axe, and that tools catch only part of the problems.
  • Mention WCAG 2.2 AA as the usual target, and contrast of 4.5:1 for body text.
  • The ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) on w3.org has tested patterns for tabs, menus, dialogs and comboboxes. Follow it rather than inventing keyboard behaviour.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const btn = document.createElement('button');
btn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', false);
const state = btn.getAttribute('aria-expanded');
console.log(typeof state);
console.log(state ? 'menu open' : 'menu closed');

menu closed

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const div = document.createElement('div');
const btn = document.createElement('button');
document.body.append(div, btn);

div.focus();
console.log(document.activeElement === div);
div.tabIndex = -1;
div.focus();
console.log(document.activeElement === div);
btn.focus();
console.log(document.activeElement.tagName);
  • A

BUTTON

Answers

  1. C. Attributes are always strings, so false becomes "false", and any non-empty string is truthy. Compare with === 'true' when reading ARIA states.
  2. B. A plain div is not focusable, so focus() does nothing. tabindex="-1" makes it focusable from script (but not with Tab). A button is focusable by default.

terms.definition: What assistive technology calls an element, such as “Add Wireless Mouse to cart”. It comes from aria-labelledby, aria-label, a label element or the element’s text, in that order of priority.
The browser’s simplified version of the DOM that screen readers read: roles, names, states and values. You can inspect it in the DevTools Elements panel.
If a native HTML element or attribute already has the semantics and behaviour you need, use it instead of adding ARIA to a generic element.
A state on a control that shows or hides something: "true" when the content is open, "false" when closed.
An element with aria-live (or role="status" / role="alert") whose text changes are announced by screen readers without moving focus.
A CSS pseudo-class that matches when the browser decides a focus ring should be shown, typically for keyboard focus but not mouse clicks.
The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. Most laws and contracts point to version 2.1 or 2.2 at level AA.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, quote the first rule of ARIA and then show you know when ARIA is needed: “a native button first; aria-expanded on it when it toggles a panel”.

quiz.question:
A teammate builds a toggle with
Filters
. What is the best fix?
options: Add role="button" to the div
Add tabindex="0" to the div
Use <button type="button">Filters</button> and add aria-expanded to it
Add aria-label="Filters" to the div
quiz.explanation: A native button is focusable and responds to Enter and Space automatically. role and tabindex on a div still need you to rebuild keyboard handling. aria-expanded then exposes the open state.

quiz.question: After adding an item, the cart badge updates silently. How do you tell screen reader users without stealing their focus?
options: Move focus to the cart badge
Update a live region, for example an element with role="status" that is already in the DOM
Show an alert() dialog
Add aria-hidden="true" to the badge
quiz.explanation: Live regions announce text changes without moving focus. The region must exist before the text changes; role="status" is polite, so it waits for the user to pause.

quiz.question: Which tabindex value should you avoid in almost all cases?
options: A positive value such as tabindex="3"
tabindex="0" on a custom widget
tabindex="-1" on a heading you focus from script
No tabindex on a native button
quiz.explanation: Positive values jump the element ahead of the natural DOM order and make the tab order unpredictable. Use DOM order, 0 for custom focusable widgets and -1 for elements you focus only from code.

quiz.question: A user deletes the third item in a list. Where should keyboard focus go?
options: Leave it on the deleted button
Move it to the top of the page
Blur it so nothing is focused
To a sensible nearby place: the next item’s control, or the list heading if the list is now empty
quiz.explanation: When the focused element disappears, focus falls back to the body and keyboard users lose their place. Move it to the next logical control and announce the change.

lessons.title: Front-end security
lessons.summaryHtml:
Front-end code runs on the user’s machine with the user’s cookies and permissions, so a single bug can let an attacker act as your user. The most common one is cross-site scripting (XSS): untrusted text ends up in the page as HTML and runs as code.

The fixes are simple habits: render user data with textContent and createElement, sanitise with DOMPurify when you truly need user HTML, validate URLs before using them in href, and add a Content Security Policy as a second wall.

You will also learn how CORS differs from CSRF, what SameSite cookies do, how to stop clickjacking, why third-party scripts need Subresource Integrity, why secrets never belong in front-end code, and the real trade-offs of storing tokens.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Your front-end code runs inside the user’s browser, logged in as the user. Anything that runs on your page can do what the user can: read the page, call your API with their cookies, change their email address, place an order. Front-end security is about making sure the only code that runs on your page is your code, and that other sites cannot trick the browser into acting for your user.

The classic mistake is treating data as code. A comment, a product name or a URL query is just text, until you hand it to innerHTML and the browser parses it as HTML, including any onerror="…" attribute inside it. That is cross-site scripting (XSS).

Why it matters

XSS has been in the OWASP Top 10 web risks for as long as the list has existed, under the wider “Injection” category today. One stored XSS in a review box can run in every visitor’s browser: stealing tokens from localStorage, posting spam as each user, or showing a fake login form on your real domain. For a client project, that is a data breach, and in many countries a reportable one.

The good news: modern front-end security is mostly a small set of habits applied every time, plus a few HTTP headers your backend or hosting sets. Juniors who know these habits stand out in code review.

How it works

XSS: three flavours, one root cause

TypeWhere the payload comes fromExample
StoredSaved on the server, shown to many usersA product review containing <img src=x onerror=…>
ReflectedIn the request, echoed straight backA search page that prints ?q= into the HTML
DOM-basedRead and written entirely by front-end JavaScriptel.innerHTML = location.hash.slice(1)

All three share one shape: untrusted data flows from a source (form input, URL, API response, postMessage, storage) into a sink that interprets strings as code: innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, eval, new Function, setTimeout with a string, or href/src set to a javascript: URL. Treat API data as untrusted too: your API may faithfully return what an attacker saved.

textContent vs innerHTML

textContent never parses HTML: <img> becomes the four visible characters. It is the default for any data. Build structure with createElement and fill it with textContent; use innerHTML only for fixed markup you wrote yourself.

// Vulnerable: review text becomes HTML
list.innerHTML += `<li><b>${r.author}</b> ${r.text}</li>`;

// Safe: structure from code, data as text
const li = document.createElement('li');
const b = document.createElement('b');
b.textContent = r.author;
li.append(b, ' ', r.text); // append() with a string adds a text node
list.append(li);

The live page below shows the same comment three ways. The left pane is the “unsafe” one, made safe for teaching: it parses the comment inside an inert <template> (where nothing loads or runs) and lists what a real innerHTML would have done.

Try it: Comment box: unsafe vs safe rendering
