const API = 'https://dummyjson.com';
const PAGE = 12;
const FIELDS = 'title,description,price,rating,thumbnail,category,discountPercentage,stock,brand';
const EMOJI = { beauty: '💄', fragrances: '🌸', furniture: '🛋️', groceries: '🥑', laptops: '💻',
  smartphones: '📱', 'home-decoration': '🪴', 'kitchen-accessories': '🍳' };
const usd = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' });
const $ = (sel, root = document) => root.querySelector(sel);
const el = (tag, className, text = '') => Object.assign(document.createElement(tag), { className, textContent: text });
const state = readUrl();
const cache = new Map();                 // request URL → data
const seen = new Map();                  // product id → product
let cart = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('ralfiz-cart') ?? '{}');
let controller, current, timer;
// ---- state ⇄ URL ⇄ API ----
function readUrl() {                     // '#?q=phone&page=2' → state
  const p = new URLSearchParams(location.hash.slice(2));
  return { q: p.get('q') ?? '', cat: p.get('cat') ?? '', sort: p.get('sort') ?? '', page: Math.max(1, Number(p.get('page')) || 1) };
}
function writeUrl(push) {                // plays need hash URLs; the lab uses ?q=…
  const p = new URLSearchParams(Object.entries(state).filter(([k, v]) => v && !(k === 'page' && v === 1)));
  history[push ? 'pushState' : 'replaceState'](null, '', p.size ? `#?${p}` : '#');
}
function apiUrl({ q, cat, sort, page }) {
  const p = new URLSearchParams({ limit: PAGE, skip: (page - 1) * PAGE, select: FIELDS });
  if (q) p.set('q', q);
  if (sort) { const [by, order] = sort.split('-'); p.set('sortBy', by); p.set('order', order); }
  const path = q ? 'products/search' : cat ? `products/category/${encodeURIComponent(cat)}` : 'products';
  return `${API}/${path}?${p}`;
}
function update(patch, push = false) {   // every control goes through here
  Object.assign(state, patch);
  writeUrl(push);
  syncControls();
  load();
}
function syncControls() {
  if ($('#q').value.trim() !== state.q) $('#q').value = state.q;
  $('#sort').value = state.sort;
  document.querySelectorAll('.chip').forEach((c) => c.setAttribute('aria-pressed', c.value === state.cat));
}
// ---- fetch pipeline: abort, skeleton, cache, four states ----
async function load() {
  controller?.abort();
  controller = new AbortController();
  const url = apiUrl(state);
  $('#status').textContent = 'Loading products…';
  $('#grid').replaceChildren(...Array.from({ length: 8 }, () => el('div', 'skel')));
  try {
    let data = cache.get(url);
    console.log(data ? 'cache' : 'GET', url.slice(API.length).replace(/&select=[^&]*/, ''));
    if (!data) {
      const res = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`The server answered ${res.status}`);
      data = await res.json();
      cache.set(url, data);
    }
    render(data);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') return;       // a newer request is running
    $('#status').textContent = 'Could not load products';
    $('#grid').replaceChildren(message('⚠️', `${err.message}. Check your connection.`, 'Retry', load));
  }
}
function render({ products, total }) {
  const pages = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(total / PAGE));
  const from = (state.page - 1) * PAGE + 1;
  products.forEach((p) => seen.set(p.id, p));
  $('#grid').replaceChildren(...(products.length ? products.map(card)
    : [message('🔎', `No products match “${state.q}”.`, 'Clear search', () => update({ q: '', page: 1 }))]));
  $('#status').textContent = total ? `Showing ${from}–${from + products.length - 1} of ${total}${state.q ? ` for “${state.q}”` : ''}` : 'No results';
  $('#pageInfo').textContent = `Page ${state.page} of ${pages}`;
  $('#prev').disabled = state.page <= 1;
  $('#next').disabled = state.page >= pages;
}
function card(p) {
  const node = $('#card').content.firstElementChild.cloneNode(true);
  node.dataset.id = p.id;
  paintThumb($('.thumb', node), p);
  $('.off', node).textContent = `−${Math.round(p.discountPercentage)}%`;
  $('.eyebrow', node).textContent = p.brand ?? p.category.replaceAll('-', ' ');
  $('.title', node).textContent = p.title;
  $('.rating', node).textContent = `★ ${p.rating.toFixed(1)} · ${p.stock < 10 ? `only ${p.stock} left` : 'in stock'}`;
  $('.price', node).textContent = usd.format(p.price);
  $('.was', node).textContent = usd.format(p.price / (1 - p.discountPercentage / 100));
  $('.add', node).setAttribute('aria-label', `Add ${p.title} to cart`);
  return node;
}
function paintThumb(box, p) {            // emoji tile; the photo covers it when it loads
  box.style.setProperty('--h', (p.id * 47) % 360);
  $('.emo', box).textContent = EMOJI[p.category] ?? '🛍️';
  $('.img', box).style.backgroundImage = `url("${p.thumbnail}")`;
}
function message(icon, text, label, action) {
  const btn = el('button', 'primary', label);
  btn.addEventListener('click', action);
  const box = el('div', 'state');
  box.append(el('span', '', icon), text, el('br'), btn);
  return box;
}
// ---- detail dialog and cart ----
function openDetail(p) {
  current = p;
  paintThumb($('#detail .thumb'), p);
  $('#dMeta').textContent = `${p.brand ?? 'Ralfiz'} · ${p.category.replaceAll('-', ' ')}`;
  $('#dTitle').textContent = p.title;
  $('#dDesc').textContent = p.description;
  $('#dRating').textContent = `★ ${p.rating.toFixed(1)}`;
  $('#dStock').textContent = p.stock;
  $('#dPrice').textContent = usd.format(p.price);
  $('#detail').showModal();              // focus moves in, and back on close
}
function addToCart(p) {
  const line = cart[p.id] ?? { title: p.title, cents: Math.round(p.price * 100), qty: 0 };
  cart = { ...cart, [p.id]: { ...line, qty: line.qty + 1 } };
  saveCart();
  $('#sr').textContent = `${p.title} added to cart`;
  $('#cartPill').classList.remove('bump');
  requestAnimationFrame(() => $('#cartPill').classList.add('bump'));
}
function saveCart() {
  localStorage.setItem('ralfiz-cart', JSON.stringify(cart));
  const lines = Object.values(cart);
  const count = lines.reduce((n, l) => n + l.qty, 0);
  const cents = lines.reduce((n, l) => n + l.cents * l.qty, 0);
  $('#cartCount').textContent = count;
  $('#cartTotal').textContent = usd.format(cents / 100);
}
async function loadCategories() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`${API}/products/categories`);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.status);
    const chip = (slug, name) => Object.assign(el('button', 'chip', name), { type: 'button', value: slug });
    $('#chips').replaceChildren(chip('', 'All'), ...(await res.json()).map((c) => chip(c.slug, c.name)));
    syncControls();
  } catch {
    $('#chips').hidden = true;           // search still works without chips
  }
}
// ---- events ----
$('#q').addEventListener('input', (ev) => {
  clearTimeout(timer);                   // debounce: wait for a 300 ms pause
  timer = setTimeout(() => update({ q: ev.target.value.trim(), cat: '', page: 1 }), 300);
});
$('#chips').addEventListener('click', (ev) => {
  const chip = ev.target.closest('.chip');
  if (chip) update({ cat: chip.value, q: '', page: 1 }, true);
});
$('#sort').addEventListener('change', (ev) => update({ sort: ev.target.value, page: 1 }));
$('#prev').addEventListener('click', () => update({ page: state.page - 1 }, true));
$('#next').addEventListener('click', () => update({ page: state.page + 1 }, true));
$('#grid').addEventListener('click', (ev) => {
  const product = seen.get(Number(ev.target.closest('.card')?.dataset.id));
  if (ev.target.closest('.add')) addToCart(product);
  else if (ev.target.closest('.title')) openDetail(product);
});
$('#dAdd').addEventListener('click', () => { addToCart(current); $('#detail').close(); });
$('#detail').addEventListener('click', (ev) => ev.target === ev.currentTarget && ev.currentTarget.close());
addEventListener('popstate', () => { Object.assign(state, readUrl()); syncControls(); load(); });
syncControls();
saveCart();
loadCategories();
load();

Search, pick a category, sort, page through results, open a product and add it to the cart. Watch the address bar change, then use the ‹ back button.

Common mistakes

1. Treating an HTTP error as success.

// Wrong: a 500 page is parsed and rendered
const data = await (await fetch(url)).json();
// Right
const res = await fetch(url, { signal });
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);

2. Showing an error for an abort. Every fast typist would see “Something went wrong”. Check err.name === 'AbortError' first and return.

3. Building cards with innerHTML and API data.

// Wrong: a product title containing markup becomes live HTML
grid.innerHTML += `<h3>${p.title}</h3>`;
// Right: template + textContent
node.querySelector('.title').textContent = p.title;

4. Putting the page number in the URL as a string and doing maths on it. '2' + 1 is '21'. Convert with Number() when you read the URL.

5. Resetting the input while the user types. If syncControls() always writes input.value = state.q, the trailing space the user just typed disappears. Only write it when the trimmed values differ.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to write debounce from memory and to explain debounce (wait for a pause) versus throttle (at most once per interval).
  • Libraries such as TanStack Query package exactly what you built: caching by key, cancelling, retries and loading/error states. Knowing the manual version lets you configure them well.
  • For large catalogues, search usually moves to the server (Postgres full-text search, Elasticsearch, Meilisearch) and the front end sends q plus filters, as here.
  • Measure with DevTools: throttle to Slow 4G, type quickly and confirm in the Network panel that cancelled requests show as “(canceled)”.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: 'red shoes', page: 2 });
params.set('sort', 'price-asc');
console.log(params.toString());
  • A q=red%20shoes&page=2&sort=price-asc
  • B q=red+shoes&page=2&sort=price-asc
  • C q=red shoes&page=2&sort=price-asc
  • D ?q=red+shoes&page=2&sort=price-asc

Snippet 2. What is logged?

function debounce(fn, ms) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms);
  };
}
const search = debounce((q) => console.log('search', q), 50);
search('p');
search('ph');
search('pho');
setTimeout(() => search('phone'), 100);
  • A 
    search p
search ph
search pho
search phone
  • B 
    search p
search phone
  • C 
    search pho
search phone
  • D search phone

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const controller = new AbortController();
controller.signal.addEventListener('abort', () => console.log('listener'));
console.log(controller.signal.aborted);
controller.abort();
controller.abort();
console.log(controller.signal.aborted, controller.signal.reason.name);
  • A 
    false
listener
listener
true AbortError
  • B 
    false
true AbortError
  • C 
    false
listener
true Error
  • D 
    false
listener
true AbortError

Answers

  1. B. URLSearchParams uses the form encoding, where a space becomes +. toString() never adds the leading ?, and set() appends a new key at the end.
  2. C. The first three calls happen within 50 ms, so each one cancels the timer before it and only “pho” runs. The fourth call comes 100 ms later, after that timer fired, so it runs on its own.
  3. D. abort() fires the abort event once; a second call does nothing. Without an argument, the reason is a DOMException named AbortError, the same error a cancelled fetch rejects with.

terms.definition: Waiting until the user stops typing for a short time (here 300 ms) before running the search, so one request is sent instead of one per key.
Creates a signal you pass to fetch; calling abort() cancels that request and makes its promise reject with an AbortError.
An older request that finishes after a newer one; without cancelling it, it would overwrite the fresh results.
Keeping filters such as q, cat, sort and page in the query string (or hash) so the view can be shared, bookmarked and restored with Back.
Grey placeholder shapes shown while data loads; they keep the layout stable and feel faster than a spinner.
An element with role="status" or aria-live="polite" whose text changes are read out by screen readers without moving focus.
A Map from request URL to parsed data, so going back to a page you already saw needs no network request.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, say “I cancel stale requests with AbortController and keep filters in the URL”. Those two sentences show you have built a real search UI, not a tutorial one.

quiz.question: A user types “phone” quickly. Without cancelling, the request for “ph” finishes last. What happens?
options: Nothing: fetch always resolves in the order requests were sent
The browser merges both responses
The “ph” results overwrite the “phone” results, so the page shows the wrong products
fetch throws a TypeError
quiz.explanation: Network responses can arrive in any order. Aborting the previous request (or ignoring stale ones) guarantees only the latest query renders.

quiz.question: Why keep q, cat, sort and page in the URL?
options: So the view can be bookmarked, shared and restored with the Back button
Because fetch can only read the URL
Because localStorage cannot store strings
To make the page load without JavaScript
quiz.explanation: The URL is the most shareable state there is. Reading state from it on load, and writing it on change, gives deep links and working history for free.

quiz.question: The search request was aborted. What should the catch block do?
options: Show the error state with a Retry button
Return quietly when err.name is AbortError, because a newer request is already running
Call load() again immediately
Clear the cart
quiz.explanation: An abort is expected, not a failure. Only real errors (network down, !response.ok) should reach the user.

quiz.question: Which is the most accessible way to tell users “Showing 1–12 of 194 products”?
options: alert() the message
Put it in the page title only
Move keyboard focus to the first product after every keystroke
Put it in an element with role="status" so screen readers announce it politely without moving focus
quiz.explanation: A status live region announces changes without stealing focus from the search box the user is typing in.

lessons.title: Web Components
lessons.summaryHtml:
Web Components let you create your own HTML tags, such as <rating-stars> or <product-card>, with built-in browser APIs and no framework. A custom element is a class that extends HTMLElement, registered with customElements.define(). The browser calls its lifecycle callbacks when it is added, removed or when an observed attribute changes.

Shadow DOM gives a component a private DOM tree whose styles do not leak in or out. Slots let users pass their own content in, CSS parts and custom properties let them theme it on purpose, and custom events carry information back out.

They work in every framework and in plain HTML, which makes them ideal for design systems and embeddable widgets.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

HTML gives you <button>, <details> and <dialog>. Web Components let you add your own: <rating-stars value="4"> or <product-card price="24.99">. They behave like built-in elements. You can write them in HTML, create them with createElement, set attributes, listen for events and style them. Their insides stay private.

It is not one API but three working together:

  • Custom elements: a class that says how your tag behaves.
  • Shadow DOM: a private DOM tree with scoped styles.
  • Templates and slots: reusable markup, with holes where the user’s content goes.

Why it matters

Imagine Ralfiz builds a rating widget used in the Store (plain JS), the admin dashboard (React) and a partner site (unknown). A React component only works in React. A Web Component is just an HTML tag, so it works everywhere, including frameworks. That is why companies build design systems and embeddable widgets (chat bubbles, payment buttons, video players) as Web Components. Shoelace, now Web Awesome, is a good example, and so is Adobe’s Spectrum Web Components. Most of them use Lit, a small library that removes the boilerplate you will write by hand today.

How it works

Custom elements and their lifecycle

A custom element is a class that extends HTMLElement, registered with customElements.define('order-status', OrderStatus). The name must contain a hyphen, so it can never clash with a future built-in tag. Tags already in the page are upgraded the moment you call define(). Before that they are unknown inline elements, which is why defining components early matters.

CallbackRuns whenUse it to
constructor()The element is created or upgradedCall super(), attach the shadow root, add listeners on this. Do not read attributes or children here.
connectedCallback()Inserted into a document (again after every move)First render, start timers, add listeners on window or document
disconnectedCallback()Removed (or moved)Clean up: clear timers, remove global listeners, disconnect observers
attributeChangedCallback(name, old, new)An attribute in static observedAttributes changesRe-render the part that depends on it

Moving an element with append() fires disconnectedCallback and then connectedCallback. So anything you set up in connected must be undone in disconnected, or it runs twice. Watch it happen:

Try it: Lifecycle callbacks, logged

HTML

<main class="panel">
  <header>
    <h2>Today’s orders</h2>
    <div class="actions">
      <button id="add" type="button">+ Add order</button>
      <button id="next" type="button">Next status</button>
      <button id="move" type="button">Move first to end</button>
      <button id="remove" type="button">Remove last</button>
    </div>
  </header>
  <ul id="orders">
    <li><span>#1042 · Desk lamp</span><order-status status="packed"></order-status></li>
    <li><span>#1043 · Canvas backpack</span><order-status status="shipped"></order-status></li>
  </ul>
</main>

CSS

* { box-sizing: border-box; }
body { margin: 0; padding: 16px; font: 14px/1.4 system-ui, sans-serif; background: #f4f6fb; color: #0f172a; }
.panel { max-width: 620px; margin: 0 auto; background: #fff; border: 1px solid #e5e7ef; border-radius: 16px;
  padding: 16px; box-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgb(15 23 42 / .05); }
header { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; gap: 8px; }
h2 { font-size: 15px; margin: 0; }
.actions { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 6px; }
button { font: inherit; font-size: 13px; font-weight: 600; border: 1px solid #d7dbe7; background: #fff;
  border-radius: 10px; padding: 6px 10px; cursor: pointer; }
button:hover { background: #f1f5f9; }
ul { list-style: none; margin: 12px 0 0; padding: 0; }
li { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; gap: 8px; padding: 10px 4px;
  border-top: 1px solid #f0f2f7; }
/* A custom element is inline and unstyled by default: give it a display */
order-status { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 6px; font-size: 12px; font-weight: 600;
  padding: 3px 10px; border-radius: 99px; background: #f1f5f9; color: #475569; }
order-status::before { content: ''; width: 7px; height: 7px; border-radius: 50%; background: currentColor; }
order-status[status=packed] { background: #fef3c7; color: #92400e; }
order-status[status=shipped] { background: #e0e7ff; color: #3730a3; }
order-status[status=delivered] { background: #dcfce7; color: #166534; }

JavaScript

const LABELS = { placed: 'Placed', packed: 'Packed', shipped: 'Shipped', delivered: 'Delivered' };

class OrderStatus extends HTMLElement {
  static observedAttributes = ['status'];   // only these trigger attributeChangedCallback

  constructor() {
    super();                                 // always first
    console.log('constructor');
  }
  connectedCallback() {
    console.log('connected ·', this.getAttribute('status'));
    this.render();
  }
  disconnectedCallback() {
    console.log('disconnected ·', this.getAttribute('status'));
  }
  attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue) {
    console.log(`attributeChanged · ${name}: ${oldValue} → ${newValue}`);
    if (this.isConnected) this.render();
  }
  render() {
    this.textContent = LABELS[this.getAttribute('status')] ?? 'Unknown';
  }
}

customElements.define('order-status', OrderStatus);   // upgrades the two tags already on the page
console.log('--- defined ---');

const list = document.querySelector('#orders');
let nextId = 1044;
document.querySelector('#add').addEventListener('click', () => {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  const badge = document.createElement('order-status');  // constructor runs here
  badge.setAttribute('status', 'placed');                // attributeChanged (not connected yet)
  li.append(Object.assign(document.createElement('span'), { textContent: `#${nextId++} · New order` }), badge);
  list.append(li);                                        // connected
});
document.querySelector('#next').addEventListener('click', () => {
  const badge = list.querySelector('li:last-child order-status');
  const order = Object.keys(LABELS);
  const i = order.indexOf(badge?.getAttribute('status'));
  badge?.setAttribute('status', order[Math.min(i + 1, order.length - 1)]);
});
document.querySelector('#move').addEventListener('click', () => {
  if (list.firstElementChild) list.append(list.firstElementChild);   // disconnected, then connected
});
document.querySelector('#remove').addEventListener('click', () => list.lastElementChild?.remove());

Press each button and read the console: the browser calls your methods at each point in the element’s life. Styling uses plain attribute selectors from the page CSS.

This first element uses no Shadow DOM at all. It just sets its own textContent, and the page styles it with attribute selectors such as order-status[status=shipped]. Custom elements are display: inline by default, so always give them a display.

Shadow DOM and templates: <rating-stars>

this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }) gives the element a shadow root, a private tree rendered instead of its children. Styles inside apply only inside, and page styles do not match inside. document.querySelector cannot see in either. Only inherited properties such as color and font flow through. :host styles the element itself from inside, and :host(:focus-visible) styles it in a given state.

A <template> holds inert markup that is parsed once. Each instance clones it with template.content.cloneNode(true), which is faster than re-parsing a string every time. The template here is a constant written by you, so setting its innerHTML is safe. Anything that comes from users still goes in with textContent.

class RatingStars extends HTMLElement {
  static observedAttributes = ['value', 'max'];
  get value() { return Number(this.getAttribute('value')) || 0; }
  set value(v) { this.setAttribute('value', v); } // reflect property → attribute
  attributeChangedCallback() { this.render(); }   // attribute → UI
}

This reflection pattern gives one source of truth: the attribute. Setting el.value = 5 in JS, or value="5" in HTML, or changing it in DevTools all end in render(). For accessibility the component calls attachInternals() and sets internals.role = 'slider' with ariaValueNow and ariaValueText. This is ARIA through ElementInternals, supported in current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari (check the MDN compatibility table for older versions), so the user’s own attributes on the host are left alone. It is focusable with tabIndex = 0 and handles the arrow keys, Home and End, like a native slider.

Try it: <rating-stars>: Shadow DOM, attributes and events

HTML

<form class="review" id="review">
  <p class="eyebrow">Order #1042 · delivered</p>
  <h2>How was your Ralfiz Store order?</h2>
  <div class="row"><span id="l1">Product quality</span><rating-stars value="4" aria-labelledby="l1"></rating-stars></div>
  <div class="row"><span id="l2">Delivery speed</span><rating-stars value="3" aria-labelledby="l2" style="--star-color: #6366f1"></rating-stars></div>
  <div class="row"><span id="l3">Packaging</span><rating-stars value="2" max="3" aria-labelledby="l3" style="--star-size: 22px"></rating-stars></div>
  <p class="summary" id="summary" role="status"></p>
  <button type="button" id="perfect">Set all to perfect</button>
</form>

CSS

* { box-sizing: border-box; }
body { margin: 0; padding: 16px; font: 14px/1.4 system-ui, sans-serif; background: #f4f6fb; color: #0f172a; }
.review { max-width: 460px; margin: 0 auto; background: #fff; border: 1px solid #e5e7ef; border-radius: 16px;
  padding: 20px; box-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgb(15 23 42 / .05); }
.eyebrow { margin: 0; color: #64748b; font-size: 12px; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: .04em; }
h2 { font-size: 17px; margin: 4px 0 12px; }
.row { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; gap: 12px; padding: 8px 0;
  border-top: 1px solid #f0f2f7; flex-wrap: wrap; }
.summary { margin: 12px 0; color: #475569; min-height: 20px; }
button { font: inherit; font-weight: 600; border: 0; border-radius: 10px; padding: 9px 14px; background: #4f46e5;
  color: #fff; cursor: pointer; }
/* page styles cannot reach inside the shadow root: this rule does not paint the stars */
span { color: #334155; }

JavaScript

const template = document.createElement('template');
template.innerHTML = `
  <style>
    :host { display: inline-flex; gap: 2px; font-size: var(--star-size, 26px); line-height: 1;
      border-radius: 8px; cursor: pointer; user-select: none; }
    :host(:focus-visible) { outline: 3px solid #c7d2fe; outline-offset: 2px; }
    span { color: #d7dbe7; transition: transform .12s, color .12s; }
    span.on { color: var(--star-color, #f59e0b); }
    span:hover { transform: scale(1.18); }
  </style>
  <div part="stars" id="stars"></div>`;

class RatingStars extends HTMLElement {
  static observedAttributes = ['value', 'max'];
  #internals = this.attachInternals();       // ARIA without touching host attributes

  constructor() {
    super();
    this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }).append(template.content.cloneNode(true));
    // Listeners on the host itself: add once, in the constructor
    this.addEventListener('click', (ev) => {
      const star = ev.composedPath().find((n) => n.dataset?.v);
      if (star) this.#commit(Number(star.dataset.v));
    });
    this.addEventListener('keydown', (ev) => {
      const keys = { ArrowRight: 1, ArrowUp: 1, ArrowLeft: -1, ArrowDown: -1 };
      if (ev.key in keys) this.#commit(this.value + keys[ev.key]);
      else if (ev.key === 'Home') this.#commit(1);
      else if (ev.key === 'End') this.#commit(this.max);
      else return;
      ev.preventDefault();
    });
  }
  get value() { return Number(this.getAttribute('value')) || 0; }
  set value(v) { this.setAttribute('value', v); }            // property reflects to attribute
  get max() { return Number(this.getAttribute('max')) || 5; }

  connectedCallback() {
    if (!this.hasAttribute('tabindex')) this.tabIndex = 0;
    this.#internals.role = 'slider';
    this.render();
  }
  attributeChangedCallback() { this.render(); }

  render() {
    const stars = [];
    for (let i = 1; i <= this.max; i++) {
      const s = document.createElement('span');
      s.textContent = '★';
      s.dataset.v = i;
      s.classList.toggle('on', i <= this.value);
      stars.push(s);
    }
    this.shadowRoot.querySelector('#stars').replaceChildren(...stars);
    Object.assign(this.#internals, { ariaValueMin: '1', ariaValueMax: String(this.max),
      ariaValueNow: String(this.value), ariaValueText: `${this.value} of ${this.max} stars` });
  }
  #commit(v) {
    const next = Math.min(this.max, Math.max(1, v));
    if (next === this.value) return;
    this.value = next;
    this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('rating-change', { detail: { value: next }, bubbles: true, composed: true }));
  }
}
customElements.define('rating-stars', RatingStars);

// ---- the page only talks to the public API: attributes, properties, events ----
const form = document.querySelector('#review');
const summary = () => {
  const all = [...form.querySelectorAll('rating-stars')];
  const pct = all.reduce((s, r) => s + r.value / r.max, 0) / all.length;
  document.querySelector('#summary').textContent = `Overall: ${Math.round(pct * 100)}% happy`;
};
form.addEventListener('rating-change', (ev) => {
  const label = document.getElementById(ev.target.getAttribute('aria-labelledby')).textContent;
  console.log(`rating-change · ${label} → ${ev.detail.value}`);
  summary();
});
document.querySelector('#perfect').addEventListener('click', () => {
  form.querySelectorAll('rating-stars').forEach((r) => (r.value = r.max));  // no event: not a user action
  summary();
});
summary();
console.log('Page CSS reaches inside?', document.querySelector('rating-stars span'));

Click or use the arrow keys on a focused rating. Each change fires one rating-change event that the page hears on the form. The Set all to perfect button sets .value from outside, so no event fires.

Notice two rules about events. The component fires rating-change only for user actions; setting .value from code does not fire it, like native inputs. And the event is created with bubbles: true, composed: true, so one listener on the form hears every rating.

Slots, parts and custom properties: <product-card>

A component often needs the user’s content: a title, a description, an icon. A <slot> in the shadow tree is a window where the element’s own children appear. <slot name="title"> shows the child with slot="title"; an unnamed slot shows everything else. Text inside a slot tag is the fallback when nothing is passed, as in the fourth card. The slotted content stays in the light DOM: the page can still query it, and page CSS still styles it.

How do users restyle a component whose styles are private? You offer them two official doors.

TechniqueInside the componentOutside, in page CSSBest for
Custom propertiesbackground: var(--accent, #4f46e5).promo { --accent: #db2777 }Colours, sizes, spacing tokens
CSS parts<button part="button">product-card::part(button) { … }Letting users restyle one whole element
::slotted()::slotted([slot=title]) { … }normal CSS on the childDefault styles for passed-in elements

Try it: <product-card>: slots, parts and theming

HTML

<main class="page">
  <header><h1>New arrivals</h1><span class="cart" id="cart">🛒 0 items</span></header>
  <section class="grid" id="grid">
    <product-card price="24.99" emoji="💡" badge="New">
      <span slot="title">Ralfiz Desk Lamp</span>
      Warm LED with three brightness levels and USB-C power.
    </product-card>
    <product-card price="39.5" emoji="🎒">
      <span slot="title">Canvas Backpack</span>
      Water-resistant, fits a 15-inch laptop.
    </product-card>
    <product-card class="promo" price="8.75" emoji="☕" badge="−20%">
      <span slot="title">Ceramic Mug</span>
      Holds 350 ml. Dishwasher safe.

    <product-card price="12"></product-card>
  </section>
</main>

CSS

* { box-sizing: border-box; }
body { margin: 0; padding: 16px; font: 14px/1.45 system-ui, sans-serif; background: #f4f6fb; color: #0f172a; }
.page { max-width: 900px; margin: 0 auto; }
header { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 12px; }
h1 { font-size: 18px; margin: 0; }
.cart { background: #fff; border: 1px solid #e5e7ef; border-radius: 99px; padding: 6px 12px; font-weight: 600; }
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(190px, 1fr)); gap: 12px; }
/* Theming on purpose: custom properties cross the shadow boundary... */

/* ...and so do parts the component exposes */
product-card::part(button):hover { filter: brightness(1.1); }
product-card::part(badge) { letter-spacing: .03em; }

JavaScript

const usd = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' });
const template = document.createElement('template');
template.innerHTML = `
  <style>
    :host { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 6px; background: #fff; border: 1px solid #e5e7ef;
      border-radius: 16px; padding: 10px; font: 14px/1.45 system-ui, sans-serif; }
    .media { position: relative; aspect-ratio: 4 / 3; border-radius: 12px; display: grid; place-items: center;
      font-size: 46px; background: var(--tint, #eef2ff); }
    .badge { position: absolute; top: 8px; left: 8px; font-size: 11px; font-weight: 700; color: #fff;
      background: var(--accent, #4f46e5); border-radius: 6px; padding: 1px 7px; }
    .badge:empty { display: none; }

    .price { font-weight: 700; font-size: 16px; }
    button { font: inherit; font-weight: 600; border: 0; border-radius: 10px; padding: 7px 12px; color: #fff; white-space: nowrap;
      background: var(--accent, #4f46e5); cursor: pointer; }
  </style>
  <div class="media" part="media"><span id="emoji"></span><span class="badge" part="badge" id="badge"></span></div>
  <h3><slot name="title">Untitled product</slot></h3>
  <p><slot>No description yet.</slot></p>
  <div class="row"><span class="price" part="price" id="price"></span>
    <button part="button" type="button">Add to cart</button></div>`;

class ProductCard extends HTMLElement {
  static observedAttributes = ['price', 'emoji', 'badge'];
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }).append(template.content.cloneNode(true));
    this.shadowRoot.querySelector('button').addEventListener('click', () => {
      this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('add-to-cart', {
        bubbles: true, composed: true,
        detail: { title: this.productTitle, price: Number(this.getAttribute('price')) },
      }));
    });
  }
  get productTitle() { return this.querySelector('[slot=title]')?.textContent.trim() ?? 'Untitled product'; }
  attributeChangedCallback() { this.render(); }
  connectedCallback() { this.render(); }
  render() {
    const $ = (id) => this.shadowRoot.getElementById(id);
    $('emoji').textContent = this.getAttribute('emoji') ?? '🛍️';
    $('badge').textContent = this.getAttribute('badge') ?? '';
    $('price').textContent = usd.format(Number(this.getAttribute('price')) || 0);
    this.shadowRoot.querySelector('button').setAttribute('aria-label', `Add ${this.productTitle} to cart`);
  }
}
customElements.define('product-card', ProductCard);

// One listener for every card, present and future
let items = 0;
let cents = 0;
document.querySelector('#grid').addEventListener('add-to-cart', (ev) => {
  items += 1;
  cents += Math.round(ev.detail.price * 100);
  document.querySelector('#cart').textContent = `🛒 ${items} items · ${usd.format(cents / 100)}`;
  console.log('add-to-cart', ev.detail);
});
console.log('Slotted title lives in the light DOM:', document.querySelector('[slot=title]').textContent);

The page passes content through slots, themes one card with --accent, restyles the button with ::part(button), and hears one add-to-cart event per click.

Example: a component the Ralfiz team can share

The product card shows the whole public API of a good component:

  1. Attributes in: price, emoji and badge are observed; render() formats the price with Intl.NumberFormat.
  2. Content in: slots for the title and description, with sensible fallbacks.
  3. Styling in: --accent and --tint custom properties plus media, badge, price and button parts. Everything else is private and can change without breaking users.
  4. Events out: add-to-cart with { title, price } in detail. The component does not know about the cart; the page decides what adding means. That keeps it reusable.
  5. Accessibility: the internal button gets an aria-label such as “Add Ceramic Mug to cart”, because four buttons all called “Add to cart” are confusing in a screen reader’s list.

Two more platform features are worth knowing. Declarative Shadow DOM (<template shadowrootmode="open"> inside the element) lets a server send the shadow tree as HTML, so components can be server-rendered; it is supported in all current evergreen browsers (Firefox since early 2024; check caniuse.com if you must support older versions). The parser only honours it in HTML it loads, not in innerHTML. Form-associated custom elements (static formAssociated = true plus internals.setFormValue()) let a component such as <rating-stars> submit a value with a <form>, like a real input. The lab shows the rating version.

Common mistakes

1. Reading attributes or children in the constructor. When the parser creates the element, they may not exist yet.

constructor() { super(); this.render(); }            // Wrong: attributes may be missing
connectedCallback() { this.render(); }               // Right

2. Adding global listeners in connectedCallback and never removing them. Every move adds another copy.

connectedCallback() {
  this.ctrl = new AbortController();
  window.addEventListener('resize', this.onResize, { signal: this.ctrl.signal });
}
disconnectedCallback() { this.ctrl.abort(); }       // removes them all

3. Events that never leave the shadow root. A CustomEvent dispatched on an element inside the shadow tree without composed: true stops at the shadow root. Dispatch on this, or set composed: true.

4. Defining the same name twice. This happens with hot reload or a script included twice, and it throws NotSupportedError. Guard it:

if (!customElements.get('rating-stars')) {
  customElements.define('rating-stars', RatingStars);
}

5. Trying to style the inside with normal selectors. rating-stars span { … } matches nothing inside the shadow root. Expose a part or a custom property instead.

Interview and real-world notes

  • When to use them: design systems shared across frameworks, widgets embedded in other sites, and long-lived pages where you want zero framework dependencies. When not to: inside a single React or Vue app, where the framework’s components integrate better with its state and tooling.
  • Frameworks consume them: React 19 passes properties and listens to custom events on custom elements. Vue, Svelte and Angular have long supported them.
  • await customElements.whenDefined('rating-stars') resolves once the element is registered. It is useful when components load lazily.
  • Use :not(:defined) in CSS to hide or reserve space for components before they upgrade, avoiding a flash of unstyled content.
  • Lit adds reactive properties, efficient template updates and decorators on top of exactly these APIs. Knowing the raw version makes Lit easy.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

    console.log(`attr ${name}: ${oldV} -> ${newV}`);

}
customElements.define('x-box', XBox);
const box = document.createElement('x-box');

box.setAttribute('color', 'red');
document.body.append(box);

  console.log(e.target === host, e.composedPath()[0] === btn));

Answers

  1. C. createElement runs the constructor at once. Only observed attributes are reported (color is ignored), and that happens immediately, before the element is connected by append().
  2. A. document.querySelector does not search inside shadow roots, so it returns null. The shadow root has its own querySelector, and mode: "open" exposes it as host.shadowRoot.
  3. D. Only the composed pick event crosses the shadow boundary. Native click is composed; outside the shadow tree its target is retargeted to the host, while composedPath() still starts at the real button.

terms.definition: A class extending HTMLElement, registered under a hyphenated tag name with customElements.define().
connectedCallback, disconnectedCallback and attributeChangedCallback: methods the browser calls when the element is inserted, removed, or an observed attribute changes.
A static array of attribute names; only these trigger attributeChangedCallback.
A separate, encapsulated DOM tree attached to an element with attachShadow(); outside CSS and querySelector cannot reach inside it.
A <slot> placeholder in the shadow tree where the element’s own children (light DOM) are shown.
An element in the shadow tree marked with part="name" that outside CSS can style with ::part(name).
An event created with composed: true, which crosses the shadow boundary so the page can hear it.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, say when you would NOT use Web Components: for a single app already in React or Vue, stay in the framework. Reach for them for design systems shared across stacks and for widgets embedded in other people’s sites.

quiz.question: Why must a custom element name contain a hyphen, as in rating-stars?
options: Hyphens make elements faster
So it can never clash with current or future built-in HTML elements, which never contain hyphens
Because JavaScript class names need hyphens
Only to enable Shadow DOM
quiz.explanation: The spec reserves hyphenated names for authors. define() throws a SyntaxError for a name without one.

quiz.question: You add rating-stars value="3". When does attributeChangedCallback run for value?
options: Only if value is listed in static observedAttributes
For every attribute, always
Only when the element is removed
Never for attributes set in HTML
quiz.explanation: For performance, the browser only reports changes to attributes you list in observedAttributes. For attributes present at upgrade it runs before connectedCallback.

quiz.question: The page has button { background: red }. What happens to a button inside a component’s shadow root?
options: It turns red
It turns red only when the component is connected
It keeps the component’s own styles, because outside selectors do not match inside the shadow tree
The page throws an error
quiz.explanation: Shadow DOM scopes styles. Inherited properties such as color and font still flow in; use ::part() or custom properties to style internals on purpose.

quiz.question: A component dispatches new CustomEvent("rating-change", { bubbles: true }) from inside its shadow root. A listener on document never fires. Why?
options: CustomEvent cannot bubble
The detail property is missing
Listeners on document only hear built-in events
The event is not composed, so it stops at the shadow root
quiz.explanation: Events created in a shadow tree need composed: true to cross the shadow boundary. Dispatching on the host element itself (this.dispatchEvent) also works.

lessons.title: From vanilla JS to frameworks
lessons.summaryHtml:
Frameworks such as React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Angular solve problems you have already met by hand. They keep the UI in sync with state, split the page into reusable components, route between pages and render on the server.

They mainly differ in how they find what changed. A virtual DOM (React, Vue) re-runs a component and diffs the new tree against the old one. Fine-grained reactivity with signals (Solid, Svelte 5, Vue’s refs, Angular) tracks exactly which values each piece of UI reads and updates only that piece.

In this lesson you build a tiny signals store in vanilla JS, compare the same Task Board in vanilla and React, and see where Next.js fits for production apps and what to learn next.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Over this track you have written the same loop again and again: an event updates state, and a render() function makes the DOM match it. Frameworks are that loop, done for you, at scale. You describe the UI for a given state, and the framework works out which DOM operations to perform. This is declarative UI. You also get components, routing, server rendering and tools that a team of developers can share.

This lesson connects what you built to what you will use at work. It explains how React and its alternatives decide what to update, and where Next.js fits for production apps.

Why it matters

Most front-end job adverts ask for React, and many ask for Next.js. Interviewers still like candidates who understand the DOM underneath. When a React list loses its checkbox state, or a page re-renders fifty times, the developer who knows why fixes it in minutes. And sometimes the right answer is no framework at all. You can only make that call if you know both sides.

How it works

What frameworks solve

ProblemIn vanilla (this track)In a framework
Keep the DOM in sync with statecommit() + a hand-written render()Declarative templates or JSX, updated automatically
Update only what changedFull re-render, or careful manual patchingVirtual DOM diff, or fine-grained signals
Reusable piecesFunctions, templates, Web ComponentsComponents with props, state and children
Pages and URLsA 30-line router (dm13)File-based or declarative routing, nested layouts
Fast first load and SEOStatic HTML plus scriptsServer-side rendering, static generation, streaming
Team conventionsWhatever you decideA shared structure, ecosystem and hiring pool

The same Task Board in vanilla and in React

Here is the heart of your dm10 Task Board, and then the same feature as a React component:

// Vanilla: you own the whole loop
function toggle(id) {
  state.tasks = state.tasks.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t));
  save();
  render();                       // you decide what to redraw, and how
}
list.addEventListener('change', (ev) => toggle(Number(ev.target.closest('li').dataset.id)));
// React: describe the UI; React updates the DOM
function TaskBoard() {
  const [tasks, setTasks] = useState(loadTasks);
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState('all');
  const visible = tasks.filter((t) => filter === 'all' || (filter === 'done') === t.done);
  const toggle = (id) =>
    setTasks((ts) => ts.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)));
  useEffect(() => localStorage.setItem('tasks', JSON.stringify(tasks)), [tasks]);
  return (
    <ul>
      {visible.map((t) => (
        <li key={t.id} className={t.done ? 'done' : ''}>
          <input type="checkbox" checked={t.done} onChange={() => toggle(t.id)} />
          {t.title}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

Almost every idea carries over. Immutable updates with map and spread are the same. visible is derived state, computed during render and never stored. key={t.id} does the job of your data-id. JSX text is escaped automatically, like textContent. What disappears is render() and every querySelector. The full component is in the lab’s reference/TaskBoard.jsx.

Virtual DOM: re-render, then diff

When state changes, React calls your component function again. The result is not DOM but a tree of plain objects describing the UI, the virtual DOM. React compares it with the previous tree (reconciliation) and applies only the differences to the real DOM. Creating objects is cheap; touching the DOM is what costs. Vue works in a similar way, with a compiler that marks which parts of a template can never change.

Try it: A virtual DOM diff, by hand

JavaScript

// h() creates a virtual node: a plain object describing an element
const h = (tag, props, ...children) => ({ tag, props: props ?? {}, children });

function TaskList(tasks) {                 // a "component": state in, tree out
  return h('ul', { class: 'tasks' },
    ...tasks.map((t) => h('li', { key: t.id, class: t.done ? 'done' : '' }, t.title)));
}

function diff(a, b, path = 'root', patches = []) {
  if (a === undefined) return patches.push(`CREATE ${path}`), patches;
  if (b === undefined) return patches.push(`REMOVE ${path}`), patches;
  if (typeof a === 'string' || typeof b === 'string') {
    if (a !== b) patches.push(`TEXT ${path}: "${a}" → "${b}"`);
    return patches;
  }
  if (a.tag !== b.tag) return patches.push(`REPLACE ${path}`), patches;
  for (const key of new Set([...Object.keys(a.props), ...Object.keys(b.props)])) {
    if (a.props[key] !== b.props[key]) patches.push(`PROP ${path} ${key}="${b.props[key]}"`);
  }
  const n = Math.max(a.children.length, b.children.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) diff(a.children[i], b.children[i], `${path}>${b.tag ?? a.tag}[${i}]`, patches);
  return patches;
}

const before = [
  { id: 1, title: 'Design logo', done: false },
  { id: 2, title: 'Write invoice', done: false },
];
const after = [
  { id: 1, title: 'Design logo', done: true },            // toggled
  { id: 2, title: 'Write GST invoice', done: false },     // renamed
  { id: 3, title: 'Call client', done: false },           // added
];
const oldTree = TaskList(before);
const newTree = TaskList(after);
console.log(JSON.stringify(newTree.children[0]));
console.log(diff(oldTree, newTree));
console.log('Patches for an identical render:', diff(newTree, TaskList(after)).length);

Two renders of the same list produce two trees. The diff finds the three real changes; a framework then applies only those to the DOM.

Keys matter in the diff. The toy diff above matches children by position. If you delete the first task, every later item appears “changed”. Real frameworks match by key, so they can move the existing <li> for task 2 up instead of rewriting three rows. That is why an index key causes bugs: after a delete, the checkbox that belonged to task 1 now sits on task 2.

Fine-grained reactivity: signals

The other family skips the tree diff. A signal is a value with get() and set(). While an effect runs, every get() records that effect as a subscriber. Later, set() re-runs just those subscribers. A computed value is a signal kept up to date by an effect. The whole idea fits in about twenty lines:

JavaScript

// ---- a tiny signals library ----
let running = null;                       // the effect currently executing
function signal(value) {
  const subscribers = new Set();
  return {
    get() { if (running) subscribers.add(running); return value; },   // track the reader
    set(next) {
      if (Object.is(next, value)) return;                               // no change, no work
      value = next;
      [...subscribers].forEach((fn) => fn());
    },
  };
}
function effect(fn) {
  const run = () => {
    const previous = running;
    running = run;
    try { fn(); } finally { running = previous; }
  };
  run();
}
function computed(fn) {                   // a signal kept up to date by an effect
  const s = signal();
  effect(() => s.set(fn()));
  return { get: s.get };
}

// ---- state ----
const PRICES = { lamp: 2499, mug: 875 };  // cents
const qty = { lamp: signal(1), mug: signal(2) };
const coupon = signal(false);
const subtotal = computed(() => qty.lamp.get() * PRICES.lamp + qty.mug.get() * PRICES.mug);
const discount = computed(() => (coupon.get() ? Math.round(subtotal.get() * 0.1) : 0));
const shipping = computed(() => (subtotal.get() - discount.get() >= 5000 ? 0 : 499));
const total = computed(() => subtotal.get() - discount.get() + shipping.get());

// ---- bindings: each effect updates exactly one piece of the page ----
const usd = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' });
function bind(id, read) {
  effect(() => {
    const text = read();
    document.getElementById(id).textContent = text;
    console.log(`effect #${id} → ${text}`);
  });
}
bind('lampQty', () => qty.lamp.get());
bind('mugQty', () => qty.mug.get());
bind('subtotal', () => usd.format(subtotal.get() / 100));
bind('discount', () => (discount.get() ? '−' + usd.format(discount.get() / 100) : '—'));
bind('shipping', () => (shipping.get() ? usd.format(shipping.get() / 100) : 'Free'));
bind('total', () => usd.format(total.get() / 100));
console.log('--- ready ---');

// ---- events only set signals; they never touch the DOM ----
document.querySelector('.checkout').addEventListener('click', (ev) => {
  const btn = ev.target.closest('button[data-item]');
  if (!btn) return;
  const q = qty[btn.dataset.item];
  q.set(Math.max(0, q.get() + Number(btn.dataset.d)));
});
document.querySelector('#coupon').addEventListener('change', (ev) => coupon.set(ev.target.checked));

Change quantities and toggle the coupon, then read the console: only the effects that read a changed signal run again.

Toggle the coupon and watch the console. The quantity effects do not run, because they never read coupon. Solid is built on this model, and it has spread widely since:

FrameworkHow it finds changesReactive primitive
ReactRe-render component + virtual DOM diffuseState, useReducer (the React Compiler adds automatic memoisation)
VueReactive tracking + compiler-optimised virtual DOMref(), computed(), watchEffect()
Svelte 5Compiler + signals (“runes”)$state, $derived, $effect
SolidSignals, no virtual DOMcreateSignal, createMemo, createEffect
AngularSignals (moving away from zone-based change detection)signal(), computed(), effect()

This toy version leaves two things out. Real libraries batch updates and run effects in dependency order, so no effect ever sees a half-updated state (a “glitch”). They also drop stale subscriptions when an effect stops reading a signal. There is also an early-stage TC39 proposal to add signals to JavaScript itself. Check its status on the tc39/proposal-signals repository before relying on it.

Example: the Task Board on signals

This version keeps the dm10 features but uses the signals library and a miniature keyed reconciler:

  1. State: tasks and filter are signals; visible and remaining are computed.
  2. Components: TaskItem() creates a row once, and patchTaskItem(row, task) updates it. That is the create/update split frameworks make for you.
  3. Keyed list: keyedList looks up existing rows by data-key and reuses them, creating only new ones. The console shows “2 reused, 1 created”.
  4. Effects: one renders the list, one updates the counter, one updates the filter buttons, one saves to localStorage. Nothing else writes to the DOM or storage.
  5. Events only call set() with new arrays, never mutating, because Object.is would see a mutated array as “unchanged”.

JavaScript

// signal / effect / computed: the same 20 lines as the checkout play
let running = null;
function signal(value) {
  const subs = new Set();
  return {
    get() { if (running) subs.add(running); return value; },
    set(next) { if (Object.is(next, value)) return; value = next; [...subs].forEach((fn) => fn()); },
  };
}
function effect(fn) {
  const run = () => { const prev = running; running = run; try { fn(); } finally { running = prev; } };
  run();
}
function computed(fn) { const s = signal(); effect(() => s.set(fn())); return { get: s.get }; }

// ---- state ----
const KEY = 'ralfiz-signal-tasks';
const tasks = signal(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY)) ?? [
  { id: 1, title: 'Send quote for the Ralfiz Store redesign', done: false },
  { id: 2, title: 'Review pull request #42', done: true },
  { id: 3, title: 'Plan sprint demo', done: false },
]);
const filter = signal('all');
const visible = computed(() => tasks.get().filter((t) =>
  filter.get() === 'all' || (filter.get() === 'done') === t.done));
const remaining = computed(() => tasks.get().filter((t) => !t.done).length);

// ---- a "component": creates a row once, patches it on every render ----
function TaskItem() {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.innerHTML = '<label><input type="checkbox"><span></span></label><button class="del" type="button">✕</button>';
  return li;
}
function patchTaskItem(li, task) {
  li.dataset.key = task.id;
  li.classList.toggle('done', task.done);
  li.querySelector('input').checked = task.done;
  li.querySelector('span').textContent = task.title;
  li.querySelector('.del').setAttribute('aria-label', `Delete ${task.title}`);
}
// keyed reconciliation in miniature: reuse rows whose key still exists
function keyedList(parent, items) {
  const old = new Map([...parent.querySelectorAll('li[data-key]')].map((n) => [n.dataset.key, n]));
  let created = 0;
  const rows = items.map((task) => {
    const row = old.get(String(task.id)) ?? (created++, TaskItem());
    patchTaskItem(row, task);
    return row;
  });
  if (!rows.length) rows.push(Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { className: 'empty', textContent: 'Nothing here.' }));
  parent.replaceChildren(...rows);
  console.log(`render: ${created} created, ${items.length - created} reused`);
}

// ---- effects: state → DOM, state → storage ----
const list = document.querySelector('#list');
effect(() => keyedList(list, visible.get()));
effect(() => { document.querySelector('#left').textContent = `${remaining.get()} left`; });
effect(() => document.querySelectorAll('[data-f]').forEach((b) => b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', b.dataset.f === filter.get())));
effect(() => localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(tasks.get())));

// ---- events: only set signals, always with new arrays ----
document.querySelector('#add').addEventListener('submit', (ev) => {
  ev.preventDefault();
  const title = ev.target.elements.title.value.trim();
  if (title) tasks.set([...tasks.get(), { id: Date.now(), title, done: false }]);
  ev.target.reset();
});
list.addEventListener('change', (ev) => {
  const id = Number(ev.target.closest('li').dataset.key);
  tasks.set(tasks.get().map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: ev.target.checked } : t)));
});
list.addEventListener('click', (ev) => {
  const del = ev.target.closest('.del');
  if (del) tasks.set(tasks.get().filter((t) => String(t.id) !== del.closest('li').dataset.key));
});
document.querySelector('.filters').addEventListener('click', (ev) => {
  if (ev.target.dataset.f) filter.set(ev.target.dataset.f);
});
document.querySelector('#clear').addEventListener('click', () => tasks.set(tasks.get().filter((t) => !t.done)));

Next.js for production web apps

React draws components; it does not decide routing, data loading or how HTML reaches the browser. Next.js is the most widely used React framework for those jobs. With the App Router, folders are routes: app/products/[id]/page.tsx serves /products/42, and layout.tsx files wrap nested pages.

Components are Server Components by default. They run on the server, can await data directly, and send HTML without shipping their code to the browser. Add 'use client' at the top of a file only for interactive parts, such as an Add to cart button. Those parts are hydrated in the browser.

// app/products/[id]/page.tsx  (a Server Component)
import AddToCart from './AddToCart';          // this file starts with 'use client'

export default async function ProductPage({ params }) {
  const { id } = await params;
  const res = await fetch(`https://dummyjson.com/products/${id}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('Product not found');
  const product = await res.json();
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>{product.title}</h1>
      <p>{product.description}</p>
      <AddToCart id={product.id} price={product.price} />
    </main>
  );
}

Pages can be rendered at build time (static), per request (dynamic server rendering), or regenerated in the background after a time limit (incremental static regeneration). They can also be streamed, so slow parts arrive later inside <Suspense>. Caching defaults have changed between major versions, so read the docs for the version you use. Server-only code is also where secrets belong. Anything prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ is bundled into the browser for everyone to read.

When vanilla is still right

  • Mostly static pages with small islands of interactivity: a marketing site, docs, a blog. Plain JS or Web Components, or a site framework such as Astro, ship far less JavaScript.
  • Widgets embedded into other people’s sites, where you cannot choose their framework.
  • Performance-critical, long-lived pieces such as a canvas editor, where you control every update anyway.
  • Learning and interviews: everything in this track is what frameworks are made of.

Common mistakes

1. Mutating state in a framework. React compares references, so a mutated array looks unchanged and nothing re-renders.

tasks.push(newTask); setTasks(tasks);           // Wrong: same array
setTasks((ts) => [...ts, newTask]);             // Right: a new array

2. Index keys on lists that change. Use a stable id: key={t.id}, not key={index}.

3. Storing derived data in state and syncing it with an effect.

useEffect(() => setLeft(tasks.filter((t) => !t.done).length), [tasks]); // Wrong: extra render
const left = tasks.filter((t) => !t.done).length;                       // Right: derive it

4. Marking everything 'use client' in Next.js. You lose the benefit of Server Components and ship more JavaScript. Push 'use client' down to the smallest interactive leaf.

5. Jumping to a framework before the platform. Framework bugs are often DOM bugs (event propagation, focus, forms, storage) in disguise.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Virtual DOM versus signals?” The virtual DOM re-runs components and diffs trees, which is simple to reason about, and memoisation limits wasted work. Signals track reads and update exactly the dependent parts, with no diff, but you must read values inside a tracking scope.
  • “Why keys?” They let reconciliation match items between renders, so the right DOM nodes, and their state, move with the right data.
  • Your learning path after this course: 1) React fundamentals (components, props, state, effects, forms) with Vite. 2) TypeScript with React. 3) Next.js App Router: routing, Server and Client Components, data fetching, server actions, deployment. 4) A data library such as TanStack Query, and a component library or Tailwind CSS. 5) Testing with Vitest, Testing Library and Playwright. 6) Accessibility and performance audits on your own projects.
  • Rebuild one of your projects from this track (Ralfiz Money or Ralfiz Store) in React and then in Next.js. Comparing your own two versions teaches more than any tutorial.

Answers

  1. D. The effect runs once when created (0) and subscribes by reading count. set(1) re-runs it, the second set(1) is skipped by Object.is, and set(2) runs it again.
  2. B. Spread makes a new outer object but copies the tasks reference, so both share one array and one task object. This is why React updates need new arrays and objects at every level you change.

terms.definition: You describe what the UI should look like for a given state; the framework works out which DOM changes to make.
A function or class that owns a piece of UI, takes inputs (props) and can be reused and nested.
A lightweight JavaScript copy of the UI tree; after each render the framework diffs the new copy with the old one and patches only the differences.
The diffing step; a stable key per list item tells the framework which item is which, so it moves nodes instead of rebuilding them.
A reactive value with get and set; reading it inside an effect subscribes that effect, and setting it re-runs only the subscribers.
React components (used by the Next.js App Router) that run only on the server, can fetch data directly and send HTML with no component JavaScript to the browser.
Attaching event listeners and state to server-rendered HTML in the browser so it becomes interactive.

quiz.question: In React, what happens when you call a state setter such as setTasks(next)?
options: The browser reloads the page
Only the text nodes that read tasks are updated directly
React re-runs the component, builds a new virtual tree, diffs it with the old one and patches the DOM differences
React writes next into localStorage
quiz.explanation: React schedules a re-render of that component (and its children), then reconciles the new element tree with the previous one to find the minimal DOM changes.

quiz.question: Why should list items have a stable key such as the task id, not the array index?
options: So the framework can match items between renders and move them instead of re-creating them or mixing up their state
Keys make items render in alphabetical order
Keys are required for CSS to work
Index keys are slower to type
quiz.explanation: With index keys, deleting the first task makes every later row “become” a different task, so checkbox and input state can end up on the wrong item.

quiz.question: With signals, why does changing the coupon only re-run the effects that show the discount and total?
options: Signals re-run every effect on every change
Signals diff the whole page
The browser tracks dependencies automatically
Each effect subscribed only to the signals it read while running, so a signal notifies just those effects
quiz.explanation: Dependency tracking happens at read time: get() records the currently running effect. That is fine-grained reactivity, and it needs no tree diff.

Every component, to be safe
